nano-ros Book

Introduction

nano-ros is a lightweight ROS 2 client library for embedded real-time systems. It runs on bare-metal microcontrollers, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, and Zephyr, as well as Linux hosts. The entire core stack is no_std compatible.

flowchart TB
    App["<b>Application</b><br/>Rust / C / C++ node code"]
    Core["<b>nano-ros core</b><br/>Executor · Node · pub/sub · services · actions · CDR"]
    RMW["<b>RMW backend</b><br/>Zenoh · XRCE-DDS · Cyclone DDS · custom"]
    Plat["<b>Platform</b><br/>clock · heap · threads · sleep · sockets · libc"]
    Wire(["ROS 2 / DDS / Zenoh wire"])
    App --> Core --> RMW --> Plat
    RMW -. wire-compatible .-> Wire

Four layers, swappable independently: the same node code runs over any RMW backend on any platform. Here is a complete Linux publisher — register a backend, open the executor, publish std_msgs/String (Hello World: N) on /chatter once a second:

use core::fmt::Write as _;
use nros::prelude::*;
use std_msgs::msg::String as StringMsg;

fn main() {
    // Pick the backend at compile time; this one line registers it.
    nros_rmw_zenoh::register().unwrap();

    let config = ExecutorConfig::new("tcp/127.0.0.1:7447").node_name("talker");
    let mut executor: Executor = Executor::open(&config).unwrap();

    let mut node = executor.create_node("talker").unwrap();
    let publisher = node.create_publisher::<StringMsg>("/chatter").unwrap();

    let mut count = 0i32;
    node.create_timer_repeating(core::time::Duration::from_millis(1000), move || {
        count += 1;
        let mut msg = StringMsg::default();
        let _ = write!(msg.data, "Hello World: {count}");
        publisher.publish(&msg).unwrap();
    })
    .unwrap();

    executor.spin(SpinOptions::default()).unwrap();
    // This is the imperative Layer-2 API; the starters use the
    // declarative `nros::node!` / `nros::main!` form — both are
    // first-class (see Concepts → Two-Layer API).
}

The same program in C and C++ is in the First Node guides: Rust · C · C++. When a project grows beyond one node, continue with Multi-Node Project Layout.

What you get

  • One node, any board. You write a node once. Moving it to another board is one line, the board = in the image’s system.toml. The target triple, linker flags, backend and pool sizes all follow from that line, so neither your code nor your build files change.
  • Talk to ROS 2 as it is. Your nodes join a stock ROS 2 graph: over Zenoh with rmw_zenoh_cpp, or over plain RTPS with rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. Topics, services and actions work in both directions.
  • Pick the middleware, keep the code. Zenoh (no agent), XRCE-DDS (agent, micro-ROS compatible) or Cyclone DDS (RTPS). Switching is one line in system.toml, then build again.
  • Fits a microcontroller. The core is no_std, with the alloc and std features opt-in, and runs on a bare-metal Cortex-M3. Whether your image needs an allocator depends on the backend you choose: Choosing an RMW Backend says which does.
  • Rust, C or C++. The core is Rust, with C and C++ APIs over it; the C API follows rclc conventions. One workspace can mix all three.
  • Your ROS 2 install’s messages. Message bindings are generated from the message definitions of the ROS 2 install you build against, so the types and their hashes match your ROS 2 peers. Source ROS 2 once for a project’s first build; later builds reuse what it recorded.
  • Real-time you can reason about. Fixed-size pools sized at build time, plus scheduling and safety features for RTOS targets: see Real-Time and Safety.
  • Checked, not only tested. Serialization, scheduling and the safety protocol are covered by model checking and machine-checked proofs, and every example is held identical across platforms by a test.

Does it work on the board I have?

Each board’s support status, where it runs (host, emulator or hardware) and how often it is checked come from the board registry, and the book shows them on generated pages: Supported Boards lists every board, Board support levels says what each status means, and each board has its own evidence page. nros board list and nros board show <board> print the same facts from the nros you installed.

A board that is not in the registry can still run nano-ros through the customization ladder: the out-of-tree STM32F4 worked example shows the pattern, and the PX4 module template brings nano-ros into PX4 firmware as an external module (PX4; C++ only, because PX4’s uORB binding is C++-only). MPS2-AN385 bare-metal is Rust-only: the C and C++ APIs need an RTOS for libc and a heap.

The ESP32 (both the ESP-IDF component and the esp-hal bare-metal board) is retired: ESP32 — retired.

posix there is the platform layer, which is genuinely POSIX-clean. The host board is named linux, and that is the narrower claim: only Linux is tested, and nros-board-linux::apply_tier_affinity calls sched_setaffinity with cpu_set_t, which libc does not define for macOS. macOS is not supported.

RMW Backends

nano-ros supports several middleware backends, selected at compile time by naming one in system.toml:

  • Zenoh (nros-rmw-zenoh) — peer-to-peer via zenoh-pico. No agent process. Compatible with ROS 2 rmw_zenoh_cpp.
  • XRCE-DDS (nros-rmw-xrce-cffi) — agent-based via Micro-XRCE-DDS. Compatible with micro-ROS agent.
  • Cyclone DDS (nros-rmw-cyclonedds) — C++ shim; full RTPS wire-compat with stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp.

Application code is identical regardless of backend — switching is editing [system] rmw and building again. (Zephyr keeps Kconfig as its own front-end, as it does for every other build knob.)

How This Book Is Organized

  • Get Started: install, build and run your first project.
  • Build a Project: workspace layout, messages, configuration, build profiles.
  • Run on a Target: nros run, and each platform’s setup.
  • Communicate: choosing a backend, QoS, ROS 2 interop, transports.
  • Real-Time and Safety: execution model, scheduling, static memory, production readiness.
  • Operate and Debug: logging, time, diagnostics.
  • Concepts and Rationale: why nano-ros is shaped the way it is.
  • Extending nano-ros: add a board, a platform or an RMW backend from outside the tree.
  • Reference: the CLI, APIs, boards, configuration.
  • Migrating: moving from an older release.

Changing nano-ros itself is a different job, with its own book: nano-ros Internals.

Choose Your Entry

This book is organized around what you are trying to do with nano-ros, not around who you are. Pick the purpose closest to yours. Each section lists the pages to read, in order.

Everyone: your first project

Every purpose starts the same way:

  1. Install the nros CLI.

  2. First Project scaffolds a talker for a Cortex-M3 board, runs it in QEMU and shows its messages in ROS 2:

    nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh
nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker
cd sensor_ws
nros run sensor_node

    No QEMU or ROS 2? The same chapter runs it on your Linux host.

  3. Anatomy of What You Just Built explains the workspace in nano-ros’s own terms. You do not need to open the bringup package before you have seen it run.

New to ROS entirely? Two ideas carry the whole book. A node is a unit that computes, and nodes talk through named topics (publish/subscribe) and request/reply services. An RMW (“ROS MiddleWare”) backend is the transport that moves the bytes. nano-ros is a small implementation of that model for microcontrollers.

If anything goes wrong in the first steps, see Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Industrial: reproducible, auditable, offline

You build products where safety and robustness matter. You need the same inputs to give the same image, every fact on a page, and an install that runs with no network.

  • What is supported, and how it is checked. Supported Boards and Board support levels are generated from the board registry. nros doctor --report prints the status of every board your bringup’s images name, as a report you can file.
  • Pinning and offline builds. Pinning a version (nros pin), and Integrating into a Vendored Tree for a company tree with air-gapped CI. nros build --offline fails, naming what is missing, rather than fetching it.
  • Your RTOS and your build tool. How Integration Works: your RTOS keeps its own build tool (west, make, CMake, your IDE) and nano-ros plugs into it. Build as a CMake subdirectory covers a tree with no system.toml.
  • Real-time and memory bounds. Execution Model and Two-Layer API, Scheduling Models and the generated Scheduling Wiring Matrix, no_std, alloc, and std, Dispatch Strategy, and the Static Pool Inventory.
  • Safety and adoption gates. Safety Protocol (E2E CRC, EN 50159 mapping) and the Production Readiness Checklist.
  • Your own board or BSP. Custom Board Package, Vendor Overlay and the STM32F4 out-of-tree worked example. A board of yours lives in your tree (NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH). A new platform (a new RTOS) still means changing nano-ros itself.
  • Comparisons. Differences from Standard ROS 2, nano-ros vs micro-ROS, Choosing an RMW Backend and the generated Per-RMW Feature Matrix.

Field solutions: a working system per customer

You build a system for each customer, often on a board you were handed, and you need it publishing data that a ROS 2 system can see, quickly.

  1. Your first project (above), on the host.
  2. Your board. Find it in Supported Boards; its evidence page says where it runs and which chapter covers it. Then read your platform’s chapter (FreeRTOS, Zephyr, NuttX, ThreadX or bare-metal). Every embedded chapter has a QEMU flow that works without hardware.
  3. Run it on the target. The target model and nros run for a host process or an emulator.
  4. Talk to ROS 2. Choosing an RMW and ROS 2 Interoperability. Cyclone DDS talks to rmw_cyclonedds_cpp directly, with no router. Zenoh needs the ROS 2 router (rmw_zenoh_cpp) on the host.
  5. Grow the system. More nodes, parameters and images: Growing your workspace, and Mixed-language workspaces for other languages. Bridging several networks: Cross-backend Bridges.
  6. Coming from rclcpp or rclpy? Setup Compared to Standard ROS 2, Porting a ROS 2 C++ node, C / C++ multi-node workspaces and the Migration Guide.

Education: labs that fit a session

You teach a course or run a lab. Every seat needs the same result, the install must be short, and each lab must fit one session.

  1. Install once per seat: Installation. Nothing in the first project needs ROS 2, a router or hardware.
  2. The first lab is the first project (above), in C++ or, on the same page, in Rust. The output it prints is the result to check on every seat.
  3. Concepts for the lecture. Anatomy, Architecture Overview and Execution Model and Two-Layer API.
  4. Embedded labs without hardware. Each platform chapter runs its example under QEMU, for example FreeRTOS or bare-metal.
  5. Labs that talk to ROS 2. Choosing an RMW; Cyclone DDS needs no router, which keeps a lab machine simple.

Installation

Three steps take a bare Linux machine to one that builds nano-ros: install a few host packages, install the nros CLI, and let nros setup provision the toolchains for your board.

A release carries everything else. The nros CLI provisions toolchains, scaffolds projects, generates message bindings and drives the build. The library ships inside the release as source, and nros build compiles it into your project. There is no prebuilt library, no system-wide install, and no nano-ros clone: your project never names a path into nano-ros.

Working on nano-ros itself? That needs a checkout and its own build of the CLI; see Contributing.

Host prerequisites

The host needs only the basics: git, curl, a C toolchain, CMake, pkg-config, Python 3, zstd, and the Python packages ROS message generation uses. nros setup provides everything toolchain-shaped later.

Debian / Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git curl ca-certificates build-essential \
    cmake pkg-config python3 python3-dev zstd \
    python3-catkin-pkg python3-empy python3-lark python3-yaml

Fedora / RHEL:

sudo dnf install -y git curl ca-certificates gcc gcc-c++ make \
    cmake pkgconf-pkg-config python3 python3-devel python3-pip zstd

Arch:

sudo pacman -S --needed git curl base-devel cmake python python-pip zstd

Fedora and Arch ship no rosidl packages, so install the Python side with pip (in a venv if your Python is externally managed):

pip install --user catkin_pkg 'empy==3.3.4' lark PyYAML

macOS is not supported. Installation Details says what each package is for.

Install the nros CLI

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"   # install.sh prints this line too

install.sh downloads the newest release for your host, checks its sha256, and installs it under ~/.nros. Add the export PATH=… line to your shell’s startup file. Check the install:

nros version        # the CLI and library versions
nros doctor         # SDK paths, toolchains, environment

Provision your board

nros setup fetches what a board needs: the cross-compiler, the emulator, the RMW host tools and the board’s SDK sources, plus a Rust toolchain if the host has none. You do not install cross-toolchains by hand.

nros setup <board> --rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds>

For a first project on Linux, use Cyclone DDS. It runs in-process, so it needs no router and no agent:

nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds

nros board list names every board. nros setup <board> --dry-run prints what a board pulls without fetching anything. Inside a workspace, a bare nros setup provisions every image it declares.

Do I need ROS 2 installed?

Yes, to build. nros build, nros run and nros configure generate your project’s message bindings from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, so the types and their hashes match the ROS 2 nodes you talk to. Every talker uses std_msgs, so install ROS 2 (the book uses Humble) and source it before the first build of a project:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

That first configure records the ROS 2 prefix in the project, so later builds and runs of that project work from a shell that has not sourced ROS. Without a sourced ROS 2 and without that record, the build stops with `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH` is unset and no configure of … has recorded one to reuse; Troubleshooting has the fix.

ROS 2 also provides:

  • the Zenoh router, ROS’s rmw_zenohd, which two Zenoh nodes meet through (Cyclone DDS needs no router);
  • ros2 topic echo and ros2 node list, to watch your nodes;
  • the existing ROS 2 graph your nodes interoperate with.

Installation Details covers the router and the XRCE agent.

  • Installation Details: other install options, provisioning in depth, pinning a project to a release, and using nano-ros from your own build.

Installation Details

Installation is the short path. This page is the rest: what each host package is for, other ways to install, provisioning in depth, ROS 2 and the RMW daemons, pinning a project to a release, and using nano-ros from a build that is not a nano-ros workspace.

Host packages

cmake builds the C/C++ quick start and every workspace root. zstd unpacks the release and the prebuilt SDK assets nros setup fetches. python3-dev is only used by a from-source build of the launch resolver, which a release ships prebuilt. The Python packages feed rosidl_adapter, the ROS message-to-IDL step the Cyclone DDS backend uses; empy must stay 3.x. On Arch, base-devel is a package group that covers pkg-config, and ca-certificates ships with the base system. Each tool’s absence produces an error naming it.

These are the only packages you install by hand. Per-board OS dependencies later on are declared in the index and printed for your package manager (apt, dnf or pacman) by:

nros setup --system          # what is missing + the exact install command

The host platform layer is POSIX-clean, but the host board is linux, and only Linux is tested. macOS is not supported: the board’s CPU-affinity code uses cpu_set_t, which macOS’s libc does not define.

Install options

install.sh installs into ~/.nros/sdk/nros/<version>/ and points ~/.nros/bin/nros at the newest version installed, so however many versions accumulate, nros means one command. It refuses an asset whose checksum it cannot verify.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0-nros4     # a specific release instead of the newest
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --dry-run                 # print what would happen, change nothing

NROS_HOME moves the install root away from ~/.nros. The repository’s GitHub Releases page lists every release.

Provisioning with nros setup

nros setup is the single command that prepares a machine to build nano-ros for a given board. The cross-compiler, emulator, RMW host tools and any SDK sources a board needs are resolved from the index the release pins and placed in a shared store (~/.nros/sdk). You do not install cross-toolchains by hand. It provides no zenoh router — that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd — and Cyclone DDS needs no daemon.

Packages are prebuilt where the index has a binary for your host, and built from source otherwise. Source builds are normal, not an error — but they cost real time and disk, so nros setup announces them before it starts:

nros setup: 1 package(s) have no prebuilt for linux-x86_64 — BUILDING FROM SOURCE: <name>
  Expect minutes (tens of minutes for a large recipe) and hundreds of MB under …

nros setup <board> --dry-run prints the whole plan, prebuilt vs source, without fetching anything.

nros setup <board> --rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds>

nros setup resolves the board’s package set union the RMW’s host packages and fetches them all — prebuilt cross-toolchain + emulator + RMW host tools + board SDK sources (no zenoh router: that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd). --rmw defaults to zenoh. For every board with a CMake build road (all of them except Zephyr, which builds with west) it also installs the pinned Corrosion, the CMake-to-cargo bridge a C/C++ configure needs: a configure never fetches it, and without it in the SDK store the configure stops and names this command.

CommandProvisions
nros setup linuxhost build; zenoh-pico + mbedtls sources (no router: see ROS 2 and the Zenoh router)
nros setup linux --rmw xrcehost build; the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent
nros setup linux --rmw cycloneddshost build; Cyclone DDS runtime + idlc
nros setup mps2-an385-freertosarm-none-eabi-gcc, patched qemu-system-arm, FreeRTOS + lwIP sources
nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttxarm-none-eabi-gcc, qemu, NuttX sources
nros setup rv-virt-threadxriscv64-*-gcc, qemu, ThreadX/NetX sources
nros setup threadx-linuxThreadX POSIX-sim sources
nros setup zephyrthe Zephyr west workspace + Zephyr SDK bits
nros setup mps2-an385-baremetalbare-metal arm-none-eabi-gcc + qemu

Provision a whole workspace

Once you have a workspace, you do not need to name its boards. Run nros setup with no board at the workspace root (the directory that holds src/), or pass --workspace <dir>. nros setup --dry-run prints the plan without fetching anything.

For example, a Rust workspace with a Linux image and a FreeRTOS image, both on zenoh:

nros new two_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd two_ws
nros new --image freertos --board mps2-an385-freertos   # adds [image.freertos]

One nros setup provisions both boards:

nros setup

Then every image builds. The first build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in that shell; the build records the prefix, and later builds of the workspace need no sourced shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build --all

It reads every system.toml in the workspace and provisions each [image.*]‘s board and RMW in one plan. For a zenoh image it reports ROS’s rmw_zenohd: the path it found, or the apt packages that provide it. It then lists the OS packages the workspace itself names, which are its build types’ host tools (for example cmake for ament_cmake) and any <depend> that is a system key, and prints the install command. Add --sudo to run that command. --check only reports.

Every <depend> must resolve before anything is fetched. A name that is not a package in the workspace, a message package, a system key, a package your ROS install provides or a rosdep key stops nros setup. The error names the package.xml that declares it, which is the same check nros build makes.

Every board also needs a Rust toolchain, whatever language you write: the runtime your project links is compiled from source when you first configure. If the host has neither rustup nor rustc + cargo, nros setup installs rustup (a pinned, checksum-verified installer) into ~/.cargo with the stable toolchain as the default — where cmake finds it without any PATH change. A host that already has Rust is left as it is. For cargo in a shell afterwards: . "$HOME/.cargo/env".

Useful flags:

nros setup --list            # every package in the index + its version
nros setup <board> --dry-run # resolve + print the plan, fetch nothing
nros setup --licenses        # license-gated packages + how to install them
nros setup --tool qemu       # one tool by name
nros setup --source freertos-kernel   # one source package by name

Each board’s exact package set lives in the index; run nros setup <board> --dry-run to see precisely what a board pulls.

A distro cross compiler is a fallback with a floor. When the store has no pinned arm-none-eabi-gcc (or riscv-none-elf-gcc), the CMake configure uses one from PATH and says so. Below GCC 11 a C++ image is refused at configure: GCC 10’s newlib libstdc++ has no std::this_thread, which ordinary ROS 2 C++ uses — Ubuntu 22.04’s apt gcc-arm-none-eabi is 10.3. Install the pin with nros setup --tool arm-none-eabi-gcc, or point -DNROS_ARM_NONE_EABI_PREFIX=<dir>/bin/arm-none-eabi at a GCC ≥ 11. A C-only image is not refused; it gets a warning.

See Supported Boards for the full board list and nros CLI for every subcommand.

Heads-up before your first example. Every nano-ros example (Linux talker, FreeRTOS talker, …) connects to its RMW host daemon at startup — a zenoh router for zenoh, the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent for xrce. Cyclone DDS is in-process — no separate daemon — so none of this applies if you ran nros setup … --rmw cyclonedds.

For xrce, nros setup … --rmw xrce installs the agent into the SDK store (~/.nros/sdk/<tool>/<version>/bin/), and you run it in a dedicated terminal before launching any example.

For zenoh, the router is not provisioned by nros setup: it is ROS 2’s rmw_zenoh_cpp/rmw_zenohd, so that nano-ros is tested against the router a ROS 2 deployment actually runs (see the RMW design). Start it with your ROS environment sourced (leave it running for the whole session):

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

It is not configured on the command line — rmw_zenohd ignores argv and reads ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE, as above. To pick a different endpoint, change the port in the listen/endpoints entry.

Without a router the talker blocks forever on Executor::open with no output. Default ports: tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 on POSIX, tcp/10.0.2.2:7447 on QEMU FreeRTOS (Slirp forwards to host). Mismatch = silent hang; see Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

After provisioning, follow the per-platform starter page (FreeRTOS, Zephyr, NuttX, …) for the board’s build + run steps.

ROS 2 and the Zenoh router

Building, yes, once per project. Running two zenoh nodes, yes, or use Cyclone. nros build, nros run and nros configure generate the message bindings from the message definitions of the ROS 2 install you sourced, so the generated layouts and type hashes are the ones your ROS 2 peers use. A release does not fall back to a copy of its own: that would pick a ROS 2 distro for you without saying so.

Source ROS 2 before the first build, run or configure of a project:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

That configure records the prefix (AMENT_PREFIX_PATH) in the project, and every later configure of the same project reuses it, so a later shell, an IDE or a CI step that has not sourced ROS still builds. A project whose packages depend on no message package at all configures without ROS 2. With neither a sourced shell nor a record, configure stops and names the setup step; see Troubleshooting.

Running is where it splits, and the reason is the router. zenoh-pico connects in client mode, so any two-process example needs a zenoh router — and that router is rmw_zenoh_cpp/rmw_zenohd, which ships with ROS 2. nano-ros does not vendor one. So:

  • --rmw cyclonedds needs no router — Cyclone is in-process, there is no daemon to start.
  • --rmw zenoh (the default) needs ROS’s router. Either install ros-<distro>-rmw-zenoh-cpp, or point NROS_RMW_ZENOHD at a rmw_zenohd you obtained another way.

The same sourced setup is what makes the router findable. nano-ros reads AMENT_PREFIX_PATH from that, so a ROS installed anywhere works, including one you built from source or a colcon overlay — it is not assumed to be under /opt/ros.

Do not expect command -v rmw_zenohd to print anything: rmw_zenohd installs into <prefix>/lib/rmw_zenoh_cpp/, and setup.bash puts only bin/ on PATH. ROS’s own way to reach it is ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd. So a silent command -v is normal and not a broken install — the ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd spelling finds it regardless.

Only what you name is used. nano-ros needs the router that ships with your rmw_zenoh_cpp: the two share a zenoh build, and a mismatch shows up as “nothing was delivered” rather than as an error. So the search is NROS_RMW_ZENOHD, then the prefixes you sourced, then $ROS_DISTRO — and nothing else. In particular:

  • PATH is not searched. A zenohd there — installed from zenoh’s own instructions, or left behind by an older nano-ros — is usually a different and older zenoh. The machine this was written on had two, at v1.4.0 and 1.7.2, against ROS’s 1.8.0.
  • /opt/ros/* is not globbed. If you have humble and jazzy installed, guessing between them is not better than saying nothing. Source the one you want, or set ROS_DISTRO.

If you do want a specific binary, name it with NROS_RMW_ZENOHD; it is used as given, with a warning if it is not an rmw_zenoh_cpp router.

If you once used an older nano-ros, run nros doctor: it reports a retired SDK store entry that is still installed, zenohd included, with the command to remove it.

TaskNeeds a ROS 2 install?
nros setupNo
The first nros build / nros run / nros configure of a project with messagesYes, sourced: the bindings are generated from it
Later builds and runs of that projectNo sourced shell: the first configure recorded the prefix
Building any node (Rust / C / C++), any RMW, any boardYes, as above: every talker uses std_msgs
Running a Cyclone DDS exampleNo router: Cyclone is in-process
Running a multi-process zenoh exampleYes — the router is ROS’s rmw_zenohd (or set NROS_RMW_ZENOHD)
Verifying with ros2 topic echo / ros2 node listYes
Interop against rmw_zenoh_cpp / a real ROS 2 graphYes

If your distro has no ROS 2 packages (Arch, for example), install ROS 2 from source or from a container image, and source its setup.bash (or your overlay’s install/setup.bash) the same way: nano-ros reads only AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, wherever the install is.

Pinning a version

A release fixes the whole surface at once: the CLI, the library source in its SDK root, and the nros-sdk-index.toml that pins every toolchain and SDK version nros setup provisions. So pinning nano-ros is pinning a release:

# install a specific release (several can sit side by side in ~/.nros/sdk/nros/):
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0-nros4

# report this project's pin (nros-toolchain.toml), or move it:
nros pin
nros pin 0.6.0-nros4

The pin is a file, nros-toolchain.toml, beside your project — commit it. With one in a directory, every nros you run there (or below it) is the pinned release: the nros on PATH hands the command to the pinned one, fetching it with that release’s own install.sh the first time. A project pinned to an older release than the one you installed, from nothing:

mkdir pinned_app && cd pinned_app
printf '[toolchain]\nversion = "0.6.0-nros4"\n' > nros-toolchain.toml

Ask for the pin. The release that answers is the pinned one, fetched on first use, and it names its own manifest:

nros pin

sdk/nros/0.6.0-nros4/share/nros/manifest.toml

and everything after it builds with that release. The pinned release is older than this page, so it is driven with the scaffold spelling it shipped with, --workspace.

nros new pinned_ws --workspace
cd pinned_ws
nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros build

nros pin <version> reports the codegen delta between the two releases before it writes anything, so an upgrade that would invalidate already-generated bindings warns first; the next nros build regenerates them. After installing a newer release, re-run nros setup <board> — it reconciles the SDK store against the new index, and packages that are already current are no-ops. See versioning for how the release number is chosen.

Consuming nano-ros

Pattern A: your project is a nano-ros workspace

This is the supported shape, in any language. A workspace is a directory of packages — node packages plus one bringup package — and it has no root build file at all, neither CMakeLists.txt nor Cargo.toml:

~/my_robot/
├── .colcon_workspace          # marks the root
└── src/
    ├── pkg_a/                 # your node package(s)
    ├── pkg_b/
    └── my_robot_bringup/      # system.toml + launch files, no code

The bringup’s system.toml names the board once per deploy target:

[system]
name = "my_robot"
rmw  = "cyclonedds"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

nros build resolves the launch files, generates what the board choice implies and the entry and build root for each [image.*] under build/, then hands off to CMake, cargo or west:

nros build                     # or: nros build linux

nros new my_robot_ws --board linux --template talker scaffolds that layout with one node package — see First Project — and nros new <pkg> --to <bringup> adds the next. A POSIX C++ workspace that already uses colcon can still be built by colcon build; the packages keep their package.xml and their own CMakeLists.txt.

A single node is the same shape with one node package; --lang <rust|c|cpp> picks its language (the First Node chapters). system.toml lives only in the bringup, never beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt.

A complete working example to read lives at examples/templates/multi-package-workspace/.

Pattern B: nano-ros inside an existing CMake tree

For a C/C++ project that is not a nano-ros workspace — an existing CMake tree with its own layout — the platform and backend are cache variables set before nano-ros is added, because there is no system.toml for the build to read them from. That is the lower-level shape and it has its own page, with the full variable table: Build as a CMake subdirectory. Reach for it when Pattern A does not fit your tree, not before.

Rust-only consumers

Nothing of nano-ros is published to crates.io (decision 2026-05-14); the crates ship as source in the release’s SDK root. The full nros crate can’t be published because it depends transitively on C/C++ sources (zenoh-pico, mbedtls); nros-core isn’t carved out for crates.io either, to avoid a hybrid distribution model with version drift between a crates.io snapshot and the SDK.

So a Rust package declares registry-style names and lets the build redirect them: nros = { version = "*" } (+ msg crates), resolved into the SDK root the nros on PATH carries (--nano-ros-path names a different one). The [patch.crates-io] block it writes goes into the generated settings file under build/, not into your package — nros build hands that file to cargo with --config, and a cargo command you drive yourself passes the same path. Copy the project anywhere; the next nros build re-points it.

A Rust package carries no build settings of its own — no target triple, no linker flag, no patch table. Its bringup’s system.toml states the board and nros build derives the rest; see examples/templates/multi-package-workspace/src/pkg_rust_publisher/ for a package in that shape, and Integrating into a Vendored Tree for the CI spelling.

Migrating from an older nano-ros

If you used nano-ros from a checkout with the old install-local recipe, see migration-install-local-removal.md for the one-page rewrite.

First Project

Support level: mps2-an385-baremetal and the Linux host. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

In this chapter you scaffold a talker for an Arm Cortex-M3 board, run it in QEMU, and watch its messages arrive in ROS 2. You write no code and edit no configuration to get there.

What this assumes: a Linux host with ROS 2 Humble and its Zenoh middleware (ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp) installed, or the container from Installation Details, and the install done, so nros is on your PATH.

What it leaves for later: the board talks to your machine over its serial port, the way a real board’s first program does. The network comes in the board’s own chapter, Bare-metal Cortex-M3. WiFi is not covered yet: it arrives with the Zephyr 4.4 line.

Provision the board

nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh

This fetches the Arm cross-compiler, a QEMU that emulates the MPS2-AN385 board, and the Rust target. Nothing is installed system-wide.

Scaffold

nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker
cd sensor_ws

That wrote two packages:

sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # your node: package.xml, Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # which board it runs on; you don't need to open it yet

sensor_node is the code: a talker that publishes std_msgs/String on /chatter once a second. sensor_node_bringup says what that code runs on. The scaffold filled it in, and this chapter never needs you to open it.

This is the shape of examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker/ in the nano-ros repository, the example kept for reading beside this chapter: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, because nros run generates it.

Run

Source ROS 2 first, then build and run. ROS 2 provides the router the board talks to, and its message definitions are what nros run generates the talker’s std_msgs bindings from. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so a later build of it needs no sourced shell (the router still does):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node --expect 'Publishing:'

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

nros run does everything between your source and a running board: it builds the firmware (the first build compiles nano-ros for the Cortex-M3 and takes a few minutes; later builds take seconds), boots it in QEMU with the board’s serial port connected to a terminal device on your host, and starts the router on that device. The talker’s own output is the board’s console. With --expect, nros run stops everything and exits 0 the moment the console prints a line containing that text, and exits 1 if the board stops first, which makes it a one-line check that the whole path works.

Without --expect it keeps streaming until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU and the router together. Start it that way in one terminal:

nros run sensor_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

See it in ROS 2

Leave nros run going. In a second terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

The talker publishes best-effort, and ros2 topic echo defaults to reliable, which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

Change it

Open src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs, change the "Hello World" text, and run nros run sensor_node again. It rebuilds what changed and boots the new image.

No QEMU, no router: run it on this machine

The same flow runs on your Linux host. Cyclone DDS needs no router, so nothing else has to be running. The build still generates the messages from ROS 2, so source it before the first run (later runs of host_ws need no sourced shell):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker --lang cpp --rmw cyclonedds
cd host_ws
nros run host_node --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

Only the board in the scaffold line changed. The node code is the same shape, and so is every command after it.

If nothing appears

  • nros run stops at once and names AMENT_PREFIX_PATH: this shell has not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace recorded it. Run source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash and run again.
  • nros run stops at once and names the router: it could not find the Zenoh router. Source ROS 2 in that shell (and install ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp if it is missing), or point NROS_RMW_ZENOHD at an rmw_zenohd binary.
  • No Publishing: line within a minute of boot: the router started but the board did not reach it. nros run names the router’s log when it stops.
  • nros run lists several names and refuses: you are in a workspace with more than one thing to run. Name one of the spellings it prints.
  • ros2 topic echo prints nothing: check the --qos-reliability best_effort flag and the RMW_IMPLEMENTATION line.

First 10 Minutes has the rest.

  • Anatomy of What You Just Built: what each package is for, and what nros run generated.
  • Growing your workspace: add a second node, another board, or a launch file.
  • Bare-metal Cortex-M3: the same board over its network.

Design background

The chapter follows RFC-0116 D5 and D6 and RFC-0121 D4 and D5. Its pointer to the copy-out talker follows RFC-0122 (behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI) D3.

Anatomy of What You Just Built

Two packages, two roles. Everything you add to this project later is another package with one of these roles, or a few more lines in the bringup. The shape never changes; it only gains packages.

If you come from ROS 2, each role is something you already know:

Your workspaceRoleIn ROS 2 terms
src/sensor_node/Node packagea composable node (rclcpp_components)
src/sensor_node_bringup/Bringup package<pkg>_bringup: configuration and launch, no code
(generated under build/)Entrythe composition container, the main()

The node package: the code

A node package is one node, as a library. It has no main() and names no board:

src/sensor_node/
├── Cargo.toml          # a library crate; dependencies only
├── package.xml         # ROS package manifest: std_msgs is declared here
└── src/lib.rs          # the Talker: a 1 s timer that publishes on /chatter

lib.rs declares what the node creates (a publisher, a timer) and what its callback does. Message types come from package.xml’s dependencies and are generated during the build; you never write them by hand.

The same node builds for any board. Nothing in this package says mps2-an385, zenoh or serial: those are the bringup’s.

The bringup package: what runs where

src/sensor_node_bringup/ holds no code, only package.xml and system.toml:

[system]
name = "sensor_node"
rmw = "zenoh"                        # which middleware
ros_edition = "humble"               # which ROS 2 your peers run
domain_id = 0

[[component]]                        # which nodes run
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Talker"
name = "sensor_node"

[image.baremetal]                    # one block per thing you deploy
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

Every configuration choice lives here, never in a node package. Moving the talker to another board is a new [image.*] block; switching middleware is the rmw line. Neither touches src/sensor_node/.

The launch file: generated until you need one

ROS 2 projects describe what to start in a launch file. This bringup has no launch/ directory, so nros run generated one from the [[component]] rows, after the first build. To see it:

cat build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

When you need what only a launch file can say (a parameter, a remap, a launch argument), add launch/system.launch.xml to the bringup and it replaces the generated one. The file is the ROS 2 launch XML schema, so a launch file from another ROS 2 project pastes in unchanged.

The entry: the binary, also generated

There is no entry package under src/. nros run (and nros build) reads each [image.*] block and generates the entry for it under build/: a main() that constructs each component, applies the launch file’s parameters, and runs them on one executor. Running the entry is launching the system; there is no separate ros2 launch step.

What is yours and what is generated

Everything under src/ is yours to edit and commit. build/ holds everything derived: generated message code, the launch file, the resolved system and the entry. Nothing in build/ is committed; if you can regenerate it, it does not belong in git.

Next

  • Your own message package
  • Growing your workspace: a second node, a second board, a launch file.
  • First Node in C or C++: the same node package in another language.

Design background

RFC-0121 D1 to D3.

First Node — Rust (Linux)

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux in about ten minutes. Uses the canonical Zenoh backend. The zenoh router comes from ROS 2 (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd) — nano-ros no longer ships one. Rather not run a router? Use --rmw cyclonedds instead: it needs no router at all (see Choosing an RMW). Either way the build generates its messages from your ROS 2 install, so you need ROS 2 sourced for the first build.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml         # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── Cargo.toml          # a library crate; names no board and no RMW
    │   └── src/lib.rs          # the Talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml         # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

The node package

talker_node is a library. It has no main(), and nothing in it names a board, an RMW or a ROS edition. src/lib.rs declares what the node creates (a publisher on /chatter, a 1 s timer) and what the timer callback does, and its last line exports the node:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
nros::node!(Talker);
}

The program’s main() is generated by the build, from the bringup. That is what lets the same node package go into a Linux image today and a Cortex-M image later without a second copy. Growing your workspace walks through lib.rs line by line.

Cargo.toml holds Rust facts only: the [lib] target, the class the package registers, and its dependencies.

[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

[package.metadata.nros.node]
class = "talker_node::Talker"
name = "talker_node"

[dependencies]
nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["rmw-cffi", "macros"] }
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

nano-ros crates are declared registry-style (version = "*"), but nothing of nano-ros is on crates.io: the build points them at the SDK the nros on PATH carries. The settings that takes (the [patch.crates-io] table, the target triple, linker flags) are generated under build/ from the bringup, never written by hand and never committed. No path in the package names where nano-ros lives, so the workspace copies anywhere.

Message packages are not listed by hand either: package.xml’s <depend>std_msgs</depend> is the one statement, and the build writes the matching # nros-managed row. To use another message package, add its <depend>; the next nros build adds the row.

The bringup package

talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement:

[system]
name = "talker_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "talker_node"
class = "talker_node::Talker"
name = "talker_node"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The [[component]] row says which node runs; [image.linux] says it runs on this machine. The --rmw you passed to nros new lives here and nowhere else, so switching RMW or ROS edition is editing rmw or ros_edition and building again.

Native (host) images read the locator and domain from environment variables (NROS_LOCATOR — the retired ZENOH_LOCATOR is refused at startup — and ROS_DOMAIN_ID). Embedded images bake theirs from the same [image.<id>] table (locator, and the address in net) — the shape shows up under the Embedded Starters section.

This is the same project as examples/linux/rust/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for Rust on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it. Its bringup goes further than the scaffold, with one image per RMW and ROS edition.

Configure

Three runtime knobs, each an env override on a built-in default:

KnobDefaultEnv override
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Zenoh modeclientNROS_SESSION_MODE

On native these stay environment variables — [image.linux] declares no locator. An embedded image bakes them from its own [image.<id>] table instead; see the Configuration Guide.

Build

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build            # builds the image `[image.linux]` declares

nros build prepares everything first: the message bindings package.xml declares, the generated main() for [image.linux], and the cargo settings derived from board = "linux", all under build/. Then it runs cargo. There is no step to run before it; when nothing changed, the preparation costs a comparison.

First build pulls dependencies (~3 minutes). Re-builds finish in seconds. When it finishes, nros build prints where the binary landed (under build/, never beside your sources) and how to run it.

Driving cargo yourself (an IDE, a CI step, --release) is supported: nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo line, against the generated entry under build/. Before you open the workspace in an IDE, run the preparation on its own so rust-analyzer finds the generated crates:

nros configure

What it writes under build/ is regenerated on every build; never edit it, and never add a .cargo/config.toml of your own to carry board facts. Your own Rust-toolchain preferences go where cargo already looks for them — a parent directory or $CARGO_HOME.

Run

Two terminals (each command below blocks; keep them open):

# Terminal 1 — zenoh router (ROS 2's own). Blocks the shell until Ctrl-C.
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# Terminal 2 — the talker. The talker logs via `log::info!`, so set
# RUST_LOG=info — without it `env_logger` only shows errors and the
# `Publishing:` lines stay hidden.
cd talker_ws
RUST_LOG=info nros run talker_node
# Expected output (on stderr):
#   [INFO  talker_node] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
#   [INFO  talker_node] Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
#   …

nros run talker_node runs the bringup whose only node is talker_node, rebuilding first if anything changed. It keeps running until Ctrl-C.

That’s the nano-ros side fully working. Optional step: verify interop with stock ROS 2.

# Terminal 3 — stock ROS 2 with rmw_zenoh_cpp. It talks to the SAME
# router already running in terminal 1 (default tcp/127.0.0.1:7447).
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

If ros2 topic echo shows no output despite the talker printing Publishing:, the routers aren’t peering — confirm both processes point at the same port (default tcp/127.0.0.1:7447).

Readiness signal. Within ~6 seconds of the program starting (session open + the first 1 s timer tick), the talker should print Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' — the count starts at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo_nodes_cpp talker. If no Publishing: line in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm RUST_LOG is set. Without RUST_LOG=info (or debug), env_logger filters out the Publishing: lines and the run looks silent even when it’s working.
  2. Confirm the router is running (terminal 1). Without it, the talker blocks on Executor::open indefinitely.
  3. Re-run with RUST_LOG=debug and look for “RMW session open failed” — usually a wrong locator or wrong port.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Retargeting

To run the same node on a board, add an image for it to src/talker_node_bringup/system.toml, named by that board’s id (Supported Boards), and provision it:

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh
nros run talker_node_bringup:baremetal

Nothing in src/talker_node/ changes: the board’s descriptor supplies the target triple, the board crate and the memory budgets. With two images the short nros run talker_node no longer picks one, so name the image you mean; nros run lists the spellings when it refuses. The platform chapters scaffold with --board <board> from the start, which writes the image for you.

  • Add a subscription: nros new listener_node --template listener --to talker_node_bringup from the workspace root adds a second node package and its component row (Growing your workspace).
  • Generate bindings for custom .msg / .srv / .action files: Message Generation
  • Cross-compile for an RTOS: pick the right Embedded Starter from the next section (FreeRTOS / Zephyr / NuttX / ThreadX / ESP32 / Bare-metal Cortex-M3).

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker kept for each platform and language, and the language workspaces that hold the paired examples.

First Node — C (Linux)

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux from C. The node is a C library built with CMake; the program around it is generated. Uses the Zenoh backend.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install — ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new c_talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang c --rmw zenoh
cd c_talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

c_talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── c_talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml           # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # a library and its registration; no board facts
    │   └── src/Talker.c          # the talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── c_talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml           # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

This is the same project as examples/linux/c/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for C on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it.

The bringup package

c_talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement, the same schema whatever language the node is written in:

[system]
name = "c_talker_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "c_talker_node"
class = "c_talker_node::Talker"
name = "c_talker_node"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The [[component]] row says which node runs; [image.linux] says it runs on this machine. Nothing in the node package names a platform, a board or an RMW — and the package.xml <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> export that used to carry that tuple is retired and refused. Moving the talker to a board is another [image.<id>] block here, with no edit to src/c_talker_node/.

On native, locator + domain come from env vars (NROS_LOCATOR, ROS_DOMAIN_ID) with built-in defaults; an embedded image declares them in its own [image.<id>] table (locator, and its address in the board network file os_config names) and they are baked at build time (see Configuration).

The node package

A C node package is a library, not a program. The scaffolded CMakeLists.txt is (comments trimmed):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(c_talker_node VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES C)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 11)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN c_talker_node::Talker
    EXECUTABLE c_talker_node
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library generates the C bindings the package declares and links nano-ros. nros_components_register_node registers the class the bringup’s [[component]] row names, the CMake spelling of ROS 2’s rclcpp_components_register_node.

There is no main(). The build generates one for each image, which opens the session and executor, creates the node, and hands both to your code. Your code is a state struct and a configure function, exported with RCLC_C_COMPONENT:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>
#include <std_msgs/msg/string.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
    char text[32];
} talker_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    talker_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, talker_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    self->count++;
    int n = snprintf(self->text, sizeof self->text, "Hello World: %d", (int)self->count);
    std_msgs__msg__String msg;
    msg.data.data = self->text;          // your buffer; nothing allocates
    msg.data.size = (size_t)n;
    msg.data.capacity = sizeof self->text;
    if (rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL) == RCL_RET_OK) {
        printf("Publishing: '%s'\n", self->text);
    }
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                  talker_t* self) {
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, String), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(talker_t, talker_configure)

configure runs once at startup, on the generated entry’s own node and executor; after that the executor calls on_tick once a second. Because the entry owns startup, the same file runs on Linux and on a board whose C runtime never calls main (Zephyr, an RTOS startup task).

--template picks a different node: listener, server / client (AddTwoInts) or action-server / action-client (Fibonacci).

Generated messages take rosidl’s C names and member shape (std_msgs__msg__String in <std_msgs/msg/string.h>, msg.data.data / .size / .capacity). Their strings and sequences point at memory you own: wire them with the generated <Msg>__init_in(&msg, &storage) over a <Msg>__Storage, or point data at your own buffer as above and as micro-ROS code does. Nothing on this path allocates, so rosidl’s allocating <Msg>__init / __fini are not declared.

Configure

Three runtime knobs:

KnobDefaultEnv override
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Node namec_talker_nodethe [[component]] row’s name (a launch file can remap it)

On an embedded image the same knobs are compile-baked from that image’s [image.<id>] table in system.toml (see Configuration).

Build

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of c_talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build from the bringup (the generated main() for [image.linux] and a CMake root that adds your package), configures it with the SDK root and the toolchain file the board names, and builds it. The C message bindings are generated during that CMake configure, from the package’s declared dependencies. There is no step to run before it.

When it finishes, nros build prints what it built and how to run it:

nros build: next for `c_talker_node_bringup:linux`:
  artifact: /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry
  run:
    nros run c_talker_node

Driving CMake yourself. The CMake root nros build configures is generated under build/, never at the workspace root, and nros build --dry-run prints the exact cmake lines it would run. To have that root in place without building (before opening the workspace in an IDE, or to run those lines by hand), prepare it on its own:

nros configure

For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace at all, see Build as a CMake subdirectory.

The first configure pulls and builds nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs (~3 minutes). Re-builds finish in seconds.

Run

Three terminals.

# 1. Start the zenoh router (ROS 2's own):
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# 2. Run the talker:
cd c_talker_ws
nros run c_talker_node
# Expected output, once a second:
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
#   …

# 3. Verify from stock ROS 2:
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

Readiness signal. Within ~6 seconds (session open + the first 1 s timer tick), the talker prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on stdout — Rust + C + C++ all start the count at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If it does not appear in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm the router is running (terminal 1). Without it, the generated entry’s session open fails at once with -4 (RCLC_RET_NOT_FOUND — connection refused) and the program stops, naming the step.
  2. Wrong locator / unreachable host → same -4 signature in stderr. Reachable host but mismatched port → talker hangs on session-open handshake rather than returning a code.
  3. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

First Node — C++ (Linux)

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux from C++. The node is a C++ library built with CMake, in the ament shape; the program around it is generated. Uses the Zenoh backend.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install — ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new cpp_talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang cpp --rmw zenoh
cd cpp_talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

cpp_talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── cpp_talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml             # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt          # a library and its registration; no board facts
    │   ├── include/cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp
    │   └── src/Talker.cpp          # the talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── cpp_talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml             # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

This is the same project as examples/linux/cpp/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for C++ on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it.

cpp_talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement — [system] for the RMW and domain, one [[component]] row naming the node, and one [image.<id>] per target naming its board. No line of the node package names a platform, a board or an RMW, so moving the talker to a board is another [image.<id>] block in the bringup; First Node — C shows the file in full. The package.xml <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> export that used to carry that tuple is retired and refused.

The node package

The CMakeLists is the ament shape you already know — this is the scaffolded file, comments trimmed (the message-package Find-stubs make find_package(std_msgs) generate bindings on the fly):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(cpp_talker_node VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES C CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.cpp)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN cpp_talker_node::Talker
    EXECUTABLE cpp_talker_node
    SHAPE configure)

nros_components_register_node has rclcpp_components_register_node’s keywords: the class the bringup’s [[component]] row names, and its executable name.

LANGUAGES C CXX (not CXX alone): the per-target register stub is a C translation unit, so C must be enabled in this directory scope or the link fails. Backend selection is [system] rmw in the bringup, not CMake code and not a configure-line cache variable.

There is no main(). The node is a class with a configure(rclcpp::Node&) method, the shape of a composable node: the generated entry initialises nano-ros, creates the node, constructs your class in static storage and calls configure on it, then spins the executor.

// include/cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp
#pragma once
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs.hpp"

namespace cpp_talker_node {

class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::String> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int count_ = 0;

    void on_tick();   // bound by &Talker::on_tick, not by a name

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

}  // namespace cpp_talker_node

// src/Talker.cpp
#include "cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp"
#include <cstdio>

namespace cpp_talker_node {

void Talker::on_tick() {
    char payload[64];
    std::snprintf(payload, sizeof payload, "Hello World: %d", ++count_);
    std_msgs::msg::String m;
    m.data = payload;
    if (pub_.publish(m).ok()) std::printf("Publishing: '%s'\n", m.data.c_str());
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}

}  // namespace cpp_talker_node

The publisher and timer are typed wrappers over the C ABI, and every call returns a Result rather than throwing: every nano-ros build is -fno-exceptions. configure returns the first failure, and the generated entry halts naming the node that failed, so there is no unchecked construction to forget. Porting a ROS 2 C++ node covers the rclcpp-shaped constructors, shared_from_this() and rclcpp::TimerBase.

--template picks a different node: listener, server / client (AddTwoInts) or action-server / action-client (Fibonacci).

Three runtime knobs:

KnobDefaultOverride
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Node namecpp_talker_nodethe [[component]] row’s name (a launch file can remap it)

On a hosted target the generated entry takes the locator and domain from the build, then from the environment variables. An embedded image declares its locator in its own [image.<id>] table and its address in the board network file os_config names, and bakes them at build time.

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of cpp_talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

nros build prepares the build from the bringup (the generated main() for [image.linux] and a CMake root that adds your package), configures it with the SDK root and the board’s toolchain file, and builds it. The C++ message bindings are generated during that CMake configure. There is no step to run before it.

When it finishes, nros build prints what it built and how to run it:

# 2. Run the talker:

  • C++ all start the count at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If it does not appear in 30 seconds:

Your own message package

You write a ROS 2 msg package once. The same src/my_msgs/ directory builds under both:

  • a nano-ros build — rosidl_generate_interfaces(...) is intercepted by nano-ros’s wrapper and routed through nano-ros codegen. No ROS 2 build tools run: even the rclcpp-shaped consumer below compiles against nano-ros’s own rclcpp CMake package. nros build still reads message definitions from your ROS 2 install, so source it for the first build (below).
  • colcon build — upstream rosidl_default_generators produces the upstream-ROS bindings (this half, and only this half, needs a ROS 2 install; it is the optional cross-build proof at the end).

Different build systems, identical source tree. No nano-ros-specific files in the msg package.

Where this fits. This chapter uses ROS 2 vocabulary (ament_cmake, rosidl, rclcpp) because its point is that stock ROS shapes work unchanged. If you came straight from First Project and none of that means anything yet, you can skim to “The Rust side” below or skip ahead to First Node — Rust and return later. The standalone tree here is for clarity — in your scaffolded my_robot workspace the same drop-in applies: put src/my_msgs/ next to your node packages.

The msg package — stock ROS shape

Drop a verbatim ROS msg pkg under src/ of your workspace:

src/my_msgs/
├── package.xml
├── CMakeLists.txt
└── msg/
    └── MyMsg.msg

src/my_msgs/package.xml:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>my_msgs</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>My ROS 2 msg package</description>
  <maintainer email="you@example.org">you</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>

  <buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend>
  <depend>std_msgs</depend>
  <build_depend>rosidl_default_generators</build_depend>
  <exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>

  <member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>

  <export>
    <build_type>ament_cmake</build_type>
  </export>
</package>

src/my_msgs/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_msgs)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
    msg/MyMsg.msg
    DEPENDENCIES std_msgs
)

ament_export_dependencies(rosidl_default_runtime)
ament_package()

src/my_msgs/msg/MyMsg.msg:

std_msgs/Header header
string payload
int32 sequence

Zero nano-ros-specific lines. Run colcon build from this dir — upstream ROS produces a working msg package. Drop the same dir into a nano-ros build (below) — nano-ros codegen produces the equivalent bindings.

The consumer — stock ROS shape

// src/my_app/src/my_app.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <memory>

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "my_msgs/msg/my_msg.hpp"

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

class MyNode : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
    MyNode() : rclcpp::Node("my_node") {
        publisher_ = this->create_publisher<my_msgs::msg::MyMsg>("topic", 10);
        timer_ = this->create_wall_timer(500ms, [this]() {
            my_msgs::msg::MyMsg m;
            m.payload = "hello";
            publisher_->publish(m);
        });
    }
private:
    rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr timer_;
    rclcpp::Publisher<my_msgs::msg::MyMsg>::SharedPtr publisher_;
};

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
    rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<MyNode>());
    rclcpp::shutdown();
    return 0;
}

src/my_app/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rclcpp REQUIRED)
find_package(my_msgs REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_app src/my_app.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app
    rclcpp::rclcpp
    my_msgs::my_msgs
    std_msgs::std_msgs
)

ament_package()

Build it with nros build

There is no nano-ros-specific file to add: a workspace has no root build file. With no bringup, nros build builds it the way colcon build does — every package it finds by its package.xml, in <depend> order, each in its own build/<pkg>/. For my_app it generates the CMake root that used to be hand-written (nano-ros, NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH at ./src/, the rclcpp / ament surface); my_msgs is not built on its own — its bindings are generated into the package that uses it.

The first nros build of the workspace needs ROS 2 sourced: it generates the bindings against your ROS 2 install’s message definitions, and refuses without one. It records the prefix, so later builds need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build
./build/my_app/cmake/pkg/my_app/my_app

In a workspace that also has a bringup (what nros new <ws> --board <board> writes), the same nros build builds my_msgs into whichever image’s packages depend on it.

Escape hatch — a hand-written umbrella. For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace, one top-level CMakeLists.txt pulls nano-ros in as a subdirectory, naming the SDK root on the configure line (Build as a CMake subdirectory has the mechanism):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_workspace LANGUAGES CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14)

# Pull nano-ros — the installed SDK root, passed as -DNANO_ROS_SDK=….
set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)
set(NROS_RMW "zenoh" CACHE STRING "Active RMW.")
set(NROS_RMW "${NROS_RMW}")
add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

# Point the message-package resolver at this workspace (must precede the
# ament-surface include so the workspace Find<pkg>.cmake auto-emit picks it up).
set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src")

# nano-ros's ament / rclcpp surface (find_package(rclcpp), ament_* verbs).
include("${NANO_ROS_SDK}/cmake/NanoRosAmentSurface.cmake")

# Bulk-build every workspace msg pkg in topo order. One line, no
# add_subdirectory(src/<pkg>) per pkg.
nros_workspace_interfaces()

# Build the consumer app.
add_subdirectory(src/my_app)

cmake -B build -S . -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build -j
./build/src/my_app/my_app

The Rust side

The same msg package feeds a Rust node with no CMake involved: declare it in your node package’s package.xml (<depend>my_msgs</depend>) and run nros build from the workspace root — that is the whole change. The package index finds src/my_msgs/ by its package.xml, generates the generated/my_msgs crate, and writes the manifest row itself (my_msgs = { path = "../../generated/my_msgs", default-features = false } # nros-managed). The shipped precedent is examples/workspaces/features/src/custom_msgs with its rust_reading_listener_pkg consumer. Full detail: Message Generation.

use my_msgs::msg::MyMsg;   // generated crate, same field names

Cross-build proof — same source under colcon (optional; needs ROS 2)

cd src && colcon build

src/my_msgs/ produces the upstream my_msgs bindings; src/my_app/ links against the upstream rclcpp + my_msgs::my_msgs. The nano-ros build above produces the same source linked against NanoRos::NanoRosCpp through the nano-ros codegen, with the smart Find-stub forwarding find_package(my_msgs) → my_msgs::my_msgs.

The interface-package search path

find_package(<pkg>) walks three layers, highest priority first:

LayerSourceNotes
1NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATHColon/semicolon-separated colcon-src/-style roots; immediate subdirs with package.xml are candidates.
2AMENT_PREFIX_PATHThe standard ROS install-prefix layout (<prefix>/share/<pkg>/{msg,srv,action}/).
3Bundled<nano-ros>/packages/cli/interfaces/<pkg>/ (in-tree bundled definitions).

Shadowing — a workspace my_msgs and an AMENT my_msgs resolve to the workspace one, with a message(STATUS ...) line noting the shadow.

Shadowing contract

When two layers carry the same package name (e.g. a workspace std_msgs and /opt/ros/<distro>/share/std_msgs/), the higher layer wins — silently and deterministically. Concretely:

  1. NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH > AMENT_PREFIX_PATH > bundled. The message-package resolver (cmake/find/_NrosFindRosMsgPackage.cmake) walks the three layers in order; the first hit wins. Lower layers are skipped entirely.

  2. The configure pass emits a message(STATUS ...) line noting the resolved path, e.g.

    -- nros: find_package(std_msgs) -> /path/to/workspace/src/std_msgs

    Grep your configure log for nros: find_package(<pkg>) to confirm which layer supplied each pkg.

  3. Intra-workspace shadowing — when two roots under NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH both ship the same pkg, the nros_workspace_interfaces() bulk orchestrator keeps the earlier-listed one and warns about the shadowed copy.

  4. No partial overrides. Shadowing is whole-package: a workspace pkg replaces ALL of an AMENT pkg’s interfaces, not a subset. If you only want to add MyExtraMsg.msg to std_msgs, ship a separate pkg (e.g. my_std_extra_msgs) — don’t shadow.

Compile-time fail-safe

Shadowing is observed at compile time: if your workspace std_msgs declares a Marker.msg and your consumer includes "std_msgs/msg/marker.hpp", the build only succeeds when the workspace copy is the one linked. AMENT’s std_msgs ships no Marker.msg, so a fall-through resolves to a missing header. The build outcome is the strongest evidence — nm on the linked binary is the symbol-level corroborator.

Reference fixture for shadowing

The canonical smoke proof for the Layer 1 > Layer 2 case ships at examples/templates/workspace-shadowing/ — a workspace std_msgs carrying a Marker.msg shadows the AMENT-installed std_msgs. The fixture’s README.md walks through the cmake + nm verification. A regression test (packages/testing/nros-tests/tests/workspace_shadowing.rs) re-runs the same proof in CI when AMENT is sourced.

Reference fixture

examples/templates/local-msg-package/ ships the exact pattern above end-to-end (two workspace msg pkgs with a dep between them, plus a consumer node). Use it as a copy-out template.

Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes

Every first build of a project needs ROS 2 sourced, because the messages are generated from it (A10). The First Project runs a talker in QEMU over Zenoh, so it also needs ROS 2 for the router; its Linux section runs on Cyclone DDS, where no router exists, so “no output” there is never a router problem. The First Node pages run on Linux over Zenoh and assume nros setup linux --rmw zenoh has run and the ROS 2 router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd) is reachable. When something goes wrong in the first ten minutes, the error you see usually points at one of the predictable misses below.

Each branch quotes the real stderr you can grep against — not a paraphrase. If your error text matches, the fix on the right is the one to try.

A. Build failures (cargo / cmake)

A1. Cargo cannot find nros

error: no matching package named `nros` found

A node package’s Cargo.toml declares nano-ros crates registry-style (nros = { version = "*" } — they are not published to crates.io); the [patch.crates-io] block that resolves them into the nano-ros SDK is GENERATED, under build/, and nros build hands it to cargo with --config. nros build and nros run write it themselves, so this error means cargo ran without it: a plain cargo build in a package, or an IDE that opened the workspace before anything was generated. Fix:

cd <the workspace root>
nros build        # or, to prepare without building: nros configure

nros configure writes the generated settings without building; nros build --dry-run prints the cargo line that uses them. Either is also what ties a copied-out workspace to an SDK (the nros binary’s own, or the one --nano-ros-path names), and runs again by itself on the next build after you move the directory.

This is not an nros setup issue — nros setup only fetches the SDK / source-package payload (zenoh-pico, mbedtls, cyclonedds, …); it does not synthesise missing Cargo dependencies.

A2. nros CLI not found

nros (codegen tool) not found on PATH or in packages/cli/target/release/
or ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin. …

(The rest of the message names how a contributor builds the CLI from a checkout; as a user you install it instead.)

The nros binary is not installed, or not on PATH. Install a release and put ~/.nros/bin on PATH:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

If ~/.nros/bin/nros exists but PATH doesn’t see it — that’s the [PATH] doctor status (D2 below), not this branch.

The nros binary ships the codegen — there is no separate nros-codegen build step. CMake projects auto-resolve nros from PATH / ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/; -D_NANO_ROS_CODEGEN_TOOL=<path> is an override, not a requirement.

A3. Rust target not installed

error: could not compile … due to previous error
the target `thumbv7m-none-eabi` is not installed

Add it:

rustup target add thumbv7m-none-eabi

The triple is the board’s, not the example’s — you will not find it in any file you wrote. Read it back from the [build] target line of the generated nros-cargo.toml under build/, which nros build writes from the board your bringup’s system.toml names.

A4. Cross linker not found

error: linker `arm-none-eabi-gcc` not found

The cross toolchain wasn’t provisioned. Run nros setup for your board (it ships a prebuilt arm-none-eabi-gcc):

nros setup mps2-an385-freertos       # or qemu-armv7a-nuttx / mps2-an385-baremetal / …

A5. Cyclone DDS runtime missing

ld: cannot find -lddsc
ld: cannot find -lcyclonedds-ddsc

The Cyclone DDS runtime wasn’t provisioned:

nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds

A6. cargo build --features rmw-cyclonedds can’t link

undefined reference to `nros_rmw_cyclonedds_register`
undefined reference to `dds_create_participant`

rmw-cyclonedds cannot link from cargo alone — the Cyclone backend is C++ + CMake, registered via nros_rmw_cffi_register_named from a CMake-built target — wired through CMakeLists.txt + Corrosion. Use the cmake build path instead, and choose the backend where backends are chosen: [system] rmw in the bringup’s system.toml.

[system]
rmw = "cyclonedds"
