cd my_ws                          # a workspace with C or C++ node packages
nros build

There is no -DNROS_RMW= to pass: a backend selected on the command line disagrees with the one the rest of the build resolves from system.toml.

A Rust node package does not take --features rmw-cyclonedds at all: its RMW is its image’s. A bringup that declares a linux_cyclonedds image (as examples/linux/rust/talker does) builds it with nros build linux_cyclonedds — the board crate’s rmw-cyclonedds builds Cyclone through nros-rmw-cyclonedds-sys.

A7. The board name is a typo

…/system.toml: board `mps2-an358` is claimed by no board descriptor under /…/nano-ros

[image.<id>] board is where a bringup names its board, and a typo there is refused by name rather than guessed at. The legal spellings are the names = [...] arrays of the board descriptors, one per board crate at packages/boards/*/nros-board.toml; several are aliases for the same board (mps2-an385-baremetal and rtic-mps2-an385 are two entry shapes on one descriptor).

The neighbouring refusals, when the image is missing rather than misspelt:

this workspace declares no `[image.*]`. An image is the buildable unit: add `[image.<id>] board = "<board>"` to system.toml.
…/system.toml: names no board; add `[image.<id>] board = "<board>"`

The first means no bringup in the workspace has a system.toml with an image, so there is nothing for nros build to plan. The second means the file is there and its [image.<id>] table has no board key.

A8. system.toml next to code

nros build refuses a system.toml in a directory that also holds a Cargo.toml or a CMakeLists.txt. A system.toml belongs to a bringup package, never to the package with the code, because it says where that code runs and the code itself must not.

To fix it, give the configuration its own package:

  1. Make src/<pkg>_bringup/ beside your node package, with a package.xml.
  2. Move system.toml into it.
  3. Delete any main that only starts the node; the entry is generated.

nros new <ws> --board <board> --template talker writes this shape, so a scaffolded project never hits it.

A9. direnv allow reminder

NROS_PLATFORM_CFFI_INCLUDE not set (direnv allow, or build via just)
FREERTOS_PORT not set

(The quoted message is emitted by the build script; “direnv allow” and “build via just” in it refer to a contributor checkout.) nros build passes these to cargo from the board’s settings, so a build driven by nros build — or by cargo with the generated --config file — does not hit it. If a cargo command you drive yourself does, you skipped the --config build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml argument.

A10. AMENT_PREFIX_PATH is unset

nros build, nros run or nros configure stops before building anything:

Error: configure: `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH` is unset and no configure of `/home/you/sensor_ws` has recorded one to reuse. Run the setup step once from a shell that has ROS 2: `source /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash` (or your overlay's `install/setup.bash`), then `nros configure`; later runs without a sourced shell reuse what it records.

The project has messages to generate (every talker uses std_msgs), and nano-ros generates them from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, so the types and their hashes match your ROS 2 peers. This shell has not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier configure of the project ran in one that had. It happens on every board and every RMW, Linux and Cyclone DDS included.

Source ROS 2 once, in this shell, and run the same command again:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # or your overlay's install/setup.bash
nros build

That configure records the prefix in the project. Later builds and runs of the same project reuse it, from any shell, an IDE or a CI step. A new project records its own, so its first build needs a sourced shell again.

B. Binary runs but no output

B1. Rust: RMW session open failed — Transport(ConnectionFailed)

[ERROR nros] RMW session open failed — Transport(ConnectionFailed)

The zenoh router isn’t running, or isn’t reachable on the locator the talker is pointed at. The router comes from ROS 2 (nano-ros no longer ships one) — start it in another terminal:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Default ports: tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 on POSIX, tcp/10.0.2.2:7451 on QEMU FreeRTOS (Slirp forwards to host), 7452 NuttX, 7453 ThreadX-RV, 7454 ESP32, 7455 ThreadX-Linux, 7447 Zephyr.

B2. C: RCLC_CHECK failed: rclc_support_init(...) -> -4

RCLC_CHECK failed at src/main.c:92: rclc_support_init(&app.support, argc, argv, &allocator) -> -4

Process exits 1 (the retval passed to RCLC_CHECK_RET). -4 = RCLC_RET_NOT_FOUND — the locator was unreachable (zenohd not running, or wrong port). Same fix as B1 above.

The C API entry point is rclc_support_init (rclc’s (&support, argc, argv, &allocator)) or, with an explicit locator, rclc_support_init_with_locator — not nros_init or nros::init, which don’t exist in the C API.

B3. C++: process exits 156 after a rclcpp::init_in failure

nros::init returned NROS_CPP_RET_TRANSPORT_ERROR (-100)

Same root cause as B1/B2 — zenohd not reachable. NROS_CPP_RET_TRANSPORT_ERROR = -100 is the C++ result code that RCLCPP_TRY_RET propagates from main(); on POSIX this becomes (unsigned char)-100 = 156 as the process exit code. Treat “exited 156 after starting” as the C++ equivalent of B1.

B4. Override the locator at runtime

When a native talker can’t reach the daemon, override the locator with the canonical env var:

NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/192.168.1.50:7447 ./build/c_talker
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7 ./build/c_talker         # also overridable

The native Rust / C / C++ talkers all read NROS_LOCATOR, then fall back to the build-time default. The retired ZENOH_LOCATOR / ZENOH_MODE are REFUSED at startup with an error naming NROS_LOCATOR / NROS_SESSION_MODE — unset them. Embedded targets have no runtime env — their locator is compile-baked from system.toml ([image.<id>] locator, or [system] locator for an image that does not state one), so editing that file and rebuilding is the override.

B5. Binary exits immediately, no error printed

Buffering: setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0) if you piped the run. POSIX terminals flush on newline; piped stdout full-buffers and may eat short outputs. Add a RUST_LOG=info (Rust) or unbuffer the C / C++ output (stdbuf -oL).

C. ROS 2 side sees nothing

C1. RMW mismatch

# On the ROS 2 side, default rmw_fastrtps_cpp will NOT see nano-ros:
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp     # for Zenoh
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp # for Cyclone

C2. QoS mismatch — echo silent, list sees the topic

ros2 topic list           # /chatter shown
ros2 topic echo /chatter  # … nothing

nano-ros publishers default to BEST_EFFORT; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE. The QoS-mismatched subscriber is created but receives no data. Force best-effort on the echo:

ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

D. Doctor + last-resort

D1. Run the doctor first

nros doctor

It prints fixit hints for the toolchain you actually need. (A just-free platform-scoped doctor spelling does not exist today; contributors with an in-tree checkout can scope via the platform recipes.)

D2. [PATH] nros built but not on PATH

The doctor reports this distinct from [MISSING] when the binary is installed at ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/nros but PATH doesn’t see it. Put the directory on PATH (and in your shell’s startup file):

export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

D3. Full sweep (slow)

nros doctor
nros setup --check

Only run this when you’re standing up every supported platform in one go. It walks the provisioning checks and can take a few minutes.

D4. File an issue

When all else fails, include:

  • the exact command you ran,
  • the full stderr,
  • rustc --version, cmake --version, qemu-system-arm --version,
  • nros --version.

What success looks like

A correctly-running Rust Linux talker (examples/linux/rust/talker) prints something like this on stderr (with RUST_LOG=info):

[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 3'

(That is the full expected output — the talker logs one line per publish, nothing else.)

A correctly-running C talker (examples/linux/c/talker) prints on stdout:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 3'

A correctly-running C++ talker prints the same Publishing: 'Hello World: N' line once per second.

The ROS 2 side (ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp) should see:

data: 'Hello World: 1'
---
data: 'Hello World: 2'
---
data: 'Hello World: 3'
---

If you see all three of these — talker logging, ROS 2 echo output, and matching counter values — interop is verified end-to-end.

See also

  • Install + first build — full setup walkthrough
  • First Node — Rust — the canonical Rust starter
  • Troubleshooting — broader issue-by-issue reference for post-first-build problems

Building and Configuring

nros build is the recommended way to build an image: it prepares everything the build needs (generated messages, the resolved system, the image’s build settings) and then runs the host build tool, as cargo build does. A project that stays in west, CMake, NuttX make or an IDE runs the preparation step, nros configure, from that tool’s own configure step instead.

This page is coming soon.

Design background

  • RFC-0120: one resolver for every build road

Growing your workspace

First Project left you with a workspace of two packages: a node and the bringup that says what it runs on. A project grows from there by one path, in four steps, and you take only the ones you need:

  1. add a node package;
  2. add its component row to the bringup;
  3. add launch/ when you need a launch argument, a remap or a parameter;
  4. add an image for another board.

Each step adds a package or a few lines to the bringup. The shape of the workspace never changes, so nothing you did in an earlier step has to be undone.

Where you start

sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # node package: package.xml, Cargo.toml (a library), src/lib.rs
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # package.xml and system.toml; no launch/ yet

The two roles, and what each one never holds:

PackageHoldsNever holds
Node packageone node: publishers, subscriptions, timers, services, callback bodiesa board, an RMW, a main()
Bringup packagesystem.toml: which nodes run, on which boards, with which RMW; optionally launch/compiled code

There is no third package to write. For each [image.*] block in the bringup’s system.toml, nros build and nros run generate the program’s entry (its main()) under build/. A workspace has no root Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt either: like a colcon workspace, it is a directory of packages.

system.toml lives only in a bringup package. A system.toml beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt is refused, and the message says where to move it.

1. Add a node package

From the workspace root:

nros new monitor_node --template listener --to sensor_node_bringup

Inside a workspace, nros new adds a package under src/ instead of writing a new workspace. --to also adds the node’s component row to the bringup (step 2). Pass --lang c or --lang cpp for a C or C++ node; the rest of this page is the same in every language.

A node package is a library with three files:

src/monitor_node/
├── package.xml          # ROS 2 manifest: one <depend> per message package
├── Cargo.toml           # a [lib] crate and its dependencies, nothing else
└── src/lib.rs           # the node; its last line is nros::node!(Listener);

It has no fn main() and names no board, RMW or board crate. That is what lets one node package go into a Cortex-M image and a Linux image unchanged: the difference between them is an [image.*] block, not a second copy of the node.

The manifests

package.xml is a standard ROS 2 manifest. Each message package the node uses is one <depend>:

<depend>std_msgs</depend>

That line is all you write for a message package. The build turns each <depend> on a message package into a dependency row in Cargo.toml, tagged # nros-managed, pointing at the crate it generates under generated/. Removing the <depend> removes the row. A row without the tag is yours and is never touched, so to override a generated row, delete its tag.

Cargo.toml registers the node class the package exports:

[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

[package.metadata.nros.node]
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"

[dependencies]
nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = [
    "alloc",
    "rmw-cffi", "macros"] }
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

This registration is the Rust spelling of nros_components_register_node(... PLUGIN pkg::Class ...) in a C or C++ package’s CMakeLists.txt. A package registers its class once, however many bringups run it. Which bringup runs it is the component row’s business (step 2). nros is never fetched from a registry: the build points it at your installed nano-ros, so no path in the manifest names where nano-ros lives and the package copies anywhere.

src/lib.rs

A Rust node implements Component (what the node creates, declared once at startup) and ExecutableNode (what each callback does), then exports both with nros::node!. The essential shape, from examples/workspaces/rust/src/talker_pkg/src/lib.rs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros::{
    CallbackCtx, ExecutableNode, Component, NodeContext, DeclarativeNode, NodeOptions, NodeResult,
    TimerDuration,
};

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "talker";

    // Per-instance slots, in order: publishers, service servers,
    // service clients, action clients, action servers.
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
        let chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<MyMsg>("/chatter")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick")
            .publishes_entity(&chatter)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    type State = i32;

    fn init() -> Self::State { 0 }

    // See the full example for the callback body.
}

nros::node!(Talker);   // exports the node; this is the last line
}
  • register declares; it does not run. It is called once at startup to declare publishers, subscriptions, timers and which callback publishes what. No message flows here.
  • on_callback is the body. The image’s executor calls it each time a callback fires; state is the node’s own mutable storage.
  • The node is the same type everywhere. ctx.create_node(...) returns the nros::Node a standalone program gets, with rclrs’s methods (create_publisher, create_subscription, timers, logger(), the graph queries). use nros::DeclarativeNode; adds the constructors that bind a callback by name, which is what lets the board run callbacks from its own tasks and lets the build measure the node without running it.
  • ENTITY_BOUNDS is static RAM. nros::node! emits a static sized from it, and a publisher slot carries a loan arena. The default (8 of each kind) measured 50,824 bytes of .bss for a one-service node, against 568 bytes when the node declared what it creates. Count the five kinds in your register(); timers and subscriptions need no slot here. Declaring fewer than register() creates is an error at boot, never a silent drop, so the exact number is safe.
  • Timers. In a timer callback, ctx.timer_info() returns the activation’s expected_call_time and actual_call_time (lateness_ns() is their difference). create_timer_for_callback_name_with_autostart(name, period, clock, false) declares a stopped timer; any callback starts it with ctx.reset_timer(nros::EntityId::new("on_tick")) and stops it with ctx.cancel_timer(..). To control timers by id, add .with_timers(n) to ENTITY_BOUNDS (16 bytes a timer).

Calling a service from a node

A node cannot make a blocking service or action call from on_callback: the executor is mid-dispatch there, and the call would deadlock it. Client calls go in ExecutableNode::tick, which the executor runs once per spin between callbacks. Arm the call in the callback and make it in tick:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn on_callback(state: &mut State, cb: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
    state.want_call = true;          // decide; do not call here
}

fn tick(state: &mut State, ctx: &mut TickCtx<'_>) {
    if state.want_call {
        state.want_call = false;
        let reply = ctx.call_for_name("add_two_ints", &request);  // blocking is safe here
    }
}
}

A service server needs no such split: requests arrive in on_callback like any other callback. In C++, rclcpp::bind_service<Svc, T, &T::method>(node, "/add_two_ints", this) binds a typed member that takes the generated Svc::Request and returns Svc::Response.

2. Add a component row

--to sensor_node_bringup added this to src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml, beside the row the scaffold wrote for sensor_node:

[[component]]
pkg = "monitor_node"
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"
FieldMeaning
pkgthe node package (its <name> in package.xml)
classthe type the package registers
namethe node’s name at runtime; a launch file can remap it
dispatchoptional: the dispatch shape, when it is not the default

It also added <exec_depend>monitor_node</exec_depend> to the bringup’s package.xml. To add a row by hand (for a node package you copied in), write both.

Run the system. The workspace’s first build, in First Project, recorded your ROS 2 prefix, so a shell that has not sourced ROS 2 builds it too; a workspace you start fresh needs ROS 2 sourced for its first build, because the messages are generated from it:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # only needed for a fresh workspace's first build
nros run

With nothing named, nros run runs the workspace’s only image, which now now holds both nodes in one program. nros run sensor_node no longer works. That spelling means “the bringup whose only node is sensor_node”, and this bringup now has two, so it refuses and prints the spellings that would resolve, here sensor_node_bringup:baremetal.

The bringup still has no launch/, so the build generates its launch file from the two rows. After a build, it is at:

cat build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

Before a build, two checks catch most mistakes in a bringup (a [[component]] row naming a package or class that does not exist, a stray build file in the bringup):

nros check --bringup src/sensor_node_bringup
nros check --workspace .

3. Add a launch file when you need one

The generated launch file starts every component with its default name and nothing else. When you need a launch argument, a remap, a namespace or a parameter, the bringup gets a launch/ directory. Start from the generated file, so that adding it changes nothing until you edit it:

mkdir -p src/sensor_node_bringup/launch
cp build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml \
   src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

From then on launch/system.launch.xml is used instead of the generated one. Deleting launch/ goes back to generation.

Keep each <node>’s pkg and exec as the generated file wrote them; the examples below write exec="…" for that value.

The file is the ROS 2 launch XML schema, read with the same parser, so a launch file from another ROS 2 project pastes in. For example, a launch argument that moves both nodes to another topic:

<launch>
  <arg name="topic" default="/chatter"/>

  <node pkg="sensor_node" exec="…" name="sensor_node">
    <remap from="/chatter" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </node>
  <node pkg="monitor_node" exec="…" name="monitor_node">
    <remap from="/chatter" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </node>
</launch>
TagPurpose
<arg name="…" default="…"/>declare a launch argument
<node pkg="…" exec="…" name="…"/>start a node
<param name="…" value="…"/>set one parameter (inside <node>)
<param from="….yaml"/>load a ROS parameter file (inside <node>)
<remap from="…" to="…"/>remap a topic or service (inside <node>)
<group ns="…">put a group of nodes in a namespace
<include file="…"/>include another launch file

Substitutions: $(var <arg>) expands a launch argument, $(find <pkg>) a package’s path, $(env <name>) an environment variable.

There is no ros2 launch step. The launch file is resolved when the image is built, and its result is compiled into the program. An image binds launch arguments, and can name another launch file in the same bringup:

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
args = { topic = "/sensor" }

[image.baremetal_sim]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
launch = "sim.launch.xml"

Parameters

<param from="…"/> takes a standard ROS parameter file, relative to the launch file:

# launch/sensor.param.yaml
/**:                      # every node
  ros__parameters:
    use_sim_time: false
sensor_node:              # this node only
  ros__parameters:
    rate_hz: 25
    limits:
      max_accel: 1.5      # reaches the node as `limits.max_accel`

<node pkg="sensor_node" exec="…" name="sensor_node">
  <param from="sensor.param.yaml"/>
  <param name="rate_hz" value="50"/>   <!-- wins over the file -->
</node>

Precedence is ROS’s: the /** block, then the node’s own block (keyed sensor_node, /ns/sensor_node or /**/sensor_node), then inline <param name= value=>. The values are baked into the program at build time, so an embedded board reads no file at run time; editing the YAML rebuilds. A from= naming a missing file is a build error.

Two capabilities in [system] features decide what the image does with them:

declaredparameter store (declare_parameter, launch values, --ros-args -p)ros2 param services
paramsyesnone
param_servicesyessix per node (get, set, list, describe, …)

params suits a small board whose nodes only read their configuration: each of the six services costs a queryable per node. What it gives up is ros2 param get|set|list|describe|dump and the use_sim_time switch.

4. Add an image

An image is one program: the bringup’s nodes, built for one board with one RMW. It is a block in system.toml, not a package. Your bringup has one, written by the scaffold:

[image.baremetal]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

Running the same two nodes on your Linux machine is one more block:

[image.linux]
board = "linux"
rmw   = "cyclonedds"       # this image only; needs no router on a host

nros run linux

Nothing in either node package changes. The board’s descriptor supplies the target triple, linker flags, cross compiler and memory budgets, so retargeting is the board line and nothing else.

KeyMeaning
boardthe nano-ros board id; Supported Boards lists them
rmwthis image’s RMW, when it differs from [system] rmw
locator, netan embedded image’s network identity (where its router is, its own address)
launcha launch file in the bringup; default [system] default_launch
argslaunch arguments bound for this image
featurescapability axes added to [system] features
os_configRTOS configuration files, in order: Zephyr prj-*.conf and overlays, or a board network file
panicpanic policy: platform, halt or own
profilea cargo or CMake build profile
before_boota function to call before the board boots (below)

[image_defaults] holds what every image shares, so eight images do not repeat their RMW eight times. A specific block’s values replace it; args merge, and os_config and features add up:

[image_defaults]
rmw = "zenoh"

The RMW, like the board, is chosen at build time; embedded targets have no RMW_IMPLEMENTATION switch. On a Linux image, ROS_DOMAIN_ID and NROS_LOCATOR still work at run time; an embedded image bakes the values from its block. See Configuration.

Naming what to run

With two images, nros run alone refuses and lists them. The target argument of nros run, nros build and nros flash accepts, in this order:

You typeIt means
sensor_node_bringup:linuxthat bringup’s image; always works
linuxthe image named linux, when only one bringup declares it
sensor_nodethe bringup whose only node is sensor_node, with its only image
nothingthe workspace’s only image

Anything else refuses and lists the <bringup>:<image> spellings that would resolve; a shortcut never picks one of several. --why says which row resolved. To make a bare nros build build a chosen set, declare it:

[system]
default_images = ["linux"]

Zephyr images

A Zephyr image also carries Zephyr’s own configuration (prj.conf, overlays), which nothing can derive. It lives in the bringup, one directory per board, and the image names the fragments it adds:

src/sensor_node_bringup/boards/native_sim_native_64/
├── prj.conf
└── prj-zenoh.conf               # named by [image.<id>] os_config

nros build writes the Zephyr application itself under build/ and runs west build on it. The board id is still nano-ros’s (zephyr), never Zephyr’s spelling. Configuring an image has the rest. A Zephyr application that keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf and is built with plain west build is not a workspace image; it has its own chapter.

What nros build generates

Everything generated lands under build/, and none of it is yours to edit or commit:

  • the generated launch file of each bringup without launch/;
  • the resolved system for each image (build/nros/models/);
  • the generated message crates;
  • each image’s entry and the build root that compiles it: a cargo package when every node is Rust, a CMake project when any node is C or C++, a Zephyr application for a Zephyr board.

nros build then runs that host tool, so compiler errors are the compiler’s. nros build --dry-run prints the command for an image, and running it yourself works too. Where each binary lands is What nros build Produces.

Customising an entry

The generated entry is one nros::main!(…) call, and the macro does a lot: it opens the executor at the size the image declares, registers every node in the launch file, and adds the lifecycle, parameter services and tiers the system asks for. Take the smallest step that does what you need:

You needUseEntry stays generated
another panic policy, build profile, Kconfig fragment or capabilityan [image.*] keyyes
one step before the runtime starts (open a device, check a calibration)before_bootyes
hardware setup every image on a board needs (clocks, DMA)the board’s init_hardware, in a board packageyes
startup none of the above can expressnros materializeno

before_boot names a function in one of the image’s node packages:

[image.linux]
board = "linux"
before_boot = "sensor_node::prepare"

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs
pub fn prepare() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    // open the device, check the calibration, wait for the peripheral
    Ok(())
}
}

The entry calls it first, before the board does anything, so nothing has booted when it runs: no executor, no session, and on bare metal no hardware setup yet. Returning Err("reason") stops the image with that reason. It works in Rust images only; a C or C++ image that sets it is refused, and so is an RTIC or Embassy board, whose framework owns the first statement. The worked example is image linux_rust_before_boot in examples/workspaces/features.

nros materialize is the last resort. It copies an image’s generated entry into src/<image>_entry/, and from then on nros build uses your copy and does not regenerate it:

$ nros build linux
$ nros materialize linux
wrote …/src/linux_entry

This entry is YOURS now — `nros build` will not regenerate it.

What you get is the same nros::main!(…) call inside its crate root. While you keep the macro, launch-file changes still reach the program; what you own is the shell around it. Replacing the macro with your own main means writing the boot, node registration, executor sizing and every capability yourself, and keeping them in step with the launch file by hand. Deleting src/<image>_entry/ returns the image to generation.

Coming from ROS 2

ROS 2nano-ros
ros2 pkg createnros new <pkg> inside the workspace; --to <bringup> adds its component row
colcon buildnros build (every default image) or nros build <image>
ros2 run <pkg> <exe>nros run <node>
ros2 launch <pkg> <file>nros run <bringup>:<image>; the launch file is compiled into the image

One image is one program, which runs its nodes in one process on one board. Several processes are several images.

Other languages

Nothing on this page is Rust-specific except the node’s source file. C and C++ node packages, and workspaces that mix languages, are C / C++ multi-node workspaces and Mixed-language workspaces. Role reference lists every field of the three roles.

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout: why every project is a workspace, why system.toml lives only in a bringup, and the target spellings nros run accepts.
  • RFC-0120: one resolver for every build road: why nros build prepares the build itself.

C / C++ multi-node workspaces

Growing your workspace describes the canonical node pkgs + bringup pkg + [image.*] shape against the Rust path (nros::node!(…) + nros::main!(launch = …)). This chapter shows the C and C++ path through the same shape, role-for-role.

The parity gap is closed. Same launch.xml, same package.xml, same system.toml, same workspace pkg-index — the only thing that changes language-side is the cmake-fn / macro surface.

TL;DR — side-by-side

RoleRustC / C++
Node pkglib.rs with nros::node!(MyNode), declared by a [[component]] row in the bringup’s system.tomlTalker.{hpp,cpp} with a configure(::rclcpp::Node&) component method (C++) / RCLC_C_COMPONENT (C); CMakeLists.txt calling nano_ros_auto_add_library + nros_components_register_node
Bringup pkgpackage.xml + system.toml, optionally launch/*.launch.xml (no Cargo.toml)identical (language-agnostic)
Image[image.linux] board = "linux" in the bringup’s system.tomlidentical (language-agnostic)
The entryGENERATED into build/<coord>/linux_entry/ — a Cargo.toml and a nros::main!(launch = "demo_bringup")GENERATED into build/<coord>/CMakeLists.txt — a nano_ros_add_executable(linux_entry BOARD … BRINGUP … LAUNCH … LANG cpp TYPED DEPLOY linux) call, plus the main TU the verb emits
Workspace rootnone — the generated entry’s own Cargo.toml is the cargo rootnone — the generated build/<coord>/CMakeLists.txt is the cmake root, calling nano_ros_workspace(WORKSPACE_ROOT … BACKEND zenoh PLATFORM posix SYSTEM demo_bringup SUBDIRS …)
Buildnros build linuxnros build linux
Runnros run linux (binary: build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/target/debug/linux_entry)nros run linux (binary: build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry)

The reference C++ workspace ships in-tree at examples/workspaces/cpp/. Copy the whole directory, rename the packages.

Workspace layout

Identical structure to the Rust template, swapping Cargo.toml → CMakeLists.txt inside each Node pkg — and, at the root, nothing at all:

my_ws/
├── .colcon_workspace             # tracked marker; there is no root build file
└── src/
    ├── talker_pkg/               # Node pkg (C++)
    │   ├── package.xml
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # nano_ros_auto_add_library + nros_components_register_node
    │   └── src/{Talker.hpp,Talker.cpp}
    ├── listener_pkg/             # Node pkg (C++)
    │   ├── package.xml
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt
    │   └── src/{Listener.hpp,Listener.cpp}
    └── demo_bringup/             # Bringup pkg (language-agnostic — copy/paste
        ├── package.xml           #          works between Rust and C++ workspaces)
        ├── system.toml           #          [system] + [[component]] + [image.*]
        └── launch/system.launch.xml

No entry package, and nothing at the root: a workspace is a directory of packages. nros build <image> writes a CMakeLists.txt and the entry’s nano_ros_add_executable(…) call into build/<coordinate>/, configures that into build/<coordinate>/cmake/, and builds — see What nros build generates. The exception is a Zephyr application, which keeps a package because west needs a real application directory.

The generated cmake root

You do not write this; nros build does, from the packages it discovered and the image it resolved. It is the cmake root — and it lives in build/<coordinate>/, not at the workspace root, which is why its first argument says where the workspace actually is. It is worth reading once, because everything below happens inside it:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_ws LANGUAGES C CXX)
find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED COMPONENTS workspace)

nano_ros_workspace(
    WORKSPACE_ROOT "../.."               # this file lives in build/<coord>/
    BACKEND        zenoh                 # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
    PLATFORM       "posix"
    SYSTEM         demo_bringup
    ORDER_FROM_DEPENDS
    SUBDIRS        "../../src/talker_pkg"
                   "../../src/listener_pkg"
)

nano_ros_workspace() does the heavy lifting in one call:

  1. Sets NROS_PLATFORM=posix + NROS_RMW=zenoh.
  2. add_subdirectory(<nano-ros>) once at root scope (so per-pkg subdirs don’t collide on re-include).
  3. include(NanoRosNodeRegister.cmake) + include(NanoRosEntry.cmake) once.
  4. add_subdirectory(<each member>) for each SUBDIRS entry.

Subdir CMakeLists begin with the dual call:

nano_ros_workspace_pkg_guard()  # no-op inside a workspace; bootstraps standalone solo

— the cmake equivalent of cargo [workspace] discipline. Every member compiles standalone (with -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<sdk-root>, or a cmake --preset from nros setup presets) or as part of the workspace; the per-pkg CMakeLists doesn’t change between modes.

Node pkg

A typed component — no main(). The pkg ships a class with a configure(::rclcpp::Node&) method that creates real entities (a Publisher, a Timer) and binds member callbacks by identity (member-fn-pointer template param, no string callback name, no interpreter). The generated entry constructs the object and calls configure(node); the executor dispatches the callbacks.

# src/talker_pkg/CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(talker_pkg LANGUAGES C CXX)
nano_ros_workspace_pkg_guard()
nros_find_interfaces(LANGUAGE CPP SKIP_INSTALL)

# The ament shape — the library owns the sources, the register
# owns the identity (keyword parity with rclcpp_components_register_node).
# Interface deps (std_msgs__nano_ros_cpp) are wired automatically.
nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.cpp)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN talker_pkg::Talker      # any qualified name — upstream namespaces port verbatim
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure)               # this walkthrough uses the configure(Node&) shape

Telling the build what the component creates

NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS, the subscriber slots and the arena are const sizes compiled into nros-node before a component TU is compiled, while a typed component wires itself in its CONSTRUCTOR, at runtime. Nothing the macros emit can supply those sizes — it exists only after linking. So somebody has to state what the image creates, ahead of the build.

That statement is a contract sidecar beside the launch file, not something in this CMakeLists. <stem>.contract.yaml next to <stem>.launch.xml in the bringup package:

# src/demo_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml
version: 1

nodes:
  talker:
    paths:
      on_timer:                                  # a path with a timer trigger
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }       # IS the periodic callback
        output: [chatter]
    pub:
      chatter: {}
  listener:
    sub:
      chatter: {}

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/Int32
    pub: [talker/chatter]
    sub: [listener/chatter]

nodes: keys are LOCAL endpoint names — an absolute path there is concatenated onto the node’s FQN and matches no topic. topics:, services: and actions: wire those endpoints to absolute names and carry the type. paths: is where timers live: the model records a path with no input as the periodic callback.

A bringup with no launch/ writes the same file at <bringup>/system.contract.yaml, beside its system.toml. Its launch file is generated from the [[component]] rows, so there is no launch/ directory to put a sidecar in; the build carries this one to where the resolver looks. That is how a one-node bringup states its QoS — and stating it is worth real memory: one sub: { chatter: { qos: { history: keep_last, depth: 1 } } } row takes a one-node Rust listener on Linux from 273,802 to 172,298 bytes of static RAM, because the zenoh backend then sizes its payload pools for the one sample the image keeps instead of the four it might have.

The name you write must be the name the code registers, ABSOLUTELY. A contract states RESOLVED names; a call site writing "chatter" or a node the launch file remaps is one the build cannot match with certainty, so it refuses that endpoint by name and the image keeps its configured pools rather than being sized from a guess.

The build folds it into the resolved SystemModel, and the entry passes that model to the sizing automatically — nothing here takes an argument for it.

The derivation is all-or-nothing per image: a component the contract does not describe makes that image derive nothing and keep its configured NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS. A count taken over only the components that answered is smaller than the image needs, and a short MAX_CBS fails entity creation at boot — so “some of them” is refused rather than guessed at.

Note that a publisher is inventoried but claims no callback slot, so the entity count and the derived MAX_CBS are legitimately different numbers.

Earlier versions stated this per component, as nano_ros_node_register(ENTITIES ...). That keyword is retired and now fails with a pointer here. It was a list beside the code with nothing comparing the two, and on the safety island one of them declared six subscriptions for a node that creates seven: every pool derived from it was short by one, and the eleventh subscription failed at boot with a transport error that named nothing.

The census: the contract checked against the code

Since the contract is still a statement beside the code, a CROSS image (any image whose board is not linux) checks it before it configures: the host image generated from the same launch file is run once in census mode — it constructs every component against a recording backend, writes what they created, and exits without spinning or dialling a router — and the configure compares that census with the contract row by row. An endpoint the code creates and the contract omits refuses as missing-in-contract (not waivable: it is the short pool); one the contract declares and the code never creates refuses as phantom (waivable per row under [census.waive]).

The configure never builds the native image itself. nros build does: before it plans a cross image, it takes that image’s census. Taking it does nothing when there is nothing to do — a model with no contract, or a census that still matches the code (freshness is by content: touching a file changes nothing, adding a subscription does). A build driven some other way (a hand-run west build or cmake) with no census, or a stale one, REFUSES at configure and prints the command that takes it; running nros build once for the image takes it too. A bringup that wants the old behaviour writes [census] on_missing = "warn" / on_stale = "warn" in its system.toml, and gets a CMake WARNING instead.

// src/talker_pkg/include/talker_pkg/Talker.hpp
#pragma once
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs.hpp"

namespace talker_pkg {

class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::Int32> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int count_ = 0;

    void on_tick();  // real body; bound via &Talker::on_tick (no name)

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

}  // namespace talker_pkg

// src/talker_pkg/src/Talker.cpp
#include "talker_pkg/Talker.hpp"

namespace talker_pkg {

void Talker::on_tick() {
    std_msgs::msg::Int32 m;
    m.data = count_++;
    (void)pub_.publish(m);
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    // Member-fn-pointer-as-template-param → no-alloc trampoline; `this` is ctx.
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}

}  // namespace talker_pkg

The generated entry constructs Talker in static storage and calls configure(node) on the real executor — the same component model the Rust nros::node!(Talker) + the C RCLC_C_COMPONENT paths use, so C++, C, and Rust Node pkgs interoperate in one launch graph.

Scaffold a C++ Node pkg with:

nros new my_talker --lang cpp --template talker --to demo_bringup

From the workspace root this adds src/my_talker/ (class my_talker::Talker) and, with --to, its [[component]] row in demo_bringup.

Bringup pkg

Language-agnostic — copy verbatim from the bringup steps. package.xml + system.toml, and launch/system.launch.xml when you want one (without it the launch file is generated from the [[component]] rows). No Cargo.toml, no CMakeLists.txt. Stock ROS 2 launch.xml from nav2 / Autoware / turtlebot3 pastes in modulo unsupported tags.

<!-- src/demo_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml -->
<launch>
  <node pkg="talker_pkg" exec="talker" name="talker"/>
  <node pkg="listener_pkg" exec="listener" name="listener"/>
</launch>

The image, and the entry it generates

Declare the program you want in the bringup’s system.toml —

[image_defaults]
rmw = "zenoh"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

— and nros build linux emits this into that generated root. BOARD and DEPLOY come from the resolved image, so a generated entry cannot disagree with the board it was generated for; there is no SOURCES, because the verb generates the translation unit carrying main:

nano_ros_add_executable(linux_entry
    BOARD   native
    BRINGUP "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../../src/demo_bringup"
    LAUNCH  default
    LANG    cpp
    TYPED
    DEPLOY  native)

At configure time the cmake fn asks the nros CLI to generate the entry and emits ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/linux_entry_nros_main_generated.cpp (the canonical int main() body that constructs each launch node’s component + calls configure(node) on the real executor via LinuxBoard::run_components), appends it to the target’s sources, and auto-links every <pkg>_<exec>_component static lib the launch XML named.

BRINGUP + LAUNCH — name your input, never the artifact

BRINGUP + LAUNCH name your input: the Bringup package and a launch selector. The build resolves that into a SystemModel build artifact (under <ws>/build/nros/models/<bringup>/ — never committed; gate check-no-tracked-models), and the entry bakes from it, so the same artifact drives the Linux runtime and every embedded image (contracts, tiers, QoS never drift). MODEL — naming the resolved artifact file directly — is a deprecated expert override; the two are mutually exclusive, and a committed model is banned outright.

nros build re-resolves the model whenever the bringup’s launch XML or system.toml changed; with nothing changed it costs a digest comparison.

Writing the entry yourself

One case needs a hand-written one: startup the declarations cannot express. nros materialize <bringup>:<image> writes the generated entry out to src/<image>_entry/, as a package with nano_ros_entry(NAME … ) in its own CMakeLists.txt, and nros build then leaves it alone. (A Rust image has a smaller step first, [image.*] before_boot; the C/C++ entry has no such hook yet.)

A Zephyr image is not a second case. nros build and nros run generate its Zephyr application under build/ from the image, like every other entry, and nros materialize is the way to own it there too (the Zephyr chapter).

The materialized package needs no source file of its own: the cmake function generates the whole body (the main above), so its CMakeLists.txt names the bringup and launch file and nothing else.

Build + boot

nros build linux
nros run linux        # or run ./build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry

nros build prepares everything first: the generated message bindings, the SystemModel (via the pinned nros-launch-resolve helper), and build/<coordinate>/CMakeLists.txt. Then it configures and builds. Each piece is redone only when its inputs changed, so there is no step to run before it. The coordinate directory names what it contains: platform, RMW, board.

Driving cmake yourself against that generated root — build/<coordinate>/CMakeLists.txt, never a file at the workspace root — still works. Run nros configure first to write it without building; nros build linux --dry-run prints the exact cmake lines.

The build produces:

  • src/talker_pkg/libtalker_pkg_talker_component.a — the Node pkg static lib (_component is the compatibility target suffix).
  • src/listener_pkg/liblistener_pkg_listener_component.a — ditto.
  • linux_entry — the image’s executable, with the generated int main() + register-call sequence + Board boot stub linked in.

cmake configure is incremental — pinned CMAKE_CONFIGURE_DEPENDS on every file the entry generator reads (depfile from the CLI), so any launch.xml / package.xml / Node pkg edit re-runs codegen.

What runs where

ConcernLives in
Node entities + real callbacksNode pkg configure(::rclcpp::Node&)
Topology + launch args + per-target deployBringup pkg system.toml + launch/*.launch.xml
int main() + executor init + spinGenerated TU emitted by the entry’s cmake fn
Board + RMW selectionThe image’s board and rmw, which become the generated BOARD / DEPLOY args

Same partition as the Rust track — the only thing that changes is the syntax the user types into the two package roles.

C / C++ scaffolding via nros new

CommandOutput
nros new <ws> --board <board> --template talker --lang cppA new workspace: a C++ Node pkg <x>_node plus its Bringup pkg <x>_node_bringup with one image
nros new <name> --lang cpp --template talker [--to <bringup>]Inside a workspace: a C++ Node pkg under src/; --to adds its [[component]] row
nros new system <name>_bringup --components a,bBringup pkg (language-agnostic — works for both Rust and C++ workspaces)
nros materialize <bringup>:<image>The image’s generated entry (for a Zephyr image, its west application) copied to src/<image>_entry/ as a package you own

--lang c scaffolds a pure-C Node pkg the same way. Pure-C and mixed C/C++ workspace examples live under examples/workspaces.

See also

  • examples/workspaces/cpp/ — the canonical reference workspace, all C++: the talker, listener, service and action Node pkgs, and one bringup per behaviour (pubsub_bringup, service_bringup, action_bringup) whose image rows are the paired examples, one per platform and role.
  • C++ Entry-pkg roadmap doc — full landing order + acceptance bar.
  • Multi-node workspace layout design §11 — LOCKED canonical shape (Bringup + Node + Entry).

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups in the language workspaces.

Mixed-language workspace

Languages mix per package, not per file. A bringup’s [[component]] row names a package and a class whatever language implements it, and node packages are linked through a C ABI register trampoline, so one image can compose node packages written in C, C++ and Rust. The workspace shape does not change with the language. The native reference shape is:

  • C Node pkgs for C code you want to keep in C.
  • C++ and Rust Node pkgs beside them, in the same workspace.
  • One Bringup pkg with the normal ROS 2 launch XML and the [image.*] rows.

The mixed workspace is in examples/workspaces/mixed/. For a pure-C workspace, use examples/workspaces/c/.

Layout

my_ws/
├── .colcon_workspace             # tracked marker; there is no root build file
└── src/
    ├── c_talker_pkg/             # C Node pkg
    ├── cpp_listener_pkg/         # C++ Node pkg
    ├── rust_heartbeat_pkg/       # Rust Node pkg
    └── demo_bringup/             # package.xml + system.toml (+ launch/)

Mixed is not a special case. The driver is chosen by the board, and cmake wins whenever the package graph crosses languages — corrosion makes cargo consumable from cmake, and nothing makes cmake consumable from cargo. So a mixed workspace builds exactly like the C++ one:

$ cd my_mixed_ws              # e.g. a copy of examples/workspaces/mixed
$ source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # the first build generates messages from ROS 2
$ nros build linux
$ nros run linux

The first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later shells need not source ROS 2.

nros build writes a CMakeLists.txt — a nano_ros_workspace(…) call listing the discovered packages, plus one nano_ros_add_executable(…) per image on that coordinate — into build/<coordinate>/, configures it into build/<coordinate>/cmake/, and builds. That generated file is the cmake root; the workspace itself has no build file at all, and neither the root nor the entry is yours to write.

C Node pkg

A C Node pkg is a typed component: no main(). It defines a state struct + a configure(node, executor, self) function and exports the C-ABI factory/configure seam via RCLC_C_COMPONENT(StateT, configure_fn) — the typed Entry creates the node and runs configure on the real executor. The component is written against the C API: configure receives an rcl_node_t * and an rclc_executor_t * over the entry’s own node and executor, so a C and a C++ component in one image share both.

# std_msgs is declared in package.xml (`<depend>std_msgs</depend>`), which
# generates its C bindings for this package.
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)
nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN c_talker_pkg::Talker
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED)

#include <stdint.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>
#include <std_msgs/msg/int32.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
} c_talker_pkg_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    c_talker_pkg_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, c_talker_pkg_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    std_msgs__msg__Int32 msg = {.data = self->count};
    (void)rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL);
    self->count++;
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                  c_talker_pkg_t* self) {
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, Int32), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(c_talker_pkg_t, talker_configure)

nano_ros_auto_add_library injects NROS_PKG_NAME (language inferred from the sources), so RCLC_C_COMPONENT exports the __nros_c_component_<pkg>_{create,configure} seam the typed Entry calls — interoperable with C++ configure(Node&) and Rust nros::node! components in one launch graph.

The image

Nothing about the language mix reaches the image declaration. One row per program, in src/demo_bringup/system.toml:

[image_defaults]
rmw = "zenoh"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The launch file (here an authored launch/system.launch.xml; without one, the file generated from the [[component]] rows) names the Node pkgs, whatever they are written in:

<launch>
  <node pkg="c_talker_pkg" exec="talker" name="talker"/>
  <node pkg="cpp_listener_pkg" exec="listener" name="listener"/>
</launch>

From that pair, nros build emits this into the generated root. LANG follows the workspace’s own sources; BOARD and DEPLOY come from the resolved image, so a generated entry cannot disagree with the board it was generated for. There is no SOURCES, because the verb generates the translation unit carrying main:

nano_ros_add_executable(linux_entry
    BOARD   native
    BRINGUP "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../../src/demo_bringup"
    LAUNCH  default
    LANG    cpp
    TYPED
    DEPLOY  native)

The generated entry translation unit calls each package’s __nros_component_<pkg>_register symbol and the CMake sidecar links the matching static libraries. The symbol keeps the legacy component spelling for ABI compatibility; the user-facing package role is still Node pkg.

Note there is no MODEL here. The resolved system is a build artifact, resolved from the launch file under build/. Naming it in a build file is a deprecated expert override, and committing one is refused.

Per-language notes

Rust. A Rust node package is a library crate ending in nros::node!(YourNode). Its message crates and the settings cargo needs (the board’s target triple, link flags, environment) are generated under build/, never beside your packages, and nros build prepares them before it hands off. In a mixed workspace the Rust packages are built through CMake (by corrosion), so their compiler errors are still cargo’s.

C. A C node package is the configure component shape above, built by the same per-package CMake as C++. Its message bindings are generated during the CMake configure.

The RMW is spelled once, whatever the languages: [system] rmw in the bringup’s system.toml, or rmw = on one [image.*] block when one image differs. The features each package needs follow from it, so switching backend is a one-word edit: Switching RMW in Config.

Scaffolding

Inside a workspace, nros new adds a node package in the language you name, and --to adds its component row to a bringup:

nros new c_talker_pkg --lang c --template talker --to demo_bringup
nros new cpp_listener_pkg --lang cpp --template listener --to demo_bringup
nros new rust_heartbeat_pkg --lang rust --to demo_bringup

To start from a complete mixed tree, copy examples/workspaces/mixed/ out instead. It runs a C talker, a C++ listener, a Rust heartbeat, and C and C++ service and action pairs, composed into one program per image.

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout

Role Reference: Node pkgs, Bringup pkgs, and Images

A nano-ros workspace has two kinds of package you write, and a third thing that is not a package at all:

  • Node pkg — a reusable, board-agnostic node library. Defines what a node does (publishers, subscribers, timers, services, actions) and registers itself with the nros::node!(T) macro. No main(), no board pick, no deploy config. (Previously called a component package; renamed to Node pkg to match ROS 2 composable-node naming.)
  • Bringup pkg — pure declarative: owns the launch topology and the images built from it. Contains a package.xml and system.toml, and optionally launch/*.launch.xml, config/ and boards/. No Cargo.toml, no compiled code. Named <system>_bringup.
  • Image — a row, not a directory. [image.<id>] in that system.toml names a board, a launch file, and a backend; nros build <id> generates the entry package from it, under build/, and hands off to cargo / cmake / west / idf.py. The workspace itself has no root build file.

The split exists because a node’s logic is portable across boards, but boot + transport + deploy config is not. One Node pkg is reused across native POSIX, FreeRTOS, and Zephyr by adding an [image.*] row per target — never a package per target.

Every project is a workspace, including one with a single node: one node package plus one bringup package, which nros new <ws> --board <board> writes together. system.toml lives only in a bringup; one beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt is refused. See One node, one bringup below.

Node pkg

A Node pkg is a normal Rust library (or C++ static library) with a few nano-ros-specific knobs:

src/talker_pkg/
├── Cargo.toml          # [lib] crate-type = ["rlib", "staticlib"] — Rust-toolchain
│                       # facts only; the node is declared by a [[component]] row
│                       # in the bringup's system.toml
├── package.xml         # ROS 2 package manifest (<exec_depend> etc.)
├── src/
│   └── lib.rs          # impl Component for Talker { … }
│                       # nros::node!(Talker);
└── launch/             # OPTIONAL — per-node launch fragment
    └── talker.launch.xml

src/lib.rs declares the user class, implements Node + ExecutableNode (init / on_callback / optional tick), and ends with nros::node!(Talker); to emit the register trampoline. Codegen owns the spin loop — your code only describes what the node has and what its callbacks do.

Key rules:

  • No fn main(). A Node pkg builds as rlib + staticlib and is linked into the entry the build generates. Codegen synthesises the spin driver; you never hand-write one.
  • class must be a namespace-qualified C++ name. The old prefix rule (class starting with the pkg dir name) is retired — pkg on the [[component]] row is the identity authority, so upstream namespaces (autoware::x::Node) port verbatim. nros check still rejects an unqualified class.
  • C++ / C analogue: nano_ros_auto_add_library(<lib> STATIC <srcs>) + nros_components_register_node(<lib> PLUGIN … EXECUTABLE …) (rclcpp_components keyword parity) + a typed component in the source — C++ a configure(::rclcpp::Node&) method, C a RCLC_C_COMPONENT(StateT, configure_fn) seam. Same conceptual shape, no Cargo.toml.
  • package.xml is mandatory. Even pure-Rust Node pkgs ship one — <exec_depend> lines drive ROS 2 launch discovery when the system runs through ros2 launch outside the nano-ros toolchain.

Bringup pkg

A Bringup pkg is pure declarative — it owns the launch topology and the image table, and contains no compiled code:

src/demo_bringup/
├── package.xml          # <name>demo_bringup</name>, <exec_depend> per node
├── system.toml          # [system] + [[component]] + [image.<id>] + [host.<name>] (+ [[domain]]/[[bridge]])
├── launch/
│   └── system.launch.xml   # ROS 2 launch schema, verbatim
├── boards/                 # optional — per-board RTOS overlays (prj.conf, *.overlay, sdkconfig.defaults)
└── config/                 # optional — params.yaml, etc.

No Cargo.toml, no CMakeLists.txt, no src/. Naming convention <system>_bringup (alias <system>_launch), matching nav2 / Autoware / turtlebot3. [image.*] lives here, so it is the package that gives a workspace images to build. (A workspace with no bringup at all still builds — every package in dependency order, each into its own build/<pkg>/, which is colcon’s default; there are simply no images.)

launch/ is optional. A bringup without it gets a launch file generated from its [[component]] rows, written to build/nros/launch/<bringup>/launch/system.launch.xml and resolved exactly as an authored one. Adding launch/system.launch.xml replaces it. A bringup with neither launch/ nor a [[component]] row is refused.

launch/*.launch.xml is the ROS 2 launch schema verbatim — <launch>, <arg>, <node>, <param>, <remap>, <group>, <include>, with $(find <pkg>) / $(var) / $(env) substitutions. Stock nav2/Autoware XML pastes in and Just Works; Python .launch.py files are resolved by the build too (the launch resolver executes them). See Add a launch file.

Image

An image is one buildable program: a topology, a board, and a backend. It is a table row in the Bringup pkg’s system.toml:

[image_defaults]           # base every block folds over
rmw = "zenoh"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
panic = "own"

[image.linux_robot1]
board  = "linux"
launch = "multihost.launch.xml"
args   = { host = "robot1" }
KeyMeaning
boardnano-ros board id, resolved through packages/boards/board-support.toml (which supplies the rustc triple, the platform, and the framework’s own board string)
launchLaunch file relative to the Bringup pkg. Absent ⇒ [system] default_launch
argsLaunch arguments bound at resolve time — how an image selects one machine out of a multi-host launch tree
rmwBackend for this image. Absent ⇒ [system] rmw
panicPanic policy: platform | halt | own
profilecargo / CMake build profile name
os_configLayer-1 files, in order: Zephyr prj-*.conf / .overlay fragments, or a board network file (.toml). os_config is read as its old alias
variantFramework build-variant name (Zephyr prj_<buildtype>.conf)
featuresCapability axes for this image, over [system]’s list
serdes, ros_editionSerialization provider and ROS edition. Absent ⇒ the [system] value

Folding is per-key: scalars are replaced by the specific block, args merges, os_config and features concatenate base-then-specific. [system] default_images = ["native"] is what a bare nros build builds; without it, nros build lists the declared images and stops.

Build one, all, or ask what would run:

$ nros build linux
$ nros build --all
$ nros build linux --dry-run     # print the handoff, run nothing

[image.<id>] says what is BUILT; [host.<name>] says where nodes RUN — which machine a node runs on. An image needs no host and a host needs no image The old [deploy.<id>] table conflated the two and is refused by name, pointing at both.

The generated entry

The entry package is derived from (launch, args, board) and generated: a workspace contains no entry packages. On the cargo driver it lands at <ws>/build/<coordinate>/<image_id>_entry/, and that package’s own Cargo.toml is the cargo root: with no workspace root to walk up to, a generated entry is simply a package with path dependencies. On the cmake driver the generated <ws>/build/<coordinate>/CMakeLists.txt is the root, and emits a nano_ros_add_executable(…) call per image on that coordinate. Beside a cargo entry sits nros-cargo.toml, the per-image settings file the build writes — triple, link flags, [env], patch rows — which cargo reads through --config. nros build writes all of it before it hands off; nros configure writes it without building, for an IDE or a hand-run cargo.

All of it is build output under build/, and none of it is written beside your source: no root build file, no .cargo/config.toml beside a package. The tracked marker that a directory is a workspace root is .colcon_workspace.

Three parts, all derivable, which is why adding a board adds a descriptor rather than a branch in the emitter:

partderived from
the no_std / no_main shellthe board’s entry_kind
board boilerplate (use panic_semihosting as _;, esp_app_desc!())the board descriptor’s entry.crate_root_extra
nros::main!(launch = …, args = …)the image

The generated entry calls nros::main! rather than an expanded form on purpose: the macro reads the launch XML at expansion time, so adding a node to the launch file is picked up by the next compile with nothing regenerated.

nros::main!() forms

// RETIRED: `nros::main!(board = X)` is a compile error — an
// out-of-tree board states `[package.metadata.nros.board] type` instead.
nros::main!(launch = "demo_bringup");                   // multi-node (CANONICAL): the bringup's default launch
nros::main!(launch = "demo_bringup:sim.launch.xml");    // multi-node, a named launch file
nros::main!(                                            // multi-host: per-host slice via launch args
    launch = "demo_bringup:multihost.launch.xml",
    args = [("host", "robot1")],
);
// DEPRECATED (expert override): name the resolved model ARTIFACT directly
// instead of the input — skips the freshness contract; bake-time warning.
nros::main!(model = "demo_bringup");

The proc-macro reads the launch file at compile time, walks the workspace pkg-index for each <node pkg=…> entry, and expands to a fn main() that delegates to <Board as BoardEntry>::run(...), dispatching one <pkg>::register(runtime)? call per launch row.

The launch forms take <bringup>[:<file>] against launch/<file>.launch.xml + system.toml [system] default_launch; the build resolves that input into a SystemModel under <ws>/build/nros/models/<bringup>/ (a build artifact — never committed; gate check-no-tracked-models), and the macro bakes from it. launch and model are mutually exclusive.

Escape hatches, smallest first: an [image.*] key (panic, profile, os_config, features); before_boot = "<pkg>::<fn>" for one step before the runtime starts; the board’s init_hardware for hardware every image on that board needs; and, last, nros materialize <bringup>:<image>, which copies the generated entry to src/<image_id>_entry/ for you to own. See Customising an entry.

C++ / C analogue: the generated cmake root emits one nano_ros_add_executable(<name> BOARD … BRINGUP … LAUNCH … LANG … TYPED DEPLOY …) per image — no SOURCES, because the verb generates the translation unit that carries main. nano_ros_entry(NAME … LANG … BRINGUP … LAUNCH …) is the hand-written spelling, which you meet only in an entry you have taken over with nros materialize. MODEL on either is the deprecated artifact-naming override, mirroring the macro. Metadata flows through ${BUILD}/nros-metadata.json rather than a sidecar TOML.

Zephyr images

A Zephyr image is no exception. Its entry is a Zephyr application — the app target find_package(Zephyr) creates — and nros build generates it under build/ like any other entry, then runs west build on it. The board comes from the image’s board key, a nano-ros board id, which the descriptor it resolves to turns into the string west build -b receives.

What Zephyr adds is authored Kconfig (prj.conf, prj-<rmw>.conf, boards/*.overlay), which nothing derives. It lives in the Bringup pkg, one directory per board, and the image names the fragments it adds:

src/demo_bringup/boards/native_sim_native_64/
├── prj.conf
└── prj-zenoh.conf      # named by [image.<id>] os_config

A change the image keys cannot express goes through the same last resort as on every other platform: nros materialize <bringup>:<image> writes the generated application into src/<image_id>_entry/ as a package you own. The Zephyr chapter has the details.

Migrating off a hand-written entry is a deletion. nros build keeps src/<image_id>_entry/ when it carries a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt; remove the directory and the next build generates its replacement. Move the board / launch / RMW / panic facts to the [image.*] row and the RTOS overlays to the Bringup pkg’s boards/<board>/ first.

Workspace shape

my_ws/
├── .colcon_workspace   # tracked marker; there is no root Cargo.toml / CMakeLists.txt
└── src/
    ├── talker_pkg/         # Node pkg (lib, nros::node!)
    ├── listener_pkg/       # Node pkg
    └── demo_bringup/       # Bringup pkg (declarative; system.toml carries [image.*])

nros build <image> writes the generated message crates and the per-image build settings, generates the entry and its build root under build/, and runs the platform’s own tool; there is no step to run before it. nros plan takes the sole bringup when there is one, or you name it: nros plan demo_bringup.

examples/workspaces/{c,cpp,rust,mixed}/ are the four canonical workspaces — each is exactly this shape, Zephyr images included.

The language workspaces (rust, c, cpp) also hold the paired examples, one bringup per behaviour: pubsub_bringup (talker and listener), service_bringup (service server and client) and action_bringup (action server and client). Each holds one [image.<platform>_<role>] row per platform and role, with a _<rmw> suffix for any RMW other than zenoh, so every role stays its own image. Run one role by naming its bringup and image:

nros run pubsub_bringup:linux_listener

A variant with different code (a callback-style client, an RTIC listener) is its own node package with its own image row; a configuration (a serial link, a custom transport) is an image row that states the knob over the same packages.

One node, one bringup

The smallest project is still this shape, with one node package. The scaffold writes both packages:

nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker

host_ws/
└── src/
    ├── host_node/              # Node pkg: package.xml, Cargo.toml (a library), src/lib.rs
    └── host_node_bringup/      # Bringup pkg: package.xml and system.toml; no launch/

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

There is no src/main.rs and no selection or board crate in the node’s manifest: the image’s generated entry names the board. nros run host_node builds and runs it. The node spelling means “the bringup whose only node is host_node, with its only image”; once the bringup has a second node or a second image, name <bringup>:<image> instead. --lang c or --lang cpp writes a C or C++ node package; the bringup is the same.

The copy-out example for each platform and language, examples/<platform>/<lang>/talker/, has this shape too: one node package and one bringup with no launch/, so its launch file is generated. It is the project to start from; the paired examples are the image rows above.

nros build (and nros configure) refuse a system.toml in a directory that also holds a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt, and the message says where to move it. Projects that own their build and have no system.toml (a CMake add_subdirectory consumer, a vendor tree, a Zephyr application you build with west) are not affected: see Build as a CMake subdirectory, Vendored tree and A Zephyr App You Build with West.

Quick reference

You want…Use
Reusable node logic, board-independentNode pkg (nros::node!())
A runnable program: N nodes on one boardAn [image.<id>] row + nros build <id>
A single-node projectnros new <ws> --board <board> --template <t>: one Node pkg plus its Bringup pkg
Same nodes on multiple boardsOne Node pkg set + one [image.*] row per board
Launch topology + the image tableBringup pkg (declarative — the one package a workspace must have)
A Zephyr imageAn [image.<id>] row with a Zephyr board; nros build generates the application
One step before the runtime starts[image.<id>] before_boot = "<pkg>::<fn>"
Startup the declarations cannot expressnros materialize <bringup>:<image>, then edit src/<image>_entry/
Board hardware bringupBoard trait family (see porting chapter)

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0065: colcon-like workspace builder (images, hosts, generated entries)
  • RFC-0098: generated leaf build config
  • RFC-0057: ament-parity component registration
  • RFC-0060: launch toolchain
  • RFC-0026: example directory layout
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups, and the single-node talker kept per platform and language.

Message Binding Generation

nros uses generated Rust bindings for ROS 2 message types. nros build generates no_std compatible bindings from each package’s package.xml dependencies before it builds (nros configure does that step alone, and nros interface generate rust the codegen alone).

Overview

The binding generator is part of the nros CLI and provides:

  • Pure Rust, no_std compatible output using heapless types
  • Automatic dependency resolution through your ROS 2 install’s ament index
  • the [patch.crates-io] rows that point the nano-ros runtime crates at the SDK root, written into the image’s generated build settings

Prerequisites

  1. package.xml in each node package - Declares ROS interface dependencies

    <?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>my_package</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>My nros package</description>
  <maintainer email="dev@example.com">Developer</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>
  <depend>std_msgs</depend>
  <depend>geometry_msgs</depend>
  <export>
    <build_type>ament_cargo</build_type>
  </export>
</package>

  2. nros tool built + on PATH

    Install a release; install.sh puts nros in ~/.nros/bin:

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

    See Installation for the full walkthrough.

  3. A ROS 2 install, sourced for the first build

    The bindings are generated from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, std_msgs included, so the generated layouts and type hashes match the ROS 2 nodes you talk to. Source it before the first nros build, nros run or nros configure of a project:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

    That configure records the prefix (AMENT_PREFIX_PATH) in the project, and later configures reuse it, so later shells need not source ROS. With neither, configure refuses and names this step. A project whose packages depend on no message package at all needs no ROS 2.

Workflow

Step 1: Create package.xml

Declare your ROS interface dependencies in <depend> tags:

<depend>std_msgs</depend>      <!-- For std_msgs::msg::Int32, String, etc. -->
<depend>example_interfaces</depend>  <!-- For service types -->

Step 2: Build

cd my_ws
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # the first build of the workspace only
nros build

Before it builds, this will:

  1. Parse package.xml to find dependencies
  2. Resolve transitive dependencies through the ament index
  3. Filter to interface packages (those with msg/srv/action)
  4. Generate bindings into the workspace’s generated/ directory
  5. Resolve the bringup’s launch file into the system model
  6. Write each image’s build settings under build/, carrying the board’s triple and flags, the resolved pool budgets, and the [patch.crates-io] rows for the nano-ros runtime crates

Each step is redone only when its inputs changed. To run them without building (before opening the workspace in an IDE, for instance), use nros configure. nros interface generate rust is the codegen-only step underneath — steps 1–4 and nothing else — and is useful when you want bindings without a workspace.

Step 3: there is no step 3 — package.xml is the dependency list

A generated message crate is a path dependency on its own directory, and nros build writes that row for you, before it plans: one per <depend> / <build_depend> / <exec_depend> that names a message package, tagged # nros-managed:

[dependencies]
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed
example_interfaces = { path = "../../generated/example_interfaces", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

So adding a message package is one edit — the <depend> — exactly as on the C/C++ road, and deleting the <depend> deletes the row on the next build. A row without the tag is yours: the build never edits or removes it, so deleting the tag is how you take a row over. The nros row is not managed — it carries a feature choice that is yours to make.

Never name a message crate by registry version (std_msgs = "*"): those crates are generated per host from your ament install, they are not published, and a bare name resolves against the public crates.io instead.

The nano-ros runtime crates are the other case — nros, nros-board-<board>, the backends — and they are registry-named with version = "*", because the build writes the [patch.crates-io] rows that redirect them into the nano-ros SDK root.

Why msg crates are RMW-agnostic

Generated msg crates carry only the wire-format data type — no backend-specific code, no per-RMW Cargo feature. A user manifest is the plain pair:

[dependencies]
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed
nros     = { version = "*" }

Transport choice and message schema are orthogonal concerns and the manifest reflects that. (Which backend you actually get is [system] rmw in the bringup’s system.toml, not a feature you pick here — see Switching RMW in Config.) This matches upstream rclcpp + rclrs, which both ship msg packages RMW-agnostic and let the RMW pick which descriptor representation it wants at runtime.

For DDS-based backends that need a per-type descriptor on the wire (Cyclone DDS today), the nros-rmw-cyclonedds shim builds those descriptors lazily on first pub/sub for a given message type, walks the static field schema exposed by nros-serdes (the Message trait with const TYPE_NAME + const FIELDS), and caches the result in a bounded no_std registry. No per-msg-pkg backend code is required.

The registry is bounded by the NROS_CYCLONEDDS_MAX_TYPES sizing knob.

Where the nano-ros sources come from

A project uses the SDK root the nros binary belongs to — a release’s own share/nano-ros — so a plain nros build works anywhere. To name a different SDK root, pass it:

nros build --nano-ros-path <sdk-root>

The build then writes the [patch.crates-io] rows into each image’s generated settings, pointing each nros* requirement at a directory in the SDK root. Nothing about the location is baked into a tracked file, so moving the workspace, or installing another release, needs no edit: the next build re-points it.

Use in code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std_msgs::msg::Int32;
use example_interfaces::srv::{AddTwoInts, AddTwoIntsRequest, AddTwoIntsResponse};

let msg = Int32 { data: 42 };
}

Command Options

nros interface generate rust is the codegen step alone — it writes bindings and nothing else:

nros interface generate rust [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --manifest <PATH>         Path to package.xml [default: package.xml]
  -o, --output <DIR>            Output directory [default: generated]
      --ros-edition <EDITION>   humble | iron | jazzy [default: humble]
      --codegen-config <PATH>   Explicit per-field capacity config (nros-codegen.toml)
      --rename <OLD=NEW>        Rename a generated package
      --force                   Overwrite existing bindings
  -v, --verbose                 Enable verbose output

It also still accepts --generate-config / --nano-ros-path / --nano-ros-git, which write a .cargo/config.toml beside a package by hand. Those are the old shape and are not the path to use: nros build writes the patches into the generated settings instead, where they are regenerated rather than committed.

Generated Output Structure

my_ws/
├── src/
│   ├── my_node/
│   │   ├── package.xml      # Your dependency declarations
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml       # Your package manifest (a library)
│   │   └── src/lib.rs       # Your code using generated types
│   └── my_node_bringup/
│       ├── package.xml
│       └── system.toml      # Board, RMW, components
├── generated/               # Generated bindings (do not edit)
│   ├── std_msgs/
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml
│   │   └── src/
│   │       ├── lib.rs       # #![no_std]
│   │       └── msg/
│   │           ├── mod.rs
│   │           └── int32.rs
│   └── builtin_interfaces/  # Transitive dependency
│       └── ...
└── build/                   # Build output (do not commit)
    └── …/<image>_entry/     # each image's generated entry and its cargo settings, incl. the patches

Generated Code Features

no_std by default:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
pub mod msg;
}

std feature for optional std support:

[features]
default = []
std = ["nros-core/std", "nros-serdes/std"]

heapless types for embedded:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct String {
    pub data: heapless::String<256>,
}

pub struct Arrays {
    pub data: heapless::Vec<i32, 64>,
}
}

Service types with Request/Response:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AddTwoInts;
pub struct AddTwoIntsRequest { pub a: i64, pub b: i64 }
pub struct AddTwoIntsResponse { pub sum: i64 }

impl RosService for AddTwoInts {
    type Request = AddTwoIntsRequest;
    type Reply = AddTwoIntsResponse;
}
}
