A timestamp message gets SecNanosecMsg, so Time::to_ros_msg() can return it:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl nros_core::SecNanosecMsg for Time {
    fn from_sec_nanosec(sec: i32, nanosec: u32) -> Self { Self { sec, nanosec } }
}
}

Emitted for every message whose field set is exactly { int32 sec, uint32 nanosec } — builtin_interfaces/msg/Time, its Duration twin, and any message of yours with that shape. It is what makes the call a publisher writes work:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
msg.header.stamp = node.now().to_ros_msg();
}

nros-core cannot name a message type — every generated crate depends on it, and your message crates are generated from your packages — so the conversion is implemented on the generated side and the trait is the seam. The C++ side spells the same thing as a template (node.now().to_msg(msg.header.stamp)); Rust has no structural bound, so it needs the named trait. There is no Result: nros’s Time already is { sec, nanosec }, so nothing can fail. (rclrs returns Result<_, TryFromIntError> because its Time is i64 nanoseconds; a ported t.to_ros_msg()? will not compile here, and deleting the ? is the fix.)

Examples

Each example on GitHub is a workspace that carries its own bringup and resolves on its own, so it builds wherever it lives. Build each from its own root:

cd my_talker_ws && nros build
cd my_service_client_ws && nros build

Regenerating Bindings

To regenerate after ROS package updates or dependency changes:

nros interface generate rust --force

Where the definitions come from

nros build reads message definitions from the ROS 2 install you sourced (or the one the project’s first configure recorded), through AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. The release carries copies of a few standard packages, but they only fill gaps under a ROS 2 install, never stand in for one: with no prefix set and none recorded, configure refuses rather than build from them, because they would silently fix a ROS 2 distro and the types would stop matching a peer on another one. A message package in your own workspace shadows the installed one of the same name.

Troubleshooting

“AMENT_PREFIX_PATH is unset and no configure of … has recorded one to reuse”

  • This shell has not sourced ROS 2, and this project has never been configured from one that had. Run source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash (or your overlay’s install/setup.bash), then build again.

“Package ‘X’ not found in ament index or bundled interfaces”

  • Source the ROS 2 environment: source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
  • Check package is installed: ros2 pkg list | grep X
  • Install if missing: sudo apt install ros-humble-X

Build errors with generated code

  • Regenerate with --force flag
  • Check nros crate compatibility

Which CMake spelling (one table)

Five codegen entry points exist in the CMake surface. They are NOT interchangeable spellings of one thing — each serves one audience, and two are back-compat only. Pick by what you are doing:

You are…UseNotes
Consuming an existing msg package from an app/node pkgfind_package(<pkg> REQUIRED)The recommended default. The smart Find-stub resolves the package through the 3-layer search (workspace → ament → bundled) and generates bindings on the fly. Zero codegen calls in your file.
Defining msgs in a message packagerosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME} msg/… DEPENDENCIES …)Recommended — the stock ROS shape, intercepted by nano-ros. Your msg pkg carries zero nano-ros-specific lines and cross-builds under colcon unchanged.
Defining msgs and you want the nano-ros verb explicitly (or C bindings)nano_ros_generate_interfaces(<name> <files…> [LANGUAGE C|CPP] [DEPENDENCIES …])The ament-shape alias. Defaults to LANGUAGE CPP like rosidl — pass LANGUAGE C for C.
Building a workspace root with several msg pkgsnros_workspace_interfaces() after set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH …/src)Bulk-builds every workspace msg pkg in topological order; one line, no per-pkg add_subdirectory.
Generating this pkg’s package.xml dependencies (no find_package flow)nros_find_interfaces([LANGUAGE C|CPP] [SKIP_INSTALL])Consume-by-manifest: resolves the transitive interface closure of your own package.xml. Used by the workspace node pkgs. Defaults LANGUAGE CPP.
—nros_generate_interfaces(<target> <files…>)Deprecated for new code. The low-level generator everything above routes through; direct calls are back-compat only.

C Code Generation (CMake)

nano_ros_generate_interfaces(… LANGUAGE C) generates C bindings for .msg, .srv, and .action files (the function defaults to C++ — the LANGUAGE C argument is what makes it the C generator). It uses a bundled codegen library — no external nros binary needed.

Prerequisites

nano_ros_generate_interfaces() becomes available automatically once the consumer’s CMakeLists.txt invokes add_subdirectory(nano-ros). The codegen tool ships inside the in-tree nros CLI binary (packages/cli/target/release/nros; the old nros-codegen submodule is retired); cmake auto-resolves it from PATH / packages/cli/target/release/ / the transitional ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/. No separate build step.

Usage

For a complete example, see the features workspace, examples/workspaces/features: its custom_msgs package defines a message, and c_reading_talker_pkg and c_reading_listener_pkg use the generated C bindings. The custom-message feature demo is a node package there, with its own image row.

Design background

  • RFC-0067: environment-invariant message dependency identity
  • RFC-0048: CMake ament consumption
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. Feature demos as node packages of the features workspace.

Configuration Guide

nano-ros config is language-agnostic and has one home per concern — no setting lives in two places, and nothing is merged across files. The authored surfaces are a universal system.toml, package.xml, and launch XML — plus Kconfig for the embedded build (Zephyr). Cargo.toml and CMakeLists.txt carry language-toolchain facts and nothing else. This guide covers what each file owns, the network identity an embedded image bakes at build time, and the standalone config.toml for hand-written no_std apps.

Retired surfaces you may find in old material: the nros.toml per-package/workspace file (rejected by the CLI), the old config.toml [network]/[zenoh]/[scheduling] schema, every [package.metadata.nros.{node,entry,component,deploy.*}] table, and the package.xml <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> tuple. The last two moved into system.toml; readers refuse them rather than reading them. The design records are listed under Design background.

One home per concern

FileOwnsPer
system.tomlEverything about the deployment — [system] (RMW, domain, capability axes like features = ["param_services"] and the [safety] block, tiers), [[component]] (what runs, and its entities), and one [image.<id>] per target (board, locator, the board network file holding its address, os_config = ["board-net.toml"], and how it runs, is flashed and is watched, [image.<id>.run], [image.<id>.flash], [image.<id>.console]). One schema for Rust, C and C++, and the same file whether the project is one package or a workspace.package, or bringup pkg
Cargo.tomlRust toolchain facts only: crate, language deps, the RMW feature menu (rmw-zenoh/rmw-cyclonedds/rmw-xrce) the generated entry selects from. No board, no target triple, no deploy block.Rust project
CMakeLists.txtC/C++ toolchain facts only: targets and language deps, via find_package(nano_ros) + nano_ros_add_executable / nano_ros_auto_add_library + nros_components_register_node (nano_ros_node_register remains as the compat spelling) / nano_ros_entry. No platform, board or RMW set().C/C++ project
build/<image>/nros-cargo.tomlGENERATED, never edited — every cargo setting the board choice implies: [build] target, [target.*] runner and rustflags, the cross compiler, the derived pool sizes as [env], the nano-ros profiles, and the [patch.crates-io] rows that resolve nano-ros’s registry-style names into your checkout. Written by nros build (or nros configure alone), passed to cargo with --config.image
package.xmlROS package identity + msg <depend>s (codegen input for nros interface generate)all
config.toml (standalone)Hand-written no_std direct-mode apps only — [node] / [eth0] / [network.<name>], compile-baked via Config::from_toml(include_str!(…)). Apps that use nros::main!() / codegen do not have one — they use [image.<id>] above.embedded single-node app (no codegen)

Boundary rule. If a knob changes what is compiled/linked as a language choice — a C++ standard, an RMW feature the entry may select — it lives in the build file. Everything else about the deployment (components, board, domain, RMW, and the physical link + router address a target boots with) lives in system.toml. Nothing a board implies is authored anywhere: it is derived from the board descriptor into the generated settings file.

Config home by language × scale

This table has one answer in all four cells, which is the point of it:

One nodeSeveral nodes
Rustsystem.toml in the bringup pkgsystem.toml in the bringup pkg
C / C++system.toml in the bringup pkgsystem.toml in the bringup pkg

A system.toml beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt is refused, so the resolver has one input shape and you have one thing to learn. Resolution is a fixed precedence ladder, not a merge: explicit CLI/build flag (--rmw / -DNROS_*) > system.toml ([image.<id>] > [system]) > the board descriptor’s [knobs] > built-in default. nros config show prints the resolved effective config with per-value provenance; nros check flags values still sourced from legacy files.

For the multi-RMW runtime topic-forwarding bridge (a separate file/feature), see nros-bridge.toml.

Embedded image config (codegen apps — the common case)

An embedded app built through nros::main!() (Rust) or the CMake entry codegen (C/C++) declares its board and its network + router config per image, in system.toml. The toolchain bakes it at compile time — there is no config file on the device and nothing is parsed at runtime. The file is the same in both languages:

# system.toml (e.g. examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker)
[system]
name      = "qemu_bsp_talker"
rmw       = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg      = "qemu_bsp_talker"
class    = "qemu_bsp_talker::Talker"
name     = "talker"
dispatch = "deferred"          # optional: callbacks hand off to a ring

[image.mps2-an385-baremetal]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:10500"
net     = { eth0 = { network = "qemu", host = 10 } }

The [image.<id>] key is the image’s name — what you pass to nros build <image> — and board is the only thing that has to change to retarget it. nros::main!() bakes the image’s network fields into a DeployOverlay that BoardEntry::run_with_deploy applies onto the board’s boot Config; the C/C++ entry codegen bakes the same values into its generated glue. Nothing is written in Cargo.toml, in package.xml or on a cmake command line.

Networks and addresses

An image’s address is a layer-1 fact: the operating system owns the network device. On Linux that is the kernel; on Zephyr and NuttX it is their own configuration (Kconfig, devicetree, defconfig); on a board where nano-ros is the OS (the reference FreeRTOS, ThreadX and bare-metal boards) it is the board package, through a small board network file the image names with os_config — one table per interface:

[image.talker]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]

# board-net.toml, beside system.toml
[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10                      # 10.0.2.10 on QEMU's network

qemu is built in: QEMU’s own user-mode (SLIRP) network, 10.0.2.0/24 with gateway and router host 10.0.2.2. Every -nic user makes a private copy of it, so two images on qemu never meet. Any other network is defined in the board network file beside the interface on it, and the image states its router as its own locator:

# board-net-sensor.toml
[eth0]
network = "lab"
address = "192.168.50.20"

[network.lab]                  # e.g. a switch or a Linux bridge with boards on it
subnet  = "192.168.50.0/24"
gateway = "192.168.50.1"

[image.sensor]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
os_config = ["board-net-sensor.toml"]
locator = "tcp/192.168.50.1:7447"

Two images on one network each define it in their own file, and the files must agree: one network has one subnet, gateway and lease policy.

Per interface:

  • network defaults to the board’s (qemu on every QEMU board), so [eth0] host = 10 is enough there.
  • host is the last octet within the network’s subnet; address is the full IPv4, or "dhcp" on a network with dhcp = true (and a board whose interface runs a DHCP client). An interface on qemu that states no address takes 10.0.2.15, the address a plain -nic user guest picks.
  • mac is optional. Left out, it is derived from the board interface’s mac_prefix and the system, image, network and interface names, so two images never share one by accident.
  • The gateway and netmask come from the network, so an interface never states them.
  • An image dials its own locator, else [system] locator. On a network other than qemu one of the two must be stated.

A board may have several interfaces. An image addresses each on its own network, one table each: [eth0], [eth1].

These fail the build, naming the image (and, for a duplicate, both images):

  • an address outside its subnet, equal to the gateway, or on a network no file defines;
  • two images with the same static address, or the same MAC, on one network other than qemu, or two files defining one network differently;
  • a board network file on a board whose network belongs to the host operating system (linux, freertos-posix, threadx-linux), or on a board that declares no interfaces (Zephyr boards take their address from Kconfig);
  • the retired spellings, each refused naming its new home: [network.<name>] and [image.<id>.net.<if>] in system.toml, and the flat ip / gateway / netmask keys on [image.<id>].

The board’s half is [board.net] in its descriptor: stack (who owns the network: host, os or board), links, network (its default network) and interfaces, each a kind (eth0 = "ethernet") or a table (eth0 = { kind = "ethernet", mac_prefix = "52:54:00", dhcp = true }). A board states no address: [board.net] ip / mac are refused.

The resolved answer for an image is written to build/nros/net/<image>.toml (under the workspace) and reaches the firmware as NROS_IMAGE_NET.

How an emulated image joins its network is a fact about how it is RUN, not built, so it has its own table, read only by the QEMU launchers and the test harness:

[image.sensor.run]
nic = { bridge = "qemu-br" }   # QEMU: -nic bridge,br=qemu-br,…

nic is "slirp" (QEMU’s own user-mode network, the default on qemu), { bridge = "<dev>" } or { tap = "<dev>" } on the host, and applies to the image’s first interface. An image on any other network with no nic is physical only, and launching it under QEMU is refused. nros run passes the -nic value to QEMU when it boots the image.

The same goes for a board that is flashed and watched on a serial port: the board’s descriptor states its flasher and console ([board.flash], [board.console], see the descriptor section), and an image overrides any key of them in its own tables:

[image.lab.flash]
command = "pyocd flash -t stm32f767zi {hex}"     # replaces the board's method
prepare = [{ say = "Set BOOT0 to 1, then press RESET", wait_for = "usb:0483:df11" }]

[image.lab.console]
baud = 921600                                     # kind stays the board's

Both are checked when system.toml is read (an unknown key, wait_for event or {placeholder} is refused) and are read by nros flash and nros monitor.

The middleware’s own file

How a session finds its peers — which router to dial, which endpoints to listen on — is the middleware’s own configuration, written in its own language. A bringup ships it beside its system.toml, and it applies to every image of that backend:

BackendFileThe same document ROS 2 reads as
zenohrmw/zenoh.json5ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI
CycloneDDSrmw/cyclonedds.xmlCYCLONEDDS_URI
 
// rmw/zenoh.json5
{
  mode: "client",
  connect: { endpoints: ["tcp/192.168.50.1:7447"] },
}

zenoh-pico has no json5 parser, so the build reads the file on the host, lowers each key to a zenoh-pico session property and bakes the result into the image. A key zenoh-pico cannot take is refused, naming the key — never dropped. With a file, the file IS the wiring: the image’s connect list replaces the default router, and an image that also states a locator is refused (a [system] locator is simply not used). On a hosted build ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI replaces the baked file at run time, whole, as it does for rmw_zenoh.

The flat rmw/zenoh.conf list (key = value) is retired and refused, naming the json5 that replaced it.

The names above are the default. To ship a different file — one per site, one for a QEMU run and one for the lab — name it:

[system]
rmw_config = "rmw/zenoh-lab.json5"      # every image's default session

[image.qemu]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
rmw_config = "rmw/zenoh-qemu.json5"     # this image's own

A named file that does not exist is refused. XRCE has no file format; its endpoint is the image’s locator.

A bridge opens one session per [[domain]], and each domain names its own file, so one image can speak to a CAN zenoh network and an Ethernet DDS one with two documents:

[[domain]]
name = "zen"
rmw = "zenoh"
config = "rmw/zenoh-zen.json5"

[[domain]]
name = "dds"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
id = 5
config = "rmw/cyclonedds-dds.xml"

[[bridge]]
name = "gw"
from = "zenoh:zen"
to = "cyclonedds:dds"

A domain with a config states no locator (the file is its wiring), and a domain config that no [[bridge]] opens is refused, since nothing would read it. An image overrides one domain’s file with a table, rmw_config = { dds = "rmw/cyclonedds-lab.xml" }: the build then writes that image its own bridge configuration (nros-bridge.<image>.toml) beside the bringup’s, and the other images keep the shared one. At run time ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI and CYCLONEDDS_URI still replace a hosted bridge’s files, and NROS_BRIDGE_<SESSION>_LOCATOR replaces that session’s file whole.

Per-image build knobs

A build knob that one image needs, and that its board does not state, goes in [image.<id>.knobs.<group>]. The table has the same shape as a board descriptor’s [knobs.<group>]:

[image.zephyr_xrce.knobs.zephyr]
heap_size = 98304            # NROS_ZEPHYR_HEAP_SIZE

[image.zephyr_xrce.knobs.xrce]
max_subscribers = 1          # NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS (-1, the default, derives it)

[image.linux.knobs.log]
max_level = "warn"           # NROS_LOG_MAX_LEVEL (a level name or 0..6)

[image.linux.knobs.executor]
max_cbs = 16                 # NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS

Each key is a row of the knob registry (packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-build/knobs.toml). The key is the row’s board key where it has one (executor.max_cbs, zenoh.tx.batch); otherwise it is the env name without NROS_, split at the first _ (NROS_ZEPHYR_HEAP_SIZE becomes zephyr.heap_size). An unknown key, a value of the wrong type or a value outside the knob’s range stops nros build with an error that names the key. The value reaches the build exactly as the knob’s NROS_* variable would: through the generated cargo config on the cargo road, the image env file on the cmake road, and the Kconfig defaults on west. It sits on the image rung (above the board, below an exported variable).

[image.<id>] env = { NAME = "value" } still carries an application’s own build variable, a name the registry does not hold. An env row that names a registry knob is an error that names its knobs spelling (release 0.6.0 accepted it with a warning).

RT/stack/priority for a single-node embedded app comes from board-crate Cargo features + Kconfig (prj*.conf on Zephyr), not a config file. Multi-node RT is declared in system.toml ([tasks.<name>.<rtos>] + [[node_overrides]]).

Periodic timers after a stall

If a tier is preempted past several periods of a periodic timer, the backlog is coalesced, not replayed: the timer fires ONCE and the missed periods are counted. Phase is preserved, so activations stay on the declared cadence grid rather than drifting by each stall. This is the default (TimerOverrunPolicy::Skip) and matches rclcpp and Zephyr’s k_timer.

Replay is available — Executor::set_timer_overrun_policy(.., CatchUp) — and is the right choice for a counter or accumulator, where every tick carries state that must not be lost. It is the wrong choice for a control loop: the replayed activations compute with stale inputs and emit a burst of commands inside a fraction of a period.

Overruns are counted per timer (Executor::timer_overruns) and reported as the timer-overrun-runtime violation. Watch that rather than a publish-rate check: under CatchUp a replayed burst makes the achieved rate look nominal — measured 100.03 Hz on a declared 100 Hz loop while the tier was stalling for up to 611 ms at a time — so a rate monitor reports health during exactly the fault it exists to catch. The rationale and the measurements are in the execution-model design record (see Design background).

Timer periods are microseconds throughout, including across the C ABI.

Standalone config.toml — hand-written no_std apps (no codegen)

A hand-written single-node app that writes its own main() and bypasses nros::main!() keeps its net config in a file, not hardcoded in Rust: a sibling config.toml, compile-baked with include_str! and parsed by the board crate’s Config::from_toml. It is the board package’s network file — the same [<interface>] / [network.<name>] shape an image’s os_config file has — plus a [node] table that stands in for the session a system.toml would declare.

# config.toml

[node]
domain_id = 0                    # ROS 2 domain ID (0–232)
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"    # the router the firmware dials

[eth0]
network = "qemu"                 # built in: QEMU user-mode, 10.0.2.0/24, gateway 10.0.2.2
host = 10                        # the address within that network → 10.0.2.10
# address = "10.0.2.10"          # or the whole address
mac = "02:00:00:00:00:00"

# A network of your own: name it on the interface instead of `qemu`.
# [network.lab]
# subnet = "192.168.50.0/24"
# gateway = "192.168.50.1"

[node.rt.freertos]               # FreeRTOS boards: raw task priorities; omit for defaults
app_priority = 3
zenoh_read_priority = 4

A board reads its own facts from the interface table: a serial link’s [uart0] baud, ThreadX Linux’s host veth as [eth0] device. One interface is brought up; a direct-mode board takes no DHCP lease, so state the address.

A file in the retired shape ([[transport]] with ip, gateway and locator) panics at boot naming the new spelling, rather than booting on the board’s defaults: ip = "10.0.2.10/24" + gateway = "10.0.2.2" is [eth0] network = "qemu" + host = 10, and the locator moves to [node].

Consumption (compile-baked; no filesystem on the target):

use nros_board_mps2_an385::{Config, run};

fn main() -> ! {
    run(Config::from_toml(include_str!("../config.toml")), |config| {
        let exec = ExecutorConfig::new(config.zenoh_locator)
            .domain_id(config.domain_id);
        // ...
    })
}

Pick by whether the app uses codegen: nros::main!() app → system.toml [image.<id>] (above); hand-written main() → config.toml.

Files that used to carry configuration and no longer do are listed in Retired configuration files.

Build-time environment variables

Read during cargo build (by build.rs). Export them in your shell.

SDK paths

You normally set none of these. nros setup puts each vendored source tree in the shared store, and every build finds it through one ladder: an environment override, then your project’s [sources] in system.toml, then a checkout submodule you are editing, then the store, then the checkout’s own copy. Ask where a tree came from with nros locate <name> --why.

Set one of these variables only to build against a tree of your own:

VariableTree
FREERTOS_DIR / LWIP_DIRFreeRTOS kernel / lwIP
THREADX_DIR / NETX_DIRThreadX / NetX Duo
NUTTX_DIR / NUTTX_APPS_DIRNuttX RTOS / apps
CYCLONEDDS_SOURCE_DIRCyclone DDS source

For a tree that belongs to one project, prefer [sources] <name> = "<path>" in its system.toml (project-relative) over an exported variable, which every build in that shell inherits.

FREERTOS_PORT, FREERTOS_CONFIG_DIR, THREADX_CONFIG_DIR and NETX_CONFIG_DIR are not yours to set: they are facts about the board, stated in its nros-board.toml and carried to the build from there.

Buffer-tuning vars (ZPICO_*, XRCE_*, NROS_*) are optional — see the Environment Variables Reference.

Binary-size knobs (embedded)

On a constrained MCU, two build-time env vars — carried in the image’s generated build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml [env], like the other NROS_* tuning, and set there from the board descriptor’s [knobs] or from your own environment — shed the parts a brokered client doesn’t need:

VariableDefaultEffect
NROS_LINK_IPonNROS_LINK_IP=0 on a serial-only node drops the IP link layer — zenoh-pico’s TCP/UDP link C (Z_FEATURE_LINK_TCP/UDP=0) and (with --gc-sections) the smoltcp platform impl. Serial link stays.
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_SOCKETS / NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_UDP_SOCKETS4 / 2Sized for DDS RTPS (3 UDP/participant). A zenoh/XRCE client multiplexes everything over one session → set both to 1 to drop the spare socket buffers (≈8 KB each).
NROS_HEAP_SIZEper-platform-crate (64 KB nros-platform-mps2-an385, 32 KB nros-platform-stm32f4)Decimal bytes for the bare-metal static heap. The defaults are generous; size to the RMW’s working set (table below). E.g. NROS_HEAP_SIZE = "24576" on a zenoh-pico node cut the mps2-an385 .data 66 → 25 KB (−41 KB).

Static-heap sizing by backend (bare-metal FreeListHeap, set via NROS_HEAP_SIZE):

BackendPeak working setRecommended heapNotes
zenoh-pico (TCP)~16 KB24–32 KB (≈2× for fragmentation)peer middleware; alloc-based session/buffers
zenoh-pico (serial)lighter than TCP16–24 KBno TCP link buffers; verified running at 16 KB
XRCE (Micro-XRCE-DDS)~3 KB (micro-ROS figure)~8 KBstatic pools, discovery offloaded to the agent — the RAM-minimal backend; a measured bare-metal XRCE figure is pending an example (no bare-metal XRCE example ships yet — XRCE bare-metal needs a custom-transport injection)

stm32f4 (thumbv7em-eabihf, cortex-m4) ¹ethernetzenoh-picorelease186.9 KB13.7 KB123.0 KB136.7 KB
stm32f4 ¹ethernetzenoh-picosize138.1 KB13.7 KB123.0 KB136.7 KB
mps2-an385-freertos (cortex-m3 + lwIP, RTOS-reused stack)ethernet (lwIP)zenoh-picorelease240.6 KB10.7 KB3.3 MB3.3 MB
mps2-an385-baremetal (serial)serial (custom XRCE transport)XRCEsize, heap 24 KB, tight XRCE pools60.3 KB25.2 KB (heap 24 KB)8.8 KB~34 KB
micro-ROS reference (XRCE)serialXRCE-DDS Client-Os< 75 KB—~3 KB~3 KB peak

¹ The two stm32f4 rows are historical: the board crates left the tree in a later cleanup, so nothing in-tree reproduces them today. They stay because a Cortex-M4F-with-its-own-stack data point is still the closest published figure for that class, and deleting a measurement is worse than dating it. The chip crate the numbers were built against (nros-platform-stm32f4) is still here.

The XRCE row uses tight per-session XRCE pools — delivered through the image’s generated [env] and read by nros-rmw-xrce-cffi’s build.rs: NROS_XRCE_STREAM_HISTORY=4, NROS_XRCE_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU=512, NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=1, NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_SERVERS=1, NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_CLIENTS=1, NROS_XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH=1, NROS_XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE=256. Vendor defaults grow xrce_session_state_t to ~390 KB (which wouldn’t fit a 24 KB heap); these knobs drop it to ~12 KB. Defaults are unchanged for hosted / non-tight-RAM consumers — the env vars are pure opt-in.

How to read this:

  • The size profile (opt-s) shrinks .text by ~10–26 % with .bss/.data unchanged (opt-level doesn’t touch static buffers — those are the env knobs above). -Oz is not used — on smoltcp examples it grows .bss +24 KB by defeating opt-3’s per-socket dead-buffer DCE (see the size-tuning notes above).
  • Switching ethernet → serial sheds ~50 KB text + ~42 KB .data (no smoltcp stack, no IP link C, tuned heap) — the structural lever.
  • FreeRTOS + lwIP cells .bss is dominated by lwIP’s heap + FreeRTOS task stacks (3 MB is the configured headroom, not nano-ros overhead).
  • The micro-ROS / XRCE row is a reference, not a nano-ros measurement — no bare-metal XRCE example ships yet (needs a custom-transport injection); the path to parity is XRCE + serial + static pools.

Size-minimal recipe

Smallest measured nano-ros configuration today (mps2-an385-baremetal serial talker, 116 KB text / 101 KB RAM):

# Cargo.toml
[profile.size]
inherits = "release"
opt-level = "s"
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
debug = false
strip = true

The gc-sections and link-script rustflags are not yours to write — they are the board’s, and they arrive in the generated build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml [target.<triple>] block:

# build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml — GENERATED, shown for orientation
[target.thumbv7m-none-eabi]
rustflags = [
    "-C", "link-arg=-Tlink.x",
    "-C", "link-arg=--gc-sections",   # 204.8 — strip unreferenced fns/data
]

The knobs that are yours are ordinary environment variables. The generated [env] never uses force, so a value you set in the calling environment wins:

NROS_LINK_IP=0 \
ZPICO_NO_SMOLTCP=1 \
NROS_HEAP_SIZE=131072 \
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_SOCKETS=1 \
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_UDP_SOCKETS=1 \
    nros build <image>

The profile is not one of them: name it on the image, as [image.<id>] profile = "size", and nros build passes it to whichever tool it drives.

NROS_LINK_IP=0 drops zenoh-pico’s TCP/UDP link C and ZPICO_NO_SMOLTCP=1 skips the smoltcp glue on bare-metal. On the heap floor: the per-entry executor backing is a single ~75 KB allocation, so a nros::main! image needs ≥128 KB (the board default) — the older 24 KB “zenoh-pico working set” figure OOMs at boot. HEAP is .bss (no flash cost); shrink below the default only on a non-nros::main! direct-mode image with a measured smaller peak. A knob you always want for a board belongs in that board’s descriptor [knobs], not on every command line.

nros new --platform baremetal already scaffolds the [profile.size] shape.

The deeper RAM win waits on XRCE on bare-metal (the ~3 KB-class client + static pools, with discovery offloaded to the agent) — tracked separately; zenoh-pico’s SUBSCRIBER_BUFFERS + alloc-based session are what keep this row’s .bss ~76 KB.

Cargo features (which RMW/platform is linked)

Features select the linked RMW backend, platform, and ROS edition. The system.toml rmw ([image.<id>], else [system]) picks which linked backend is active — the two are different layers (link vs run). Matrix + mutual-exclusion rules: Platform Model.

[dependencies]
nros = { path = "…/nros", default-features = false, features = [
    "rmw-cffi",            # generic C-vtable runtime registry
    "platform-bare-metal", # or platform-{freertos,nuttx,threadx,zephyr,posix}
    "ros-humble",          # or ros-iron
    "std", "alloc",        # optional, target-dependent
] }
# Exactly one RMW backend crate; its registration runs before main:
nros-rmw-zenoh = { path = "…/nros-rmw-zenoh", features = ["platform-bare-metal", "link-tcp", "ros-humble"] }
# …or nros-rmw-xrce-cffi / the cyclonedds CMake backend

Runtime environment (native host only)

On the native host build, ExecutorConfig::from_env() reads at process start (embedded targets bake their config at build time instead):

VariableDescriptionDefault
ROS_DOMAIN_IDROS 2 domain ID0
NROS_LOCATORRouter addresstcp/127.0.0.1:7447
NROS_SESSION_MODEclient / peerclient
ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATE*TLS CA cert (path / base64)(none)

By deployment scenario

ScenarioConfig sourceCargo featuresNotes
Desktop (POSIX)env (ExecutorConfig::from_env())rmw-cffi, platform-posix, std + zenoh deprun the router locally (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd, ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false')
QEMU bare-metalsystem.toml [image.<id>] ip/mac/gateway/locatorrmw-cffi, platform-bare-metal, ros-humble + zenohTAP/slirp bridge
FreeRTOS hardware[image.<id>] + board features (RT)…, platform-freertos, …FREERTOS_DIR/LWIP_DIR
ESP32 WiFi[image.<id>] (ssid/password via build env)…, platform-bare-metal, …SSID/PASSWORD build env
Zephyr moduleKconfig overlay (prj-<rmw>.conf)(Kconfig → features)

Design background

  • RFC-0004: configuration and transports
  • RFC-0098: generated leaf build config
  • RFC-0031: RMW selection and lowering
  • RFC-0109: network config layers
  • RFC-0015: RTOS orchestration (multi-node RT tiers)
  • RFC-0002: RT execution model (timer overrun policy, § 4.4a)
  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact (source lookup ladder)

Build Profiles

nano-ros builds both C/C++ and Rust code on your behalf. You choose the optimization level once, and nano-ros propagates it to every crate and library it builds for you.

The image is where you say it, beside the board it is built for:

[image_defaults]
profile = "nros-relwithdebinfo"   # the base every image folds over

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.mps2]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
profile = "nros-minsizerel"       # this one is going on a board

nros build carries that through to whichever tool builds the image — the cargo profile flag on the cargo driver, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE on the cmake one. You do not repeat it on the command line, and you do not define the nros-* profiles anywhere: the build writes them into the image’s generated cargo settings file under build/ (build/linux/nros-cargo.toml for a single-package project), along with everything else the board choice implies.

From a CMake build type

When you drive CMake yourself — a single-package C or C++ project builds with its own CMake configure (from the CMakePresets.json that nros setup presets writes, which names the SDK root; nros build passes it for you), and needs no sync — set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE as you would in any CMake project. nano-ros derives the cargo profile for the Rust it builds underneath from it:

CMAKE_BUILD_TYPEcargo profilewhat it means
Debugdevdebuggable, minimal optimization
RelWithDebInfonros-relwithdebinfoopt-level 2, debug info, no LTO — the default
MinSizeRelnros-minsizerelopt-level "s", fat LTO — smallest images
Releasereleaseopt-level 3, fat LTO — fastest code
(unset)nros-relwithdebinfothe development default
 
cmake --preset linux -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
cmake --build build/linux

Your C/C++ sources get -Os from CMake as usual, and the Rust nano-ros builds for you gets --profile nros-minsizerel. You do not need to add anything to any Cargo.toml — nano-ros supplies the definition of its own nros-* profiles.

An unrecognized build type is an error rather than a guess, so a custom type never silently produces an optimization level you did not ask for.

Choosing the Rust profile separately

NROS_CARGO_PROFILE overrides the mapping when you want the two halves to differ — for example a small C/C++ image with debuggable Rust:

cmake --preset linux \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel -DNROS_CARGO_PROFILE=nros-relwithdebinfo

Using your own profile

Name any profile you like. When the name is not one of nano-ros’s nros-* profiles, you own the definition — nano-ros passes the name through and injects nothing, so your settings are authoritative:

[profile.prod]
inherits = "release"
opt-level = 3
lto = "fat"

Put that where cargo already looks for a profile: the package’s own Cargo.toml for a single-package project, or a .cargo/config.toml in a directory above your project. There is no workspace-root Cargo.toml to put it in — a nano-ros workspace has no root build file, and the cargo root is the generated entry under build/, which is regenerated on every build.

A config file is a first-class home for a profile, not a workaround: it is exactly how the nros-* presets reach cargo. An undefined name still fails the way it always did — error: profile 'prod' is not defined — while a name the generated settings file defines resolves and builds.

cmake --preset linux \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DNROS_CARGO_PROFILE=prod

Which profile is active?

A CMake configure prints it, with the target/ subdirectory it builds into:

-- nano-ros: cargo profile `nros-minsizerel` (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel) → target/nros-minsizerel

Notes for embedded targets

  • Images grow at the default. nros-relwithdebinfo trades size for build speed. For flashing to a constrained board, build MinSizeRel.
  • Two platforms pin their own profile regardless of what you choose, and will say so: NuttX Rust images (a codegen miscompile at lto = "off") and FreeRTOS QEMU images (the emulated Cortex-M3 misses zenoh-pico’s handshake window at low optimization).

What nros build Produces

nros build ends at an artifact and stops. It discovers your packages, resolves the image, checks the toolchain, generates the root build file and the entry, and then hands off to the native tool — cargo, cmake or west. The last stage is an exec, so the artifact is exactly the one that tool would have produced had you run it yourself.

This page answers the question the build does not: what are you holding, and where is it?

Running it: nros run and nros flash

nros run starts an image whose board is a host process or an emulator: it builds the image if it is stale, starts the router the image’s link needs, streams the console and stops everything when it ends (--expect <text> grades the console, --dry-run --why prints the plan it would execute). How a board is launched is stated once, in its descriptor’s [board.run], so the command nros build prints as its next step is the one nros run executes.

Real silicon is flashed, not run: nros run refuses a hardware image and names nros flash --monitor. nros flash builds the image if stale, runs the board’s human steps ([board.flash] prepare), flashes through the method its descriptor’s [board.flash] names (west, or a command template), and with --monitor watches the console on the same port; --expect <text> grades it as nros run does. nros monitor opens the console of a board that is already running. The port comes from --port, NROS_PORT, the bench file (nros bench scan) or the one attached device that matches the board.

The commands quoted below are the board tooling’s, reproduced here as a reference for a board no flash method covers yet.

There is also no install step: nros build never runs cmake --install, writes no install/ prefix and stages nothing. Whatever the native tool wrote in its own build tree is the deliverable.

Where it lands

Which tool builds an image is decided by its platform and by whether the workspace crosses languages:

platform / shapedriverthe artifact
Rust-only workspace, any non-Zephyr boardcargo<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<image>_entry/target/[<triple>/]<profile>/<image>_entry
any workspace containing C or C++cmake<ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/<image>_entry
a zephyr boardwest<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<bringup>__<image>_west/zephyr/zephyr.{elf,bin,exe}

The coordinate is the platform and the RMW — posix-zenoh, freertos-cyclonedds — plus, for CMake, the board, because CMake pins one compiler per configure and two boards on one platform would otherwise share a cache: posix-zenoh-linux, freertos-zenoh-mps2-an385-freertos.

Everything above is under build/, and that is the rule rather than a coincidence: a workspace has no root Cargo.toml and no root CMakeLists.txt. It is a directory of packages, like a colcon workspace, and every generated thing — the entry, the root build file, the cargo settings, the compiled output — lives in build/.

After a successful build nros build prints the artifact itself, and the board’s own command that runs or flashes it — never running either:

nros build: next for `c_talker_node_bringup:linux`:
  artifact: /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry
  run:
    /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry

What the run: (or flash) line is depends on the board: the binary for a host board, the board’s QEMU runner with the provisioned qemu-system-* for an emulated one, west build -d <dir> -t run / west flash -d <dir> for Zephyr. --dry-run and --check build nothing, so they print no such block.

One path the build also prints is easy to mistake for the binary:

nros build:   entry → …/build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry

That is the generated entry package — source that nano-ros wrote for you, under build/ because it is build output. The compiled program is elsewhere; see below.

cargo

Every image gets its own cargo settings file, build/<coordinate>/<entry>/nros-cargo.toml, and nros build points cargo at it:

cargo build --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml \
            --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml

That file states the image’s target-dir, so each image compiles into its own tree rather than sharing one target/. It also carries the board’s triple, linker flags and cross compiler, the resolved pool budgets as [env], the in-repo [patch.crates-io] rows, and the nros-* build profiles. It is generated on every build — read it, never edit it.

The artifact is the generated entry’s binary, inside that entry’s own target dir:

<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<image>_entry/target/[<triple>/]<profile-dir>/<image>_entry

The triple level appears whenever the board pins one — which it does in the generated [build] target, not on your command line.

A Linux image on Cyclone DDS, for instance, is build/posix-cyclonedds/linux_entry/target/debug/linux_entry.

<profile-dir> is debug unless the image declares [image.<id>] profile = …, in which case it is that profile’s directory (cargo’s rule: a profile builds into the directory of its own name, and dev into debug).

Next step: on a host board, run it. It is an ordinary executable.

./build/linux/target/debug/talker

For a QEMU board, the generated settings file also carries that board’s runner, so cargo run through the same --config boots the image — see Build Profiles for driving cargo yourself.

A multi-process zenoh example also needs a router; that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd, not something nano-ros ships — see Deployment Workflow and Install.

C, C++ and mixed workspaces (cmake)

CMake is chosen whenever the package graph contains anything that is not Rust, on the host and when cross-compiling alike. The generated root is <ws>/build/<coordinate>/CMakeLists.txt, it is configured into <ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/, and each image’s executable lands at the top of that directory:

<ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/<image>_entry

For example, examples/workspaces/c builds [image.linux] to build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry and its FreeRTOS image to build/freertos-zenoh-mps2-an385-freertos/cmake/freertos_entry. (Node packages also build their own executables, under cmake/pkg/<pkg>/<pkg>; the image is the one at the top level.)

The file has no extension in either case. On the host it is a host executable; for a cross board it is a statically linked ELF for that architecture — the FreeRTOS one above is ELF 32-bit LSB executable, ARM, EABI5, statically linked.

Next step:

  • host — run it directly.
  • QEMU — the ELF is what -kernel takes, with the machine and CPU your board’s guide names.
  • hardware — hand the ELF to your flasher (probe-rs, OpenOCD, a vendor tool). nano-ros has no opinion about which.

Zephyr (west)

nros build resolves your application and its overlays and runs west build from the workspace root with each image’s OWN build directory, <ws>/build/<coordinate>/<bringup>__<image>_west (west’s default, build/ under the cwd, would put every image of a workspace in one tree and refuse the second). Pass -- -d <dir> to choose another. Zephyr writes its image under zephyr/ inside it; for demo_bringup:zephyr on zenoh:

<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.elf   # always
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe   # native_sim — a host executable
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.bin   # cross targets — the raw image
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.map   # the link map

Which of .exe and .bin appears is Zephyr’s choice, not nano-ros’s: a native_sim build produces zephyr.exe, a Cortex-M build produces zephyr.bin.

Next step — Zephyr’s own verbs, against the image’s build directory (nros build prints whichever the board supports):

west build -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west -t run   # native_sim and emulated boards
west flash -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west          # hardware: the board's flash runner
./build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe    # native_sim: the same as -t run

The -d is not optional here: without it west uses build/ under the current directory, which is not where nros build put the image. west flash picks its runner from the board’s own board.cmake; nano-ros adds nothing to it.

Finding it yourself

When in doubt, ask the build what it is about to do. --dry-run prints the stages and the exact command, and performs no I/O:

nros build <image> --dry-run

The tool named in that command owns the output location, and its own documentation is the authority — which is the whole point of handing off rather than wrapping.

For the generation side of this — which root file is written, why the entry is derived rather than hand-written, and what the coordinate directory holds — see What nros build generates.

Integrating nano-ros into a Vendored Tree

This page is for the engineer whose company has its own source tree — a BSP, possibly a forked RTOS, an existing build system — and needs nano-ros to be part of it: pinned, reproducible, buildable offline, upgradable on their schedule. It collects the contracts the other chapters mention in passing into one place.

nano-ros is distributed as a release: one archive holding the nros CLI and the library source it builds against (the SDK root). Nothing is on crates.io and there is no prebuilt library. So “vendoring” nano-ros means pinning and mirroring a release, not copying its repository into your tree: your tree holds your packages and the bringup’s system.toml, and the release supplies everything else.

Pinning the release

Install the exact release your tree is tested against:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0-nros4
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"
nros pin 0.6.0-nros4          # record it in the project's nros-toolchain.toml

Rules that keep the pin trustworthy:

  • Pin a version, never “latest”. A moving target unships the pairing you tested.
  • Move the pin forward only. nros pin <newer> reports the codegen delta before it writes anything, so an upgrade that invalidates generated bindings warns first.
  • A release’s toolchain pins are decisions, not lags. Its nros-sdk-index.toml fixes the cross-compilers, the Cyclone DDS that ROS ships, a wire-stable zenoh-pico. Take what the release pinned.

What a fresh machine needs, in order

Three things, and the order matters:

  1. The nros CLI, installed as above. Nothing else works without it.
  2. ~/.nros/bin on PATH for interactive use. CI can skip this and call $NROS_HOME/bin/nros by absolute path.
  3. Provisioned toolchains. nros setup <board> --rmw <rmw> fetches the cross-compiler, emulator, and SDK sources for exactly that pair into the shared store at ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk. --dry-run prints the plan first. (The zenoh router is deliberately not provisioned — it comes from a ROS 2 install, ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd.)

Then nros build from the workspace root. It produces the message bindings and the build settings each [image.*] implies before it builds — see the next section.

The Rust side: everything the build reads is generated, outside your source tree

Two things a Rust node package needs are generated, not authored: the message crates, and every build setting the target implies — the triple, the runner, the link flags, the resolved [env], and the [patch.crates-io] table that resolves registry-style names (nros = { version = "*" }) to the release’s SDK root. You state the target once, as a board name in the bringup’s system.toml, and the build derives the rest:

[system]
name = "my_app"
rmw  = "cyclonedds"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

nros build writes those settings under build/, one set per [image.*] row, beside the entry it generates for that image and never beside your package, then hands them to cargo:

nros build            # or: nros build <image-id> for one image

A CI job that drives cargo itself prepares the same files first, without building, and runs the line nros build --dry-run prints:

nros configure                  # prepares every image, builds nothing
nros build <image-id> --dry-run # prints the cargo line, with its --config

nros configure is also the step to cache on: a run with nothing changed is a no-op, and its stamp under build/nros/configured/<image>/ holds the digest of every input that image read, which makes a CI cache key.

This is what makes a tree cheap to move: there is no .cargo/config.toml to copy, no include line whose relative path cannot resolve from your directory, and no table of absolute paths under version control to invalidate. After relocating the workspace or installing another release, the next build rewrites what is under build/ and touches nothing you track. Switching an image to another board is editing its one board = line.

Message dependencies are path deps that the build writes for you from package.xml’s <depend>s (std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false } # nros-managed); never registry-name a message crate — a bare std_msgs = "*" can resolve against the public crates.io.

The CMake side

Two entry points, both source-backed:

  • find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED) — the ament-shaped entry (nano_rosConfig.cmake at the SDK root). Located via -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<sdk-root>, which nros build and the CMakePresets nros setup presets writes pass; a raw cmake names it (no shell exports it). The SDK root is the installed release’s share/nano-ros (nros locate nano-ros prints it, for the version the project is pinned to).
  • add_subdirectory(<sdk-root> nano_ros) — the lower-level shape. See Build as a CMake subdirectory for the cache-variable table.

Corrosion is never fetched at configure time: without it in the SDK store the configure stops and names nros setup --tool corrosion. nros setup <board> installs it too, for every board with a CMake road.

Air-gapped / mirrored CI

The offline contract, all of it:

  1. Mirror the release asset. install.sh takes NROS_INSTALL_URL=<url> — a mirror, an air-gapped copy, a test server. The asset’s .sha256 must sit beside it and is still required.
  2. Mirror or pin the SDK index. nros setup reads the index the release ships; NROS_INDEX_URL=<url> fetches a newer one from a mirror, nros setup --index <path> uses a copy you already have, and NROS_OFFLINE=1 forbids the fetch, and also runs every cargo that nros starts with CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true, so dependencies come from cargo’s own cache (item 5). The index names every asset’s upstream ([tool.*], [source.*] sections); for a full mirror, rehost those URLs in your copy.
  3. Pre-install Corrosion: nros setup --tool corrosion (or the nros setup <board> you already run) stages it into the SDK store, where the configure finds it without the network. Verify the configure line prints nano-ros: Corrosion <ver> via <origin> — never infer the version from having run an installer.
  4. Cache NROS_HOME and the Rust toolchain. The CLI, the SDK root and every SDK nros setup fetches land under ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}; point NROS_HOME at a shared or cached location and it is reusable across jobs and machines of the same host triple. The Rust toolchain is the exception: nros setup installs it with rustup, which keeps it in ${RUSTUP_HOME:-~/.rustup} and ${CARGO_HOME:-~/.cargo} (the crate registry cache too). Cache those two directories beside NROS_HOME, or the offline host’s nros setup tries to download rustup again.
  5. Prepare each workspace while online. nros configure in the workspace fetches the crates its images need into cargo’s cache and writes everything generated, so the offline build has nothing left to download.

What lives in your tree, and what does not

An application, a message package, a board overlay crate, and a custom transport all live entirely in your tree. A board the tooling can see does too: point NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH (env, or CMake cache var for nano_ros_use_board()) at a directory of board crates in your tree, laid out like the SDK’s packages/boards/. Board keys stay global (a name under two roots errors).

A new platform (your own RTOS port) is the one extension that still edits nano-ros itself (nros-platform’s feature list and type alias, plus a cmake/platform/ module). That is a fork of nano-ros, built and maintained the way Contributing describes — see Custom Platform for the edits.

Upgrading the pin

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version <newer>
nros pin <newer>              # reports the codegen delta first
nros setup <board>            # reconcile the SDK store with the new index
nros build                    # in each consuming workspace

What nros build generates is keyed to the CLI that wrote it, so the first build after a pin move regenerates it; there is no separate step to remember.

Checklist

  • One release version, installed with --version, recorded with nros pin, moved forward only
  • CI drives nros build (or a raw cmake --preset from the CMakePresets.json that nros setup presets writes) — no reliance on an interactive shell
  • CI runs nros configure before any cargo line it drives itself (nros build needs nothing before it); no build setting hand-written into a package
  • Air-gapped: release asset mirrored (NROS_INSTALL_URL), index pinned (--index / NROS_OFFLINE), Corrosion staged, NROS_HOME cached
  • Your own boards found through NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH, not copied into the SDK
  • Router comes from the ROS 2 install on the host that runs it — nothing in the release provides one

Related

  • Build as a CMake subdirectory — cache variables, link targets
  • How Integration Works — per-RTOS build hosting
  • Vendor Overlay Board Crate — board glue that lives in your tree
  • Worked Example — STM32F4 Out of Tree
  • Install — the interactive first-time flow this page assumes you are automating

Build as a CMake subdirectory

This is the escape hatch, not the path. If your project is a nano-ros package or workspace, you state the board once in the bringup’s system.toml and let nros build drive CMake — you never set a cache variable by hand, because the build root it generates sets them from that one board name. Start at First Project and Growing your workspace instead.

This page is for the C or C++ project that is not a nano-ros workspace: an existing CMake tree with its own layout and its own conventions, that wants nano-ros as a subdirectory and nothing else. There the cache variables below are how you say what you are building for, because there is no system.toml to read it from. nros build sets exactly these variables in the root it generates.

The SDK root’s top-level CMakeLists.txt (the SDK root is the share/nano-ros directory of the installed release, nros locate nano-ros prints it) exposes everything via add_subdirectory(...). The higher-level, ament-shaped alternative is find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED) — nano_rosConfig.cmake at the SDK root, located via -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<root>, which nros build and the CMakePresets nros setup presets writes pass for you (a raw cmake names it; no shell exports it) — which every in-tree example reaches through the workspace helpers. Either way there is NO install step: there is no install prefix and no find_package(NanoRos) (capital) config pipeline. Pinning a release for a company tree (offline CI, upgrade workflow) has its own page: Integrating into a Vendored Tree.

Layout

my_app/
├── CMakeLists.txt
└── main.c

nano-ros itself is the installed SDK root; the configure names it:

cmake -B build -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build

User project CMakeLists.txt

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_app C)

# Pick platform + RMW BEFORE add_subdirectory.
set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)   # posix | freertos | nuttx | threadx | zephyr | baremetal
set(NROS_RMW     zenoh)    # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds

add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

add_executable(my_app main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE NanoRos::NanoRos)
if(COMMAND nros_platform_link_app)   # defined by zephyr/threadx platforms only
    nros_platform_link_app(my_app)
endif()

# Optional — generate C bindings for ROS 2 .msg / .srv / .action files.
# (LANGUAGE defaults to CPP; full spelling table → user-guide
# "Message Generation".)
nano_ros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs LANGUAGE C
    DEPENDENCIES builtin_interfaces)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE std_msgs__nano_ros_c)

That’s the whole story for the host-POSIX / zenoh case. CMake’s transitive target propagation pulls in libnros_c.a, libnros_rmw_zenoh_staticlib.a, the POSIX platform shim, system libraries (pthread, dl, m), and the per-build nros_config_generated.h header automatically.

Cache variables

VariableDefaultValues
NROS_PLATFORMposixposix, freertos, nuttx, threadx (legacy spellings: freertos_armcm3, nuttx_armv7a, threadx_linux, threadx_riscv64). esp_idf is no longer accepted and is REJECTED. Zephyr and bare-metal are not add_subdirectory platforms — they enter via the Zephyr module / cargo directly
NROS_BOARD(unset)required for threadx (threadx-linux or rv-virt-threadx)
NROS_SKIP_BOOTSTRAPOFFON skips the configure-time submodule bootstrap — which only a source checkout has; an installed SDK root takes its sources from nros setup. Corrosion is never fetched: a configure without it in the SDK store stops and names nros setup --tool corrosion
NROS_FEATURES(empty)extra cargo features forwarded to the Rust build
NROS_RMWzenohzenoh, dds, xrce, cyclonedds
NROS_ROS_EDITIONhumblehumble, iron, jazzy
NROS_BUILD_CODEGENONON / OFF

Variables MUST be set(...) BEFORE add_subdirectory(...) — the sub-project consumes them at include time.

In a nano-ros package or workspace none of these are yours to set. The CMake root nros build generates writes NROS_PLATFORM and NROS_BOARD itself, both derived from the one [image.<id>] board you named in system.toml, and passes the backend from [system] rmw through the workspace helper. Setting them by hand there means two answers to one question.

What about installing?

nano-ros has no install(...) rules. It is consumed in source form — never out of an installed prefix. If you need a shippable artefact, your user project owns the install layout; ship your binary, not nano-ros itself.

For RTOS users who want a more idiomatic surface than raw add_subdirectory, see the integration shells under integrations/<rtos>/ in the SDK root — they translate NuttX / PX4 manifests into the same root CMake. Each shell is a ~20-line wrapper around add_subdirectory(<sdk root>).

What the in-tree examples do instead

Worth reading as the contrast, because it is the shape most projects want. The C node package nros new c_talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang c scaffolds is a dozen lines and sets no cache variable at all:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(c_talker_node LANGUAGES C)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN c_talker_node::Talker
    EXECUTABLE c_talker_node
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED)

The board, the RMW, the domain and the network identity are not in that file — they are in the bringup’s system.toml, and the build reads them from there. nros build generates the CMake root that adds the package and the image’s entry, under build/, and passes the board’s toolchain file; its message bindings are a CMake-time output.

All the C/C++ examples follow that shape. The add_subdirectory mechanism on this page sits underneath it.

The Target Model

Every place an image can run is described the same way: a launcher or a flasher (a host process, an emulator, or a tool that programs a board), a console (where the image’s output appears), and a link (how its middleware reaches the rest of the system). nros reads these from the board’s descriptor, so the same commands work on every board.

  • nros run launches an image on the host or in an emulator.
  • nros flash programs a real board, and nros monitor attaches to its console.
  • nros bench records which board on your machine is on which port.

This page is coming soon. Until then, see the nros CLI reference.

Design background

  • RFC-0118: target execution model

Running an Image: nros run

nros run builds the image if it is stale, starts what its link needs, and streams the console, for host images and emulators. nros run --expect '<line>' exits successfully when that line appears, which makes it a one-line smoke test. On a real board it refuses and names the flashing step instead.

This page is coming soon. Until then, see nros run in the nros CLI reference and Deployment Workflow.

Design background

  • RFC-0118: target execution model

Flashing and Monitoring a Board

nros flash programs a real board with a built image, and nros monitor attaches to its console. Both read how to do it from the board’s descriptor.

This page is coming soon. Until those verbs are available for your board, flash with the board vendor’s own tools; see Deployment Workflow.

Your Bench: nros bench

nros bench records which board on this machine is connected to which serial port and debug probe, so nros flash and nros monitor find it without being told each time.

This page is coming soon.

Run Plans

Before it runs anything, nros run resolves a run plan: which launcher or flasher, which console and which link, and where each fact came from. The facts come from five levels, highest first: the command line, the image, your machine’s bench file, the board’s descriptor, and the runner’s defaults. --plan prints the plan without running it.

How integration works

You already have an RTOS project that builds and runs — an STM32Cube or NXP MCUXpresso tree, a Pico SDK app, an ESP-IDF project, a vendored Zephyr or NuttX workspace. This section is about adding nano-ros to that project, without changing who is in charge.

The principle

nano-ros is a library your project imports. Your RTOS keeps its own build tool. You keep building with west, make, idf.py, cmake, or your IDE, exactly as before. nano-ros never compiles your kernel, never owns your linker script, and never replaces your build system.

What nano-ros contributes to your build is small and fixed:

  • a Rust static library (the client runtime, behind a stable C ABI),
  • generated code for your messages and system configuration,
  • a thin C shim that your build compiles, so it sees your config headers (FreeRTOSConfig.h, lwipopts.h, sdkconfig, …).

The last point is why the shim is source, not a prebuilt: config-header mismatches between your kernel and a prebuilt binary are silent ABI breaks. Your compiler, your headers, your flags.

One shape per host build

Each supported host build system gets a small “shell” — build glue plus the host’s own package manifest — that makes nano-ros look native to it. Pick your row:

Your buildHow nano-ros plugs inShell in the repoStart here
Zephyr (west)west modulezephyr/ (module.yml, Kconfig, CMakeLists.txt)Zephyr (west module)
NuttX (make + Kconfig)apps/external/ appintegrations/nuttx/ (Make.defs, Kconfig, Makefile)NuttX (apps/external)
ESP-IDF (idf.py)retired — integrations/nano-ros/ is gonenone ships todayESP32 (ESP-IDF component) — retired; for an ESP32-C3 use ESP32 (esp-hal)
FreeRTOS, CMake projectadd_subdirectory(nano-ros)cmake/platform/nano-ros-freertos.cmakeBuild as a CMake subdirectory, FreeRTOS (QEMU)
ThreadX, CMake projectadd_subdirectory(nano-ros)cmake/platform/nano-ros-threadx.cmakeBuild as a CMake subdirectory, ThreadX
PX4 (make px4_…)EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION copy-outintegrations/px4/module-template/PX4 (integration shell)
PlatformIO (pio run)library + pre-build codegen scriptlibrary.json (repo root) + integrations/platformio/integrations/platformio/README.md in the repo
IDE project (no CMake)emitted drop-in sourcesplanned — no shell ships todaysee note below

Notes on the rows that need them:

  • Vendored FreeRTOS — STM32Cube, MCUXpresso, Pico SDK, and upstream FreeRTOS-Kernel all count. Your SDK builds the kernel and network stack; your CMake project does add_subdirectory(nano-ros) and links NanoRos::NanoRos. See the honest caveat in FreeRTOS: who builds the kernel?
  • PX4 is a hookless host: its configure step cannot run nano-ros codegen from inside, so codegen runs ahead of the PX4 build, emitting module directories PX4 then builds natively. PlatformIO works the same way, via a pre-build script.
  • IDE hosts (STM32CubeIDE, MCUXpresso IDE, IAR, Keil) have no build hook nano-ros can join. A drop-in emitter (prebuilt static library + shim sources + an integration README) is designed but not shipped yet. Today, the practical route is your IDE’s external-CMake or makefile support driving the CMake subdirectory path.

In every row the division of labor is the same: your build owns compile and link; nano-ros owns the adapter shell and the host-time code generation. Generated configuration is baked to C at build time on your host — system.toml and launch files never reach the device.

Two homes for configuration

When you integrate against your own board, you author facts in exactly two places. The split is by what kind of fact it is:

1. A board package — facts intrinsic to the board. A directory in your workspace with a package.xml and an nros-board.toml: the board’s name, RTOS platform, target triple, architecture, entry shape. These are true of every copy of that board on every desk, so they are reusable and shareable. Discovery: the CLI’s board catalog scans <nano-ros>/packages/boards/ plus every root named by NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH (PATH-style list of directories shaped like packages/boards/), so an out-of-tree board dir is seen without copying it into the checkout.

2. An [image.<id>] block, and a [board_config.<board>] beside it — facts about this checkout, this machine, this application. It lives in your bringup package’s system.toml, next to your nodes and launch files:

[image.my-board]
board = "my-board"         # joins to the board package by name
                           # the rustc triple comes from that board's descriptor

[board_config."my-board"]  # site facts: where YOUR SDK lives, which config
sdk.vendor = "{env:VENDOR_SDK_DIR}"     # headers are yours — keyed by BOARD

SDK paths, config-header locations, serial ports: anything another developer’s checkout would spell differently belongs here, keyed per deploy target, and never in the board package.

If a fact would survive being published with the board, it is a board fact. If it names a path on your disk, it is a deploy fact.

When nros build drives the build

The rows above are for a project whose build already exists. A nano-ros workspace (Growing your workspace) has no build of its own to integrate into: nros build generates each image’s entry and the build root that compiles it under build/, then runs the platform’s own tool on it. Which tool follows from the image:

The imagenros build runs
a Zephyr boardwest build, on a generated Zephyr application
any C or C++ node packageCMake (Rust packages join it through corrosion)
every node package Rustcargo, on the generated entry package

The tool is not hidden behind nano-ros. Compiler errors are the compiler’s, unchanged. nros build <image> --dry-run prints the exact command for an image, and running it yourself works. No command line names a --target: the board’s triple, linker flags and QEMU runner are in the settings generated for that image. On Zephyr, nros build prints Zephyr’s next command for the image’s own build directory, west build -d <dir> -t run for an emulated board or west flash -d <dir> for one with a flash runner.

Per platform

The nros setup name to provision each platform, where its copy-out talkers live, and its chapter:

platformnros setup <board>copy-out talkers underchapter
Linux hostlinuxexamples/linuxNative host build
FreeRTOS (QEMU MPS2-AN385)mps2-an385-freertosexamples/mps2-an385-freertosFreeRTOS
NuttX (Arm)qemu-armv7a-nuttxexamples/qemu-armv7a-nuttxNuttX
NuttX (RISC-V)rv-virt-nuttxexamples/rv-virt-nuttxNuttX
ThreadX (Linux sim)threadx-linuxexamples/threadx-linuxThreadX
ThreadX (QEMU RISC-V 64)rv-virt-threadxexamples/rv-virt-threadxThreadX
Zephyrzephyrexamples/zephyrZephyr
Bare-metal Cortex-M3mps2-an385-baremetalexamples/mps2-an385-baremetalBare-metal
Arm FVP (Cortex-A SMP)zephyr + the Arm FVP (nros setup --tool arm-fvp, x86_64 only)—ARM FVP

Each platform directory holds one copy-out talker per language, at <lang>/talker/: a workspace with one node package and a bringup with no launch/, whose launch file is generated. Copy its directory anywhere and build it there; it is the example to start from.

The paired examples are not separate directories. Talker and listener, service server and client, and action server and client are image rows of the language workspaces examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, under one bringup per behaviour: pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup. An image id is <platform>_<role>, plus _<rmw> for any RMW other than zenoh, so one role on one platform is one command:

nros run pubsub_bringup:freertos_listener
nros run service_bringup:zephyr_service_server_xrce

Variants with different code are node packages of their own, configurations such as a serial link are image rows that state the knob, and the Linux feature demos (logging, parameters, lifecycle, custom messages) live in examples/workspaces/features. The multi-node workspace examples all live under examples/workspaces. Coverage Matrix shows which platform, language and RMW combinations have examples.

FreeRTOS: who builds the kernel?

One honest exception to the principle. On the QEMU reference board, nano-ros can build the FreeRTOS kernel and lwIP for you — point FREERTOS_DIR at a kernel checkout and cmake/platform/nano-ros-freertos.cmake compiles it into the image. That is a convenience for the out-of-the-box demo, and it is the one place nano-ros compiles an RTOS.

With a vendored kernel — STM32Cube’s Middlewares/Third_Party/ FreeRTOS, MCUXpresso’s or the Pico SDK’s bundled kernel — do not use that path. Your SDK’s build owns the kernel, its port selection, and FreeRTOSConfig.h; nano-ros compiles against your include directories and links in as a library, the same as every other row in the table.

Native (Host) Build

Use the host (linux) board for first experiments, CI smoke tests, and ROS 2 interoperability checks on Linux. It uses OS sockets, the host process environment, and the same project layout as the embedded targets.

The host board is named linux ([image.<id>] board = "linux") because that is all it supports: the platform layer (nros-platform-posix) is POSIX, but the host board crate’s apply_tier_affinity calls sched_setaffinity with cpu_set_t, which libc does not define for macOS, Windows or FreeBSD. Only Linux is supported. Neither native (every general-purpose host) nor posix (the platform) names a board: board = "…", nros setup, and nros new --board refuse both with a hint naming linux.

When to Use It

  • You want the shortest path to a working nano-ros publisher or subscriber.
  • You are validating message generation, CMake integration, or ROS 2 interop before moving to an RTOS.
  • Your deployment target is Linux or an embedded Linux system.

Setup

Install the nros CLI (Installation), then provision the native host. For a host build there is no cross-toolchain to fetch — nros setup linux installs the client stack (and for xrce the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent) into a shared store. The zenoh router is NOT installed: it comes from a ROS 2 install (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd). Rather not run a router? Use --rmw cyclonedds — it needs no daemon. Either way the first build generates the messages from your ROS 2 install, so it needs ROS 2 sourced.

With the nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin):

# Provision the Linux host (zenoh RMW is the default):
nros setup linux --rmw zenoh        # or: --rmw xrce / --rmw cyclonedds

linux is this board’s one name; posix names the platform layer underneath it, and native names no board at all (Retired names).

For a colcon consumer workspace that already has nano-ros under src/:

colcon build && source install/setup.bash

Workspace Layout

A host project is a workspace, like every other board’s:

nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust   # or --lang c / cpp
cd host_ws

host_ws/
└── src/
    ├── host_node/              # node package: package.xml + Cargo.toml (or CMakeLists.txt), the node
    └── host_node_bringup/      # package.xml and system.toml: board, rmw, domain, components

The node package is a library with no main(); the bringup’s [image.linux] block (board = "linux") is what makes it a host program. The examples on GitHub are copy-out ready: nothing in one names a path into the SDK. nros finds its own SDK; --nano-ros-path names another.

Code Example

A Rust node package’s src/lib.rs declares what the node creates and what its callbacks do, and exports the node; the entry that opens the executor and spins it is generated:

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "talker";
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
        let chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<StringMsg>("/chatter")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick").publishes_entity(&chatter)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

// impl ExecutableNode for Talker { … the timer callback publishes "Hello World: N" … }

nros::node!(Talker);

Use the full First Node — Rust walkthrough for generated messages and runnable commands, and Growing your workspace for each line of lib.rs.

Build and Run

Start the RMW host daemon (the router comes from ROS 2). For zenoh:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Then build and run the node from the workspace root, in a shell that has sourced ROS 2. The first build generates the messages from it and records the prefix, so later runs need no sourced shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run host_node

nros run builds first if anything changed. nros build alone prints the binary’s path under build/, which runs directly too. For a workspace that lives in a colcon consumer workspace, colcon build && source install/setup.bash && ros2 run … works as well.

Configuration

Native examples can read runtime settings from the shell:

export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
export NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/127.0.0.1:7447

The same fields are compiled into embedded targets through their platform-specific configuration files. See Configuration for the full layering.

Deployment

Host deployment is normal process deployment: install the workspace, source install/setup.bash, set environment, and run the binary. For ROS 2 interop, run ROS 2 Interoperability and set the ROS side to rmw_zenoh_cpp.

Design background

  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance

FreeRTOS (QEMU MPS2-AN385)

Support level: mps2-an385-freertos, freertos-posix, s32z270-freertos, mps3-an536-freertos. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on FreeRTOS + lwIP, cross-compiled for Cortex-M3 and booted in QEMU MPS2-AN385. Slirp networking; no host TAP / bridge / sudo. Rust, C, and C++ talkers are on GitHub as reading material; this page scaffolds your own.

Prereqs. nros setup mps2-an385-freertos is the single command that prepares your machine for this board. It fetches a prebuilt toolchain set into the shared store at ~/.nros/sdk — the arm-none-eabi-gcc cross-compiler, the patched qemu-system-arm emulator, and the FreeRTOS kernel + lwIP sources. You do not hand-install a cross-toolchain. The zenoh path DOES need a ROS 2 install for the router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd); the xrce path needs only the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent, which nros setup installs.

Setup

With the nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), provision the board (--rmw defaults to zenoh; pick xrce or cyclonedds to match the example you intend to run):

nros setup mps2-an385-freertos --rmw zenoh

This fetches the cross-compiler, the patched qemu-system-arm, and the FreeRTOS + lwIP sources into ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk (plus the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent when you pick --rmw xrce). The zenoh router is NOT installed — it comes from your ROS 2 install.

Project layout

nros new scaffolds a workspace for the board, in any of the three languages:

nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang c      # or --lang cpp
cd fr_ws

nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang rust
cd fr_ws

fr_ws/
└── src/
    ├── fr_node/                 # node package: package.xml + CMakeLists.txt (or Cargo.toml), the talker
    └── fr_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

fr_node is a library: no main(), no board, no RMW. The bringup’s system.toml holds one image, [image.freertos], with board = "mps2-an385-freertos". The program’s entry, the FreeRTOS startup task that runs your node, is generated from that image at build time.

Nothing else states the deployment. The Rust side has no .cargo/ to edit — the thumbv7m-none-eabi triple, the -Tmps2_an385.ld --nmagic --gc-sections link group, the QEMU runner and the [patch.crates-io] rows all come from the board and are written by nros build under build/. A C or C++ node package has no <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> tuple in its package.xml and names no board in its CMakeLists.txt.

The board crate (nros-board-mps2-an385-freertos) wraps the kernel + lwIP + LAN9118 driver build; the generated entry depends on it, so nothing you write names it.

Configure

Board, RMW, domain and network identity are declared in the bringup’s system.toml and baked at compile time — there is no config file on the device. With a locator and an address added, src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml reads:

[system]
name = "fr_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "fr_node"
class = "fr_node::Talker"
name = "fr_node"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7800"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]    # [eth0] network = "qemu", host = 15

locator is where the router is (the QEMU guest reaches the host’s router through the Slirp gateway 10.0.2.2); os_config names the board network file, board-net.toml beside system.toml in the bringup. The file is the same whatever language the node is written in. Nothing about the deployment lives in Cargo.toml, in CMakeLists.txt, or in the package.xml <export> block.
