Switching board is editing [image.<id>] board and rebuilding: nros build picks the cross-toolchain file the board names, and the generated entry brings the board crate, its RMW and nros-platform’s FreeRTOS feature.

Task stacks / priorities come from the board crate’s defaults (Cargo features), not a config file — see the Configuration Guide.

The 10.0.2.0/24 subnet is QEMU Slirp’s default; 10.0.2.2 is the Slirp gateway that forwards to host loopback. No TAP, no sudo.

Ports: read your image’s own locator. The image above dials host port 7800; with no locator, as scaffolded, an image dials the board’s default (tcp/10.0.2.2:7447).

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → per-platform lanes.

Build

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

In the workspace root (fr_ws/, where nros new left you), whatever the language:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build first (message bindings, the resolved launch model, the generated entry for [image.freertos]), then hands off to cargo or CMake with the board’s cross-toolchain file and the SDK root. There is no step to run before it.

The first build cross-compiles nano-ros’s dependencies and the FreeRTOS kernel

  • lwIP (~3 min for C / C++, ~5 min for Rust). The ELF lands under build/. nros build --dry-run prints the native commands without building.

After a successful build nros build prints what it built and the command that runs it — a block like

nros build: next for `fr_node_bringup:freertos`:
  artifact: /home/you/fr_ws/build/…/freertos_entry
  run:
    nros run fr_node

Driving the native tool yourself is the escape hatch, not the path. nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo build … or cmake lines, run against the generated entry under build/. To write that entry without building (an IDE, a CI cache step), run:

nros configure

For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace at all, see Build as a CMake subdirectory.

See When nros build drives the build for which tool builds each image.

Run on QEMU

Three terminals: the router, the board, and a stock ROS 2 peer.

1. The router — ROS’s rmw_zenohd, on the port your image’s locator names (7447 when it names none, as a scaffolded image; 7800 in the example shown above). It must listen on 0.0.0.0 for the Slirp gateway: Slirp forwards the guest’s 10.0.2.2:<p> to the host’s <p>.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

2. The board — from the workspace root:

nros run fr_node

nros run rebuilds if anything changed, then boots the image in QEMU with the board’s runner: the store’s patched qemu-system-arm (nros setup mps2-an385-freertos installed it), the LAN9118 on Slirp, and -icount shift=auto, which keeps the board’s timer in step with Slirp’s I/O. It streams the semihosting console until you press Ctrl-C.

The scaffolded talker publishes std_msgs/String once a second, in every language:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

3. A stock ROS 2 peer. The talker publishes best-effort; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing. Force best-effort to receive:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

It prints a data: line per message:

data:

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it.

Readiness signal. Within ~20 seconds of QEMU boot, the image prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on its semihosting stdout — a std_msgs/String counted from 1, like the official ROS 2 demo talker. QEMU cold-boot through FreeRTOS init + lwIP DHCP + zenoh session open typically takes 10–15 s. If no Publishing: line in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm the router is running on the host on the port the image dials — the locator in its system.toml (Slirp forwards 10.0.2.2:<p> → host:

    ). Without it the talker makes one connection attempt and stops with Failed to open session; a board that should wait for a late router sets [knobs.zenoh.limits] connect_forever = true (or connect_timeout_ms for a bounded wait).

  2. Check the talker’s early log for lwIP DHCP timeout or Failed to open session.
  3. Bridge tip: ros2 topic echo /chatter from a stock ROS 2 install (with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp) confirms end-to-end interop.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Run on the POSIX simulator

The freertos-posix board runs the FreeRTOS kernel as an ordinary Linux process (FreeRTOS’s POSIX port) — no QEMU, host networking. It is a C / C++ board (it has no Rust entry shape). Provision it, point the image of a C or C++ workspace at it, and run:

nros setup freertos-posix --rmw zenoh
# in src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml:  [image.freertos] board = "freertos-posix"
nros run fr_node

The image dials the router on the host directly (no Slirp gateway), so start rmw_zenohd on the port its locator names, as in Run on QEMU step 1.

Flash a real board

No in-tree FreeRTOS board is flashed by a documented flow, and none is claimed: the MPS2-AN385 boards above are QEMU machines.

  • NXP S32Z270 (s32z270-freertos; its status is on its board page). No emulator models its Cortex-R52 RTU, so nothing here boots it. It builds like the other boards — the licensed pieces (NXP’s GCC/ARM_CR52_GIC FreeRTOS port, the RTD NETC Ethernet driver, the S32 Config Tools PBcfg) are yours to supply, as its descriptor explains — and the ELF is flashed with your own S32 tooling (S32 Design Studio, a Lauterbach/PEmicro probe); nano-ros adds no flash step:

    nros setup s32z270-freertos --rmw zenoh
# in src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml, a second image:
#   [image.s32z] board = "s32z270-freertos"
nros build s32z
# → nros build prints the ELF path; flash it with your S32 tooling

  • Your own FreeRTOS board is a board package of your own — see Adding a FreeRTOS Board — and is flashed with whatever that board’s vendor uses (probe-rs, OpenOCD, a vendor IDE).

Neither flash path is run by any probe (a CI runner has no board): both stand unverified until run against a named board. How often the QEMU line above runs is on each board’s page under Supported Boards.

GitHub source

The copy-out talkers for this board, one per language. Each is the same project this page scaffolds: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own.

  • Rust: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/rust/talker/
  • C: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/c/talker/
  • C++: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/cpp/talker/

Next

  • Subscriber, services and actions: the freertos_* image rows of the language workspaces, examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, one bringup per behaviour (pubsub_bringup, service_bringup, action_bringup). nros run pubsub_bringup:freertos_listener runs the listener; freertos_listener_xrce is the same role over XRCE.
  • No RTOS: the Bare-metal Cortex-M3 page is the same board without FreeRTOS.
  • Your own board / RTOS: the Board Integration matrix maps each user profile (Cargo-first, vendor-IDE, Zephyr, NuttX, ESP32-C3, niche fork) to the shortest bring-up path.
  • RTOS-specific debugging: FreeRTOS LAN9118 Debugging.

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups.

Zephyr (west module)

Support level: native_sim, mps2_an385, the S32K344 safety island. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on Zephyr via the in-tree zephyr/ west module. nano-ros ships as a Zephyr module — west discovers it from your workspace’s west.yml, drops in a prj.conf Kconfig surface, and the standard west build / west flash flow takes care of the rest.

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → in-tree examples.

Just want a working starter? Clone the nano-ros-zephyr-example repo (west init -m …) — a manifest + zenoh talker app pinned to a tested Zephyr, with the same quickstart as below baked in. The steps here explain what it does so you can adapt it to your own workspace.

Prereqs. Run nros setup zephyr --rmw <rmw> once (see Prerequisites below) — it provisions the Zephyr west workspace + Zephyr SDK bits, the emulator, and your RMW’s host daemon into the shared store. No hand-installed Zephyr SDK, west, or cross-toolchain. nros build generates the messages from your ROS 2 install, so its first build of a workspace needs ROS 2 sourced. Python: 3.10+ on Zephyr 3.7 LTS, but ≥ 3.12 on Zephyr 4.x (4.x’s find_package(Python3) requires 3.12 — see the version matrix below). nano-ros’s imported west fragment zephyr/west.yml is a manifest-only file — it does NOT pull Zephyr itself; that has to be in your parent manifest (zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr).

Which Zephyr? — 3.7 LTS and 4.x both supported

nano-ros consumes as a module on both the 3.7 LTS line (supported to Jan 2027; the safety-island default) and the current 4.x rolling line. You build against whatever Zephyr your workspace already pins — nano-ros adapts. The two lines differ only in how you select an RMW and apply nano-ros’s Zephyr patches:

CapabilityZephyr 3.7 LTSZephyr 4.x
Min Python3.103.12 (find_package(Python3))
RMW selectionthe image’s rmw in system.tomlthe image’s rmw in system.toml (an app with no system.toml: the -S nros-<rmw> snippet)
nano-ros patchesapplied during nros setup zephyr provisioningapplied during nros setup zephyr provisioning
Examples as samples / Twister—samples: + Twister (sample.nano-ros.*)
zenoh (native_sim)✅ build + e2e✅ build + e2e
cyclonedds (native_sim)✅ build + e2e✅ build · publish · receive · multicast-join (stable 2-node run pending a tracked k_mutex fix)
xrce✅build path WIP

native_sim networking uses NSOS (host loopback) on both lines — no TAP/bridge/root. The copy-out, snippet, patch-apply, and dual-line build flows are exercised in CI; the lanes are in Internals → Zephyr in-tree examples.

Project layout

A nano-ros project on Zephyr is a workspace like on every other platform, beside the west workspace that holds Zephyr. Your code is node packages; the bringup’s system.toml names the board. The Zephyr application is generated: nros build writes it under build/ and runs west build on it.

my_zephyr_ws/                          # the west workspace: Zephyr and its modules
├── .west/
├── manifest/west.yml
├── zephyr/                            # cloned by `west update`
└── modules/
c_ws/                                  # the nano-ros workspace
├── src/
│   ├── c_node/                        # your node package
│   └── c_node_bringup/
│       ├── package.xml
│       └── system.toml                # [image.zephyr] board = "zephyr"
└── build/                             # generated, the Zephyr application among it

Quick start builds exactly this. An application that owns its west build and has no bringup (its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf, with nano-ros added as one more module) is the subject of its own chapter, A Zephyr App You Build with West.

Prerequisites

nros setup zephyr provisions what the index declares for the board — the Zephyr SDK ([board.zephyr] packages = ["zephyr-sdk"]) and the RMW transport sources (zenoh-pico + mbedtls for zenoh, the cyclonedds fork) — from a pinned index into ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk. The Zephyr sources and modules themselves are a west workspace, which you keep the standard Zephyr way. It provides no zenoh router: that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd (see the RMW design); Cyclone DDS needs no daemon at all.

  1. Get the nros CLI — install a release with scripts/install.sh (Installation); it lands in ~/.nros/bin.
  2. Provision the board + RMW: 
    nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh       # Zephyr SDK + zenoh-pico + mbedtls
nros setup --source px4-rs          # workspace cargo-load dep
  3. Point Zephyr at the SDK if your shell does not already find it — export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)", which prints where nros setup installed it (or register it via the SDK’s setup.sh -c).
  4. Source ROS 2 for the first build. nros build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install’s definitions, std_msgs included, so the types match your ROS 2 peers: source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash before the first nros build, nros run or nros configure of a workspace. That configure records the prefix, so later shells need not source ROS.

The zenoh router must be running before an example connects (ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd); for xrce, the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent nros setup … --rmw xrce installed; for cyclonedds, nothing.

Quick start: a talker on native_sim, from nothing

The sections after this one explain each piece; this is the whole path in order, for a C talker on native_sim (a host executable, so no emulator). Zephyr’s own host tools come first — west and the build tools Zephyr’s Getting Started lists; nros setup installs no system packages. On Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Provision the board and RMW (the Zephyr SDK, zenoh-pico, mbedtls):

nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"

A west workspace that pins Zephyr 3.7 and fetches only the modules nano-ros’s boards build with (nros setup zephyr lists them; import: true would fetch every vendor HAL, ~2.5 GB more):

mkdir -p my_zephyr_ws/manifest && cd my_zephyr_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools]
    # Rust support: only a Rust app builds with it. Pinned to the revision
    # nano-ros's own west.yml pins for the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"

Scaffold a workspace beside the west workspace: a C talker node package and its bringup, whose image runs on board zephyr (Zephyr’s native_sim/native/64). nros build writes the Zephyr application for that image under build/ and runs west build on it, from the west workspace NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE names. You write no CMakeLists.txt and no prj.conf.

The board package also applies nano-ros’s nros-nsos snippet, which routes the image’s sockets to the host’s (Zephyr’s NSOS) instead of a TAP interface. Without it native_sim tries to create one (eth_posix: Cannot create zeth), which needs privileges a container or an ordinary user does not have, and the image never reaches the router.

The first build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. It records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new c_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang c --rmw zenoh
cd c_ws
nros build

That wrote two packages, the same shape every platform’s scaffold has:

c_ws/
└── src/
    ├── c_node/            # the talker: package.xml, CMakeLists.txt, its C source
    └── c_node_bringup/    # package.xml, and system.toml: [image.zephyr] board = "zephyr"

Run it against a router on the host’s loopback — native_sim uses the host’s sockets, and the image dials tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 unless the bringup’s system.toml states a locator:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

With the router running, run the talker:

nros run c_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

An application you already build with west. A Zephyr application that keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf and has no bringup is not a workspace image: it adds the nano-ros module to a plain west build, as A Zephyr App You Build with West shows.

The same talker in Rust. The scaffold is the same with --lang rust, and so is everything nros build does with it. Make it beside the west workspace above.

zephyr-lang-rust needs three things the C app does not: the Rust target the Zephyr board implies (x86_64-unknown-none for native_sim/64 on an x86_64 host), rustup’s clippy (it lints every Rust app as part of the build), and clang and libclang, for the bindings it generates from Zephyr’s headers. nros setup in the workspace installs the target and clippy, and with --sudo the two packages (without it, it prints the install command). nros build refuses a Rust Zephyr image that lacks any of them, naming the command.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
. "$HOME/.cargo/env"     # the cargo `nros setup` installed (Installation)
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new rs_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd rs_ws
nros setup --sudo
nros build

With the router above running, run it:

nros run rs_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

Configure

nano-ros’s Zephyr module ships in the installed SDK — the SDK root (the release’s share/nano-ros; nros locate nano-ros prints it) holds its zephyr/module.yml. You do not add nano-ros to your west.yml: nros build names the module on the west build line it runs (-DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES=<sdk root>), and a west build you run yourself passes the same:

west build -b native_sim/native/64 apps/my_app -- \
    -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)"

Your west.yml pins Zephyr itself (and whatever modules your application uses) the standard Zephyr way:

manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyr
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyr
      revision: v3.7.0          # or your chosen 3.7 LTS / 4.x SHA
      path: zephyr
      import: true               # pulls Zephyr's own modules

The transport sources the module compiles (zenoh-pico, mbedtls, the Cyclone DDS fork) come from nros setup zephyr --rmw <rmw>, not from west.

Then nano-ros’s half of the configuration goes in the bringup’s system.toml, and Zephyr’s own half in prj.conf fragments (in a workspace, under the bringup’s boards/<board>/, as Growing your workspace shows):

# src/c_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "c_node_bringup"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[image.zephyr]
board = "zephyr"            # the concrete board is west's `-b`
rmw = "zenoh"               # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
# locator = "tcp/192.0.2.10:7447"
# [image.zephyr.knobs.zenoh]
# max_publishers = 4

# prj.conf — Zephyr settings only; never a CONFIG_NROS_* knob here
CONFIG_NROS=y               # enables the module; everything else is the image's
CONFIG_NETWORKING=y
CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y
CONFIG_NET_TCP=y

The module renders the image into a Kconfig fragment merged after prj.conf: the RMW from rmw, the language API from your app, the endpoint from locator, the domain from domain_id, and every env knob (any symbol in the Kconfig reference, spelled without CONFIG_). A CONFIG_NROS_* line in prj.conf would be overridden by it, so it is at best dead. Several images in one file — one per RMW — are picked with west build … -- -DNROS_IMAGE=<id>; see Configuring an image. An app with NO system.toml gets no rendering and is configured in its own prj.conf (A Zephyr App You Build with West).

CONFIG_NROS=y activates the shell, which maps Kconfig values to NROS_* CMake cache vars and add_subdirectory()s the root nano-ros CMake. NanoRos::NanoRos is linked into your app library transparently.

Configuring an image: system.toml, not prj.conf

An image’s nano-ros configuration lives in ONE place, the bringup’s system.toml. The nano-ros Zephyr module renders the selected image into a Kconfig fragment and merges it last, after every conf file. So the prj*.conf files hold Zephyr’s own settings only (networking, POSIX, stacks, heaps) and never a CONFIG_NROS_* line: one there is either dead (the image overrides it) or a second source that can disagree with the first. A gate (check-leaf-conf-nros-knobs) refuses one in the tree.

What the module renders, and from where:

You write in system.tomlThe build gets
[image.<id>] rmw = "xrce"CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE=y
(nothing — the package’s language)CONFIG_NROS_{C,CPP,RUST}_API=y
locator = "tcp/…" (zenoh)CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR
locator = "udp/<host>:<port>" (XRCE)CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_ADDR + _PORT
domain_id = 7 (image, [defaults] or [system])CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID
[image.<id>.knobs.zenoh] max_queryables = 12CONFIG_NROS_MAX_QUERYABLES=12 — a registry knob, spelled as a board’s [knobs] is (see Configuration)
[image.<id>.knobs.xrce] max_subscribers = 0CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=0 — likewise
env = { NROS_ZEPHYR_TASK_STACK_SIZE = "16384" }CONFIG_NROS_ZEPHYR_TASK_STACK_SIZE=16384 — any other option in the reference below, spelled without CONFIG_
os_config = ["prj-xrce.conf"]that Zephyr-native fragment, added ahead of your own EXTRA_CONF_FILE

An env row with no Kconfig symbol is not lost: it reaches the image’s cargo builds as an [env] row instead. A row whose type does not fit its symbol, or that only exists under another RMW, is refused at configure time, naming the system.toml line.

One image per RMW

A bringup built for several backends states one image per RMW, and picks one at build time. From examples/zephyr/c/talker/system.toml:

[system]
name = "nros_zephyr_talker_c"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0
default_images = ["zephyr_zenoh"]

[image.zephyr_zenoh]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "zenoh"
os_config = ["prj-zenoh.conf"]

[image.zephyr_xrce]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "xrce"
os_config = ["prj-xrce.conf"]
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:2018"

[image.zephyr_xrce.knobs.xrce]
max_subscribers = 0
max_service_servers = 0
max_service_clients = 0

[image.zephyr_cyclonedds]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
os_config = ["prj-cyclonedds.conf"]

nros build                    # the default_images: zephyr_zenoh
nros build zephyr_xrce        # another image — its own west build dir

Each image builds into its own directory, build/<platform>-<rmw>/<package>__<image>_west, so switching images never reuses another image’s cache.

To run west yourself on one image, nros build zephyr_xrce --dry-run prints the west build line for that image’s generated application and its own build directory.

Precedence, last wins: the conf files, then a 4.x -S nros-<rmw> snippet, then the image’s rendering, then any -DCONFIG_… on the command line (how a test harness passes a per-run port). A snippet naming a DIFFERENT RMW than the image is refused rather than silently overridden; one that agrees is redundant. An application with no system.toml gets no rendering, so for it the snippets and Kconfig defaults still choose.

What each RMW’s Zephyr-native fragment needs

The image’s os_config file carries what the backend needs from Zephyr itself:

  • Zenoh (the Kconfig default): TCP and POSIX threads for zenoh-pico — CONFIG_NET_TCP=y, CONFIG_POSIX_API=y, and pthread pools big enough for it (examples/zephyr/rust/talker/prj-zenoh.conf uses CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_MUTEX_COUNT=64, CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_COND_COUNT=16).
  • XRCE-DDS: CONFIG_NET_TCP=y, on top of the BSD sockets (CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS=y) every image’s shared prj.conf enables. The agent endpoint is the image’s locator.
  • Cyclone DDS: brokerless RTPS, wire-compatible with stock ROS 2 (rmw_cyclonedds_cpp). Its source is C++, so CONFIG_CPP=y even for Rust callers; it needs a large stack (CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE=524288), pthread pools, and CONFIG_NET_IPV4_IGMP=y for SPDP multicast. The bool prerequisites (thread-local storage, dynamic threads, NET_TCP, …) are selected by CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS. Its ddsrt_malloc draws on the nano-ros platform heap, 1 MiB by default under Cyclone — raise it with [image.<id>.knobs.zephyr] heap_size = … on the image, not in the conf.

On native_sim, add the NSOS host-socket offload (CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS_OFFLOAD=y + CONFIG_NET_NATIVE_OFFLOADED_SOCKETS=y) so discovery uses host BSD sockets instead of zeth/TAP. See examples/zephyr/rust/talker/prj-cyclonedds.conf for the full fragment.

Build

If your workspace is a fresh manifest-only dir (no .west/), initialise it first so west knows which west.yml is the manifest:

cd my_zephyr_ws
west init -l .                           # one-time; points west at the
                                         # local west.yml in cwd
west update                              # clones Zephyr + its modules into the workspace

(If you started from west init -m <remote>, both calls above are already done — go straight to west build below.)

nros build on Zephyr: it hands off, it does not take over

On every platform nros build generates the image’s entry under build/ and runs the platform’s tool on it. On Zephyr the entry is a Zephyr application and the tool is west build. What stays yours is the west workspace: west init / west update populate it, it pins your Zephyr, and nano-ros never writes into it.

So for a Zephyr image nros build:

  1. writes the application for that image under build/, from the image’s board and the bringup’s nodes (or uses src/<image>_entry/, if you have taken it over with nros materialize);
  2. resolves your Zephyr — $ZEPHYR_BASE, else $NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE, else an in-tree zephyr-workspace/, else a sibling ../nano-ros-workspace. Note it is a Zephyr that is needed, not a .west/ directory: with ZEPHYR_BASE set, west build runs from anywhere, which is what lets the application live under your workspace’s build/, outside the west workspace;
  3. runs west build from there with the image’s overlays (EXTRA_CONF_FILE, APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR) already applied.

If it cannot find a workspace it does not guess. It prints the command and where to run it:

$ nros build demo_bringup:zephyr
Error: no west workspace found, so `west build` cannot be run for `zephyr`.

Zephyr differs from the other drivers: YOU own the west workspace and the
application, and `west` only runs inside a workspace …

Run this from your west workspace:

    west build -b native_sim/native/64 …/build/…/demo_bringup__zephyr_west

Point nros at your workspace:

    NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE=<dir>   # the dir containing zephyr/

That is deliberate and it is the same boundary nros setup --system draws when it composes an install command and prints it rather than running sudo for you: where the tool is yours, nano-ros hands you the command instead of assuming it may act.

nros build is the flow this chapter teaches: it applies the image’s overlays, picks the build directory and, when it finishes, prints the artifact and the Zephyr command that runs or flashes it. It never becomes a required layer between you and west — a Zephyr app you build with west stays the escape hatch, for an application that owns its west build and has no bringup.

Starting from nothing: nros new

nros new rs_ws --board zephyr --template talker writes a workspace whose bringup already has a Zephyr image, as in the quick start. Inside a workspace, a further node package is board- and RMW-agnostic — it names no platform, which is what lets the same package be deployed to Linux and to a Cortex-M without an edit:

nros new talker_pkg --template talker --to demo_bringup

It writes the package and, with --to, adds the [[component]] row to that bringup. There is no Zephyr application to scaffold: nros build and nros run generate it from the image.

Owning the application: nros materialize

The generated application takes the image’s keys (board, os_config, the RMW) and the board package’s Kconfig and devicetree overlay, and most changes are one of those. When a change is none of them, and the application’s own CMakeLists.txt or prj.conf has to change, take it over:

nros materialize zephyr

That writes the generated application into src/zephyr_entry/ as a package of yours, and from then on nros build builds that copy and does not regenerate it. Deleting src/zephyr_entry/ returns the image to generation. It is the last resort, for the reasons Customising an entry gives.

The whole flow, end to end

Four commands, run from your workspace. This is the examples/workspaces/rust transcript, verbatim:

# 0. tell nros where your west workspace is — the directory containing
#    `zephyr/`. On the command line:
#
#      nros build demo_bringup:zephyr --zephyr-workspace /path/to/zephyr-workspace
#
#    or once for the shell, if you would rather not repeat it:
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE=/path/to/zephyr-workspace

# 1. build. This generates the message bindings the workspace's packages
#    depend on, resolves the application, applies the image's overlays and
#    runs `west build` for you.
nros build demo_bringup:zephyr

# 2. start the router ROS itself uses — the one `rmw_zenoh_cpp` ships, so it
#    cannot drift from the RMW your ROS 2 nodes use. Separate terminal; it
#    keeps running. Listens on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447.
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# 3. run the image — `nros build` printed this, with its own build dir
#    (build/<coordinate>/<bringup>__<image>_west):
west build -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west -t run
#    (on native_sim that runs ./build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe)

*** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***
<inf> nros_net_wait: Network ready (NSOS — host kernel sockets)
<inf> rust: rustapp: nros: zephyr workspace entry up (2 nodes)
<inf> rust: talker_pkg: Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
<inf> rust: talker_pkg: Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

and from a ROS 2 shell on the same router, the nodes are ordinary ROS nodes:

$ export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
$ ros2 topic echo /chatter --once
data: 'Hello World: 6'
---

Step 2 is not optional and its ORDER does not matter, but the locator does: zenoh-pico is a client, so with no router the image gets

<err> rust: nros: zephyr entry — executor open failed: Transport(ConnectionFailed)

which names no port. Both sides default to tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 — the port rmw_zenohd listens on and a rmw_zenoh_cpp node connects to. Override with the image’s locator = "tcp/…" in system.toml and ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:<port>"]' on the router, and change both.

What an image declares

The Zephyr images in examples/workspaces/* are the worked examples:

[image.zephyr]
board = "zephyr"
conf  = ["prj-zenoh.conf"]      # the RMW overlay this app requires

None of them sets entry: nros build generates each image’s application.

  • os_config names the app’s own Kconfig fragments, in order. They are looked for beside the board config dir, then beside the application, then beside the bringup — the app rung matters because a Zephyr app keeps its prj-<rmw>.conf next to the CMakeLists.txt west builds. These entries FATAL_ERROR without an RMW overlay, so the image has to say which one.
  • board is a nano-ros board id, which nano-ros resolves to the Zephyr board target. See below.
  • entry names the application package. Normally leave it out: an entry declares the deploy target it serves — its own system.toml in Rust, nano_ros_add_executable(... DEPLOY zephyr) in CMakeLists.txt — and one package usually claims a given board. Set it when the derivation cannot answer, which happens two ways and says which:
    • several packages claim the board — deriving would be a coin flip, so nros build lists the candidates rather than picking one. Reachable for C/C++ entries, which are matched by their DEPLOY token;
    • none does — nros build falls back to the Bringup directory, and you see a conf fragment “not found” in a path that is not your application’s. A hand-written application that picks its board with nano_ros_use_board(...) inside its own CMakeLists.txt is this case: the DEPLOY scan does not read that call. Usually the better fix is to delete the application — nros build generates one and hands it the board package’s own Kconfig and devicetree overlay, which is all nano_ros_use_board added.

If you live in west: west nros

Everything above assumes you stand in your nano-ros workspace and name the Zephyr one. If you work the other way round — inside the west workspace — west already knows where Zephyr is, so it can tell nros for you:

cd ~/zephyr-workspace
west nros build --workspace ~/my_robot demo_bringup:zephyr

No ZEPHYR_BASE, no NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE, no --zephyr-workspace. Every argument after nros is passed straight through, so anything nros accepts works here unchanged.

It picks up automatically in any workspace whose manifest lists nano-ros — a checkout of this repository, or a mirror of a release you vendor (see Pin and mirror a release). With the installed SDK alone there is no west nros: west reads extension commands from a manifest project, and the installed SDK root is a versioned directory under ~/.nros that no west.yml can name. Name the Zephyr workspace to nros instead, which is what west nros does for you:

nros build --zephyr-workspace ~/zephyr-workspace demo_bringup:zephyr

west nros is the only nano-ros west extension; to run an image, use the stock west build -t run. Two things worth knowing:

  • It only exists inside a west workspace. West loads extension commands from the manifest, so from an unrelated directory you get west: unknown command "nros". That is why this is an addition rather than a replacement: it swaps which of the two trees you have to name, trading the Zephyr path (which differs per machine) for your own workspace path (which you chose).
  • It never overwrites a ZEPHYR_BASE you set yourself — an exported one is a deliberate choice, and this only fills in a missing answer.

Which boards you can name

board names a board in nano-ros’s catalog, and the board’s descriptor states the Zephyr id west build -b receives:

# packages/boards/zephyr/nros-board.toml
names = ["zephyr"]                        # what your images say

[board.zephyr]
west_board = "native_sim/native/64"       # what west is given

So an image writes board = "zephyr", never board = "native_sim/native/64": the Zephyr spelling is the descriptor’s to state, and an image that authors it is refused with the id to write instead.

Nor is it free-form. A board the catalog does not know is refused with the list of ones it does, because the descriptor supplies more than the -b string — the platform, the toolchain, the entry kind, the declared capabilities. There is no safe default for those.

A board is a package — put it in your workspace. Drop an nros-board.toml beside a package’s package.xml and it joins the catalog like any other package in src/:

my_robot/src/
├── talker_pkg/
└── my_board/
    ├── package.xml
    └── nros-board.toml

# src/my_board/nros-board.toml
[[board]]
names = ["my-board"]              # what your images say
west_board = "qemu_cortex_m3"     # what west is given
platform = "zephyr"
toolchain = "stable"
platform_feature = "platform-zephyr"
link_kind = "none"
entry_kind = "zephyr-staticlib"

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml
[image.zephyr]
board = "my-board"

No environment variable, nothing outside the tree, nothing copied into the nano-ros checkout. west_board is what lets the friendly name be the one your workspace uses, which is also what the shipped Zephyr descriptors do (under [board.zephyr]). Leave it out only when your board name already is the west board target and you have no other name for it.

For a board shared by several workspaces there is no single workspace to put it in, and $NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH still covers that: PATH-style, naming directories shaped like packages/boards/.

nros new board <name> --for-platform zephyr scaffolds the descriptor. Note this is the nano-ros descriptor; an out-of-tree Zephyr board definition (its devicetree and board.yml) is contributed the Zephyr way, through your module’s board_root.

Adding your own drivers, modules and boards

Everything Zephyr lets you extend, you still extend the Zephyr way. nros build runs a plain west build, so the extension points are untouched. The first row edits the application’s CMakeLists.txt, so it needs an application you own (nros materialize); the rest do not:

you wantyou donros build involvement
an out-of-tree modulelist(APPEND ZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES <dir>) before find_package(Zephyr)none
a driver in that modulezephyr_library() + zephyr_library_sources(), gated on your own Kconfignone
its devicetree bindingdts/bindings/ + settings: {dts_root: .} in the module’s zephyr/module.ymlnone
an out-of-tree board / SoC / arch / snippetthe matching *_root in the same module.yml (board_root, soc_root, arch_root, snippet_root, module_ext_root)none
turning your Kconfig on for one imagea os_config fragment on [image.*]passed as EXTRA_CONF_FILE
a devicetree overlay for one imagean .overlay in the same os_config listpassed as EXTRA_DTC_OVERLAY_FILE

Only the last two rows are ours, and they are how an IMAGE differs from its siblings — the module itself is a property of the application, not of one image, so it belongs in the app’s CMakeLists.txt where you would have put it anyway.

nros build passes exactly four things to west of its own — APPLICATION_CONFIG_DIR, EXTRA_CONF_FILE, EXTRA_DTC_OVERLAY_FILE, FILE_SUFFIX, all Zephyr’s own variables — and there is deliberately no image key for arbitrary -D defines. Something your application always needs belongs in its CMakeLists.txt, which keeps one place to look.

Customizing the west command itself

Anything after -- goes to west. west build has two argument zones, and nros build routes each token to the right one using west’s own flag list:

nros build demo_bringup:zephyr -- --pristine        # a west option
nros build demo_bringup:zephyr -- -t run            # build, then run it
nros build demo_bringup:zephyr -- -DMY_OPT=1        # a cmake option
nros build demo_bringup:zephyr -- -p always -DX=1   # both, in one go

which becomes, respectively, the west option zone and the cmake zone:

west build -b <board> <app> -p always -- -DEXTRA_CONF_FILE=… -DX=1

nros build --dry-run prints that line without running it, so you can always see exactly what west is being asked to do — and copy it if you would rather drive west yourself.

Two flags are refused rather than routed, because the image already decides them and a build must not be able to disagree with its own declaration:

$ nros build demo_bringup:zephyr -- --sysbuild
Error: `--sysbuild` is decided by the image, not by the command line.
It comes from the presence of a `sysbuild.conf` beside the application.

Change it there, so one build cannot disagree with the declaration it was
resolved from.

The other is -b/--board, which comes from the image’s board.

Verified by building one. An out-of-tree module with its own Kconfig, a driver source gated on it, a devicetree overlay declaring a node and a binding shipped from the module’s dts_root, added to examples/workspaces/rust’s entry and enabled through the image:

[image.zephyr]
os_config = ["prj-zenoh.conf", "prj-user-extra.conf", "user-widget.overlay"]

*** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***
user_extra: out-of-tree driver init, widget-id=42
<inf> rust: rustapp: nros: zephyr workspace entry up (2 nodes)
<inf> rust: talker_pkg: Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'

The driver’s BUILD_ASSERT(DT_NODE_EXISTS(DT_NODELABEL(user_widget))) is what makes that a test rather than a screenshot: without the overlay reaching the build, it fails to compile instead of quietly doing nothing.

A mistake in your module surfaces as Zephyr’s own error, unmediated — a wrong kconfig: path in module.yml reports

ERROR: "kconfig" key in …/extra_module/zephyr/module.yml has value
"../Kconfig" which does not point to a valid Kconfig file.

which is the message you would get from a plain west build, because it is a plain west build.

Driving west yourself

An application with no bringup, built with a plain west build and configured in its own prj.conf, is covered in A Zephyr App You Build with West: adding the module, the Kconfig settings that replace system.toml, messages, and running it.

Rust applications

Two things differ for a Rust app (C/C++ apps skip this section):

  1. The Rust crate’s [lib] must be named rustapp (crate-type = ["staticlib"]) — a zephyr-lang-rust contract: its rust_cargo_application() links librustapp.a. The Cargo package name is free.

  2. Generate the interface crates and the dependency wiring for YOUR layout before the first west build, which does not run nano-ros’s preparation for a Rust app. From your app dir, run (after the Prerequisites nros setup, which provides the codegen toolchain), in a shell that has sourced ROS 2 (the message definitions come from it; this configure records the prefix for later runs):

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros configure

    This writes generated/<pkg>/ (the message crates) and a .cargo/config.toml whose [patch.crates-io] points the nros-* crates into the nano-ros SDK root and the generated interfaces at generated/*. --nano-ros-path <dir> names another root (the SDK ROOT, the directory holding nano_rosConfig.cmake).

Run

nros build ends by printing what to type next, read from the finished build itself — the emulators Zephyr’s board declares (run_<emu> targets in build.ninja) and its flash runner (zephyr/runners.yaml). For an image in build directory <dir> that is one or both of

west build -d <dir> -t run        # an emulated board: native_sim, QEMU
west flash -d <dir>               # a board with a flash runner

Both are Zephyr’s own commands; nano-ros adds nothing to them. The router comes first either way:

# Start the router (ROS's `rmw_zenohd` — nano-ros ships no router of its
# own) on port 7447, the port your app dials by default (an image with no
# `locator` gets "tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"; change either side to match):
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd &

Run on native_sim

board = "zephyr" is Zephyr’s native_sim/native/64: the image is a host executable, and its sockets are the host’s (NSOS), so it reaches the router on loopback with no network setup.

nros build demo_bringup:zephyr
west build -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west -t run
# — the same as running the executable directly:
./build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe

(A build you drove with plain west build, into west’s default build/: west build -t run, or ./build/zephyr/zephyr.exe.)

Run on QEMU (mps2-an385)

The Cortex-M3 witness is Zephyr’s mps2/an385 under QEMU, with Zephyr’s own IP stack on the emulated SMSC911x. An image names it board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"; west build -t run boots it under the QEMU the Zephyr SDK ships (nros setup zephyr installed it). In the Rust workspace above, a second image is that board. nros setup board comes first: it applies nano-ros’s patch set to your west workspace, without which zephyr-lang-rust’s cargo command carries none of nano-ros’s settings for the board (among them the C cross compiler the zenoh-pico crate builds with), and adds the board’s Rust target. The image is one more block in the bringup:

nros setup board mps2-an385-zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE"
cat >> src/rs_node_bringup/system.toml <<'TOML'

[image.zephyr_m3]
board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"
TOML
nros setup --sudo
nros build zephyr_m3

The guest sits on QEMU’s user-mode network, and the board package states it: its prj.conf gives the image 10.0.2.15 (gateway 10.0.2.2) and the locator tcp/10.0.2.2:7447, and nros build applies it, so there is nothing to set. The Slirp gateway 10.0.2.2 is the host, so the router above is reachable. An image whose router listens elsewhere states its own locator in system.toml.

With two images in the bringup, name the one to run:

nros run zephyr_m3

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

Verify from stock ROS 2

# The scaffolded talker publishes std_msgs/String (the talker in
# "A Zephyr App You Build with West" publishes std_msgs/Int32).
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

The Zephyr boot banner runs first, then the talker fires: it prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1', Publishing: 'Hello World: 2', … (Rust + C + C++ all count from 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker).

Readiness signal. On native_sim, expect the first publish line (Publishing: 'Hello World: 1') within 5 seconds of boot; on a QEMU board (mps2-an385-zephyr, or a qemu_cortex_a9 you built yourself) expect it within ~15 seconds (QEMU cold boot + Zephyr init). If no publish line in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm CONFIG_NROS=y lit up via west build -t menuconfig; without it the module shell never add_subdirectory’s nano-ros.
  2. Check CONFIG_NETWORKING=y, CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y, CONFIG_NET_TCP=y in prj.conf — Zephyr networking is opt-in.
  3. Confirm zenohd reachable from the simulated network (Slirp needs 10.0.2.2:7447 on QEMU; native_sim uses host loopback).
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Zephyr 4.x build gotchas.

  • Could NOT find Python3 ... required is at least "3.12" — 4.x needs Python ≥ 3.12. Provision one without sudo (e.g. uv venv --python 3.12 .venv312 && uv pip install west -r zephyr/scripts/requirements.txt) and run west through it (.venv312/bin/python -m west build ...), so the ROS descriptor-codegen subprocess still uses the system ROS Python.
  • attempt to assign the value ... to the undefined symbol ETH_NATIVE_POSIX — that symbol was renamed ETH_NATIVE_TAP in 4.x; the version-aware NSOS overlay handles it (contributors: the in-tree just zephyr build-one recipe applies it automatically).

Flash a real board

The boards above are native_sim and QEMU machines, and the ARM FVP is a model (its chapter). The hardware boards nano-ros ships a package for are the Nucleo-F767ZI (board = "nucleo-f767zi-zephyr"), whose Renode twin boots the same image (its chapter), and the Raspberry Pi Pico W (board = "rpi-pico-w-zephyr"), whose Wokwi twin does; the Pico W’s own chapter is still to come. Any board Zephyr supports is reached with a board package that names it (west_board, see Which boards you can name), and flashed with the runner Zephyr’s own board definition declares:

# src/my_board/nros-board.toml names west_board = "nucleo_f767zi" (say);
# in system.toml:  [image.nucleo] board = "my-board"
nros build demo_bringup:nucleo
west flash -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__nucleo_west

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

nros build prints that west flash line when the build’s zephyr/runners.yaml names a flash runner. The runner (J-Link, nrfjprog, OpenOCD, pyOCD, …) and its probe are Zephyr’s and your bench’s; nano-ros adds nothing to them. The board must also have a network nano-ros can use.

Zephyr 4.x: select the RMW with a snippet

On 4.x, nano-ros ships west snippets so you pick the RMW on the build line instead of hand-writing the overlay:

west build -b native_sim/native/64 -S nros-cyclonedds apps/my_app
#                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  nros-zenoh | nros-cyclonedds | nros-xrce

The snippet (shipped via the module’s snippet_root) carries the RMW-common Kconfig — equivalent to merging prj-<rmw>.conf. It is for an app with NO system.toml: with one, the image’s rmw decides and merges after the snippet, so a snippet that agrees is redundant and one that names a different RMW is refused at configure time. The prj-<rmw>.conf / -DCONF_FILE path still works (and is the only option on 3.7).

nano-ros patches into your workspace

nano-ros needs a few patches to Zephyr’s native_sim NSOS driver (recvmsg, IPv4-multicast) so the host-loopback-based examples work. Both supported lines (3.7 LTS and 4.x) take the same path — nros setup zephyr reads zephyr/patches.yml and applies each patch against the workspace’s Zephyr tree, sha256-checked. No extra step on your side beyond the provisioning command (already run during Prerequisites).

To re-apply (e.g. after a west update reset the tree):

nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh

(Earlier nano-ros revisions documented a west patch apply flow on 4.x — that required a workspace-side west extension that doesn’t ship with stock Zephyr. Both lines now use the provisioner. Cyclone-DDS-on-Zephyr patches stay baked into the pinned cyclonedds submodule, not delivered through patches.yml.)

Start from an example

The copy-out talkers under examples/zephyr/<lang>/talker/ on GitHub, one per language, are copy-out clean, with no reference back into the nano-ros repository. Each is the same project as the quick start’s: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, whose launch file is generated. Their node sources are a starting point to copy into your own node packages.

The other roles are image rows of the language workspaces, examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, one bringup per behaviour: pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup. A Zephyr image id is zephyr_<role>, plus _<rmw> for any RMW other than zenoh, so

nros run pubsub_bringup:zephyr_listener_xrce

builds and runs the XRCE listener. The release does not ship examples/; nros new <ws> --board zephyr --template <role> --lang <c|cpp|rust> writes any role as a workspace of your own.

Cyclone idlc and the descriptor-gen scripts are located via the module’s exported cache vars (NROS_CYCLONE_IDLC, NROS_CYCLONE_SCRIPTS_DIR, NROS_CYCLONE_CMAKE_DIR); message-package dirs come from NROS_<PKG>_DIR env (defaulting to /opt/ros/humble/share/<pkg>). No /opt/ros or repo-relative paths are baked into the example.

See the zephyr/ module dir + its Kconfig for the canonical in-repo surface.

GitHub source

  • Zephyr module shell: zephyr/
  • Copy-out talkers: examples/zephyr/rust/talker/, examples/zephyr/c/talker/, examples/zephyr/cpp/talker/
  • The other roles: the zephyr_* image rows of the language workspaces’ pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup
  • Module manifest: zephyr/module.yml
  • Kconfig surface (canonical — every CONFIG_NROS* symbol the doc cites lives here): zephyr/Kconfig
  • Patches applied by nros setup zephyr (the west patch flow is retired): zephyr/patches.yml

Next

  • Pick a real board (Nordic, NXP, STM32, …): a board package naming its west_board, then Flash a real board.
  • Cyclone DDS on Cortex-A/R: see the DDS section of Choosing an RMW Backend for the required Kconfig deltas.
  • Build nano-ros’s own Zephyr examples without west: Zephyr in-tree examples (contributor).

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups.

A Zephyr App You Build with West

Support level: native_sim. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

In this chapter you add a ROS 2 talker to a Zephyr application that you already build with west build, run it on native_sim against a ROS 2 router, and then flash the same application to a real board. The application keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf; nano-ros joins it as one more Zephyr module.

What this assumes: a Linux host with ROS 2 Humble and its Zenoh middleware (ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp), the install done so nros is on your PATH, and some familiarity with west: a manifest, west update, west build -b <board>.

What it leaves for later: a project with several nodes, several boards, or a launch file. That is a nano-ros workspace, which the Zephyr chapter builds.

When to choose this

There are two ways to put a ROS 2 node on Zephyr.

  • A nano-ros workspace (nros new my_ws --board zephyr). Your code is node packages; a bringup package says which board each image runs on. nros build writes the Zephyr application for you and runs west build on it, and nros run starts it. You write no CMakeLists.txt for Zephyr and no prj.conf. Start there if you are starting fresh, or if the project will grow past one node. The Zephyr chapter covers it.
  • Your own west application (this chapter). The Zephyr application already exists, owns its build, and has its own drivers, devicetree and prj.conf. You want a ROS 2 node inside it, and you want west build and west flash to stay the commands you type.

The second road has no bringup and no system.toml. Everything nano-ros needs to know about the image comes from prj.conf, the way any Zephyr module is configured.

Set up the host and the west workspace

Zephyr’s host tools come first: west and the build tools Zephyr’s Getting Started lists. nros setup installs no system packages. On Debian or Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Provision the Zephyr SDK and the zenoh transport sources nano-ros compiles, then point Zephyr at that SDK:

nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"

nros locate tool zephyr-sdk prints where nros setup installed the Zephyr SDK version this release of nano-ros pins, so the line keeps working when that version changes. If you already have a Zephyr SDK that your workspace builds with, keep using it: set ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR to that one instead, or register it with the SDK’s own setup.sh -c.

If you already have a west workspace, skip the next block. This one pins Zephyr 3.7 and fetches only the modules nano-ros’s boards use:

mkdir -p my_zephyr_ws/manifest && cd my_zephyr_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools]
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"

The last project, zephyr-lang-rust, is Zephyr’s Rust support, at the revision nano-ros builds with on Zephyr 3.7. Only a Rust application uses it; leave it out if you write none.

nano-ros supports both the Zephyr 3.7 LTS line and the 4.x line; the version table lists what differs between them.

Add nano-ros to the build

nano-ros’s Zephyr module ships inside your nano-ros install. nros locate nano-ros prints the directory that holds it, and you hand that directory to west as an extra module:

west build -b native_sim/native/64 apps/my_app -- \
    -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)"

You do not add nano-ros to west.yml, and nothing is cloned. The command needs no network, so it is also safe inside your own scripts and CI.

If you would rather not type the option on every build, ask for the path once in the application’s CMakeLists.txt, before find_package(Zephyr):

execute_process(COMMAND nros locate nano-ros
    OUTPUT_VARIABLE NROS_MODULE_DIR
    OUTPUT_STRIP_TRAILING_WHITESPACE
    COMMAND_ERROR_IS_FATAL ANY)
list(APPEND ZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES "${NROS_MODULE_DIR}")

With either form, a plain west build picks the module up.

Write the application

The application is a stock Zephyr application with four files:

my_zephyr_ws/
├── zephyr/
├── modules/
└── apps/
    └── my_app/
        ├── CMakeLists.txt     # find_package(Zephyr), then the node
        ├── package.xml        # the message packages the node uses
        ├── prj.conf           # Zephyr's settings and nano-ros's
        └── src/
            └── Talker.c       # the node

The node, in C

The node is a component: a struct that holds its state and a configure function that creates its publishers, subscriptions and timers. You do not write main(). The module generates the application’s entry point, which initialises the RMW session, creates the node and executor, calls your configure, and then spins the executor.

mkdir -p apps/my_app/src
cat > apps/my_app/src/Talker.c <<'EOF'
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#include <rclc/rclc.h>
#include <std_msgs/std_msgs.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
} talker_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    talker_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, talker_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    std_msgs__msg__Int32 msg = {.data = self->count};
    if (rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL) == RCL_RET_OK) {
        printf("Published: %d\n", (int)self->count);
    }
    self->count++;
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                  talker_t* self) {
    setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IONBF, 0);
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, Int32), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000ULL * 1000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(talker_t, talker_configure)
EOF

It publishes a counter as std_msgs/Int32 on /chatter once a second. RCLC_C_COMPONENT registers the struct and its configure function with the generated entry point. The rest is the ROS 2 rclc API.

The build file

cat > apps/my_app/CMakeLists.txt <<'EOF'
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20.0)
find_package(Zephyr REQUIRED HINTS $ENV{ZEPHYR_BASE})
project(my_app)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN my_app::Talker
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED
    DEPLOY zephyr)
EOF

find_package(nano_ros) and find_package(std_msgs) are provided by the module. nano_ros_auto_add_library compiles your node source. nros_components_register_node registers the component, and DEPLOY zephyr is what makes the module generate the entry point into Zephyr’s app target. Your application’s other sources still go into app with target_sources, as before; nothing else about the file changes.

The C++ form

The same node in C++ is a class with a configure member. In place of Talker.c, write its header and its source:

mkdir -p apps/my_app/src
cat > apps/my_app/src/Talker.hpp <<'EOF'
#pragma once
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs.hpp"

namespace my_app {
class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::Int32> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int count_ = 0;
    void on_tick();

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};
}  // namespace my_app
EOF

cat > apps/my_app/src/Talker.cpp <<'EOF'
#include "Talker.hpp"
#include <cstdio>

namespace my_app {
void Talker::on_tick() {
    std_msgs::msg::Int32 m;
    m.data = count_;
    if (pub_.publish(m).ok()) {
        std::printf("Published: %d\n", count_);
    }
    ++count_;
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::setvbuf(stdout, nullptr, _IONBF, 0);
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}
}  // namespace my_app
EOF

::setvbuf turns off stdout’s buffering, so each line shows as soon as it is printed. It is the global one because Zephyr’s C++ library declares it only there.

The build file differs from the C one in two places: the project declares C++, and the registration names the class’s header.

cat > apps/my_app/CMakeLists.txt <<'EOF'
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20.0)
find_package(Zephyr REQUIRED HINTS $ENV{ZEPHYR_BASE})
project(my_app LANGUAGES C CXX)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.cpp)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    HEADER Talker.hpp
    PLUGIN my_app::Talker
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED
    DEPLOY zephyr)
EOF

Everything after this point is the same for the C and the C++ node.

Configure

nano-ros reads its settings from Kconfig, so they go in prj.conf beside Zephyr’s own, and west build -t menuconfig shows them under nros ROS 2 client library:

cat > apps/my_app/prj.conf <<'EOF'
# Zephyr: console and networking
CONFIG_LOG=y
CONFIG_PRINTK=y
CONFIG_NETWORKING=y
CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y
CONFIG_NET_UDP=y
CONFIG_NET_TCP=y
CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS=y
CONFIG_NET_L2_ETHERNET=y
CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONTEXTS=16
CONFIG_DNS_RESOLVER=n
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC=1000

# zenoh-pico runs on POSIX threads and wants room
CONFIG_POSIX_API=y
CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_MUTEX_COUNT=64
CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_COND_COUNT=16
CONFIG_POSIX_THREAD_THREADS_MAX=16
CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE=16384
CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE=65536
CONFIG_SYSTEM_WORKQUEUE_STACK_SIZE=4096
CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT=32
CONFIG_NET_PKT_TX_COUNT=32
CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT=64
CONFIG_NET_BUF_TX_COUNT=64

# nano-ros
CONFIG_NROS=y
CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API=y
CONFIG_STD_CPP17=y
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH=y
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR="tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"
CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
EOF

The nano-ros lines, one by one:

SettingWhat it chooses
CONFIG_NROS=yTurns the module on. Without it nano-ros adds nothing to the build.
CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API=yThe runtime library the generated entry point links. The entry point is C++ even when your node is C, so a C or C++ node both set this. CONFIG_NROS_RUST_API is for a Rust application (below).
CONFIG_STD_CPP17=yThe C++ standard the entry point compiles with.
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH=yThe middleware: CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH, CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE or CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS.
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATORWhere the zenoh router is. tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 is the default and suits native_sim, which uses the host’s sockets.
CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_IDThe ROS 2 domain. It must match the ROS_DOMAIN_ID of the nodes you talk to.

CONFIG_NROS_C_API is for an application that calls the C API (rclc/*.h) from its own main and registers no component. An application that registers its node with nros_components_register_node(... DEPLOY zephyr) is driven by the generated entry point, which is C++, so it sets CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API=y even when the node is C.

For XRCE-DDS, set CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE=y and name the agent with CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_ADDR and CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_PORT instead of a locator. Each middleware also needs some Zephyr settings of its own; What each RMW’s Zephyr-native fragment needs lists them.

Every other nano-ros setting (executor slots, buffer sizes, the zenoh session’s limits) is a Kconfig symbol too, set the same way. The Kconfig reference lists them with their defaults. Do not set CONFIG_NROS_ROS_EDITION: there is no such symbol, and Zephyr stops the build on a symbol it does not know.

On Zephyr 4.x you can also select the middleware on the build line with one of the module’s snippets, -S nros-zenoh, -S nros-xrce or -S nros-cyclonedds, instead of the CONFIG_NROS_RMW_* line (Zephyr 4.x: select the RMW with a snippet).

Messages

You do not run a generator. The build generates the C or C++ types for every message package the application depends on, and package.xml is where you list those packages, the same file a ROS 2 package uses:

cat > apps/my_app/package.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>my_app</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>A Zephyr application with a ROS 2 talker</description>
  <maintainer email="you@example.com">You</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>

  <depend>std_msgs</depend>

  <export>
    <build_type>nros_cmake</build_type>
  </export>
</package>
EOF

Each <depend> also gets a find_package(<pkg> REQUIRED) line in CMakeLists.txt. The C node then includes <std_msgs/std_msgs.h> and the C++ node "std_msgs.hpp".

The message definitions come from the first of these that has the package: the directories in NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH, then a sourced ROS 2 install (AMENT_PREFIX_PATH), then copies nano-ros carries of a few standard packages. Those copies are one ROS 2 distro’s, so build from a shell that has sourced your ROS 2 install (source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash): the types then match your ROS 2 peers. A Rust application’s nros configure (below) does not fall back to the copies at all. For your own messages, keep them in a ROS 2 interface package (its package.xml and msg/ directory) anywhere on disk, add the directory that holds it to NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH, and depend on it like any other.

Build

From the top of the west workspace, build for native_sim:

west build -b native_sim/native/64 -S nros-nsos apps/my_app -- \
    -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)"

native_sim builds the application as a program for your machine, so there is no emulator. The nros-nsos snippet routes its sockets to the host’s (Zephyr’s NSOS). Without it, native_sim tries to create a TAP interface (eth_posix: Cannot create zeth), which needs privileges an ordinary user or a container does not have, and the talker never reaches the router.

Run on native_sim

ROS 2 provides the router. Start it on the port the talker dials:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

With the router running, in another terminal, start the talker:

./build/zephyr/zephyr.exe

Published: 1
Published: 2

west build -t run does the same. To see the messages from ROS 2, in a third terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/Int32 --qos-reliability best_effort

The talker publishes best-effort. ros2 topic echo asks for reliable delivery unless told otherwise, and then receives nothing.

Flash a real board

The board here is ST’s Nucleo-F767ZI (Zephyr’s nucleo_f767zi). Its ST-LINK debugger is also a USB serial port, so the talker can reach the router over that cable, with no network on the board at all. Zenoh calls this a serial link.

Provision the board, and add its HAL, hal_stm32, to the west workspace. nros setup board applies nano-ros’s changes for the board to the workspace:

nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --rmw zenoh
sed -i 's/net-tools]/net-tools, hal_stm32]/' manifest/west.yml
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
nros setup board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$PWD"

Zephyr reads boards/<board>.conf and boards/<board>.overlay from the application directory after prj.conf, for that board only, so the native_sim build stays as it is. The settings turn the IP stack off, carry zenoh over USART3 (the ST-LINK port), move the console to USART6 (pins D0 and D1, for a USB-to-UART adapter), and size the image for the board’s 384 KiB of RAM:

mkdir -p apps/my_app/boards
cat > apps/my_app/boards/nucleo_f767zi.conf <<'EOF'
# zenoh over USART3, the ST-LINK USB serial port; no IP stack
CONFIG_NETWORKING=n
CONFIG_NROS_TRANSPORT_SERIAL=y
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR="serial/serial@40004800#baudrate=115200"
CONFIG_SERIAL=y
CONFIG_UART_INTERRUPT_DRIVEN=y
CONFIG_RING_BUFFER=y
CONFIG_MAIN_THREAD_PRIORITY=5

# no network driver brings up the RNG, so zenoh's session id uses this one
CONFIG_TEST_RANDOM_GENERATOR=y

# 384 KiB of RAM
CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE=16384
CONFIG_NROS_MAX_LARGE_SUBSCRIBERS=0
EOF
cat > apps/my_app/boards/nucleo_f767zi.overlay <<'EOF'
/ {
	chosen {
		zephyr,console = &usart6;
		zephyr,shell-uart = &usart6;
	};
};
EOF

Build for the board, into its own build directory:

west build -p always -b nucleo_f767zi -d build-board apps/my_app -- \
    -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)"

Zephyr warns that prj.conf’s networking settings (NET_IPV4, NET_TCP and the rest) were assigned y but got n. That is expected: the board file turned networking off, and the warnings do not stop the build.

Plug the board in, start the router on its serial port (the ST-LINK port is usually /dev/ttyACM0), and flash it with Zephyr’s own runner:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["serial//dev/ttyACM0#baudrate=115200"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

west flash -d build-board

ros2 topic echo, as on native_sim, then shows the counter:

data: 1
---
data: 2
---

Without the board, the same image runs in the board’s emulator: the probe for this chapter boots build-board/zephyr/zephyr.elf in Renode’s nucleo_f767zi machine, with USART3 on a host serial port, instead of flashing it, and checks that ros2 topic echo hears it. The flash runner (OpenOCD, pyOCD, J-Link and so on) and the probe are Zephyr’s and your bench’s; nano-ros adds nothing to them.

To use the board’s Ethernet instead, leave out the serial lines: keep CONFIG_NETWORKING=y with the board’s Ethernet driver and an address, and set CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR to the router’s address on that network, for example "tcp/192.0.2.10:7447", with the router listening on tcp/0.0.0.0:7447.

A Rust application

A Rust application is built by Zephyr’s Rust support (zephyr-lang-rust, the last project in the manifest above): its CMakeLists.txt calls rust_cargo_application(), which builds the application’s crate with cargo and links it into the image. The node is the same talker, written as a nano-ros Rust component.

zephyr-lang-rust needs three things a C application does not: the Rust target the Zephyr board implies (x86_64-unknown-none for native_sim/native/64 on an x86_64 host), rustup’s clippy (it lints every Rust application as part of the build), and clang with libclang, for the bindings it generates from Zephyr’s headers. nros setup board adds the target and applies nano-ros’s changes to the west workspace, without which zephyr-lang-rust’s cargo command carries none of nano-ros’s settings for the board. From the top of the west workspace:

. "$HOME/.cargo/env"     # the cargo the install set up
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends clang libclang-dev
rustup component add clippy
nros setup board zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$PWD"

The application is a crate whose library is named rustapp and built as a static library: rust_cargo_application() links librustapp.a, whatever the package is called. In place of the C application’s source and build file, write the crate, its build script and its node:

mkdir -p apps/my_app/src
cat > apps/my_app/CMakeLists.txt <<'EOF'
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20.0)
find_package(Zephyr REQUIRED HINTS $ENV{ZEPHYR_BASE})
project(my_app)

rust_cargo_application()
EOF
cat > apps/my_app/Cargo.toml <<'EOF'
[package]
name = "my_app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
name = "rustapp"
crate-type = ["staticlib"]

[dependencies]
zephyr = "0.1.0"
log = "0.4"
nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["alloc", "rmw-cffi", "macros"] }
nros-platform = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["platform-zephyr"] }
nros-rmw-zenoh = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["platform-zephyr"] }
std_msgs = { version = "*", default-features = false }

[build-dependencies]
zephyr-build = "0.1.0"
nros-zephyr-build = "*"

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"
lto = true
debug = false
EOF
cat > apps/my_app/build.rs <<'EOF'
fn main() {
    zephyr_build::export_kconfig_bool_options();
    nros_zephyr_build::bake_nros_config();
}
EOF
cat > apps/my_app/src/lib.rs <<'EOF'
#![no_std]

extern crate zephyr;

use nros::{
    Callback, CallbackCtx, Component, DeclarativeNode, ExecutableNode, NodeContext, NodeOptions,
    NodeResult, TimerDuration,
};
use std_msgs::msg::Int32;

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "talker";
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
        let chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<Int32>("/chatter")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick").publishes_entity(&chatter)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    type State = i32;
    const HAS_TICK: bool = false;

    fn init() -> Self::State {
        0
    }

    fn on_callback(count: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
        if callback.as_str() == "on_tick" {
            let msg = Int32 { data: *count };
            if ctx.publish_to_topic::<Int32, 16>("/chatter", &msg).is_ok() {
                log::info!("Published: {}", *count);
            }
            *count += 1;
        }
    }
}

nros::node!(Talker);

// Keeps the zenoh backend in the static library, then generates the
// application's entry point around the component.
nros::force_link_backend!(nros_rmw_zenoh);
nros::zephyr_component_main!(crate::Talker);
EOF

Write prj.conf and package.xml as for the C application (Configure, Messages), then change two lines of prj.conf: a Rust application selects CONFIG_NROS_RUST_API (which needs CONFIG_RUST, Zephyr’s switch for zephyr-lang-rust) instead of CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API, and needs no C++ standard:

sed -i -e '/^CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API=y$/d' -e '/^CONFIG_STD_CPP17=y$/d' apps/my_app/prj.conf
cat >> apps/my_app/prj.conf <<'EOF'
CONFIG_RUST=y
CONFIG_NROS_RUST_API=y
EOF
``` The other settings stay as they are. `build.rs` hands the Kconfig
values to the crate, among them the locator and the domain, so they are still
set in `prj.conf` alone.

The crate names the nano-ros crates and `std_msgs` but does not say where they
come from. `nros configure`, run in the application directory, generates the
Rust types for the message packages `package.xml` lists, under `generated/`,
and writes `.cargo/config.toml`, which points the nano-ros crates at your
nano-ros install and the message crates at `generated/`. Run it before the
first `west build`, and again when `package.xml` changes. It generates the
types from your ROS 2 install, so source it first; the configure records the
prefix, and a later `nros configure` of the application needs no sourced
shell:

```bash probe=49 track=installed variant=west-app-rust
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cd apps/my_app && nros configure && cd ../..

From there the application builds and runs as the C one does: the same west build line, and the same run on native_sim. The log line reads <inf> nros: rustapp: Published: 1, from Zephyr’s logger.

If it doesn’t work

Could not find a package configuration file provided by "nano_ros". The module is not in the build. Check that nros locate nano-ros prints a directory, and that the build line passes it as -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES after the --.

attempt to assign the value ... to the undefined symbol NROS_.... The symbol is misspelled or does not exist. Search for it in west build -t menuconfig (/ searches). CONFIG_NROS_ROS_EDITION is a common one: it does not exist.

No Published: line within 30 seconds.

  1. Check that the router is running and listening on the port in CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR.
  2. On native_sim, check that the build line has -S nros-nsos. A line eth_posix: Cannot create zeth in the output means it did not.
  3. Check CONFIG_NETWORKING=y, CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y and CONFIG_NET_TCP=y in prj.conf. Zephyr’s networking is opt-in.

A message with an unbounded string or sequence field fails to generate, asking for a bound. nano-ros sizes its buffers at build time, so a field with no stated maximum needs one. Put it in an nros-codegen.toml beside package.xml:

[fields]
"std_msgs/String.data" = 256

The Zephyr 4.x line says Could NOT find Python3 ... required is at least "3.12". Zephyr 4.x needs Python 3.12 or newer for west and its build scripts.

For anything else, Troubleshooting: First 10 Minutes walks through the common failures.

Design background

A nano-ros project is normally a workspace, and its bringup’s system.toml says what runs where. An application that owns its own build stays outside that model on purpose (RFC-0121 D6): nano-ros joins the build the way any library would, and asks the build for nothing back. For Zephyr, that application is a guest (RFC-0085 D14): it loads nano-ros as a module, states the middleware, locator and domain in Kconfig, and builds with west alone. With no system.toml beside it, the module gives every nano-ros setting its Kconfig prompt, so prj.conf, menuconfig and -DCONFIG_* are the one source of its configuration.

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0085: Zephyr workspace and west handoff

Nucleo-F767ZI (Zephyr, Renode twin)

Support level: nucleo-f767zi-zephyr. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

One talker on an ST Nucleo-F767ZI (STM32F767ZI, Cortex-M7) running Zephyr 3.7, talking to ROS 2 over the board’s USB serial port. You do not need the board: Renode emulates it on your machine, and its USART3, the UART the Nucleo’s ST-LINK carries to your USB port, is wired to your host the way the cable would be. No network is configured anywhere in this chapter; ethernet comes after it.

This chapter assumes a Linux x86_64 host (or the container the install page describes) with a C/C++ compiler, ROS 2 Humble with ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp, and the install done, so nros is on your PATH. It uses Zephyr’s own tools the way the Zephyr chapter does; read that one for what each piece is. WiFi is deferred to the Zephyr 4.4 line, where the Pico W’s WiFi driver exists, so no chapter here opens over WiFi yet.

Provision the board

Zephyr’s host tools first: west and the build tools Zephyr’s Getting Started lists (nros setup installs no system packages). On Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Then the board:

nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"
