That fetches what the board needs into a shared store under ~/.nros: the Zephyr SDK, the zenoh-pico sources, the Rust target, and Renode, the emulator the board runs in here. It installs no router: the router is ROS’s rmw_zenohd, from the ROS 2 install above.

A west workspace that pins Zephyr 3.7 and fetches only the modules this board builds with, hal_stm32 among them (import: true would fetch every vendor HAL):

mkdir -p nucleo_ws/manifest && cd nucleo_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools, hal_stm32]
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"

Last, give the workspace the patches nano-ros carries for Zephyr 3.7:

nros setup board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --zephyr-workspace .

Scaffold the talker

nros new nucleo_ws --board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --template talker --lang c
cd nucleo_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages: src/nucleo_node/, the C talker, and src/nucleo_node_bringup/, whose system.toml ends in the [image.zephyr] block naming the board. The Zephyr application itself is generated under build/ when you build. The board reaches the zenoh router on your host through USART3, which Zephyr calls serial@40004800, at 115200 baud. Say so with one line at the end of the bringup’s system.toml:

echo 'locator = "serial/serial@40004800#baudrate=115200"' >> src/nucleo_node_bringup/system.toml

The line lands in the [image.zephyr] block, under the board = "nucleo-f767zi-zephyr" line the scaffold wrote. The board’s own configuration already turns Zephyr’s IP stack off and gives USART3 to zenoh; its console is USART6.

Run in the twin

Source ROS 2, then build and run. ROS 2 provides the router, and its message definitions are what the build generates the talker’s std_msgs code from. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later runs of it need no sourced shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run nucleo_node --expect 'Publishing:'

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

nros run generates what the build reads (the message code and the board’s build settings, under build/), builds the firmware through west (the first build takes a few minutes; later ones take seconds), boots it in Renode’s nucleo_f767zi machine with USART3 on a terminal device of your host, starts rmw_zenohd on that device, and then lets the board run. What it prints is the board’s console, USART6: *** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***, then the talker’s Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' and on. With --expect it stops everything and exits 0 at the first console line containing that text, and exits 1 if the board stops first.

Without --expect it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C. Start it that way in one terminal:

nros run nucleo_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

See it from ROS 2

In a second terminal, ask ROS 2 for the topic. The router nros run started also listens where a ROS 2 node on this machine looks for one, so nothing needs to be configured:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

The talker publishes best-effort, so the echo asks for best-effort too. Ctrl-C in the first terminal stops Renode and the router together.

Ethernet

The Nucleo’s on-chip ethernet MAC works in Renode: the talker reached a router over tcp/ with Zephyr’s eth_stm32_hal driver in an early spike. That run needed a host tap device bridged to Renode’s virtual switch, which takes CAP_NET_ADMIN (the spike made one inside a rootless network namespace), and nros run does not set one up yet. So this chapter stops at serial; the ethernet chapter comes with that support.

Flash a real board

On the bench, nros flash programs the same image through Zephyr’s own runner for the board, OpenOCD over the Nucleo’s ST-LINK:

nros flash

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

On the real board USART3 is the ST-LINK’s virtual COM port, so the zenoh link arrives on your host as a USB serial device (/dev/ttyACM0, say), and the router listens there instead of on Renode’s terminal device. The console, USART6, is on the board’s pins rather than on the USB cable.

If it didn’t work

  • nros run names what failed and the log it wrote. no runner package drives or the plan's tools name no renode: run the nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr step again, which installs Renode.
  • A router that would not start usually means rmw_zenohd was not found (source your ROS 2 setup in that terminal) or another router already holds port 7447 on this machine.
  • A build that cannot find hal_stm32: the west workspace predates the hal_stm32 line in its allowlist; add it and run west update again.
  • Everything else: Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes.

Where to go next

  • What each Zephyr piece is - Zephyr (west module).
  • The same talker on QEMU, with no Zephyr - First Project.
  • Talk to a real ROS 2 system - ROS 2 Interoperability.

NuttX (apps/external)

Support level: qemu-armv7a-nuttx, rv-virt-nuttx. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on NuttX. nano-ros plugs into the standard NuttX app discovery as an external app under apps/external/nano-ros/, exposing Kconfig knobs under Application Configuration → External Modules → nano-ros. Use this entry when your NuttX board ships its own kernel build and you want to add ROS 2 communication.

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → in-tree examples.

Prereqs. Install the nros CLI once per machine, then run nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx --rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds> (--rmw defaults to zenoh). This fetches a mostly-prebuilt toolchain set into ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk — the NuttX cross-compiler, the emulator and the NuttX sources — so you do not hand-install a cross-toolchain. The zenoh router is ROS’s rmw_zenohd and comes from a ROS 2 install; the xrce path needs only the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent, which nros setup … --rmw xrce installs:

nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx --rmw zenoh

(nros is the installed CLI — Installation.)

The NuttX-managed road below (apps/external, NuttX’s own make) also needs a NuttX ≥ nuttx-12 checkout of your own with an apps/ sibling; the nros build road does not.

Project layout

NuttX’s “external apps” pattern places the app shim under $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/<name>/:

$NUTTX_DIR/                              # NuttX kernel checkout
$NUTTX_APPS_DIR/                             # sibling: apps tree
└── external/
    └── nano-ros/                        # symlink to the SDK root's
        ├── Make.defs                    #   integrations/nuttx/
        ├── Makefile
        ├── CMakeLists.txt               #   (cmake-driven NuttX builds)
        └── Kconfig
nx_ws/                                   # your application: a workspace
└── src/
    ├── nx_node/                         # node package: package.xml, Cargo.toml | CMakeLists.txt, the node
    └── nx_node_bringup/                 # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

Wire the shell into your NuttX apps tree. Two commands, both run once:

nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx --rmw zenoh    # toolchain + NuttX sources + SDK
sdk="$(nros locate nano-ros)"   # this project's nano-ros SDK root
"$sdk/scripts/nuttx/stage-external-apps.sh" "$NUTTX_APPS_DIR"

The staging script writes $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/Make.defs + Kconfig and symlinks the integration shell in as external/nano-ros. (The SDK root carries integrations/ in releases cut after 0.6.0-nros4.) Menuconfig surfaces it under Application Configuration → External Modules.

The script stages the integration shell only. A bringup with several components is not built through the apps tree: give it an [image.<id>] with board = "qemu-armv7a-nuttx" and run nros build — see [image.nuttx] in examples/workspaces/rust. The script’s old --bringup <dir> / --image <id> flags staged a per-bringup app that could not build an image, and now refuse.

If you’d rather wire it yourself (e.g. into a vendored apps tree):

ln -s "$sdk/integrations/nuttx" \
      $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/nano-ros
# then copy integrations/nuttx/external-Make.defs.in →
# $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/Make.defs and add a matching
# $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/Kconfig that `source`s the shell.

Configure

NuttX uses Kconfig as its single source of truth. After the symlink above:

cd $NUTTX_DIR
make menuconfig
# Navigate to:
#   Application Configuration → External Modules → nano-ros
#   [*] nano-ros ROS 2 client
#       RMW backend  →  zenoh           # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
#       ROS 2 edition →  humble

Networking Kconfig requirements live under Networking Support — enable CONFIG_NET, CONFIG_NET_TCP, CONFIG_NET_IPv4. For QEMU nsh_smp configurations the defaults already include these.

Those Kconfig knobs govern what the integration shell compiles into libnros_c.a — NuttX’s build owns that, the way Zephyr’s Kconfig owns its lane. They are not where your application states its deployment, and the two must name the same RMW.

Your application’s deployment — board, RMW, domain id, and an optional locator — is declared in the bringup’s system.toml and baked at compile time. With a locator added, src/nx_node_bringup/system.toml reads:

[system]
name = "nx_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "nx_node"
class = "nx_node::Talker"
name = "nx_node"

[image.nuttx]
board = "qemu-armv7a-nuttx"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:8200"

The file is the same whatever language the node is written in — a C or C++ node’s package.xml has no <nano_ros …/> tuple and its CMakeLists.txt names no board. Nor does anything here name a target triple: armv7a-nuttx-eabihf is a fact about the board, and it lives in the board descriptor. The next build picks an edit to this file up, regenerating the message bindings and the build settings the board choice implies.

The guest network shape (eth0 10.0.2.15, Slirp gateway 10.0.2.2 — QEMU’s own network, which the board’s [board.net] network = "qemu" names) comes from the board; add a locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:<port>" field to [image.<id>] to dial a non-default router port. The prebuilt test fixtures bake distinct per-language allocator ports so parallel suites don’t collide on one router. Start the router (ROS’s rmw_zenohd) on the port your app dials — it must listen on 0.0.0.0, not loopback, because the guest reaches it through QEMU’s Slirp gateway:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:8200"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Build

Two roads, and they differ in who owns the NuttX kernel build.

nros build — the path for a nano-ros workspace. The board in the bringup (qemu-armv7a-nuttx for Arm virt, rv-virt-nuttx for RISC-V rv-virt) picks the cross toolchain and the NuttX board config; nros build links your node into a bootable NuttX kernel ELF. Provision the board (no NuttX checkout of your own is needed on this road — nros setup fetches the kernel and apps sources), then scaffold a workspace for it and build:

nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx --rmw zenoh --sudo

The NuttX kernel build needs two host packages a fresh Debian/Ubuntu host may lack — the Python venv module and unzip. nros setup names any that are missing before fetching anything; --sudo lets it run the one install command it composed for your package manager (sudo apt-get install -y python3-venv unzip here) before the download starts. Leave --sudo off and it only prints that command, and never runs sudo for you.

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros new nx_ws --board qemu-armv7a-nuttx --template talker --lang c    # or --lang cpp
cd nx_ws
nros build

A Rust node is the same scaffold with --lang rust. For it, nros build configures and exports the NuttX kernel from the board’s defconfig first (the same step the C/C++ road runs inside its configure; a current export is a no-op), then builds the entry with the board’s pinned nightly:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros new nx_ws --board qemu-armv7a-nuttx --template talker --lang rust
cd nx_ws
nros build

Either way nros build prepares the build itself (message bindings, the generated entry), and the kernel ELF lands under build/; nros build prints its path with the QEMU line that boots it. nros build --dry-run shows the native commands.

NuttX’s own build — the integration shell in a NuttX-managed tree. NuttX owns the build verb there, make from the configured kernel, the way Zephyr owns west build. NuttX’s make does not prepare a nano-ros workspace, so prepare it first, in the workspace, because the generated message bindings must exist before anything compiles against them:

cd nx_ws
nros configure                      # bindings + settings from the bringup

cd $NUTTX_DIR
make                                # full kernel + apps build

The Cargo build of nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs runs as a sub-step of the NuttX app build; libnros_c.a is linked at the final app link stage. The kernel ELF is $NUTTX_DIR/nuttx.

For a CMake-driven NuttX build, NuttX’s own CMake takes one BOARD_CONFIG=<board>:<config> and finds apps/ beside the kernel tree (-DNUTTX_APPS_DIR=<dir> names another):

cmake -S "$NUTTX_DIR" -B build -DBOARD_CONFIG=qemu-armv7a:nsh -GNinja
cmake --build build                 # the ELF is build/nuttx

Stock qemu-armv7a:nsh has no networking; merge the nano-ros requirements into it as described under Auto-configure glue below.

Run on QEMU (Arm virt)

QEMU is the store’s build (nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx installed it), on QEMU’s virt machine with virtio-net on Slirp — the line nros build prints. Two terminals: the router, then the board.

1. The router on the host (Slirp forwards 10.0.2.2:<port> → host). It must listen on 0.0.0.0 for the Slirp gateway; match whatever locator your app bakes — 7447 when it states none, as a scaffolded image; 8200 in the example above:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

2. The board — from the workspace root:

nros run nx_node

nros run boots the kernel ELF with the board’s runner: the store’s qemu-system-arm on the virt machine, virtio-net on Slirp, and -icount shift=auto. (A make-built kernel is $NUTTX_DIR/nuttx; boot it with the same QEMU line, which nros build --dry-run prints.)

An image nros build produced starts its application itself. The scaffolded talker publishes Hello World: N once a second, in every language:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

A stock ROS 2 peer can echo it:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

A make-built kernel boots to the NSH prompt instead; run your app’s PROGNAME there — the make-driven build registers every nano-ros example as a built-in command via Application.mk’s -Dmain=<PROGNAME>_main rename, e.g. nsh> nuttx_c_talker (C) or nsh> nuttx_cpp_talker (C++).

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it (Ctrl-A x for a QEMU you started yourself).

Readiness signal. Once the image boots (a make-built kernel: once you type the app’s NSH command, e.g. nuttx_c_talker), expect its first line on the NSH console within ~6 seconds — Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' from the scaffolded and in-tree Rust, C and C++ talkers, which start the count at 1 like the official ROS 2 demo talker. If no Publishing: line:

  1. Confirm the app actually ran — ps should show your task.
  2. Confirm networking — ifconfig shows a configured interface. With the virtio-net + Slirp wiring above, eth0 comes up at 10.0.2.15 (the board’s default on QEMU’s network; an image’s net address overrides it).
  3. Confirm zenohd reachable; the image’s locator must match the router’s listen port.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Run on QEMU (RISC-V rv-virt)

The rv-virt-nuttx board (rv32imac) boots on QEMU’s RISC-V virt machine. The store’s QEMU is built for Arm and RISC-V 64 only, so this board needs a qemu-system-riscv32 from your distribution (Debian/Ubuntu: qemu-system-misc):

nros setup rv-virt-nuttx --rmw zenoh --sudo
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-misc

Name it with QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32 and nros build prints a line that uses it; without it the printed line asks nros locate tool qemu-system-riscv32, which then has nothing to answer. Scaffold for this board and build:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros new nx_ws --board rv-virt-nuttx --template talker --lang c
cd nx_ws
export QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32="$(command -v qemu-system-riscv32)"
nros build

A Rust node builds for this board the same way as for Arm. The kernel step uses rv-virt’s own defconfig, and the target is the board’s riscv32imac-unknown-nuttx-elf spec, built with build-std:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32="$(command -v qemu-system-riscv32)"
nros new nx_ws --board rv-virt-nuttx --template talker --lang rust
cd nx_ws
nros build

Start the router as above (on the port your image’s locator names), then boot it; nros run uses the qemu-system-riscv32 that QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32 names:

nros run nx_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

Auto-configure glue (NSH built-in registration)

The make-driven build above relies on a host-side glue layer. In-tree that is scripts/nuttx/stage-external-apps.sh plus kconfig-tweak. If you wire the integration shell into your own NuttX tree by hand, reproduce the same three steps:

  1. Bring the required symbols into your config. Stock NuttX qemu-armv7a/nsh ships without CONFIG_NET=y, virtio-net, or TLS_NELEM. If you have no config of your own, copy the board defconfig packages/boards/nros-board-nuttx-qemu/nuttx-config/arm/defconfig to $NUTTX_DIR/.config and run make olddefconfig. If you already maintain a vendor defconfig, do NOT clobber it — merge the nano-ros requirements into it instead (CONFIG_NET=y, the virtio-net / netdev options, CONFIG_TLS_NELEM=8, CONFIG_LIBCXXTOOLCHAIN=y, CONFIG_ALLSYMS=n; diff the board defconfig against nsh for the authoritative list) and re-run make olddefconfig.
  2. Stage the integration shell. Run scripts/nuttx/stage-external-apps.sh "$NUTTX_APPS_DIR" to symlink integrations/nuttx/ into $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/external/. Remove $NUTTX_APPS_DIR/Kconfig so NuttX’s mkkconfig.sh rediscovers the new apps/external/Kconfig.
  3. Flip the nano-ros Kconfig knobs via kconfig-tweak. The recipe enables NROS, NROS_C_API, NROS_CPP_API, every NROS_EXAMPLE_<EX>_<LANG>, sets TLS_NELEM=8, disables LIBCXXNONE + enables LIBCXXTOOLCHAIN, and disables ALLSYMS for the bootstrap link. Re-run make olddefconfig so the newly-visible dependencies settle, then make.

kconfig-tweak ships in the kconfig-frontends package on most distros. Without it the recipe skips ("NuttX skip: kconfig-tweak not on PATH"); install it before retrying.

Flash a real board

nano-ros has no NuttX hardware board of its own: both boards above are QEMU machines. On real hardware the image is an ordinary NuttX application, so it goes to the board the way NuttX’s documentation for that board says — build the board’s own BOARD_CONFIG with the integration shell staged as above, then flash nuttx (or nuttx.bin / nuttx.hex) with the board’s tool:

cmake -S "$NUTTX_DIR" -B build -DBOARD_CONFIG=<board>:<config> -GNinja
cmake --build build
openocd -f board/<your-board>.cfg -c "program build/nuttx verify reset exit"

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

(OpenOCD is an example; NuttX boards also flash with J-Link, dfu-util, esptool or a vendor tool, as the board’s page says.)

GitHub source

  • NuttX integration shell: integrations/nuttx/
  • Copy-out NuttX QEMU talkers, one per language, each the same project as the one this page scaffolds: examples/qemu-armv7a-nuttx/rust/talker/, examples/qemu-armv7a-nuttx/c/talker/, examples/qemu-armv7a-nuttx/cpp/talker/
  • The listener, service and action examples: the nuttx_* and riscv_nuttx_* image rows of the language workspaces, examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, under pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup (nros run pubsub_bringup:nuttx_listener)
  • Kconfig schema: integrations/nuttx/Kconfig

  • DDS on NuttX: bump the netbuffer Kconfig knobs (similar to the Zephyr DDS profile under Choosing an RMW Backend).

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups.

ThreadX (Linux sim / RISC-V64 QEMU)

Support level: threadx-linux, rv-virt-threadx. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on Microsoft Azure RTOS ThreadX + NetX Duo (BSD socket layer). Two flavours:

  • threadx-linux — ThreadX user-space simulator on Linux. Fast build, host network stack, ideal for development.
  • threadx-riscv64 — QEMU virt machine with the RISC-V64 GCC toolchain. Full kernel + NetX Duo TCP/IP stack.

Rust, C, and C++ are supported on both flavours.

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → per-platform lanes.

See the coverage matrix for the per-RMW cell status.

Prereqs. Install the nros CLI once, then run nros setup <board> --rmw <rmw> for the flavour you need (see Setup). It provisions the cross-compiler, emulator, and ThreadX/NetX sources — no hand-installed riscv64 cross toolchain or qemu-system-riscv64. The zenoh path additionally needs a ROS 2 install for the router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd); xrce needs only the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent, which nros setup installs.

Setup

nros setup is the single canonical command to prepare a machine to build nano-ros for a board. Most components are prebuilt per platform per RMW — the cross-compiler, emulator, and SDK sources (the ThreadX/NetX sources, and for threadx-linux the POSIX-sim sources) are fetched from a pinned index into a shared store at ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk. The zenoh router is NOT among them — it comes from a ROS 2 install; only the xrce agent is provisioned by nros setup.

Packages are prebuilt where the index has a binary for your host and built from source otherwise. --dry-run prints the plan for your host. See Installation Details for the full explanation.

With the nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), provision the ThreadX flavour you need (+ the RMW; --rmw defaults to zenoh). The POSIX-sim flavour:

nros setup threadx-linux --rmw zenoh

and, if you need the RISC-V64 QEMU flow:

nros setup rv-virt-threadx --rmw zenoh

The RMW host daemon must be running before any example: for zenoh the ROS 2 router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd), for xrce the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent (installed by nros setup … --rmw xrce).

Project layout

nros new scaffolds a workspace for one board, in any of the three languages. threadx names two boards, so name the one you want with --board:

nros new tx_ws --board threadx-linux --template talker --lang c   # or rv-virt-threadx; --lang cpp
cd tx_ws

nros new tx_ws --board threadx-linux --template talker --lang rust
cd tx_ws

nros new tx_ws --board rv-virt-threadx --template talker --lang rust
cd tx_ws

tx_ws/
└── src/
    ├── tx_node/                 # node package: package.xml + CMakeLists.txt (or Cargo.toml), the talker
    └── tx_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

tx_node is a library with no main() that names no board; the ThreadX startup that runs it is generated from the bringup’s image at build time.

The two flavours differ in the board = line of their image — nothing else. Everything else follows the board. threadx-linux builds for the host triple (its Rust entry is still #![no_std]), so its board contributes no target triple; rv-virt-threadx cross-compiles, and its triple, link group and emulator all come from the board descriptor — never from your package. nros build resolves the choice into the generated entry and its settings under build/, and the entry is what depends on the board crate, so nothing you write names it.

ThreadX-linux runs as a regular host process — no QEMU. NetX Duo uses the nx_bsd_* BSD socket shim layered on the host TCP stack (threadx-linux variant) or on its own NetX Duo TCP/IP stack (riscv64 variant).

Why there are two board crates and one arch port

The two flavours look like one board with two targets, and they are not. nano-ros ships three ThreadX packages, in three layers:

PackageLayerWhat it owns
nros-board-threadxfamily driverthe kernel/NetX build and the generic run_entry boot path both boards call
nros-board-threadx-port-riscv64arch porta fork of upstream’s ports/risc-v64/gnu: tx_port.h + five context-switch .S files
nros-board-threadx-{linux,qemu-riscv64}board overlaydefaults, console/exit/panic, and the network bring-up

The arch port is the reason the two boards did not merge. Upstream’s RISC-V64 port types ULONG as unsigned long — 8 bytes on rv64 — but NetX Duo’s packet code does ULONG * arithmetic assuming 4-byte words, so nano-ros retypes it to unsigned int, matching upstream’s own Linux and AArch64 ports. That retype shifts every field offset inside TX_THREAD, and the port’s context-switch assembly loads those fields at hard-coded offsets — so the header change forces the assembly to be forked with it. threadx-linux needs none of this, because upstream’s Linux port already types ULONG as 4 bytes.

That is architecture code, not board code: a second RISC-V64 ThreadX board would need every line of it unchanged, and folding it into a crate that also serves Linux would mean cfg-gating RISC-V assembly there. If you are porting to another RISC-V64 ThreadX board, depend on the arch port and write only the overlay — see Custom boards.

One rule matters if you build ThreadX outside the shipped recipes: the arch port’s inc/ must be searched before $THREADX_DIR/ports/risc-v64/gnu/inc. Get that wrong and the build succeeds against upstream’s 8-byte ULONG, and the symptom is corrupted packets at runtime rather than a compiler error. A _Static_assert(sizeof(ULONG) == 4, …) in packages/boards/nros-board-common/c/threadx_hooks.c turns that mistake into a build failure with a name on it.

Configure

Deployment is declared in the bringup’s system.toml, one image per flavour, and baked at compile time. The scaffold names its image after the platform, [image.threadx]. For the hosted flavour, with a locator added:

[system]
name = "tx_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "tx_node"
class = "tx_node::Talker"
name = "tx_node"

[image.threadx]
board = "threadx-linux"
locator = "tcp/127.0.0.1:9000"

The QEMU flavour adds the guest’s network identity, because it boots behind QEMU Slirp. Added beside the first, it takes a name of its own:

[image.threadx_rv]
board = "rv-virt-threadx"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:9400"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]    # [eth0] network = "qemu", host = 15

Both blocks can live in one bringup; the node package does not change. With two images, nros run tx_node no longer picks one, so name it (nros run threadx, nros run threadx_rv). Whatever the node’s language, the bringup carries the same keys; a C node’s CMakeLists.txt declares targets and nothing about the deployment, and its package.xml carries no <nano_ros …/> tuple. Anything the image does not state — the rest of the network shape — comes from the board crate’s defaults; see the Configuration Guide.

ThreadX-Linux normally uses a veth pair (tap-tx0) for an isolated host link, but nros setup threadx-linux does not create the interface — the test fixtures fall back to a loopback path when tap-tx0 is absent, which is fine for the happy-path tutorial. Bring up tap-tx0 by hand (ip link add … type veth …) only when you need real-network bridging. The QEMU-RISC-V64 fixture uses Slirp’s default 10.0.2.2 gateway just like the FreeRTOS QEMU flow.

Build

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

In the workspace root (tx_ws/, where nros new left you), whatever the language and flavour:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build first (message bindings, the generated entry for the image, its cargo or CMake settings), then hands off. There is no step to run before it.

First setup builds ThreadX + NetX Duo (~3 min). Subsequent builds finish in seconds. The binary lands under build/; nros build --dry-run prints the exact paths and the cargo or cmake lines, for driving the tool yourself (run nros configure first to write the generated entry without building). See When nros build drives the build.

After a successful build, nros build prints the artifact and the command that runs it.

Run on the Linux simulator

threadx-linux is an ordinary host process — no QEMU. First the router (ROS’s rmw_zenohd), on the port your image’s locator names — 7447 when it names none, as a scaffolded image; 9000 in the example above:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

Then the image, from the workspace root:

nros run tx_node

The scaffolded talker publishes std_msgs/String once a second, in every language:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

Run on QEMU (RISC-V 64)

rv-virt-threadx boots on QEMU’s RISC-V virt machine, UART on stdio, virtio-net on Slirp. Three terminals: the router, the board, and a stock ROS 2 peer.

1. The router, on the image’s port (7447 for a scaffolded image; 9400 in the example above). The guest dials 10.0.2.2:<p> through QEMU Slirp, so it listens on 0.0.0.0:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

2. The board — from the workspace root:

nros run tx_node

nros run boots the image with the board’s runner: the store’s qemu-system-riscv64 (nros setup rv-virt-threadx installed it) on the virt machine, with virtio-net on Slirp. A C or C++ node on this board runs the same way.

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

3. A stock ROS 2 peer (either flavour). The talker publishes best-effort; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing. Force best-effort to receive:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data:

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it.

Readiness signal. threadx-linux: Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' within a few seconds of the program starting on a warm cache; a cold first nros build compiles the Rust image (~80 s) before the first publish lands. threadx-riscv64 (QEMU): within ~15 seconds of QEMU boot. If no Publishing: line:

  1. Confirm the router is reachable on the image’s locator (threadx-linux uses 127.0.0.1; riscv64 QEMU uses 10.0.2.2).
  2. threadx-linux: if you brought up tap-tx0 by hand, confirm it is up; without it the fixtures use the loopback fallback, which is fine for this tutorial (nros setup threadx-linux does not create the interface).
  3. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Flash a real board

No real ThreadX board is supported. Both boards here are simulated — a Linux process and a QEMU machine — and nano-ros ships no ThreadX board package for physical hardware. A board of your own starts from the porting guide, with the nros-board-threadx family crate and the riscv64 arch port as the pieces to reuse; it is then flashed with that board vendor’s tooling.

Multi-tier scheduling

ThreadX supports the multi-tier workspace scheduling model: declare per-tier ThreadX priorities in the bringup’s system.toml with [tasks.<name>.threadx] priority tables, and the generated entry routes the app onto run_tiers — one executor per tier, all sharing one session, with per-tier stacks carved from the ThreadX byte pool. ThreadX priorities follow the native convention: lower number = higher priority. Tiers are sorted descending by raw priority number, so tiers[0] (the numerically-largest, i.e. lowest-priority tier) boots first and then adopts its declared priority. See Scheduling Models for the mechanics.

GitHub source

The copy-out talkers, each the same project as the one this page scaffolds:

  • ThreadX-Linux Rust: examples/threadx-linux/rust/talker/
  • ThreadX-Linux C: examples/threadx-linux/c/talker/
  • ThreadX-RISC-V64 Rust: examples/rv-virt-threadx/rust/talker/
  • Board crates: packages/boards/nros-board-threadx-linux/, packages/boards/nros-board-threadx-qemu-riscv64/

Next

  • Subscriber, service and action: the threadx_* and riscv_threadx_* image rows of the language workspaces, examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, under pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup (nros run pubsub_bringup:threadx_listener).
  • DDS on ThreadX: Cyclone DDS is the surviving DDS backend (nros-rmw-cyclonedds) — select it with [system] rmw = "cyclonedds" in the bringup’s system.toml and build again; see Choosing an RMW Backend.
  • Real hardware: same code runs against ThreadX vendor BSPs (Renesas Synergy, MIMXRT, etc.); replace the QEMU board crate with a vendor board crate.

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups.

Bare-metal Cortex-M3 (QEMU)

Support level: mps2-an385-baremetal. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on bare-metal Cortex-M3 (QEMU MPS2-AN385) — no RTOS, no kernel scheduler. Pure cooperative spin via zpico_spin_once. Rust only. nros-c / nros-cpp are not supported on bare-metal targets (they assume a hosted RTOS for startup / heap / libc); see the examples coverage matrix for the policy.

When to use this path: ultra-constrained Cortex-M0+ / M3 / M4 targets with no OS scheduler, no pthread. If you have FreeRTOS or any RTOS, use the FreeRTOS starter instead — it’s more ergonomic and produces smaller code overall.

Prereqs. Install the nros CLI once per machine (scripts/install.sh, see Installation), then provision this board. nros setup fetches a prebuilt bare-metal toolchain (arm-none-eabi-gcc, qemu-system-arm) plus the Rust thumbv7m-none-eabi target into a shared store — no manual cross-compiler install. It provides no zenoh router: that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd (see the RMW design), so running a zenoh image needs it from a ROS 2 install.

# Provision the bare-metal Cortex-M3 board (zenoh RMW is the default):
nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh

One key, not two: qemu-arm-baremetal is a retired spelling of the same entry. A board name states the reach of its build, and this build is true for one silicon part. Nothing extra is provisioned for physical hardware — no probe/flash tooling. For a real STM32F4 see the out-of-tree worked example.

Project layout

Scaffold a workspace for the board:

nros new bm_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd bm_ws

bm_ws/
└── src/
    ├── bm_node/                 # node package: package.xml, Cargo.toml (a library), src/lib.rs
    └── bm_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

bm_node is the talker, a library with no main() that names no board. The bringup’s system.toml holds one image, [image.baremetal]. There is no .cargo/ to edit: the target triple, the linker script, the --gc-sections flag, the QEMU runner and the [patch.crates-io] rows that resolve nano-ros’s crates all come from the board, and nros build writes them under build/ together with the generated entry it compiles.

The board crate is nros-board-mps2-an385 (note: no -freertos suffix — this is the bare-metal variant) which provides:

  • Cortex-M3 startup + linker script
  • LAN9118 driver for smoltcp
  • BoardIdle::wfi() for cooperative wait

Direct-exec or RTIC — one crate, two entry shapes

The same crate serves both bare-metal entry models. Both are names of the same board descriptor, so you pick the entry shape with the image’s board line — never a different board crate, and never an edit to the node package:

Entry shape[image.<id>] board =board crate feature the entry enables
direct-exec (inline spin loop)"mps2-an385-baremetal"board-entry
RTIC (framework-owned #[rtic::app], deferred dispatch)"rtic-mps2-an385"rtic

The generated entry depends on the board crate with the feature its shape needs, so an RTIC image differs from a direct-exec one in its board line. The RTIC examples in the Rust language workspace, examples/workspaces/rust (an RTIC talker and listener, and the RTIC service and action roles), are node packages of their own, each with an image row in its behaviour’s bringup that names rtic-mps2-an385.

The RTIC surface used to be a separate nros-board-rtic-mps2-an385 crate; it was folded in here because it depended on this crate and re-declared its Config — the two copies had drifted to different default IPs, which nothing catches until a node fails to reach the router.

Which network the defaults describe is stated by the board: its nros-board.toml says [board.net] network = "qemu", so Config::default() sits on QEMU’s own user-mode network (10.0.2.15/24, gateway and router 10.0.2.2) — the network every QEMU board shares. Config::qemu_slirp() is the same network at the RTIC entry’s own address (10.0.2.10, router port 7450). Either way, an image that sets its locator in its [image.<id>] and its address in a board network file ([eth0] network = "qemu", host = N) table overrides the default — which every in-tree example does, and which you should too. The address goes in the image’s board network file, named by os_config (below).

Configure

The whole deployment statement is the bringup’s system.toml. It is baked at compile time: the generated entry folds the image’s network identity into a DeployOverlay the board’s boot Config applies. With a locator and an address added, src/bm_node_bringup/system.toml reads:

[system]
name = "bm_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "bm_node"
class = "bm_node::Talker"
name = "bm_node"
dispatch = "deferred"

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:10500"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]

and the image’s address sits in the board network file it names, board-net.toml beside system.toml in the bringup (the board package owns the device, so its address lives in the board’s own file):

[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10

board picks the silicon and everything that follows from it; rmw picks the backend. Everything the board implies — triple, linker script, runner, cross compiler, [patch.crates-io], the board crate and its features — follows the board = line on the next nros build, so no linker flag and no triple ever moves by hand. The node package’s Cargo.toml names no board crate, RMW backend or panic handler: those are the generated entry’s dependencies. So changing board = to "mps2-an385-freertos" and building again builds the FreeRTOS image with no other edit.

QEMU Slirp networking — no host TAP / bridge / sudo. The zenoh default port is 7447; this example dials 10500 (the locator above), so start the router (ROS’s rmw_zenohd) on that port:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:10500"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

or edit the locator above to the port you prefer.

Build

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

In the workspace root (where the scaffold step left you):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build           # builds the image `[image.baremetal]` declares

nros build prepares the build first (message bindings, the generated entry for [image.baremetal], the cargo settings the board implies), then runs cargo. There is no step to run before it.

First build (~5 min) cross-compiles all of nano-ros’s Rust deps for thumbv7m-none-eabi. Re-builds finish in seconds. The ELF lands under build/, never beside your sources; nros build prints its path and a run: line when it finishes.

Driving cargo yourself (an IDE, a CI step, --release) is supported: nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo line, against the generated entry under build/. To write that entry and its settings without building, before you open the workspace in an IDE, run:

nros configure

What it writes is regenerated on every build; never edit it, and never add a .cargo/config.toml of your own to carry board facts. Your own Rust-toolchain preferences go where cargo already looks for them — a parent directory or $CARGO_HOME. See When nros build drives the build.

Run on QEMU

Three terminals: the router, the board, and a stock ROS 2 peer.

1. The router — ROS’s rmw_zenohd, on the port your image’s locator names (Slirp forwards the guest’s 10.0.2.2:<p> to the host’s <p>). The scaffold states no locator, so the board dials 10.0.2.2:7447; the example above dials 10500. It must listen on 0.0.0.0 for the Slirp gateway:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

2. The board — from the workspace root:

nros run bm_node

nros run rebuilds if anything changed, then boots the talker in QEMU with the board’s runner: the patched qemu-system-arm that nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal provisioned into the SDK store, the LAN9118 on Slirp, and -icount shift=auto, which keeps the board’s timer in step with Slirp’s I/O. It streams the semihosting console until you press Ctrl-C.

Expected serial-over-semihosting output:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
...

3. A stock ROS 2 peer. The talker publishes best-effort; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing. Force best-effort to receive:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it.

Readiness signal. Within ~15 seconds of QEMU boot (no RTOS init delay, but smoltcp + zenoh handshake still takes a few seconds), expect Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on semihosting stdout — the count starts at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If no Publishing: line:

  1. Router not running — talker spins on smoltcp poll until killed.
  2. No network on the guest — if you boot the ELF with your own QEMU line, an explicit -nic/-netdev that does not reach the LAN9118 (or -nic none, -nodefaults) leaves it unwired. The board’s runner passes -nic user,model=lan9118.
  3. Cooperative spin starvation — if you added a long-running callback, the entire executor stalls; bare-metal has no preemption.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Flash a real board

Nothing in-tree is flashed: mps2-an385 is a QEMU machine, and nros setup provisions no probe or flash tooling for it. A real Cortex-M board is a board crate of your own — Worked Example — STM32F4 Out of Tree takes one through the whole ladder — and its ELF goes to the board with the probe tool its vendor supports. Add an image for it to the bringup ([image.stm32f4] board = "<your board id>"); once that board package declares its flash runner, nros flash names the image:

nros flash bm_node_bringup:stm32f4
# or by hand, on the ELF path `nros build` printed:
#   probe-rs run --chip STM32F407VGTx <elf>
#   openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f4x.cfg \
#       -c "program <elf> verify reset exit"

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

The chip, interface and triple above are the STM32F4-Discovery’s; yours come from your board.

GitHub source

  • Bare-metal talker, the copy-out example for this board and the same project as the one this page builds: examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker/
  • Board crate: packages/boards/nros-board-mps2-an385/

Constraints to be aware of

  • No alloc by default. Pure no_std + heapless for bounded collections. If you need alloc, opt in via the alloc feature on your board crate and supply a #[global_allocator].
  • No wake primitive. Cooperative single-thread spin only; the executor’s nros_platform_wake_* slots return Unsupported.
  • No preemption. A long-running user callback blocks every other dispatchable handle until it returns.
  • nros-c / nros-cpp NOT supported. These wrappers assume hosted-RTOS libc + heap. Pure-Rust API only on this target.

For Cortex-M3 with an RTOS, switch to the FreeRTOS starter.

Next

  • Subscriber / service / action: the bare-metal image rows of the Rust language workspace, examples/workspaces/rust, under pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup. The serial talker and listener are image rows there too, stating transport = "serial" over the same packages.
  • Wake-callback opt-in: the wake-callback (latency-probe) bench under packages/testing/nros-bench/wake-latency-cortex-m3/ shows how to feed a backend’s transport-notify into the cooperative spin loop on bare-metal.
  • Real hardware: the same code runs on an STM32F4-Discovery with a board crate of your own and a different linker script — see Worked Example — STM32F4 Out of Tree, which takes that board through the customization ladder end to end.

PX4 Autopilot (external module)

Single-node starter on PX4 Autopilot via the external-module copy-out template. PX4’s EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION pattern lets downstream firmware drop in nano-ros without forking PX4 itself. C++ only — PX4’s uORB binding is C++-only (Rust + C not in the coverage matrix).

Prereqs. A PX4-Autopilot ≥ v1.16 clone, the matching cross toolchain (e.g. gcc-arm-none-eabi for Pixhawk targets), and python3 with the PX4 development requirements installed (bash ./Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh once).

Project layout

PX4 external modules live outside the PX4 source tree and are hooked in at configure time. The template — shipped in the SDK root at integrations/px4/module-template/ (the SDK root is the installed release’s share/nano-ros, nros locate nano-ros prints it) — has the PX4-required src/modules/<name>/ shape:

my_drone_firmware/
├── PX4-Autopilot/                          # PX4 source tree (submodule)
└── px4-modules/                            # passed via EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION
    └── nano-ros/                           # copy-out from integrations/px4/module-template/
        └── src/
            ├── CMakeLists.txt              # populates config_module_list_external
            └── modules/
                └── nano_ros_app/
                    ├── CMakeLists.txt      # px4_add_module(... MAIN nano_ros_app)
                    └── nano_ros_app.cpp    # the user-editable app

Prereq. PX4 is your own checkout — the firmware tree you already build. Clone it (or use the one you have) and initialize its submodules; nano-ros is tested against PX4 v1.17.0.

git clone --branch v1.17.0 https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot.git
git -C PX4-Autopilot submodule update --init \
    --depth 1 --recommend-shallow --recursive

PX4’s own Python dependencies come from its Tools/setup scripts (e.g. PX4-Autopilot/Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh) — run those per PX4’s documentation if the firmware build complains about missing Python modules.

Copy the template into your firmware repo; PX4 is pointed at the copy at build time:

mkdir -p px4-modules
sdk="$(nros locate nano-ros)"   # this project's nano-ros SDK root
cp -r "$sdk/integrations/px4/module-template" px4-modules/nano-ros

(Releases after 0.6.0-nros4 ship the template; with an older one, copy it from GitHub.)

PX4 enforces the src/modules/<name>/ layout exactly. To make the module your own, rename nano_ros_app in all three places at once: the directory, the module list in src/CMakeLists.txt, and the MAIN name in the module’s own CMakeLists.txt. PX4 has no central module registry, so copying the template into your tree is how it is distributed.

PX4’s own make <target> is the build verb, and it configures and builds ONE tree, PX4-Autopilot/build/<target>/. The module joins it through EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION, passed on that same make line — PX4’s Makefile forwards it to its CMake configure — and pointing at the dir that contains the template’s src/ (that’s px4-modules/nano-ros, not its parent: PX4’s root CMakeLists.txt does add_subdirectory("${EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION}/src" …)).

The template finds nano-ros itself: an explicit -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<path> cache variable wins, otherwise it asks the nros on PATH, which answers with the SDK that binary belongs to. No environment variable is read. To name the root anyway, pass it through PX4’s CMAKE_ARGS:

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros" \
    CMAKE_ARGS="-Dnano_ros_ROOT=$sdk"    # optional

Not replayed. No probe track runs the PX4 SITL build yet, so this line is unmeasured on the installed track (tracking issue).

Inside the module, the canonical pattern bridges uORB → nano-ros. The module is a PX4Module subclass that runs in its own work queue, opens an nros executor, and forwards uORB messages onto a zenoh / DDS topic (or vice versa). Edit nano_ros_app.cpp to add your topic bindings.

Configure

The template does not ship a Kconfig overlay (no Kconfig.projbuild files). Module enablement is implicit once EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION points at the template. Which RMW backends the module registers is the BACKENDS list of nros_px4_add_module(...) in src/modules/nano_ros_app/CMakeLists.txt — the template ships BACKENDS uorb — not a cache variable. (Adding a Kconfig overlay so the module appears under menuconfig → External modules is a follow-up task; for now the template is always enabled.)

Build

One make, one tree. For the SITL simulator (POSIX target — easier to develop against), or for a Pixhawk (px4_fmu-v5_default here; use your board’s PX4 target):

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"
make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_fmu-v5_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"

The firmware lands in PX4’s own tree, PX4-Autopilot/build/<target>/ (px4_fmu-v5_default.px4 for the Pixhawk). The first build cross-compiles nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs alongside PX4’s NuttX kernel + apps (~10 min on a fresh checkout). Note that the module links prebuilt nano-ros archives (nros_px4_add_module resolves them at configure time and, when one is missing, stops naming the command that builds it).

Run on the SITL simulator

PX4’s SITL runs the autopilot as a host process against a simulator. With Gazebo (Harmonic) installed per PX4’s documentation:

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default gz_x500 \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"
# In the PX4 console:
pxh> nano_ros_app start

# Verify from stock ROS 2 on the same network (only after you have
# added uORB → nano-ros forwarders to nano_ros_app.cpp — the shipped
# template forwards nothing on its own):
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /vehicle_local_position px4_msgs/msg/VehicleLocalPosition

Flash a real board

PX4’s own upload target flashes over the bootloader USB, with the same EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION as the build (it rebuilds if anything changed):

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_fmu-v5_default upload \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

QGroundControl can flash the same build/px4_fmu-v5_default/px4_fmu-v5_default.px4 instead. Start the module from the NSH console (nano_ros_app start) or the board’s startup script.

No probe runs the upload line (a CI runner has no board): it stands unverified until run against a named board. PX4 SITL is the replay that can run in CI, and it is not yet run there either.

Readiness signal. After nano_ros_app start in the PX4 console, the shipped template logs nano-ros uORB backend registered and returns immediately — it doesn’t start a publisher loop or print a “bridge started” line on its own. You’re expected to edit nano_ros_app.cpp to wire your uORB → nano-ros forwards. If nano_ros_app reports register failed, check:

  1. Module didn’t register — the template logs nros_rmw_uorb_register() -> <rc> on startup (search the PX4 boot log for nros_rmw_uorb_register). A non-zero <rc> usually means a NuttX kernel-config / feature-gate mismatch.
  2. Once you’ve added forwarders, zenohd must be reachable from the autopilot’s network (Pixhawk: configured via QGroundControl or param set).
  3. uORB topic not advertised yet — start the upstream PX4 module that publishes it (commander start etc.) first.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

GitHub source

  • PX4 external-module template: integrations/px4/module-template/
  • Worked PX4 example, the source of truth for the register-check shape (including the weak nros-rmw-cffi register stub on the Rust side): packages/testing/nros-px4-register-check/
  • PX4 integration roadmap notes: integrations/px4/README.md

Constraints to be aware of

  • uORB binding is C++-only. The PX4 example collapses uORB registration to a C++ port; Rust / C variants exist for non-PX4 RTOSes but not for PX4.
  • PX4’s NuttX kernel. Underneath, PX4 runs NuttX; if you need to debug at the kernel layer, the NuttX starter page applies too.
  • uORB throughput vs zenoh hops. uORB is in-process pub/sub at ~µs latency; zenoh adds network-RTT. Plan accordingly when bridging high-rate streams.

Next

  • Add your own uORB topics to the bridge: see the nano_ros_app.cpp template’s topic-table section.
  • Multi-vehicle: PX4-XRCE-Agent → nano-ros XRCE backend gives you the standard PX4-ROS bridge with nano-ros on the autopilot side.
  • For pure-NuttX (no PX4) firmware: see the NuttX starter.

ARM FVP (FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R)

Run nano-ros on Arm’s Base_RevC AEMv8-R Fast Models — the Cortex-A SMP profile under Zephyr 3.7 (board id fvp_baser_aemv8r/fvp_aemv8r_aarch64/smp). The FVP is the canonical local proxy for the safety-island reference platforms that follow the same hwv2 Zephyr shape; pair this chapter with the Zephyr (west module) starter for the build half.

Status. The run half — invoking FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R and piping UART 0–3 to stdout — is landed.

The two standalone talker lanes were retired: their runners had been deleted, so they built images nothing booted. What remains is the part with consumers — the board-crate import surface and the workspace Entry. FVP support is intended to grow back from those. See the archived FVP runtime roadmap.

Verified where? The run half is maintainer-run: a maintainer boots the image by hand (the recipe is in the contributor lanes linked below), and no installed probe track replays this chapter. fvp-aemv8r-smp’s status and the date of its last boot are on its evidence page; a probe track follows an automated run, not the other way round. Read the output below as what a maintainer last saw, not as a gate.

When to use

  • You need to exercise a Cortex-A SMP Zephyr image on a developer laptop without dedicated silicon.
  • You’re bringing up a new hwv2 safety-island target — the FVP is the closest in-tree reference for board.cmake + SMP boot + Cyclone DDS shape.
  • You’re validating stock-Cyclone-DDS RMW interop locally before promoting to a hardware bench.

The FVP is not a replacement for QEMU on Cortex-M (mps2-an385, mps3-an547); those targets are covered by FreeRTOS (QEMU) and the Zephyr starter. The FVP is also not the same surface as Corellium’s AVH cloud FVP — AVH packages firmware as .coreimg and provisions via a remote API; local FVP loads a raw ELF via -a cluster0.cpu*=<elf>. AVH is out of scope for this chapter.

Prereqs

  • A working Zephyr 3.7 workspace — run nros setup zephyr once if you haven’t (see the Zephyr starter).

  • The Arm Base_RevC AEMv8R Fast Models binary. nano-ros fetches it:

    nros setup --tool arm-fvp

    nros setup board fvp-aemv8r-smp does it as one of its steps, so most people never run the line above directly. It is a pinned Arm CDN permalink with a checked SHA256 ([tool.arm-fvp] in nros-sdk-index.toml), installed to ~/.nros/sdk/arm-fvp/<version>.

    x86_64 Linux only — Arm publishes no other host build of this model. On another architecture you can still build the image; you cannot run it here.

    Until 2026-09-06 this page said the model was license-gated and that fetching it was your responsibility. It is not: the permalink answers 200 with no authentication, which is how autoware-safety-island had been downloading it in CI the whole time. The mistaken policy cost every reader of this page a manual install.

After installing, export one of the discovery env vars:

# Preferred — Zephyr's canonical name; takes highest priority.
export ARMFVP_BIN_PATH=/opt/Arm/FastModels/Base_RevC_AEMv8R/models/Linux64_GCC-9.3

# Alternative — directory layout from the gated installer; the
# resolver scans `models/Linux64_GCC-*/` underneath it.
export ARM_FVP_DIR=/opt/Arm/FastModels/Base_RevC_AEMv8R

If neither is set, FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R is discovered via PATH as a last-ditch fallback.

Installer surface

For a model you extracted yourself, rather than the one nros setup --tool arm-fvp fetched, run the discovery script:

ARM_FVP_DIR=/path/to/extracted/fvp \
    scripts/installers/arm-fvp-installer.sh

The installer locates FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R under $ARM_FVP_DIR, symlinks the containing directory to ~/.nros/sdks/arm-fvp/current/ (atomic via ln -sfn), and prints the export ARMFVP_BIN_PATH=… line for your shell rc. Run scripts/installers/arm-fvp-installer.sh --print-env later to re-emit the export. It downloads nothing: nros setup --tool arm-fvp is the fetch.

Doctor check

nano-ros checks that the model resolves via ARMFVP_BIN_PATH, ARM_FVP_DIR, PATH, or the SDK store (where nros setup --tool arm-fvp installs it), and warns — never hard-fails — when it can’t. A warning rather than an error because a contributor who is not working on the FVP should not be blocked by its absence; nros setup --tool arm-fvp is the fix when they are.

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → per-platform lanes.

Build

The FVP is a Zephyr board, fvp-aemv8r-smp, so an image names it in its bringup’s system.toml and nros build hands it to west like any Zephyr image (the Zephyr chapter has the workspace flow). The worked example is examples/workspaces/realtime-cpp’s [image.fvp], a Cyclone DDS image:

[image.fvp]
board = "fvp-aemv8r-smp"
rmw = "cyclonedds"

The build generates the messages from your ROS 2 install, so the first one runs in a shell that has sourced it; it records the prefix, so later builds need no sourced shell:

nros setup zephyr --rmw cyclonedds     # the Zephyr workspace + SDK
nros setup fvp-aemv8r-smp              # the model (x86_64 Linux only)
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build demo_bringup:fvp

The model must be resolvable when the build configures: Zephyr caches the FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R path then, so an image configured before the model was installed (or before ARMFVP_BIN_PATH was set) has to be reconfigured (nros build demo_bringup:fvp -- --pristine). nros build says so in the note it prints after the build.

Run on the FVP

nros build ends by printing Zephyr’s run target for the image’s build directory; it invokes FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R with the board’s cluster and UART settings and pipes the UARTs to your terminal:

west build -d build/zephyr-cyclonedds/demo_bringup__fvp_west -t run

Not replayed. No probe track builds or boots the FVP image yet, so this line is unmeasured on the installed track (tracking issue).

The model is a free download, not licence-gated (see Prereqs); what keeps it off a CI lane is cost and its x86_64-only host build. It runs until you stop it (Ctrl-C).

Expected output

The Zephyr 3.7 boot banner appears on UART0 first, followed by the talker. The exact line counts depend on CONFIG_BOOT_BANNER and your locator config, but the markers to look for are:

*** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***
[00:00:00.xxx,000] <inf> nros: session up (domain 0)
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
...

For the cpp/cyclonedds recipe, the same banner is followed by Cyclone DDS reader-match logs and std_msgs/String publish lines. Verify ROS 2 interop by running a sibling listener in another terminal:

# stock ROS 2 — reads the FVP's Cyclone DDS publisher
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String

The same std_msgs/String payload (Hello World: N) + byte-equal CDR framing must appear on both sides — that’s the stock-RMW interop contract (byte-compatible with rmw_cyclonedds_cpp).

Cross-references

  • Environment Variables — ARM_FVP_DIR / ARMFVP_BIN_PATH — the discovery contract.
  • Zephyr (west module) — the parent Zephyr starter; the FVP is a board-target slice of it.
  • examples/workspaces/realtime-cpp/src/demo_bringup/ — the workspace image ([image.fvp]) this chapter builds and boots. Its west application is generated by nros build; its Kconfig lives in boards/fvp_baser_aemv8r_fvp_aemv8r_aarch64_smp/.

Choosing an RMW

Every nano-ros binary picks its RMW (ROS Middleware) backend at build time. There are three: Cyclone DDS, Zenoh (zenoh-pico), and XRCE-DDS. This page helps you pick one and explains how each backend connects your device to a ROS 2 network. The mechanics of changing your pick are in Switching RMW Backends.

Start with Cyclone DDS

For getting started, use Cyclone DDS. It is the one backend that needs no daemon, router, or agent: a nano-ros node publishes with nothing else running, and a stock ROS 2 node using rmw_cyclonedds_cpp sees it directly — same RTPS wire protocol, same discovery, no translation layer in between.

The reason the other two are not the starting point: nano-ros ships no bridge process of its own. The zenoh router is ROS 2’s own rmw_zenohd, so the zenoh backend requires a ROS 2 installation just to start the router; the XRCE backend requires a running Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent. Cyclone DDS requires neither.

Current maturity: pub/sub and services interoperate with stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. Which status events and other features it wires is listed in the Per-RMW Feature Matrix; the remaining known limitations are in docs/reference/cyclonedds-known-limitations.md.

Zenoh — ROS 2 interop and small embedded targets

Choose the Zenoh backend (built on zenoh-pico) when:

  • You are integrating with a ROS 2 fleet running rmw_zenoh_cpp.
  • Your target is a small MCU: ~16 KB of heap and ~100 KB of flash are enough, versus ~32 KB+ RAM for Cyclone DDS.
  • Your network cannot do UDP multicast (RTPS discovery needs IGMP; zenoh-pico in client mode runs over plain TCP).

The zenoh backend needs a router, and the router comes from your ROS 2 installation — it is the same rmw_zenohd that ROS 2 zenoh nodes use:

ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

That invocation works on any host with rmw_zenoh_cpp installed, regardless of where ROS 2 lives — never hard-code an install path to the router binary. See ROS 2 Interop for the full three-terminal walkthrough.

XRCE-DDS — smallest footprint, serial transport

Choose the XRCE-DDS backend when:

  • RAM is the constraint: ~3 KB of client RAM, and the backend allocates only when a session or entity is created — never per message. (It is not heap-free: each allocation goes through nros_platform_alloc, and their number follows the entities you declare.)
  • You need a serial (UART) transport — the only backend that works on an MCU with no networking hardware. See Serial Transport.
  • You are joining an existing micro-ROS / DDS deployment: the agent bridges to any DDS-based RMW.

The MCU cannot participate without the Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent (MicroXRCEAgent) running on a host; if the agent stops, the device loses all connectivity.

What each backend supports

The Per-RMW Feature Matrix is the one capability table in this book. It is generated from the backend sources, so it is current: services, status events, graph introspection, zero-copy loans and the rest, per backend. In short, all three backends do publish/subscribe, service servers and clients, and status events; they differ in the less common features (for example, XRCE-DDS has no graph introspection, and only Zenoh has the zero-copy loan API). The version of each backend’s upstream library is listed on Support Status.

How each backend works

The three backends differ less in what they can do than in the shape of the network around your device: what else has to run, who handles discovery, and what happens when a process goes away.

Zenoh

The Zenoh backend uses zenoh-pico, a lightweight C client for the Zenoh protocol. The MCU takes part in the Zenoh network directly; there is no protocol translation layer.

  1. The MCU runs zenoh-pico in client mode and connects to a zenoh router (rmw_zenohd, ROS 2’s own) over TCP, UDP or TLS.
  2. zenoh-pico creates publishers and subscribers directly on the Zenoh network.
  3. ROS 2 nodes running rmw_zenoh_cpp connect to the same router. The router forwards messages without interpreting them; it is not a protocol translator.
  4. The device takes part in ROS 2 graph discovery through liveliness tokens, so ros2 topic list and ros2 node list see it.

Zenoh itself defines a peer mode in which two zenoh-pico devices talk directly with no router. nano-ros does not ship it: zenoh-pico is built without its multicast transport and scouting, because every nano-ros deployment reaches its peers through a router or an agent and those code paths cost flash on an MCU. Setting NROS_SESSION_MODE=peer is therefore refused at session open, with a message saying so.

If the router stops, the device loses routing but keeps running. Footprint: roughly 16 KB+ of RAM (heap required) and 100 KB+ of flash.

XRCE-DDS

The XRCE-DDS backend uses Micro-XRCE-DDS-Client, the same client library micro-ROS uses. It follows an agent-based model: a small client on the MCU delegates entity creation to an agent process.

  1. The MCU runs the XRCE-DDS client and connects to an Agent process over UDP or serial (UART, HDLC framing).
  2. The client asks the Agent to create entities (“a publisher on topic X with type Y”).
  3. The Agent creates full DDS entities on the client’s behalf and bridges data between the XRCE protocol and the DDS data space.
  4. ROS 2 nodes using any DDS-based RMW (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS) communicate through the Agent.

The Agent is mandatory and handles discovery; the client does none of its own. If the Agent stops, the device loses all connectivity.

Heap use on the MCU is small and bounded: the backend allocates when a session or entity is created, never per message. Each XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS slot is heap, so size it to the subscriptions you declare. Footprint: roughly 3 KB of client RAM and 75 KB of flash. The upstream client also defines a CAN FD transport, but nano-ros builds do not enable it.

Cyclone DDS

The Cyclone DDS backend uses Eclipse Cyclone DDS, the same DDS implementation ROS 2 uses through rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. It is a C++ library that registers itself with the nano-ros runtime through the RMW C ABI.

  1. Selecting cyclonedds for the image links the backend and registers it before the executor opens; you do not call a register function yourself.
  2. The executor’s session, publisher, subscriber and service operations dispatch to Cyclone, which creates the DDS domain, participant, topics, writers and readers. Cyclone runs its own receive threads.
  3. ROS 2 nodes using stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp interoperate directly: same wire protocol, same discovery, and no key rewriting (unlike rmw_zenoh’s <domain>/<topic>/<type>/… key expressions).

Discovery is SPDP / SEDP over UDP multicast, or a static unicast peer list. The domain is configured from a built-in configuration rather than an XML file, so no XML parser is linked. Cyclone allocates with malloc, so a heap is required: plan for roughly 32 KB+ of RAM and 150 KB+ of flash on an embedded link (the POSIX shared library, libddsc.so, is about 1.4 MB). When a peer goes offline, only its samples stop arriving; there is no central process whose loss takes the network down.

Getting the Cyclone library. Selecting cyclonedds for an image is all you have to do; the build provides Cyclone itself. It uses a prebuilt install if you point at one (-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<install> or -DCycloneDDS_DIR=); otherwise it builds Cyclone from source, by default from the pinned sources that ship with nano-ros, or from your own copy with -DCYCLONEDDS_SOURCE_DIR=<path>. A plain nros build therefore needs no separate Cyclone step. The idlc code generator is a host tool, found on PATH (for example from a ROS 2 install) or through -DIDLC_EXECUTABLE=.

Zephyr on Cortex-A / Cortex-R needs the aarch64-zephyr-elf toolchain in your Zephyr SDK install; toolchain setup for these targets is in docs/reference/zephyr-armv8r-setup.md.

The footprint figures in this section are order-of-magnitude planning numbers, not measurements; they vary with features, message set and optimisation level. Size your own image with arm-none-eabi-size; the RAM knobs are listed in the Static Pool Inventory.

Cyclone DDS network configuration per platform

Cyclone DDS speaks RTPS over UDP multicast and unicast. On every RTOS the network stack needs IGMP enabled, enough network buffers for the SPDP / SEDP discovery burst, and a way to join a multicast group. The settings per platform:

Zephyr

# IGMP for SPDP multicast discovery (239.255.0.1:7400+).
CONFIG_NET_IPV4_IGMP=y

# Multicast group slots — RTPS uses up to 4 builtin groups per
# participant (SPDP + SEDP pubs / subs / topics).
CONFIG_NET_IF_MCAST_IPV4_ADDR_COUNT=4

# Net-buffer pools — defaults of 14 / 36 are too small for the SEDP
# burst when more than two service / action entities exist on each
# participant. Symptom of undersizing: runtime starvation as the
# discovery exchange backs up.
CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT=256
CONFIG_NET_PKT_TX_COUNT=128
CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT=512
CONFIG_NET_BUF_TX_COUNT=256
CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE=512

# Heap — Cyclone DDS (malloc) + heapless mailboxes.
CONFIG_COMMON_LIBC_MALLOC_ARENA_SIZE=4194304
CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE=524288

On qemu_cortex_a9, also use a board overlay to enlarge the GEM driver’s RX / TX descriptor rings (default 32), so a brief pause in draining does not immediately drop frames:

&gem0 {
    promiscuous-mode;
    rx-buffer-descriptors = <128>;
    tx-buffer-descriptors = <64>;
};

On native_sim, Zephyr’s offloaded-sockets driver does not forward IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP to the host kernel, so multicast discovery does not work there. The native_sim configuration discovers peers by unicast to 127.0.0.1 instead (see Troubleshooting); use qemu_cortex_a9 to exercise multicast DDS on Zephyr.

FreeRTOS + lwIP

// FreeRTOSConfig.h / lwipopts.h
#define LWIP_IGMP            1   // SPDP multicast
#define LWIP_SO_RCVTIMEO     1   // Cyclone DDS recv timeouts
#define LWIP_BROADCAST       1
#define IP_REASSEMBLY        1   // RTPS DATA_FRAG fragments
#define MEMP_NUM_NETBUF      32  // discovery burst headroom

NuttX

CONFIG_NET_IGMP=y
CONFIG_NET_BROADCAST=y
CONFIG_NET_UDP_NRECVS=4
CONFIG_NET_RECV_TIMEO=y

ThreadX + NetX Duo

tx_user.h / nx_user.h:

#define NX_ENABLE_IGMPV2          // IGMP v2 for RTPS multicast
// NetX BSD layer init must call `bsd_initialize` early — required
// for `setsockopt(SO_RCVTIMEO)` support.

Bare-metal smoltcp

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Bridge config in the board crate.
let mut config = smoltcp::iface::Config::new(...);
config.multicast_groups = vec![Ipv4Address::new(239, 255, 0, 1)];
// MulticastConfig::Strict in smoltcp 0.x; the bridge must expose
// a `join_multicast_group` API.
}

POSIX

No configuration is needed: the kernel handles IGMP and setsockopt. Make sure the loopback interface is up (it is by default).

Decision summary

  • Default / getting started / DDS fleet → Cyclone DDS. Nothing to run beside your node; direct rmw_cyclonedds_cpp interop. Needs ~32 KB RAM and a network stack with IGMP.
  • rmw_zenoh_cpp fleet, small MCU, or TCP-only network → Zenoh. Needs the router from your ROS 2 install (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd).
  • Tiny MCU, serial link, or micro-ROS deployment → XRCE-DDS. Smallest footprint and no per-message allocation, but the agent is mandatory.

Any of the three handles standard publish/subscribe and services, integration with ROS 2 desktop nodes, and development under QEMU.

You do not have to pick exactly one per system: a single binary can link multiple backends and bridge between them, for example zenoh devices to a Cyclone DDS stack, or XRCE devices to a Zenoh network — see Cross-backend Bridges.

Once you have picked, Switching RMW Backends shows the exact edits per build system.

Design background

  • RFC-0031: RMW selection and lowering
  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance and the unstable seam

Switching RMW Backends

nano-ros selects its RMW backend at build time — there is no RMW_IMPLEMENTATION environment variable to flip at runtime the way desktop ROS 2 does. Which edit you make depends on how your project is built. This page lists the exact change per builder; for help picking a backend in the first place, see Choosing an RMW.

Backend names are the same everywhere: zenoh, xrce, cyclonedds. When nothing selects a backend, the default is zenoh.

Workspace (C, C++, mixed or Rust)

One edit, in the bringup’s system.toml:

[system]
rmw = "cyclonedds"          # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds

or, for one image only, rmw = "…" inside its [image.<id>] block. Then

nros build

A workspace has no root build file to edit: nros build writes the CMake root under build/ with BACKEND taken from the image’s rmw, and for a Rust image it generates the entry that gives the board crate the backend feature. Each image builds into its own directory, so no object files from another backend linger.

A CMake tree that is not a workspace

A CMake project with no system.toml that consumes nano-ros in source form — either find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED) (the ament-shape entry point, nano_rosConfig.cmake at the SDK root, located via -Dnano_ros_ROOT) or a raw add_subdirectory (Build as a CMake subdirectory) — picks its backend on the configure line. nros setup presets writes the package a CMakePresets.json that already carries the SDK root and the board’s toolchain (from the presets nros setup <board> wrote), so the configure line names only the backend:

nros setup presets                       # once per package
cmake --preset linux -DNROS_RMW=cyclonedds   # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
cmake --build build/linux

Use one build directory per backend (-B build-zenoh, -B build-cyclonedds, …) if you switch back and forth.

A Rust node package

A Rust node package needs no edit at all. Its Cargo.toml names no rmw-<x> or ros-<edition> feature and no board crate, and no code calls a backend’s register(): the generated entry boots through the board crate, which links the backend the image selects and registers it. The workspace section above is the whole change.

Several backends from one bringup

A bringup whose nodes run on more than one backend declares one image per RMW in its system.toml and builds the image it names:

# src/talker_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "talker_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
default_images = ["linux"]

[image_defaults]
board = "linux"

[image.linux]

[image.linux_cyclonedds]
rmw = "cyclonedds"

nros build linux_cyclonedds

The full-system declaration model — how the one value in system.toml is lowered to cargo features and CMake cache variables — is specified in the RMW selection-and-lowering design (see Design background below).

Embedded targets

On embedded platforms the backend is fixed at compile time like everything else — there is nothing to switch on the device. Each platform surfaces the same choice through its own configuration mechanism; on Zephyr, for instance, the image’s rmw in system.toml is rendered into a Kconfig choice (CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH / CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE / CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS, exactly one), never written in a conf file. One image per backend, each with the Zephyr settings that backend needs:

[image.zephyr_zenoh]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "zenoh"
os_config = ["prj-zenoh.conf"]

[image.zephyr_cyclonedds]       # Cyclone: Cortex-A/R and native_sim targets
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
os_config = ["prj-cyclonedds.conf"]

A Cyclone DDS image also needs multicast-capable networking on the target; the per-platform settings are in Choosing an RMW.

See the platform guides for the concrete per-platform workflow:

  • Zephyr
  • FreeRTOS
  • NuttX
  • ThreadX
  • ESP32

and When nros build drives the build for which builder applies where.

Design background

  • RFC-0031: RMW selection and lowering
  • RFC-0048: CMake / ament consumption
  • RFC-0098: generated leaf build config

QoS, Status Events, and Discovery

This page covers runtime event behavior that application authors need after choosing an RMW backend: liveliness, deadline misses, lost messages, and the places where nano-ros deliberately differs from standard ROS 2 waitset-style event handling.

Transport-level status events let an application observe conditions the underlying middleware detects: a remote node going silent, a publisher missing its rate, a subscriber dropping samples. nano-ros exposes a core subset useful for embedded RTOS deployments — liveliness changes, deadline misses, and message loss.

This page describes the event surface, the dispatch model, and the patterns that motivate having events at all on RTOS targets.

The event kinds

Nine event kinds: the five core kinds below, plus Iron’s matched and incompatible-type pairs (below). Three core kinds on subscribers, two on publishers.

Subscriber events

KindFires whenUse
LivelinessChangedA tracked publisher’s liveliness state changes (publisher started asserting / stopped)Safety-island fail-over: trigger MRM when remote control node goes silent
