add_subdirectory("/path/to/nano-ros" nano_ros)

# 2) Point the message-package resolver at this workspace's src/ (must
#    precede the ament-surface include so workspace-pkg Find<pkg>.cmake
#    auto-emit picks it up).
set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src")

# 3) nano-ros's ament / rclcpp surface.
include("/path/to/nano-ros/cmake/NanoRosAmentSurface.cmake")

# 4) Bulk-build every workspace msg pkg in topo order (one line instead of
#    N add_subdirectory(src/<pkg>) lines).
nros_workspace_interfaces()

# 5) Build consumer apps.
add_subdirectory(src/my_node)

No nros_generate_interfaces(<pkg>) calls per consumer — the smart Find-stub does the codegen at find_package(<pkg>) time.

Reference fixture

examples/templates/local-msg-package/ ships the pattern end-to-end: two workspace msg pkgs (local_msgs, extra_msgs) with intra-workspace dep + a C++ consumer pulling msgs from BOTH the workspace AND AMENT (std_msgs, geometry_msgs, sensor_msgs) via one find_package shape. Cross-build proof: the same src/ builds under colcon build (CI-gated).

Legacy nros_generate_interfaces(<pkg>) shape

(The full current-vs-legacy spelling table lives in Message Generation.)

Per-package nros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs LANGUAGE CPP SKIP_INSTALL) calls still work (back-compat preserved) but are deprecated for new code — they bypass the ROS-convention smart Find-stub + workspace discovery. Existing in-tree examples will migrate as part of Phase 210.E.3.

Running the ported node on a microcontroller

The same source runs on an RTOS, main included. Build glue for each platform sits beside the source, and the source itself does not change. examples/templates/cpp-port-minimal-publisher carries two such directories, mps2-an385-freertos/ and zephyr/, each with a CMakeLists.txt built around one line:

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
nano_ros_add_executable(minimal_publisher ../src/minimal_publisher.cpp ROS2_MAIN)

The board comes from the directory’s system.toml, as for any nano-ros image. Every nano_ros_add_executable reaches your main: no C runtime calls int main(int argc, char** argv) on a board, so the build renames main in your sources only (never in the board’s own startup) and calls it from the platform’s entry, with argc == 0. ROS2_MAIN adds what a ported program needs on top of that:

  • It gives the ported code the C++ standard library. A ported node uses std::string, std::to_string and <chrono> literals.
    • On FreeRTOS the toolchain compiles C++ -ffreestanding, which makes <string> an #error, so the flag is removed for this package’s directory. nano-ros’s own code stays freestanding.
    • On Zephyr, select the full library in prj.conf: CONFIG_REQUIRES_FULL_LIBCPP=y and CONFIG_GLIBCXX_LIBCPP=y.
  • It asks for the std-shaped API (NROS_CPP_STD), the same one the ament verbs give a ported package on a host.

Where the node connects is decided when the image is built, because a board has no environment to read it from: the NROS_ENTRY_LOCATOR cache variable on FreeRTOS, the image’s locator in system.toml on Zephyr (rendered into CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR). rclcpp::init(argc, argv) reads it in every source file that includes <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>.

A node with a hand-written spin loop also works. The other two templates, rclcpp-compat-smoke/ and topic-state-monitor-port/, have the same two directories, and their main is the common shape:

while (rclcpp::ok()) {
    node->tick();
    rclcpp::spin_some(node);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
}

On FreeRTOS the board provides what the C++ library needs for this: std::this_thread::sleep_for sleeps the calling task, and std::chrono::steady_clock counts from boot, because the board has no real-time clock. A package that uses another library, such as diagnostic_updater, names it the usual way, ament_target_dependencies(<name> diagnostic_updater). On Zephyr the dependency goes to app, where the sources are compiled.

Zephyr’s native_sim cannot run a ported node. There Zephyr links its own C library, and the host’s libstdc++ cannot run on top of it. Use a Cortex-M board such as mps2/an385 in QEMU, which is what the template targets.

A whole workspace on a board

A ported workspace keeps each package’s own CMakeLists.txt, unchanged. Only the root that configures the packages is new. examples/templates/ament-workspace-port has three roots over one stock package:

  • FreeRTOS: find_package(nano_ros), then add_subdirectory for each package, with system.toml naming the board. Build with nros build.
  • Zephyr: find_package(Zephyr) first, then the same two lines, plus a package.xml and the Kconfig fragments beside them. Build with nros build.
  • posix: the same root you already use.

On a board, nano-ros reads the stock CMake verbs this way:

  • add_executable builds an image, as nano_ros_add_executable(... ROS2_MAIN) does. The board’s entry calls your main, and the image gets its locator and domain from system.toml.
  • add_library(... SHARED) builds STATIC, because an image is one binary.
  • A package that finds rclcpp gets the C++ standard library. Its directory is compiled without -ffreestanding.
  • ament_target_dependencies(<target> std_msgs) on a C++ target generates the message package if nothing has yet.
  • A plain target_link_libraries(<exe> <lib>) keeps working beside nano-ros’s own links.
  • A package that calls find_package(ament_cmake) is a ported package: its C++ is hosted even if it never finds rclcpp, and a message package it finds is generated in C++, so target_link_libraries(<lib> PUBLIC ${std_msgs_TARGETS}) reaches the headers.
  • find_package(<sibling>) reaches a library package of the same workspace when the root sets NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH and calls nros_workspace_interfaces() before adding the packages. Zephyr has the same call.
  • -Wpedantic -Werror and -fPIC on a package’s directory are fine. On Zephyr the image’s kernel link is never position-independent, whatever the package adds.
  • std::mutex and std::recursive_mutex exist although the RTOS toolchains’ libstdc++ has no threads: nano-ros defines them over the platform’s mutex for the ported package. std::condition_variable, std::thread and std::promise are still absent there.

What porting Nav2 packages to FreeRTOS and Zephyr needed edited in the source:

  • Exceptions. An RTOS image is built -fno-exceptions, so a throw does not compile. Guard it with #if defined(__cpp_exceptions) and abort in the other arm. A try / catch around a call needs the same guard.

  • Linux scheduling. Nav2’s setSoftRealTimePriority() calls sched_setscheduler. On an RTOS a thread’s priority is its tier’s (system.toml [tasks.*]), so make the call a no-op there.

  • Per-request client callbacks. No std::promise, so no Client<S>::SharedFuture: read the future on a later tick (the client row in the table below).

  • Parameters with no default. A board has no command line. State the launch file’s parameters in the image instead, and leave the source alone:

    [image.<id>]
params_files = ["config/x.param.yaml"]
ros_args = ["--ros-args", "-p", "update_rate:=10.0"]

    The build bakes both into the image, and rclcpp::init applies them ahead of whatever command line there is, so a host’s real arguments still win. A C (rclc) program does not read them.

What a workspace image still has to state:

  • Pool sizes: let the census answer. Say that the image’s entities are what its program creates, and state no size:

    [[component]]
pkg = "my_pkg"
class = "my_pkg::MyNode"
name = "my_node"        # the executable, when the workspace builds several
entities = "census"

    The configure then builds the same sources for the host, runs the program once in census mode, and sizes the publisher, subscriber, queryable, liveliness and executor-callback pools from what it created. Nothing has to be built twice by hand, and a current census is reused. This works on the add_subdirectory and find_package roads, for a host image and a FreeRTOS one, and for a Zephyr application. On Zephyr the census also decides whether an in-image client reaches an in-image server (local_queryable) and, when it records a parameter, the parameter store and the nros heap’s default. A program that creates several nodes is counted node by node. The census run constructs the node, so it needs the node’s parameters: state them with params_files (above). One Zephyr pool stays yours to state, because Zephyr sizes it in Kconfig: zenoh-pico takes a POSIX condition variable per subscriber and queryable, and the configure refuses a CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_COND_COUNT below what the census needs, naming the number to set in your prj-zenoh.conf.

  • Message bounds. An unbounded sequence or string in a message the node publishes gets the default bound, which can make one message megabytes. Bound it in nros-codegen.toml, for example [packages."diagnostic_msgs"] sequence = 4 and string = 64.

  • Parameter capacities and the app stack. The default capacities fit: both ported Nav2 nodes boot on FreeRTOS’s default 64 KiB app stack, at peaks of 12.5 and 16.8 KiB. [knobs.params] (max_string_value_len, max_array_len, max_byte_array_len) still shrinks the parameter store’s RAM. If a node needs more stack, raise it with set(NROS_FREERTOS_APP_STACK_KB <KiB>) in the root. The boot line app task stack peak <used> of <total> says what it needed.

  • The heap. On FreeRTOS, NROS_FREERTOS_HEAP_KB on freertos_config; on Zephyr, [image.<id>.knobs.zephyr] heap_size. A Zephyr heap that runs out while a subscription is created reports ConnectionFailed, not an out-of-memory.

  • The Zephyr board. Name the board package, board = "mps2-an385-zephyr", not the generic zephyr (which lowers to native_sim). The package carries the board’s QEMU network, sizing and entropy Kconfig, so the leaf names only its own os_config fragments.

What “just works” without source edits

nano-ros covers the patterns a typical ROS 2 C++ node uses:

rclcpp surfacenano-ros mappingNotes
class MyNode : public rclcpp::Noderclcpp::Node — ours, and the same name.Ctor takes (name), (name, options) or (name, ns, options).
std::make_shared<MyNode>()worksauto node = std::make_shared<MyNode>() and rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<MyNode>()) are unchanged. rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr node = std::make_shared<…>(…) does not compile — write auto; see “Node::SharedPtr observes, it does not own” below. shared_from_this() works too, with the same caveat.
rclcpp::Node::make_shared("name")std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>(…), the owning std::shared_ptrHosted builds. auto node = rclcpp::Node::make_shared("x"); is unchanged; assigning the temporary straight to a global rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr is not — keep it in a local first (auto node = …; g_node = node;).
create_publisher<M>(topic, qos)shared_ptr-returning wrapperqos can be rclcpp::QoS(10) or an int.
create_subscription<M>(topic, qos, callback)registered on the executor arena; dispatched by any spin verbCapturing lambdas + std::function + std::bind all work. The callback may take const M& (no allocation, every target) or, on hosted builds, upstream’s M::UniquePtr / M::SharedPtr / M::ConstSharedPtr / std::shared_ptr<const M>: each delivery is then copied into a fresh heap object the callback owns and may keep. A freestanding build refuses the pointer shapes at compile time, naming const M&.
create_wall_timer(period, callback)registered on the executor arena; dispatched by any spin verbstd::chrono::duration arg, capturing-lambda callback. Returns rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr, which is rclcpp::Timer::SharedPtr — one flat type, two names. See below.
rclcpp::create_timer(node, clock, period, cb)the clock-taking verb; a RCL_ROS_TIME clock follows /clockHumble’s only form. create_wall_timer stays on the steady clock.
create_service<S>(name, handler) with upstream’s std::shared_ptr<Request> / std::shared_ptr<Response> handler (optionally with std::shared_ptr<rmw_request_id_t> first)lent from the dispatch: the handler gets pointers to the request and response the dispatch decodedHosted builds; a plain function, a lambda with or without captures, or std::bind(&Node::on_request, this, _1, _2) (a handler’s state is copied into the service’s executor entry, and whatever it returns, such as Autoware’s bool, is ignored). The handler must not KEEP a pointer past its call: that aborts, naming why. The request header is zero-filled.
rclcpp::executors::SingleThreadedExecutor + add_node + spinthe process executor every node already lives onadd_node checks rather than attaches. MultiThreadedExecutor is a compile error naming the alternative: an executor dispatches on one task, and parallelism is a tier, not a callback group.
executor.spin_some() / rclcpp::spin_some(node)drain what is ready, without waitingThe bound is milliseconds (spin_some(5)), not a std::chrono duration.
client->wait_for_service(1s) / wait_for_action_server(10s)the millisecond wait, convertedHosted builds. The budget is still required; a negative duration is refused at the call.
rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, client->send_request(req))spins until the reply arrivesThe timeout is milliseconds.
auto fut = client->async_send_request(std::make_shared<S::Request>(…)) / fut.get() / fut.wait_for(1s) / client->remove_pending_request(fut)the poll client’s rclcpp::Future, under upstream’s verbsHosted builds, except remove_pending_request. get() returns the reply as an owning std::shared_ptr<Response> but never blocks: call it after spin_until_future_complete returned SUCCESS (before the reply it logs a refusal and returns nullptr). wait_for returns std::future_status and spins the executor while it waits. Each future is keyed by its request’s sequence number, as upstream’s is: several may be in flight on one client, each gets its own reply, and a reply that arrives after remove_pending_request (or prune_pending_requests) is dropped. How many is capped by the transport’s own outstanding-request limit (NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PENDING_GETS on zenoh); a send past it returns an empty future (valid() false). What it returns is upstream’s FutureAndRequestId: the future as .future, the request’s sequence id as .request_id (auto [future, id] = … works), and share() hands back a SharedFutureAndRequestId whose future is a std::shared_future<SharedResponse> every copy of which gets the same response; remove_pending_request takes the id too. .future is an rclcpp::Future, not a std::future. A freestanding build has send_request(req) + fut.try_take(resp); get() and share() there are compile errors naming them.
#include "rclcpp_action/rclcpp_action.hpp"an umbrella over Server<A> / Client<A> and the two free factoriesSee Actions below.
rclcpp::init(argc, argv) / shutdown() / ok() / spin(n) / spin_some(n)wraps rclcpp::init_in/shutdown_in/ok/spin_once--ros-args -r from:=to is honoured, beneath any remap the launch file sets for the same name. -p [node:]name:=value and --params-file <file> are honoured in an image with a parameter store: the value replaces the default when the node declares the parameter (scalars only from a file; a value of the wrong type is logged and the default kept). Any other ROS argument (__node, log flags) aborts, naming it.
RCLCPP_INFO / WARN / ERROR / DEBUG / FATALdispatched through the NROS_LOG_* family into nros_logCarries the logger, so get_logger("x") selects a real per-logger level, and FATAL is a distinct severity. Reaches LOG_ERR/printk on embedded, where the legacy NROS_* sink is a no-op. _THROTTLE variants are REFUSE-LOUD.
get_logger().get_child("sub")a real child logger, <parent>.subIts level, when unset, follows the nearest ancestor’s, so set_level on the node logger reaches it. A full name over 48 bytes or a full runtime-logger arena emits through the PARENT and set_level on it is refused — never a silent move of the parent’s threshold. Iron/Jazzy images publish children on /rosout; Humble ones, as upstream, do not.
executor.spin_once() / client->wait_for_service() / action_client->wait_for_action_server()the budget is requiredUpstream defaults all three to “block forever”, which nano-ros has no form of; the no-argument call is a compile error naming the alternative rather than a silently substituted 10 ms / 5 s budget. Write spin_once(10), wait_for_service(10000).
rclcpp::QoS / KeepLast(n) / SystemDefaultsQoS()one class with upstream’s implicit (depth) ctorChainable setters inherited.
diagnostic_updater::Updater + DiagnosticStatusWrapperpackages/api/nros-diagnostic-updaterPublishes /diagnostics.
rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A>ours, under upstream’s namesHosted builds take upstream’s goal-handle shapes as written; freestanding builds key goals by id. See Actions below.
class MyNode : public rclcpp_lifecycle::LifecycleNodeours, under upstream’s name (<rclcpp_lifecycle/lifecycle_node.hpp>)It IS an rclcpp::Node. The on_configure(const State&) … on_shutdown overrides, CallbackReturn::SUCCESS, configure() / activate() / … and get_current_state() keep upstream’s signatures; the REP-2002 services are registered by the constructor. create_publisher<M>(topic, qos) returns a managed LifecyclePublisher<M>::SharedPtr that sends only while Active. One managed node per executor.
RCLCPP_COMPONENTS_REGISTER_NODE(class) + rclcpp_components_register_node(lib PLUGIN "ns::Class" EXECUTABLE exe)the macro defines the component’s factory in its own source file; the cmake verb emits a thin int main() per registration that declares the class and calls that factorySingle binary, no class_loader. The PLUGIN’s qualifiers must be namespaces (a class nested in a class cannot be forward-declared). A component library built SHARED is built static.
plain CMake components: add_library(<c> SHARED …), ament_target_dependencies(<c> rclcpp …), rclcpp_components_register_nodes(<c> "ns::Class"), a hand-written main (add_executable + target_link_libraries)each SHARED or MODULE library builds static, and the configure prints a line saying so; the plural verb and ament_environment_hooks are accepted and do nothingOne image is one binary with one runtime. ament_target_dependencies works beside a target_link_libraries in either signature (plain or PRIVATE). A hand-written main gets the link pass the ament verbs give theirs. IMPORTED libraries keep their type. A project that overrides add_library itself replaces this.
find_package(ament_cmake_auto / rclcpp / rclcpp_components / diagnostic_updater / std_msgs / …)find modules at cmake/find/~28 of the most-cited ROS 2 packages; a message package not among them is found by the resolver from NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH / AMENT_PREFIX_PATH.
ament_auto_find_build_dependencies() + ament_auto_add_library / ament_auto_add_executablereads package.xml; each target gets the package’s include/ and every dependency nano-ros has a module forA dependency nano-ros does not provide (a project helper such as autoware_utils) is listed at configure and not looked up; a source that includes it fails on the include.
a project’s own message packages (autoware_vehicle_msgs, tier4_control_msgs, …) installed under AMENT_PREFIX_PATHgenerated by nano-ros codegen from the installed .msg / .srvNever the installed package’s upstream C++. Source the project’s install first (below).
create_callback_group(rclcpp::CallbackGroupType::MutuallyExclusive), SubscriptionOptions::callback_group, create_subscription<M>(topic, qos, cb, options)accepted; an unnamed group runs on the node’s default contextOne executor task already keeps every callback mutually exclusive, so Reentrant runs them one at a time too. A NAMED group (create_callback_group("name")) is the tier-mapped one.
create_service<S>(name, cb, rmw_qos_profile_services_default, group)upstream’s trailing QoS and grouprmw_qos_profile_t has upstream’s fields and enum values. A profile converts to rclcpp::QoS, QoS(QoSInitialization::from_rmw(p), p) builds one, and qos.get_rmw_qos_profile() reads it back. rmw_qos_profile_system_default is absent, because every field of it is a placeholder for the RMW to fill in, and the RMWs fill it in differently. A file that also includes <nros/rmw_entity.h> is refused, because that header defines the RMW backend’s own struct of the same name.
pub_->publish(msg); as a statementallowed on a ported (ament-built) target, even under -Wall -Werror; a failure is loggedCode written for nano-ros keeps the [[nodiscard]] Result.
several packages in one workspace (a library package such as Nav2’s nav2_util, a cmake-only one such as nav2_common, and the node that finds them)find_package(<sibling>) resolves to the sibling configured earlier in the same run: <pkg>::<pkg> over what it exported with ament_export_libraries / _targets / _dependencies, its include/, and its ament_package(CONFIG_EXTRAS …) files runAdd each package before the packages that find it; the configure refuses an out-of-order find by name. Every package configures in ONE CMake run, so ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR} is the workspace root, not the package: write ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR} (rare: 0 of 417 Autoware CMakeLists name it).
find_package(<pkg>) for an upstream C++ library nano-ros does not ship (bondcpp, tf2_ros, …)refused at configure, naming the package and the installed file CMake fell back toRemove the dependency, or port the library into your workspace as a package of its own.
rclcpp::Time(msg->header.stamp)implicit, from any {sec, nanosec} message, on the ROS clock
msg.header.stamp = now();, stamp + rclcpp::Duration::from_seconds(0.1)a {sec, nanosec} message converts from rclcpp::Time, and + / - a Duration
last_cmd_.twist == geometry_msgs::msg::Twist()a generated message has field-wise operator== / operator!=Messages only; a service’s or action’s own Request / Goal structs have none.
rclcpp::Node::WeakPtr parent + parent.lock()the same non-owning handle; lock() hands it backlock() cannot tell a destroyed node from a live one, because the handle owns nothing; it answers null only for an unset handle.
rclcpp::Clock::SharedPtr clock_ = get_clock();a pointer to the node’s clockstd::make_shared<rclcpp::Clock>(...) does not convert; hold a rclcpp::Clock by value.
timer_->cancel(); / timer_->reset(); as a statementallowed on a ported target under -WerrorAs publish(): the result is still readable.
descriptor.floating_point_range.resize(1)a bounded sequence resizes within its boundPast the bound it is refused and returns false, where rosidl throws.
rclcpp::spin(node->get_node_base_interface())spins the node
get_node_base_interface()->get_context()->add_pre_shutdown_callback(f)rclcpp::Context views the executor’s shutdown hooks; f runs on rclcpp::shutdown()The hooks share the executor’s table (NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SHUTDOWN_CBS, default 2). A full table returns an invalid handle.
a package that depends on rclcpp_lifecycleits runtime carries lifecycle (with param_services on a host), and ros2 lifecycle get /<node> finds itOn a board the cmake road gives it lifecycle alone. A Zephyr application states it in system.toml: [system] features = ["lifecycle"].
std::static_pointer_cast<Derived>(shared_from_this()) (Nav2’s nav2_util::LifecycleNode)does not compileThe handle owns nothing, so there is no std::shared_ptr to cast. Drop the override; rclcpp_lifecycle::LifecycleNode::shared_from_this() returns its own type.
pub_->get_subscription_count()takes the executor and an out-parameterSee Publisher::get_subscription_count. Nav2 calls it only in its tests.
declare_parameter(name, rclcpp::ParameterValue(...)[, descriptor]), get_parameter(name) as an rclcpp::Parameter, set_parameter(rclcpp::Parameter(...))the same store the typed declare_parameter<T> uses; the descriptor may be an rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterDescriptorHosted builds. A byte or string array can be built but not declared. A wrong-type as_double() answers 0.0, not an exception.
add_on_set_parameters_callback(std::bind(&C::cb, this, _1)) with cb(std::vector<rclcpp::Parameter>) returning SetParametersResultruns on every write, local or ros2 param set; successful = false refuses it; the returned handle unregisters on destructionOne parameter per call, because writes are validated one at a time. The reason does not reach the remote caller. Keep the handle as a member of your node class, so it goes before the node does.
node->get_node_parameters_interface()has_parameter, declare_parameter, get_parameter and get_parameter_overrides() through ->get_parameter_overrides() lists this node’s -p / --params-file values as a std::map<std::string, rclcpp::ParameterValue>, one copy per node, so Nav2’s declare_or_get_parameter compiles.
pub_->publish(std::move(msg)) with a std::unique_ptr<M>publishes *msg; the message is freed when the call returnsHosted builds. Every publish serializes, so there is no intra-process hand-over to save a copy. A null pointer is refused and logged.
rclcpp::Client<S>::SharedPtr client_ = create_client<S>(name); + client_->async_send_request(req, callback) with a void(Client<S>::SharedFuture) callbackthe handle holds the poll client; the callback runs from the executor when the reply arrives, with a SharedFuture whose get() returns itHosted builds with std::promise. The client registers one 1 ms timer for its callbacks, cancelled while none is waiting. A removed request’s callback never runs. wait_for_service(1s) inside a callback waits without spinning, so on a polled backend it runs out its budget. On an RTOS toolchain (no std::promise) store the client as rclcpp::Owned<rclcpp::PollClient<S>>, keep the FutureAndRequestId that async_send_request(req) returns, and read it on a later callback with future.is_ready() and get().
diagnostic_updater::Updater updater_{this};publishes /diagnostics on its own timer, every period (setPeriod), as upstream’s doesupdate() still works and is no longer required.
DiagnosticTask, FrequencyStatus, TimeStampStatus, Heartbeat, HeaderlessTopicDiagnostic, TopicDiagnosticupstream’s classes, levels and messages; updater.add(task)A clock argument is a const rclcpp::Clock*, so node->get_clock() still passes. The tasks take no lock, so a node that calls tick() from its own thread must keep that call from overlapping an update. DiagnosedPublisher is absent, because a nano-ros publisher handle can be moved but not copied. Keep the publisher and a TopicDiagnostic, and call tick(stamp) next to each publish.
the six parameter services (ros2 param get/set/list)on for an ament package built on a host: every node serves them, as upstream’s doesComes from the package’s package.xml naming ament_cmake; set NROS_FEATURES to declare the capabilities yourself. Values come from --ros-args --params-file <yaml> or -p. On a board they are off unless declared (param_services in NROS_FEATURES, or [system] features on Zephyr): they cost six queryables and their RAM.

Measured: the stock rclcpp examples

packages/api/nros-cpp/tests/compile/rclcpp-examples/ holds 13 files from ros2/examples (humble and jazzy) verbatim, each beside its port. The repository’s C++ check compiles and links every port against nros-cpp, boots it on a stub middleware, and fails if the number of edited lines changes in either direction (edits.json). Today:

exampleedited lineswhat the edits are
minimal_publisher lambda / member_function0—
minimal_subscriber member_function0—
minimal_subscriber lambda (jazzy)0—
minimal_timer lambda / member_function0—
minimal_client0—
minimal_service3global Node::SharedPtr from a temporary
minimal_subscriber not_composable3global Node::SharedPtr from a temporary
minimal_publisher not_composable11the try/catch goes: no exceptions
multithreaded_executor18MultiThreadedExecutor, callback groups
minimal_action_client member_functions2seq.back() on a generated sequence
minimal_action_server member_functions6the goal runs in the accepted callback, not on a thread of its own

The remaining causes, largest first:

  • Callback groups and the multi-threaded executor (18 lines).
  • Exceptions (11 lines). There is nothing to catch.
  • The action server’s thread per goal (6 lines). The stock handle_accepted detaches a std::thread that drives the goal handle; a goal handle used from a thread you started races the executor (nano-ros starts no threads behind it and a one-level image has no executor lock). The port calls execute(goal_handle) in the accepted callback and drops the rclcpp::Rate::sleep, which would re-enter the executor from that callback.
  • A global Node::SharedPtr assigned from make_shared (2 lines each).
  • seq.back() on a generated sequence (2 lines). FixedSequence / HeapSequence are not std::vector; write seq[seq.length() - 1].

Upstream’s goal-handle shapes are drop-ins, so the two action examples need 6 and 2 edited lines; the total is 43.

Actions: goal handles on a hosted build

The action types keep upstream’s names and concepts, and GoalResponse / CancelResponse / ResultCode keep upstream’s enumerators and values.

On a hosted build (-DNROS_CPP_STD, what the porting flow sets) the stock spellings are drop-ins:

  • rclcpp_action::create_server<A>(node->get_node_base_interface(), …clock, …logging, …waitables, name, handle_goal, handle_cancel, handle_accepted) and rclcpp_action::create_client<A>(…base, …graph, …logging, …waitables, name), or the (node, name, …) shape. Each returns X<A>::SharedPtr, which is rclcpp::Owned<X<A>>: the entity by value, so a member Server<A>::SharedPtr action_server_; works and nothing is shared. The get_node_*_interface() getters return a handle naming the node, whose only use is these two calls.
  • The callbacks take upstream’s shapes, std::bind-ed members included: handle_goal(const GoalUUID&, std::shared_ptr<const Goal>), handle_cancel(std::shared_ptr<ServerGoalHandle<A>>), handle_accepted(std::shared_ptr<ServerGoalHandle<A>>).
  • ServerGoalHandle<A> answers get_goal_id, get_goal, is_active, is_executing, is_canceling, and publish_feedback / succeed / abort / canceled take upstream’s std::shared_ptrs. Each call forwards to the server, keyed by the goal id; the goal itself lives in the server’s static arena, and the handle is a token over it. execute() moves a goal accepted with ACCEPT_AND_DEFER to EXECUTING and publishes the status; for ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE the server does that itself before handle_accepted, as upstream’s does.
  • Client<A>::SendGoalOptions carries upstream’s goal_response_callback (a ClientGoalHandle<A>::SharedPtr, null when rejected), feedback_callback (std::shared_ptr<const Feedback>) and result_callback (WrappedResult{goal_id, code, result}), and async_send_goal(goal, options) binds them to that goal. Giving a result callback requests the result once the goal is accepted, as upstream does.
  • async_get_result(goal_handle, result_callback) and async_cancel_goal(goal_handle, cancel_callback), plus async_cancel_all_goals / async_cancel_goals_before(stamp), return upstream’s std::shared_future (of a WrappedResult, or a CancelResponse::SharedPtr with return_code and goals_canceling), so rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, f) then f.get() work unchanged. The future drives the client while it is polled or waited on.

What stays different, each a compile error or written below:

  • async_send_goal returns rclcpp::Future<GoalAccept>, the goal-keyed future send_goal_future returns, not a std::shared_future of a goal handle. auto f = client->async_send_goal(goal, opts); compiles; a caller that waits on f gets the acceptance (the future never blocks without spinning).
  • A cancel reply is taken by the executor’s spin, as upstream’s is: the spin settles the async_cancel_* future and runs its cancel_callback, so code that keeps only the callback ports as written. A nano-ros server acts on the zero-id cancel-all / cancel-before forms as an rclcpp server does.
  • A goal handle is driven from the executor’s task. Do not hand it to a thread you start (see the 6 lines above). It names its server by address, so the server must not move while a handle is in use; a SharedPtr does not move it.
  • No get_goal_stamp: the arena keeps no acceptance time.
  • It is not a Waitable (no execute / is_ready / set_on_ready_callback): the executor drives the server directly.
  • wait_for_action_server returns Result and the budget is required (see the table above).

On a freestanding build there is no allocator for a goal handle, so ClientGoalHandle::SharedPtr, ServerGoalHandle::SharedPtr, rclcpp_action::create_server, async_send_goal and an assignment to SendGoalOptions’ upstream fields are each a compile error naming the goal-id-keyed form:

  • Server. Declare the Server<A>, initialise it with node.create_action_server(srv, name), and install set_goal_callback_with_ctx / set_cancel_callback_with_ctx / set_accepted_callback_with_ctx (function pointers with a void* context). The callbacks receive the 16-byte goal id; feedback and termination are calls on the server keyed by it — srv.publish_feedback(id, fb), srv.succeed(id, result), abort, canceled — taking the message by const reference.
  • Client. client.set_callbacks(SendGoalOptions{goal_response, feedback, result, context}) installs raw callbacks once for every goal the client sends; send_goal_async(goal, goal_id) sends. send_goal_future / get_result_future are the future-shaped spellings, each keyed by its goal. rclcpp_action::create_client works here too (no allocator involved).

Two things the compiler will not tell you

Everything else on this page either works or fails to compile. These two compile and behave slightly differently, so they are written down rather than left for a debugging session.

Node::ok() — nano-ros cannot throw, so YOU have to ask

Upstream’s rclcpp::Node constructor THROWS when the node cannot be created. nano-ros is built -fno-exceptions, so the constructor cannot: it records the failure and the node answers false to ok().

rclcpp::Node node("talker");
if (!node.ok()) return 1;        // <- this line replaces upstream's try/catch

A generated entry already does this and halts naming the node, so a workspace component needs nothing. A hand-written main does not, and a node that failed to create will otherwise go on to create publishers that quietly do nothing. There is no diagnostic for it — the object exists either way, which is the whole point of not throwing — so checking ok() after constructing a node by hand is on you.

The same shape applies to init(), the two-phase form:

rclcpp::Node node;
if (!node.init("talker").ok()) return 1;

Result carries [[nodiscard]] on C++17 and later, so that one the compiler does warn about.

Node::SharedPtr observes, it does not own

rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr is rclcpp::Handle<rclcpp::Node> on every target, embedded included: a copyable reference that does not keep the node alive. A node is constructed by your main (or the generated entry) and outlives everything it is handed to, so storing and copying it works as upstream’s does. Two consequences:

  • shared_from_this() returns that handle. It is safe to pass to anything that holds it for less than the node’s lifetime (diagnostic_updater::Updater(shared_from_this(), 1.0) is the common case), and NOT safe to store somewhere that outlives the node. It never throws where upstream would raise bad_weak_ptr. nano-ros cannot derive from std::enable_shared_from_this<Node>: its std::weak_ptr member exists only where <memory> does, so two translation units of one firmware image could disagree about the object’s layout.
  • rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr node = std::make_shared<MyNode>(); is a compile error. The shared_ptr there is a temporary, and a handle to it would dangle at the end of the line; the compiler names the deleted conversion. Write auto node = std::make_shared<MyNode>(); instead. A shared_ptr you keep converts to Node::SharedPtr freely, and rclcpp::spin(…) accepts the temporary directly.

rclcpp::TimerBase is a NAME here, not a hierarchy

rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr timer_; compiles unchanged, and you should keep writing it — it is the only spelling that works against real ROS 2 as well as against nano-ros, since upstream has no rclcpp::Timer.

What differs is behind the name. nano-ros has no timer hierarchy: TimerBase is an ALIAS for the one flat rclcpp::Timer, so is_same<TimerBase, Timer>::value is true and neither spelling carries a vtable. The executor dispatches through a raw function pointer, so a polymorphic base would be cost with no caller.

Consequences worth knowing:

  • Timer::SharedPtr is a small handle, not a std::shared_ptr. Its callback lives in the executor, so the handle does not own the timer. Dropping or overwriting timer_ leaves the timer firing; destroying the node stops it. timer_.reset() releases the timer for good. timer_->reset() restarts it, as upstream. A member declared as std::shared_ptr<rclcpp::TimerBase> does not compile: spell it rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr.
  • The same holds for Subscription<M>::SharedPtr, Service<S>::SharedPtr and Client<S>::SharedPtr: dropping the handle leaves the entity running, and sub_.reset() / srv_.reset() / cli_.reset() releases it for every copy at once. A one-shot timer or subscription that resets ITSELF from its own callback works: the release takes effect when the callback returns.
  • rclcpp::WallTimer<...> and rclcpp::GenericTimer<...> do not exist. The clock axis is the second verb rclcpp::create_timer(node, clock, period, cb) plus a runtime field, not a type parameter.
  • DERIVING from rclcpp::TimerBase gets you a concrete handle with a non-virtual destructor. Upstream code almost never does this; if yours does, it needs rework. There is no timer hierarchy here: the executor dispatches through a raw function pointer, so a polymorphic base would be a vtable nothing calls, and TimerBase is a name that promises WallTimer and GenericTimer siblings we deliberately do not have. The clock axis is a runtime field plus the second verb rclcpp::create_timer, not a type parameter.

A real package: Autoware’s autoware_external_cmd_selector

This node was ported (Autoware 0.45.0; 12 subscriptions, 7 publishers, a service, two parameters, diagnostic_updater, a component registered with rclcpp_components_register_node(... EXECUTABLE ...)) through a workspace umbrella like the one above. Its package needed no source edit and no CMakeLists edit, and it runs against a stock ROS 2 Humble rmw_zenoh_cpp peer: topics, the service, ros2 param, /diagnostics. Three things it needed from the person porting it:

  1. Source the project’s install before configuring. Its CMakeLists calls find_package(autoware_cmake) and its message packages come from Autoware’s own install; both reach a machine through source <autoware>/install/setup.bash. nano-ros reads what that puts on AMENT_PREFIX_PATH and CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH: autoware_cmake’s own macros run over nano-ros’s ament verbs, and each message package is generated by nano-ros codegen, never taken from the installed upstream C++.

  2. Raise the pool sizes. A package built this way declares no entity counts, so every pool sits at its embedded default, and start-up stops at the first one that fills, naming its knob. Unless the census derives them from the program (see “Pool sizes” above), set them in the environment of the configure and build:

    export NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS=40 NROS_ZENOH_MAX_LIVELINESS=128 \
       NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PUBLISHERS=32 NROS_ZENOH_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=32 \
       NROS_ZENOH_MAX_QUERYABLES=32

    Those are what this node needed with headroom; a smaller node needs less.

  3. Name the router. NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/<host>:7447 at run time, the same router the ROS 2 side’s rmw_zenoh_cpp uses.

What’s documented as “needs adapt” (codegen-side, not surface-side)

These are cosmetic codegen differences nano-ros’s per-package codegen and the upstream rosidl_default_runtime codegen don’t share; both are tracked as ROS-convention codegen work.

  • Message string fields. nano-ros codegen emits rclcpp::FixedString<N>, upstream emits std::string. Assigning a std::string needs a one-token adapter: message.data = s.c_str(). The reverse (std::string{}.c_str()) is what RCLCPP_INFO already takes.
  • Generated message header path. CLOSED (alias headers): nano-ros codegen emits BOTH the per-message form <std_msgs/msg/string.hpp> (upstream-shape) AND the umbrella <std_msgs/std_msgs.hpp>. Use whichever the original source picks.

What’s out of scope (will need code adapt or a follow-up phase)

  • Persisting parameters. A --params-file <yaml> on the command line is read (scalars), as is -p, and declare_parameter<T>(name) with no default takes its value from there (the Autoware port below declares both of its parameters that way). Parameters then live in a volatile store the standard parameter services can update until the next boot; nothing writes them back.

  • A message with an unbounded string or sequence (std_msgs/String’s data) — a subscription to it stops the compile at NROS_UNBOUNDED__<pkg>_msg_<type>__field_<field>. The receive buffer is sized from a bound, and an unbounded field has none. Give it one in a nros-codegen.toml at the workspace root or beside the package’s CMakeLists.txt:

    [fields]
"std_msgs/String.data" = 256

    The wire format does not change. The other levels ([defaults], [packages.*], [types.*]) and the storage modes are in the message field capacity design.

  • create_generic_publisher(topic, type, qos) / create_generic_subscription(topic, type, qos, callback) by type name — a compile error naming the alternative. rclcpp loads the type’s typesupport at run time; nano-ros links its types at build time, and the wire key needs the type’s RIHS01 hash, which nothing derives from a name. Pass the hash: create_generic_publisher(topic, type, type_hash, qos) returns a GenericPublisher with publish_serialized(data, len), and create_generic_subscription(topic, type, type_hash, qos, callback) calls callback(const uint8_t* data, size_t len) with each message’s CDR bytes. A generated type states both as M::TYPE_NAME and M::TYPE_HASH.

  • class_loader, dlopen composition, a component that is not an rclcpp::Node (get_node_base_interface()) — nano-ros has no runtime loader and no node interfaces. Build the components into one image with a hand-written main, as ros2/demos manual_composition does.

  • tf2, image_transport, pluginlib — out of nano-ros scope. Project- specific helpers (autoware universe_utils, PX4 uORB shims) are not nano-ros’s to ship; the porting user vendors them or replaces the call sites with raw nros-cpp ones.

When the port hits a gap

Known open follow-ups: pool sizing on the ament road, the per-request client callback, listing parameter overrides, and the in-tree migration of legacy nros_generate_interfaces(<pkg>) call sites. If your port surfaces a new gap, file an issue with a reduced case — a fix lands either tree-side (in packages/api/nros-cpp/, cmake/NanoRosAmentSurface.cmake or cmake/find/) or as a codegen change, each with its own in-tree test.

In-tree regression fixtures:

  • local-msg-package — mixed workspace (workspace + AMENT msg sources) C++ + Rust consumers.
  • cpp-port-minimal-publisher — ROS 2 tutorial minimal_publisher.cpp verbatim.
  • rclcpp-compat-smoke — minimal source-compat regression test.
  • topic-state-monitor-port — multi-sub / wall-timer / diagnostic_updater exercise.

Your ported code stays yours: nano-ros does not take a copy of it as a fixture. What lands is the fix, tested by code written for the test: the Autoware port above left behind tests/cmake-ament-surface-tests.sh and packages/api/nros-cpp/tests/compile/ament_port_surface_runtime.cpp, neither of which contains a line of Autoware’s.

Differences from standard ROS 2

Coming from rclcpp, rclrs, or rclc? This page calls out where nano-ros looks the same, where it diverges, and the reason behind each choice. It is an orientation page — the per-language API references (Rust / C / C++) cover the surface itself.

The short version: nano-ros keeps ROS 2’s vocabulary (Node, Publisher, Subscription, Service, Client, ActionServer, ActionClient, Timer, Executor, QoS, message codegen) so existing nodes port cleanly. The trade-offs that come from running on a Cortex-M3 with 64 KB of heap shape every place where the surface diverges.

Same vocabulary, same wire format

  • ROS 2 entity model unchanged. A node owns publishers, subscriptions, services, clients, action servers, action clients, timers, and parameters.
  • Topic / service / action names follow ROS 2 conventions (/talker_node/chatter, /add_two_ints, /fibonacci).
  • Message types stay rosidl-shaped (std_msgs/msg/Int32, geometry_msgs/msg/Twist, …). CDR encoding on the wire.
  • Default backend (nros-rmw-zenoh) is bit-compatible with the upstream rmw_zenoh ROS 2 RMW. A nano-ros publisher and an rclcpp subscriber on the same zenohd router exchange messages without a bridge — see ROS 2 Interoperability.

Where it diverges, and why

1. The executor is the entry point

Standard ROS 2 starts with a global init (rclcpp::init / rclrs::Context::default_from_env / rclc_support_init) followed by node creation, then optionally an executor.

nano-ros inverts this: an Executor opens the RMW session and owns the runtime budget. Every node, publisher, subscription, service, client, action handle, and timer is allocated out of the executor’s arena.

Executor::open(&config) → Node → Publisher / Subscription / Service / Client / Timer

Why. The arena is fixed-size and known at compile time (NROS_EXECUTOR_ARENA_SIZE / NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS). On a 64 KB heap MCU we cannot afford the indirection of a global allocator behind every create_publisher call. The executor-as-arena pattern moves the size negotiation up to the application’s startup code, where it belongs.

2. Both manual-poll and callback paths are first-class

rclcpp is callback-only — every subscription needs a callback, the executor dispatches them. rclrs <0.7 was manual-poll only. rclc exposes both but treats manual-poll as the second-class path.

nano-ros treats them as equals. A subscription created via node.create_subscription(...) exposes take(). A subscription registered via executor.node_mut(nid).create_subscription::<M, _>("/topic", callback) runs the callback during spin_once. Pick whichever fits the control loop.

A C++ callback may also take upstream’s const rclcpp::MessageInfo& as its second argument (hosted builds). A C++ poll subscription has upstream’s polling form, sub.take(msg, info), on hosted and freestanding builds. The fields are what the backend reports per sample, so on XRCE and uORB they are all zero. info.is_reported() (a nano-ros extension) says whether the backend reported metadata for that sample at all.

Why. Embedded apps often want the predictability of an explicit poll inside a real-time loop. Callback dispatch is great for event-driven services but adds indirection that real-time engineers have to bound by hand. Offering both means the application picks.

3. No foreign async runtime, on purpose

rclrs 0.7+ added spin_async beside its synchronous executor. nano-ros does not offer one. A future polled by tokio or Embassy runs when THAT scheduler decides, so nano-ros could not state when a callback runs or at what priority, and the real-time promise is the first thing nano-ros offers. Concurrent waits are written as callbacks on tiers instead, each tier an OS thread at a priority nano-ros derives.

4. Heap is optional

ROS 2 RMW implementations all assume std + a heap. Even rclrs’s no_std story is “soon”.

nano-ros runs in three modes that map onto target capability:

ModeCargo featuresWhat works
stdstd (default on POSIX)Everything. POSIX threading, full async runtime.
no_std + allocalloc + a #[global_allocator]Everything except features that need std::sync::Mutex. Used by FreeRTOS / NuttX / ThreadX / Zephyr.
no_std cooperativeno std/alloc platform threading (bare-metal board crates, RTIC apps)Cooperative single-task — no threading at all. Used by bare-metal MPS2-AN385, single-core RTIC.

Why. Heap presence is not a binary “embedded yes/no” — it is a spectrum. Stm32-class boards have a heap; Cortex-M0+-class might not. The feature axis lets the same application code target both.

5. Backend selection at compile time, not runtime

Standard ROS 2 uses an RMW_IMPLEMENTATION env var read at process start. The plugin loader pulls a shared library, dispatches calls through C function pointers.

nano-ros bakes the backend in at compile time. The consuming Cargo.toml adds the backend crate directly (nros-rmw-zenoh / nros-rmw-cyclonedds / nros-rmw-xrce-cffi) alongside nros with the rmw-cffi feature; CMake options (-DNROS_RMW=zenoh) decide it for C/C++ builds. The backend’s #[ctor] registers its vtable with the nros-rmw-cffi runtime registry before main.

Why.

  • Dead-code elimination. A 32 KB Flash budget cannot afford to link every backend’s C client and pick at runtime. Linking only the selected backend cuts the binary substantially (the three backends differ by an order of magnitude in linked C footprint — measure your own image with size; no benchmarked figure exists).
  • No plugin loader. Most embedded targets have no dlopen. The cost of the plugin abstraction is a permanent overhead with no payoff there.
  • Cross-compile sanity. RMW_IMPLEMENTATION baked into the binary means the build system already knows which backend’s C client to link — no separate “find shared library at runtime” step.

The trade-off is real: changing backends requires a rebuild. This is the right trade-off for the embedded use case; it would be the wrong trade-off for desktop ROS 2.

A binary can still link multiple backends and run them in parallel — one node on backend A, another on backend B, the executor draining both each tick. The Cross-backend Bridges chapter walks the build knobs (NROS_RMW=... primary selector, explicit per-backend register(), NROS_RMW= none cmake escape hatch) and the three shipped examples.

6. Message codegen lands inside your build, not a sibling library

Standard ROS 2 uses ament + rosidl to compile message packages (std_msgs, geometry_msgs, …) into separate shared libraries that your application links against.

nano-ros’s nros build (Rust) and nano_ros_generate_interfaces() (C / C++ via CMake — one of five entry points; see the spelling table) write message type definitions into your build tree. No _msgs library, no ament overlay, no colcon workspace required.

Why. An embedded cross-build has no ROS 2 runtime to link against, so the types are generated into the build instead of installed as libraries. The message definitions still come from your ROS 2 install: nros build reads them through AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, which you source once per project (the first configure records it), so the generated layouts and type hashes are the ones your ROS 2 peers use.

7. QoS profile is the full DDS field set; backends advertise per-policy support

Standard ROS 2 supports the full DDS QoS profile family (reliability, durability, history, depth, deadline, lifespan, liveliness, liveliness_lease_duration, avoid_ros_namespace_conventions) and performs profile matching between endpoints.

nano-ros’s rmw_qos_profile_t carries the same field set; standard profile constants (NROS_RMW_QOS_PROFILE_DEFAULT, _SENSOR_DATA, _SERVICES_DEFAULT, _PARAMETERS, _SYSTEM_DEFAULT) match upstream rmw_qos_profile_* field-for-field. ROS 2 apps porting across pull the equivalent constant unchanged.

Each backend advertises which policies it can enforce via Session::supported_qos_policies(). The runtime validates the requested QoS at entity-create time and returns IncompatibleQos synchronously when the backend can’t honour a requested policy:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if session.supported_qos_policies().contains(QoSPolicyMask::DEADLINE) {
    // backend honours deadline; safe to set deadline_ms
} else {
    // app handles deadline monitoring itself
}
}

No silent downgrade. The runtime never quietly drops a requested policy. Apps either get the QoS they asked for or a hard error.

Why upstream-shaped struct, not a smaller subset. ROS 2 QoS is the established vocabulary; mismatched APIs make porting painful. The field set is small (24 bytes); apps that don’t request a policy leave its field at zero (“off”). Per-backend implementation is a separate question — which policies actually fire — answered by the support mask.

Why synchronous error instead of runtime event. Upstream’s RMW_EVENT_REQUESTED_INCOMPATIBLE_QOS event surfaces mismatches at run time. Most QoS mismatches are configuration errors visible at startup; the runtime path doesn’t need to handle them. The few that aren’t (cross-process QoS-mismatched discovery) the wire protocol handles itself — DDS endpoints negotiate via DDS Discovery, zenoh endpoints communicate intent through the topic-key encoding.

Manual liveliness assertion. Publishers configured with MANUAL_BY_TOPIC / MANUAL_BY_NODE liveliness call assert_liveliness() explicitly to refresh the lease. Available on every language surface (Rust Publisher<M>::assert_liveliness(), C rcl_publisher_assert_liveliness(&pub), C++ pub.assert_liveliness()).

Which backend actually asserts. cyclonedds implements it (dds_assert_liveliness on the writer: renews the lease and sends a Heartbeat). zenoh-pico does not — its liveliness is a session-scoped keepalive, it has no per-topic lease a call can renew, and what assert_liveliness() refreshes there is a LOCAL watchdog that fires this publisher’s own LivelinessLost on expiry. That local behaviour is real, but under a manual kind zenoh-pico, XRCE-DDS and uORB answer UNSUPPORTED rather than Ok, because an Ok from a call that put nothing on the wire is the one thing a caller uses this function to rule out. AUTOMATIC and NONE answer Ok everywhere: there was nothing to assert.

See Status events for the runtime-event side of liveliness, deadline, and message-lost.

Per-backend coverage is documented in RMW vs upstream § 7.

8. No runtime backend swap, no runtime introspection

Standard ROS 2 ships ros2 topic list, ros2 node info, dynamic endpoints discovery, rmw_get_* introspection.

nano-ros has none of that at runtime. The backend is fixed at compile time, the wire-protocol introspection is whatever the backend natively exposes (zenoh-pico’s z_query for SPDP, Cyclone DDS’s SPDP/SEDP discovery, …). Use the host-side ROS 2 tools for introspection and connect via the rmw_zenoh interop path.

Why. Every byte of “introspect what’s running” is overhead a microcontroller can’t justify when a host-side ROS 2 environment is one router-hop away.

9. Parameters: node-local server, no descriptors, no callbacks (yet)

Standard ROS 2 (rclcpp::Node) ships a rich parameter surface: declare_parameter<T> with ParameterDescriptor (description, ranges, read-only, dynamic typing), set_parameter returning a SetParametersResult, atomic multi-set, three callback hooks (pre_set / on_set / post_set), parameter overrides from the launch file or CLI, and a service-backed remote-introspection surface (/<node>/get_parameters, /<node>/set_parameters, …).

nano-ros keeps the vocabulary (declare_parameter<T>, get_parameter<T>, set_parameter<T>, has_parameter) but trims the surface for embedded use. There is ONE store, and it is in Rust: the nros_params::ParameterServer the executor owns, which is also what the six rcl_interfaces/srv/* servers read. C++ reaches it through methods on rclcpp::Node; C through rclc’s own parameter-server API, <rclc_parameter/rclc_parameter.h> (rclc_parameter_server_t, one per node); Rust through the Node (node.declare_parameter::<T>(name), rclrs’s builder, plus get_parameter / set_parameter and the rest), as rclrs does; the executor’s own parameter methods are deprecated or internal.

If you have older nano-ros code: rclcpp::ParameterServer<Cap> is gone and so is the caller-storage store it wrapped as a thing to reach for. Both were node-LOCAL: the parameter services read a different object, so ros2 param list never saw what you declared. The C caller-storage family and the nros_executor_*_param* functions are gone too: C uses rclc’s rclc_parameter_server_t, which declares into the same executor-owned store.

What we keep

  • Same five scalar types: bool, int64_t, double, string, plus the bool / int64_t / double / byte / string array variants on the C side (rclc_parameter_{declare,get,set}_*_array; string arrays not yet).
  • Same lifecycle: declare → get → set, with declare-once-then-typed-get semantics.
  • Optional service-backed exposure (~/get_parameters / ~/set_parameters / ~/list_parameters / …) when the param-services feature is enabled. This pulls in ROS 2 wire compat: declared parameters are visible to ros2 param list /<node> and ros2 param set. The services use the rcl_interfaces message bounds: a list_parameters reply carries at most 64 names and 64 prefixes, and when more match it is cut there and the node logs one warning (the reply message has no field to say so). A set_parameters request is answered per parameter, so a value or name past those bounds gets successful = false with a reason while the rest are applied.
  • /parameter_events, from every language. A node whose parameters are served publishes rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent with rmw_qos_profile_parameter_events (RELIABLE, VOLATILE; depth 1000 hosted, NROS_PARAM_EVENTS_DEPTH on an RTOS): one start-up event naming what the node already holds, then one per declare, set and undeclare, with node set to the node’s fully qualified name. C++ gets it from Node::start_parameter_services(), Rust from [param_services] (or Executor::register_parameter_services), C from rclc’s notify_changed_over_dds (default on; false opts that node out; C++‘s NodeOptions().start_parameter_event_publisher(false) does the same). One publisher per executor serves every node, so param_services costs one publisher slot and one liveliness token on top of the six services per node, and no queryable. An event too big for NROS_PARAM_SERVICE_BUFFER_SIZE is not published (logged as an error), never truncated. To subscribe to OTHER nodes’ events, a hosted C++ build has rclcpp::ParameterEventHandler: per-parameter callbacks taking rclcpp::Parameter, and whole-event callbacks taking the image’s generated rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterEvent. A freestanding build, C and Rust use a plain /parameter_events subscription.

What we drop, and why

Upstream featurenano-ros statusWhy dropped
ParameterDescriptor (description, ranges, read-only, dynamic_typing)not exposeddescriptor metadata is host-side concern; embedded server enforces type at declare-time, range checks belong in set callbacks (deferred — see below)
add_pre_set_parameters_callback / add_on_set_parameters_callback / add_post_set_parameters_callbackone rclc_parameter_callback_t per C server — rclc’s (old, new, context), fired before the write, false refusesthree callbacks → three indirection slots × N subscribers; one callback covers the safety-island validation use case (reject if out of range)
set_parameter returning SetParametersResult (successful: bool, reason: string)returns rcl_ret_tstring reason would force heap or fixed-buffer; ret code captures the binary outcome
set_parameters_atomicallynot exposedatomic multi-set requires transaction log; not justified by current embedded use
declare_parameters (multi-declare with namespace)C++ only, hosted only: rclcpp::Node::declare_parameters<T>(prefix, map)upstream’s argument is a std::map, so it needs an allocator; returns Result, not the std::vector<T> of values in effect (read back with get_parameter<T>). Rust and C declare one at a time
Parameter overrides from CLI / launch / yamlnot exposedembedded apps configure via Kconfig / Config struct; runtime overrides come over the wire via ~/set_parameters (when param-services is on)
Storage allocation policyone executor-owned table, NROS_MAX_PARAMETERS slots, keyed by nodeno per-node heap; capacity is a build knob, sized once like the executor arena rather than multiplied by the node count

Storage shape difference

rclcppnano-ros
Containerstd::map<string, ParameterValue> per node (heap)one fixed table on the executor, keyed by (node, name)
String valuestd::string (heap)fixed slot, copy semantics
Array paramsstd::vector<T> (heap)rclcpp::Seq<T, N> in, elements copied into the store’s own slot — nothing for the caller to keep alive
Total fixed costunboundedNROS_MAX_PARAMETERS slots, known at build time, shared by every node

Class shape difference

rclcpp::Node owns the parameter store; nano-ros’s node borrows one the EXECUTOR owns. The call shape is upstream’s:

// rclcpp
auto node = std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>("ctrl");
node->declare_parameter<double>("ctrl_period", 0.15);
double v = node->get_parameter("ctrl_period").as_double();

// nano-ros
rclcpp::Node node;
RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::Node::create(node, "ctrl"));
double period = node.declare_parameter<double>("ctrl_period", 0.15);
double v = 0.0;
node.get_parameter<double>("ctrl_period", v);

// an array parameter, with no heap: `Seq<T, N>` is the value, the store
// owns the elements
rclcpp::Seq<double, 8> w = node.declare_parameter("mpc_weights",
                                                rclcpp::Seq<double, 8>{1.0, 2.0});

Why the executor owns it. Templating Node on a capacity would propagate through every create_publisher / create_subscription site, so the store cannot be a member; and a store per node is a store per node’s worth of fixed arena on a target that has one. One executor-owned table, keyed by node, is both — /talker’s rate is not /listener’s, and the arena is sized once (NROS_MAX_PARAMETERS). It is also the table the services answer from, which is the property the split shape could not have: the parameter you declare is the parameter ros2 param get returns.

Why no Box<dyn FnMut> callback yet. The same constraint that shapes the QoS event callbacks applies here: nano-ros’s #[no_std] core forbids alloc-style indirection. A future descriptor-+-validation-callback path will use a function pointer + void* user_context pair, registered at declare-time. Tracked under the upstream parity backlog.

Going further. When upstream’s full parameter surface matters — describe_parameter, ranges, three-stage validation callbacks, override files — fall back to running a host-side ROS 2 node that exposes them and uses the embedded node only as the leaf publisher / subscriber.

What this means in practice

If you are coming from rclcpp:

  • Open an Executor, then create the node from it.
  • Decide poll vs. callback per subscription, not globally.
  • If the platform has std, nros::init() looks identical; if it is RTOS / bare-metal, plan the executor arena up front.
  • Pick nros-rmw-zenoh for ROS 2 interop; everything else is a different trade-off.

If you are coming from rclrs:

  • The umbrella crate is nros, not split into rclrs_*. nros::prelude gives you everything.
  • Executor::open(&config) is the equivalent of Context::default_from_env() + Executor::new(...).
  • The async surface is on the executor + handles themselves (re-exported at the crate root). Compatible with tokio out of the box.

If you are coming from rclc:

  • The C entry points carry rclc’s own names (rclc_node_init_default, rclc_publisher_init_default, rclc_subscription_init_default), in rclc’s argument order and at rclc’s arity. Memory ownership rules are the same — the caller owns storage, the API initialises it.
  • See the C API reference for the full surface.

Going deeper

  • API surface, type by type → per-language references at Rust / C / C++.
  • Why the executor / RMW / platform layers split this way → Architecture Overview.
  • Cooperative no_std model → no_std Support.

Design background

  • RFC-0113: RT unified wait (why there is no async executor)

nano-ros vs micro-ROS

The closest peer project to nano-ros is micro-ROS. Both ship a full embedded ROS 2 framework — client library + RMW + tooling targeted at MCU-class hardware. This page is an apples-to-apples comparison.

Why not compare to rmw_zenoh or ros2_rust? Scope mismatch. rmw_zenoh is a single RMW backend; nano-ros is a full client stack. ros2_rust (rclrs) targets hosted Linux only — it can’t run on the bare-metal or RTOS targets nano-ros and micro-ROS both address. Comparing nano-ros to either would be misleading.

Pick nano-ros when…

  • You want Rust as a first-class API, not bolted on. Memory safety + ownership semantics extend to your application code.
  • You want multi-backend flexibility — same binary can speak Zenoh + DDS, or you want to pick Zenoh’s peer-to-peer model over XRCE’s agent dependency.
  • You need scheduling primitives beyond priority callbacks — EDF / Sporadic / ARINC-653 TT classes, per-callback runtime accounting, formal SchedContext API.
  • You’re targeting safety-aware deployments that benefit from the E2E CRC + sequence tracking and the Kani / Verus harness coverage.
  • You want a lean source-only consumption model: git clone + add_subdirectory(<repo>). No crates.io drift, no pre-built per-distro binaries.

Pick micro-ROS when…

  • You’re already in the micro-ROS ecosystem (existing rclc code, established Agent deployment, ROS 2 Jazzy / Iron support).
  • Your toolchain is C-only and you don’t want to introduce Rust into the build pipeline.
  • Your target’s flash budget is tight (~30 KB ceiling) — the rclc + XRCE client is smaller than nano-ros + Zenoh.
  • You need commercial support contracts today (Bosch, eProsima, PIWeb).

Migration sketch

If you’re porting from micro-ROS to nano-ros:

Several rows below are now identity on the C side: nano-ros’s C API uses rcl/rclc’s spellings, so rclc_publisher_init_default and rclc_executor_t are what nano-ros calls them too. The migration is a rename only where the shape differs.

  • rcl_node_init → Executor::create_node (Rust) / rclc_node_init_default (C — same name as micro-ROS, but the ARGUMENTS are rclc’s order (node, name, namespace, support)).
  • rclc_executor_t → nros::Executor (Rust) / rclcpp::Executor (C++); unchanged in C.
  • rclc_publisher_init_default → Node::create_publisher::<M> (Rust) or the identically-spelled rclc_publisher_init_default (C).
  • micro-ROS’s rmw_uros_set_custom_transport → nano-ros’s custom transport pattern via nros_platform_* C ABI (see Custom Transport).
  • XRCE Agent deployment stays the same — point nano-ros’s XRCE backend at the same Agent.

Migration Guide for ROS 2 Users

This page maps standard ROS 2 concepts to their nano-ros equivalents. It is not an API reference; use it as a checklist when moving an existing rclcpp, rclc, or rclrs node toward nano-ros.

Concept map

You have (ROS 2)You get (nano-ros)Where

package.xmlkept, verbatim. What it deploys to is not in it — that is the bringup’s system.tomlAnatomy
.launch.xml / .launch.pykept — nros configure resolves them into a SystemModel the image bakes inAdd a launch file
ros2 launch pkg filenros build <image>, then run its binary — the launch product is compiled inAdd an image
colcon buildnros build <image> — it generates the root and hands off to cmake / cargo / west. Running those yourself still works when you point them at the generated build root, and colcon build still works for POSIX C++ workspacesC/C++ workspaces
rosdep installnros setup <board> --rmw <rmw>Install
RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=… at runtimecompile-time backend, one line: [system] rmw = "…" in the bringup’s system.toml, then nros buildSwitching RMW

find_package(rclcpp)find_package(nano_ros) — ament-shaped, source-backedPorting a C++ node
