For *_get_actual_qos the deciding fact was measured: an Agent-side profile cannot override a BIN-created entity’s QoS, and a BIN-created requester/replier ignores its requested QoS altogether.

10. Error returns

Upstream. Single error type for everything:

typedef int32_t rmw_ret_t;
#define RMW_RET_OK              0
#define RMW_RET_ERROR           1
#define RMW_RET_TIMEOUT         2
#define RMW_RET_UNSUPPORTED     3
/* ... */

Pointer-returning calls indicate failure with NULL and set a thread-local error string via rmw_set_error_string.

nano-ros. Same named-constant style (<nros/rmw_ret.h>), different sign convention, no thread-local error string:

typedef int32_t rmw_ret_t;
#define NROS_RMW_RET_OK                       0
#define NROS_RMW_RET_ERROR                   -1
#define NROS_RMW_RET_TIMEOUT                 -2
#define NROS_RMW_RET_BAD_ALLOC               -3
#define NROS_RMW_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT        -4
#define NROS_RMW_RET_UNSUPPORTED             -5
#define NROS_RMW_RET_INCOMPATIBLE_QOS        -6
#define NROS_RMW_RET_TOPIC_NAME_INVALID      -7
#define NROS_RMW_RET_NODE_NAME_NON_EXISTENT  -8
#define NROS_RMW_RET_LOAN_NOT_SUPPORTED      -9
#define NROS_RMW_RET_NO_DATA                -10
#define NROS_RMW_RET_WOULD_BLOCK            -11
#define NROS_RMW_RET_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL       -12
#define NROS_RMW_RET_MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE      -13

Two return-shape conventions, picked by call shape:

ReturnsSuccessFailure
rmw_ret_t + entity-struct out-param (create_session, create_publisher, create_subscription, …)NROS_RMW_RET_OK, out->backend_data non-NULLnegative named constant
rmw_ret_t (destroy_session, drive_io, publish, send_response, …)NROS_RMW_RET_OKnegative named constant
int32_t byte count (take, take_request, take_response)>= 0 (bytes received)negative rmw_ret_t

Differences from upstream.

  • Negative for error. Upstream uses positive integer codes (RMW_RET_ERROR = 1); nano-ros uses negative so the byte-count convention can be unified into the same int32_t return.
  • No thread-local error string. No rmw_set_error_string, no rmw_get_error_string. The thread-local heap allocation that pattern needs is unaffordable on embedded targets. Backends log verbose diagnostics at the failure site through the platform’s printk equivalent — never buffered, never thread-local.
  • Smaller code-set. 13 codes total (vs upstream’s ~25). The set started from upstream’s and dropped codes that don’t apply (e.g., DDS event codes, RMW_RET_NODE_INVALID). Adding a code is a <nros/rmw_ret.h> header change only.

Why same style. Named constants make switch statements possible at call sites; bare negative ints don’t.

Publisher GID, message-info & service info: functional-parity, different shape

Three upstream rmw.h capabilities exist in nano-ros in a different shape — the functionality is present, but the upstream-exact C entry points are deliberately not mirrored. Recorded here so the divergence reads as a decision.

Message-info: surfaced via a builder, not a take_with_info slot

Upstream’s rmw_take_with_info fills an rmw_message_info_t (source + received timestamp, publisher GID, publication + reception sequence numbers) alongside the payload.

nano-ros provides the same information — MessageInfo carries all five fields — but through a different seam:

  • Application API (present). A subscription opts into message-info with the message_info() builder: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
node.subscription::<Msg>("/topic")
    .message_info()
    .build(|msg, info: Option<&MessageInfo>| {
        if let Some(i) = info {
            log::info!("from {:?} at {:?}", i.publisher_gid(), i.source_timestamp());
        }
    })?;
}
    C mirrors this with rclc_executor_add_subscription_with_info (the callback receives the payload plus the attachment/metadata arguments directly — there is no info struct on the C side), which registers into a rcl_subscription_t that rclc_executor_remove_subscription takes back out.
  • Two backend channels. The hot take vtable slot returns bytes only. A backend that fills the optional take_with_info slot reports rmw_message_info_t in caller-owned storage, and the runtime dispatches it whenever it is present — that is how a C/C++ backend (Cyclone) reports metadata. A Rust backend behind the adapter writes a MessageInfoSlot side-channel instead, which the runtime pairs with the payload. Either way the message_info() builder sees the same MessageInfo.

received_timestamp follows upstream’s meaning: the subscriber’s own wall clock (nros_platform_time_now_ns, ns since the Unix epoch) when the sample ARRIVED, the clock and the moment rmw_zenoh_cpp stamps (system_clock::now() in its sample callback). Zero means “not stamped”:

backendreceived_timestamp on a sample
zenoh-picostamped by the ring producer (the sample callback)
XRCE-DDSstamped by the topic callback, inside drive_io
Cyclone DDS0 — Cyclone 0.10’s sample info has no reception time, and a stamp at take time is a different fact. Humble rmw_cyclonedds_cpp writes 0 for the same reason; Jazzy’s stamps the take time
uORB0

Publisher identity: one GID, from one source

Upstream exposes rmw_get_gid_for_publisher(pub, out_gid) and stamps every sample with the writer’s GID, so a subscriber can name the publisher that sent a message. nano-ros does both, and the two answers are the same bytes:

backendget_gid() and MessageInfo::publisher_gid
zenoh-picoXXH3-128 of the entity’s liveliness keyexpr, 16 bytes zero-extended to 24 — rmw_zenoh_cpp’s own derivation, so a stock peer’s ros2 topic info --verbose prints the same GID
cycloneddsthe DDS writer GUID, 16 bytes zero-extended; the take path reports it through the take_with_info slot
XRCE-DDSget_gid(): the DDS GUID graph.c derives for the endpoint (probed participant prefix + the Agent’s endpoint counter), 16 bytes zero-extended — the GID ros_discovery_info lists and a stock ros2 topic info --verbose prints. No GID on a take: a topic sample carries no writer GUID through the Agent (the take reports only its receive time)
uORBUNSUPPORTED; no metadata on a take

The field is 24 bytes, upstream’s RMW_GID_STORAGE_SIZE. The 16 is zenoh’s wire width and stays there: rmw_zenoh_cpp’s attachment reader rejects any other length.

One upstream divergence worth knowing when comparing against a stock peer: a Humble rmw_cyclonedds_cpp subscriber puts the 8-byte publication handle in message_info.publisher_gid, not the writer GUID it reports everywhere else, so its take-side gid matches no gid query. Ours reports the GUID.

Service info: a sibling slot on each side

Upstream’s rmw_take_request fills an rmw_service_info_t beside the request: the client’s request_id (writer GUID + the sequence number that client assigned) and the source_timestamp / received_timestamp pair.

nano-ros splits that take across two vtable slots:

  • take_request returns the payload bytes and int64_t *seq_out, the backend’s reply-correlation token that send_response takes back. That is everything a server needs to answer, and it is all this slot returns.
  • take_request_with_info (optional, appended) is the same take plus a caller-owned rmw_service_info_t *, declared in <nros/rmw_entity.h> field for field as upstream’s. seq_out stays beside the struct instead of becoming its request_id.sequence_number: a backend’s token (a reply-slot index on Cyclone, XRCE and zenoh) is not the client’s sequence number, and the runtime needs both. When a backend fills this slot the runtime takes every request through it; when it does not, the runtime falls back to take_request, and only a Rust backend’s side table can then report anything.

A field the backend cannot report is zero (all-zero writer_guid = no request id, timestamp 0 = not stamped), and the runtime turns each zero into None, never into a value:

backendchannelrequest_idsource_timestampreceived_timestamp
zenoh-picoRust adapter side tablefrom the query attachment (rmw_zenoh_cpp layout)from the attachmentstamped by the queryable callback
Cyclone DDStake_request_with_inforequest-header GUID + publication handle, header sequence (stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp layout)the DDS sample’s source timestampnot reported — Cyclone 0.10 has no reception time (Humble upstream writes 0 too)
XRCE-DDStake_request_with_infothe Agent’s SampleIdentity (client request-writer GUID + sequence), as rmw_microxrcedds fills itnot reported — no timestamp reaches the client librarystamped by the request callback
uORB—uORB has no services——

received_timestamp is the server’s own wall clock (nros_platform_time_now_ns) when the request arrived, which is what rmw_zenoh_cpp stamps (system_clock::now() when the query arrives); it is zero on a platform with no wall clock.

What an application sees:

  • Rust. create_service_with_info (or the builder’s .service_info()) hands the callback a nros::ServiceInfo — rclrs’s shape, except every field is an Option: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
executor.node_mut(nid).create_service_with_info::<AddTwoInts, _>(
    "/add_two_ints",
    |req: &AddTwoIntsRequest, info: &nros::ServiceInfo| {
        if let Some(id) = info.request_id {
            log::info!("request #{} from {:?}", id.sequence_number, id.writer_guid);
        }
        AddTwoIntsResponse { sum: req.a + req.b }
    },
)?;
}
  • C. rclc_executor_add_service_with_request_id (typed) and rclc_executor_add_service_raw_with_request_id (CDR bytes) pass the callback an rmw_request_id_t *, rclc’s shape. The timestamps are not surfaced in C.
  • C++. An rclcpp service handler taking three arguments — (std::shared_ptr<rmw_request_id_t>, request, response) — receives the request header; the two-argument handler does not. As in C, the timestamps are not surfaced.

The client side has the same split. take_response returns the reply bytes and the sequence_id that send_request handed out, which is what the runtime matches a reply against. take_response_with_info (optional, appended) is the same take plus a caller-owned rmw_service_info_t * — upstream rmw_take_response’s request_header. Its fields mean what a client’s mean upstream: the request_id the reply answers (this client’s request-writer GUID and the sequence number of its request), the SERVER’s clock when it sent the reply, and this client’s clock when the reply arrived.

backendrequest_idsource_timestampreceived_timestamp
zenoh-picofrom the reply attachment (rmw_zenoh_cpp layout: the client’s gid and sequence number)from the attachment — the replier’s send time; our server restamps the request attachment it echoesstamped by the reply callback, as rmw_zenoh_cpp’s ZenohReply is
Cyclone DDSthe echoed request header’s GUID + the reply sample’s publication handle, header sequence (stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp, which shares one take for both sides)the reply sample’s source timestampnot reported — Cyclone 0.10 has no reception time
XRCE-DDSnot reported — the Agent owns the request writer, so its GUID never reaches the client (the sequence number is still matched on)not reportedstamped by the reply callback
uORB———

What an application sees on the client side:

  • Rust. Promise::take_with_info() / wait_with_info() return the reply with its nros::ServiceInfo — rclrs’s client.call::<_, (Response, ServiceInfo)>(..), every field an Option: 
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut promise = client.call(&request)?;
let (reply, info) = promise.wait_with_info(&mut executor, timeout)?;
if let (Some(sent), Some(got)) = (info.source_timestamp, info.received_timestamp) {
    log::info!("reply took {} ns on the wire", got.to_nanos() - sent.to_nanos());
}
}
    The callback client has the same read: Node::create_client_with_callback_with_info hands its closure (&Reply, &ServiceInfo), the client twin of create_service_with_info.
  • C. rclc_executor_add_client_with_request_id passes the callback an rmw_request_id_t *, rclc’s shape: the sequence number the reply was matched on, and the writer GUID where the backend reports it. The timestamps are not surfaced in C.
  • C++. PollClient<S>::take_response(response, request_header) — upstream rclcpp::Client::take_response — takes the next reply with its rmw_request_id_t, as C’s callback receives it: the sequence number always, the writer GUID where the backend reports it. As upstream’s, it takes whatever reply is next and touches no pending future, so the header is what a caller correlates on. It returns a Result (TryAgain when nothing is waiting) where upstream returns bool and throws. The timestamps are not surfaced in C++, as upstream rclcpp surfaces none on a client.
