Zenoh-pico Symbol Reference

This page documents the ~55 FFI symbols that zenoh-pico requires at link time. These symbols are provided by zpico-sys’s C alias translation unit (c/zpico/platform_aliases.c, built by the default-on platform-aliases feature), which forwards each z_* / _z_* call to the canonical nros_platform_* ABI. When porting to a new platform, you implement an nros-platform-<name> crate (see Custom Platform) that supplies the nros_platform_* symbols — you do not provide the z_* symbols directly.

There is no separate zpico-platform-shim crate: the forwarders live in the zpico-sys alias TU.

This page serves as a reference for understanding what the alias TU maps and what capabilities your nros-platform-<name> crate must provide.

Platform crate structure

packages/platform/nros-platform-<name>/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    ├── clock.rs
    ├── memory.rs
    ├── sleep.rs
    ├── random.rs
    ├── time.rs
    ├── threading.rs          # no-op stubs or real RTOS impl
    ├── socket_stubs.rs       # if using smoltcp
    └── network.rs            # if using smoltcp

Cargo.toml must have zero nros-* dependencies. It may depend on:

  • Hardware HAL crate (e.g., stm32f4xx-hal, esp-hal)
  • zpico-smoltcp (if using smoltcp networking)
  • embedded-alloc (for heap on bare-metal)
  • RTOS bindings crate

Required FFI symbols

Clock (critical)

The clock is the most important primitive. zenoh-pico uses it for session keep-alive, query timeouts, and transport timeouts. It must be backed by a hardware timer or OS tick — never by a software counter that only advances when polled.

// Monotonic clock — returns an opaque timestamp (lower 32 bits of ms)
usize   z_clock_now(void);

// Elapsed time since a previous z_clock_now() value
c_ulong z_clock_elapsed_us(usize *time);
c_ulong z_clock_elapsed_ms(usize *time);
c_ulong z_clock_elapsed_s(usize *time);

// Advance a timestamp value by a duration
void    z_clock_advance_us(usize *clock, c_ulong duration);
void    z_clock_advance_ms(usize *clock, c_ulong duration);
void    z_clock_advance_s(usize *clock, c_ulong duration);

If using smoltcp (bare-metal networking), also provide:

// Called by zpico-smoltcp for TCP/IP timestamping
u64 smoltcp_clock_now_ms(void);

Implementation checklist:

  1. Identify a hardware timer (SysTick, GPT, DWT) or use the OS tick API (xTaskGetTickCount, k_uptime_get, clock_gettime)
  2. Handle 32-bit timer wraps — track a wrap count in an atomic or use a 64-bit counter
  3. Never advance the clock inside smoltcp_network_poll() — read the hardware timer directly
  4. Verify with QEMU: use -icount shift=auto to synchronize virtual time with wall-clock time

Reference implementations:

PlatformClock sourceFile
MPS2-AN385CMSDK APB Timer0 (25 MHz)nros-platform-mps2-an385/src/clock.rs
STM32F4ARM DWT cycle counternros-platform-stm32f4/src/clock.rs
FreeRTOSxTaskGetTickCount()Use OS tick directly
NuttXclock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)POSIX API

Memory

zenoh-pico allocates heap during session open and entity creation. Typical minimum: 64 KB heap.

void *z_malloc(usize size);
void *z_realloc(void *ptr, usize size);
void  z_free(void *ptr);

Options:

  • embedded-alloc FreeListHeap (bare-metal)
  • RTOS heap (pvPortMalloc / tx_byte_allocate)
  • System malloc (POSIX, NuttX)

Sleep

i8 z_sleep_us(usize time);
i8 z_sleep_ms(usize time);
i8 z_sleep_s(usize time);

All return 0 (_Z_RES_OK). On bare-metal, busy-wait using the clock. On RTOS, delegate to vTaskDelay / tx_thread_sleep / k_sleep.

If using smoltcp, poll the network stack during busy-wait sleep to avoid missing packets.

Random

zenoh-pico needs randomness for session IDs, SN initialization, and scouting nonces.

u8   z_random_u8(void);
u16  z_random_u16(void);
u32  z_random_u32(void);
u64  z_random_u64(void);
void z_random_fill(void *buf, usize len);

A simple xorshift32 PRNG is sufficient. Seed it with hardware entropy (RNG peripheral, ADC noise, semihosting wall-clock time) during init.

Time

System time (wall clock). Used for logging and z_time_now_as_str().

u64         z_time_now(void);
const char *z_time_now_as_str(char *buf, c_ulong buflen);
c_ulong     z_time_elapsed_us(u64 *time);
c_ulong     z_time_elapsed_ms(u64 *time);
c_ulong     z_time_elapsed_s(u64 *time);
i8          _z_get_time_since_epoch(ZTimeSinceEpoch *t);

Where ZTimeSinceEpoch is:

#[repr(C)]
struct ZTimeSinceEpoch {
    u32 secs,
    u32 nanos,
}

On bare-metal without an RTC, return monotonic time or zeros.

Threading

For single-threaded platforms (bare-metal, RTIC), provide no-op stubs. For RTOS platforms, implement real task/mutex/condvar operations.

Task operations:

i8   _z_task_init(ZTask *task, ZTaskAttr *attr, void*(*fun)(void*), void *arg);
i8   _z_task_join(ZTask *task);
i8   _z_task_detach(ZTask *task);
i8   _z_task_cancel(ZTask *task);
void _z_task_exit(void);
void _z_task_free(ZTask **task);

Mutex operations:

i8 _z_mutex_init(ZMutex *m);
i8 _z_mutex_drop(ZMutex *m);
i8 _z_mutex_lock(ZMutex *m);
i8 _z_mutex_try_lock(ZMutex *m);
i8 _z_mutex_unlock(ZMutex *m);

Recursive mutex operations:

i8 _z_mutex_rec_init(ZMutexRec *m);
i8 _z_mutex_rec_drop(ZMutexRec *m);
i8 _z_mutex_rec_lock(ZMutexRec *m);
i8 _z_mutex_rec_try_lock(ZMutexRec *m);
i8 _z_mutex_rec_unlock(ZMutexRec *m);

Condition variable operations:

i8 _z_condvar_init(ZCondvar *cv);
i8 _z_condvar_drop(ZCondvar *cv);
i8 _z_condvar_signal(ZCondvar *cv);
i8 _z_condvar_signal_all(ZCondvar *cv);
i8 _z_condvar_wait(ZCondvar *cv, ZMutex *m);
i8 _z_condvar_wait_until(ZCondvar *cv, ZMutex *m, u64 *abstime);

Single-threaded stubs: Return 0 for all mutex/condvar operations. Return -1 for _z_task_init (task creation is not supported).

RTOS implementations: Map to xTaskCreate/xSemaphoreCreateMutex (FreeRTOS), tx_thread_create/tx_mutex_create (ThreadX), or pthread_create/pthread_mutex_init (NuttX, POSIX). zenoh-pico requires recursive mutexes (configUSE_RECURSIVE_MUTEXES=1 on FreeRTOS).

Sockets

If using smoltcp (bare-metal), socket operations are handled by zpico-smoltcp. Your platform crate provides thin shims:

#[repr(C)]
struct ZSysNetSocket { i8 _handle, bool _connected }

i8   _z_socket_set_non_blocking(const ZSysNetSocket *sock);  // Return 0
i8   _z_socket_accept(const ZSysNetSocket *in, ZSysNetSocket *out);  // Return -1
void _z_socket_close(ZSysNetSocket *sock);
i8   _z_socket_wait_event(void *peers, ZMutexRecRef *mutex);  // Return 0

If using OS sockets (POSIX, NuttX, Zephyr), zenoh-pico’s built-in socket layer handles everything — no socket stubs needed.

libc stubs (bare-metal only)

Bare-metal targets without a C runtime need standard C library functions:

usize  strlen(const char *s);
int    strcmp(const char *s1, const char *s2);
int    strncmp(const char *s1, const char *s2, usize n);
char  *strchr(const char *s, int c);
char  *strncpy(char *dest, const char *src, usize n);
void  *memcpy(void *dest, const void *src, usize n);
void  *memmove(void *dest, const void *src, usize n);
void  *memset(void *dest, int c, usize n);
int    memcmp(const void *s1, const void *s2, usize n);
void  *memchr(const void *s, int c, usize n);
c_ulong strtoul(const char *nptr, char **endptr, int base);
int   *__errno(void);

RTOS platforms (FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, Zephyr) ship their own libc — you do not need these stubs.

Network poll callback (smoltcp only)

If using smoltcp for networking, provide a poll callback that zpico-smoltcp calls to process network events:

void smoltcp_network_poll(void);

And a Rust API for the board crate to register the network state:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub unsafe fn set_network_state(
    iface: *mut Interface,
    sockets: *mut SocketSet<'static>,
    device: *mut (),
);

pub unsafe fn clear_network_state();
}

Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create the platform crate (nros-platform-<name>) – see Custom Platform for the full guide
  2. Implement and verify the clock — this is the #1 cause of porting failures. Print clock_ms() in a loop and verify monotonic advance
  3. Implement remaining primitives — memory, random, sleep, time, threading, sockets. Each module is independent
  4. Wire into nros-platform — add a feature and ConcretePlatform alias
  5. Create the board crate — see Custom Board Package
  6. Add the platform feature to nros with mutual exclusivity checks
  7. Write an example — see Creating Examples
  8. Add test infrastructure — for an in-tree platform, see Internals → Per-platform contributor lanes

Platform capability summary

CapabilityBare-metalRTOS (FreeRTOS/ThreadX)POSIX-like (NuttX/Zephyr)
ClockHardware timerOS tick APIclock_gettime
Memoryembedded-allocRTOS heapSystem malloc
SleepBusy-wait + pollvTaskDelaynanosleep
ThreadingNo-op stubsReal tasks + mutexespthreads
Socketssmoltcp shimslwIP or NetX socketsBSD sockets
RandomSeeded xorshiftRTOS RNG or xorshift/dev/urandom
libcHand-written stubsRTOS libcSystem libc
Network pollsmoltcp_network_pollStack-specific pollNot needed

Common pitfalls

See Platform Porting Pitfalls for detailed failure modes including poll-driven clocks, DMA buffer placement, QEMU I/O starvation, recursive mutexes, stack sizing, and heap sizing.

XRCE-DDS Symbol Reference

XRCE-DDS has a minimal platform abstraction layer. It is single-threaded, heap-less, and delegates networking to user-provided transport callbacks. The 2-3 required FFI symbols (uxr_millis, uxr_nanos) are provided by nros-rmw-xrce’s C alias translation unit (src/platform_aliases.c, compiled into nros-rmw-xrce-cffi on every target), which forwards them to the canonical nros_platform_* ABI. When porting to a new platform, you implement an nros-platform-<name> crate (see Custom Platform) that supplies the nros_platform_* symbols — you do not provide the uxr_* symbols directly.

There is no separate xrce-platform-shim crate: the uxr_* forwarders live in the nros-rmw-xrce alias TU.

Platform crate structure

The XRCE-DDS clock symbols are a subset of what the platform crate provides. Your nros-platform-<name> crate provides the canonical monotonic clock, nros_platform_clock_ns, and the alias TU maps it to the uxr_* symbols XRCE-DDS expects.

packages/platform/nros-platform-<name>/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    └── lib.rs          # clock + other primitives

Cargo.toml must have zero nros-* dependencies. It may depend on:

  • Hardware HAL crate (e.g., stm32f4xx-hal, esp-hal)
  • xrce-smoltcp (if using smoltcp networking)

Required FFI symbols

Clock (2 symbols)

XRCE-DDS uses the clock for session timeouts and time synchronization.

// Monotonic millisecond clock
i64 uxr_millis(void);

// Monotonic nanosecond clock
i64 uxr_nanos(void);

These must be backed by a hardware timer or OS tick — same rules as the zenoh-pico clock.

Reference implementations:

PlatformClock sourceFile
MPS2-AN385CMSDK APB Timer0 (25 MHz)nros-platform-mps2-an385/src/clock.rs
Zephyrk_uptime_get()xrce-zephyr/src/xrce_zephyr.c
POSIXclock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)Built-in time.c from XRCE library

smoltcp clock (1 symbol, if using smoltcp)

If using xrce-smoltcp for bare-metal networking:

u64 smoltcp_clock_now_ms(void);

This is the same symbol used by zpico-smoltcp — shared clock implementations work for both RMW backends.

Transport callbacks

Instead of requiring socket FFI symbols, XRCE-DDS uses a custom transport abstraction. You register four callbacks via uxr_set_custom_transport_callbacks():

bool   open(uxrCustomTransport *transport);
bool   close(uxrCustomTransport *transport);
size_t write(uxrCustomTransport *transport, const uint8_t *buf, size_t len, uint8_t *errcode);
size_t read(uxrCustomTransport *transport, uint8_t *buf, size_t len, int timeout_ms, uint8_t *errcode);

These are typically provided by a transport crate, not the platform crate:

TransportCrateDescription
smoltcp UDPxrce-smoltcpBare-metal networking via smoltcp
Zephyr UDPxrce-zephyrZephyr BSD sockets
POSIX UDPBuilt-inUses XRCE library’s POSIX transport

The transport crate registers its callbacks during initialization. Your platform crate does not need to implement sockets.

What you do NOT need

Unlike zenoh-pico, XRCE-DDS does not require:

  • Memory symbols — XRCE-DDS is heap-less; all buffers are statically sized
  • Sleep symbols — polling is driven by uxr_run_session_time()
  • Random symbols — no session ID randomization needed
  • Threading symbols — single-threaded by design
  • libc stubs — Micro-XRCE-DDS has minimal C dependencies

This makes XRCE-DDS the easiest RMW backend to port to new platforms.

Platform-conditional compilation in xrce-sys

The xrce-sys crate uses Cargo features to select platform behavior:

FeatureEffect
posixCompiles built-in time.c (uses clock_gettime, BSD sockets)
bare-metalSkips time.c; expects uxr_millis()/uxr_nanos() from platform crate
zephyrCompiles xrce_zephyr.c (Zephyr kernel APIs)
freertosRTOS-specific; skips time.c
nuttxRTOS-specific; skips time.c
threadxRTOS-specific; skips time.c

When adding a new platform, you may need to add a feature to xrce-sys that skips the default time.c compilation and lets your platform crate provide the clock symbols.

Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create the platform crate — nros-platform-<name>/ (see Custom Platform)
  2. Implement the canonical clock primitive — nros_platform_clock_ns(); the alias TU (nros-rmw-xrce/src/platform_aliases.c) derives uxr_millis() / uxr_nanos() from it for you
  3. Implement smoltcp_clock_now_ms() if using smoltcp transport
  4. Add a feature to xrce-sys for the new platform if needed
  5. Choose or implement a transport crate — reuse xrce-smoltcp for bare-metal, or implement a new transport if the platform has its own networking stack
  6. Create the board crate — see Custom Board Package
  7. Add the platform feature to nros with mutual exclusivity checks
  8. Write an example and tests

Example: bare-metal MPS2-AN385

The simplest reference is nros-platform-mps2-an385. It supplies the canonical nros_platform_clock_ns; the XRCE alias TU (nros-rmw-xrce/src/platform_aliases.c) then derives uxr_millis / uxr_nanos from it — you never hand-write the uxr_* symbols:

/* nros-rmw-xrce/src/platform_aliases.c — provided for you, not the porter */
int64_t uxr_millis(void) {
    return (int64_t) (nros_platform_clock_ns() / 1000000u);
}
int64_t uxr_nanos(void) {
    return (int64_t) nros_platform_clock_ns();
}

So a porter only implements the canonical primitive in their platform crate (nros_platform_clock_ns), plus smoltcp_clock_now_ms() if using the smoltcp transport. The MPS2-AN385 platform reads it from a hardware timer with wrap detection.

Common pitfalls

  • Agent connectivity — XRCE-DDS requires a Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent running on the host. Ensure the agent is reachable from the target before debugging the platform layer.
  • Reliable stream history — STREAM_HISTORY must be >= 2 (recommend 4). History=1 fails to recycle slots between separate uxr_run_session_until_all_status calls.
  • Flush after request_data — uxr_buffer_request_data must be flushed with uxr_run_session_time immediately after being called. Unflushed requests in the reliable output stream cause intermittent timeouts.

Platform Porting Pitfalls

Hard-won lessons from porting nros to bare-metal ARM (QEMU MPS2-AN385), bare-metal RISC-V, STM32F4, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, and Zephyr. Read this before adding a new platform or debugging mysterious failures on an existing one.

Memory Layout

DMA buffer placement

On MCUs with multiple SRAM regions, DMA descriptors and buffers must be in DMA-accessible memory. The STM32F4 has 64 KB of CCM RAM that is NOT DMA-accessible — placing Ethernet descriptors there causes silent data corruption with no error interrupt.

Fix: Use linker script sections to force placement:

/* stm32f4.x — place DMA descriptors in SRAM1, not CCM */
.eth_descriptors (NOLOAD) : ALIGN(4) {
    *(.eth_descriptors .eth_descriptors.*)
} > RAM

In Rust, annotate the buffer:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[link_section = ".eth_descriptors"]
static mut ETH_DMA_DESC: MaybeUninit<[u32; 256]> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
}

Stack sizing

Bare-metal and RTIC applications share a single stack. FreeRTOS/Zephyr give each task its own stack. In both cases, zenoh-pico’s internal processing needs significant stack space:

ContextMinimum stack
Bare-metal / RTIC main stack8 KB
FreeRTOS zenoh read task2 KB
FreeRTOS zenoh lease task1 KB
Zephyr zpico work queue thread2 KB

Stack overflow on embedded targets causes silent corruption — there is no guard page. FreeRTOS can detect overflow with configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW=2 and the high-water-mark API (uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark), but only after the fact.

Heap sizing

zenoh-pico allocates heap memory during session open, publisher/subscriber creation, and message processing. Typical heap consumption:

PlatformMinimum heap
MPS2-AN385 (bare-metal)64 KB
STM32F464 KB
FreeRTOS (lwIP + zenoh)256 KB (configTOTAL_HEAP_SIZE)

Undersized heaps cause _Z_ERR_SYSTEM_OUT_OF_MEMORY (-78) during z_open() or entity creation, not during message I/O.

Rust struct move invalidation

When Rust returns a struct from a function, it moves the value to a new address. If C code stored a pointer to the original location (e.g., during init()), that pointer is now dangling.

Symptom: Callback crashes or garbage field values after struct is returned from an init function.

Fix: Use static storage, Box::pin(), or index-based references instead of raw pointers. See Troubleshooting: Subscriber Callback Crashes.

Clock Sources

Use hardware timers, not poll-driven counters

Every platform must provide a monotonic millisecond clock via smoltcp_clock_now_ms() (for smoltcp timestamping) and z_clock_now() / z_clock_elapsed_*() (for zenoh-pico timeouts). This clock must be backed by a hardware timer or OS clock — never by a software counter that only advances when spin() or poll() is called.

A poll-driven clock causes:

  • Incorrect timeouts: zenoh-pico uses z_clock_elapsed_ms() for session keep-alive, query timeout, and transport timeout. If the clock only advances during poll, idle periods (waiting for network I/O, sleeping between spins) are invisible to the timeout logic.
  • Timeout storms: After a long idle period, the next poll advances the clock by a large jump, causing multiple timeouts to fire simultaneously.
  • Broken RTIC integration: RTIC tasks yield with Mono::delay() between spins. A poll-driven clock doesn’t advance during the delay, making all timeouts effectively infinite.

Platform clock status

PlatformClock sourceNotes
MPS2-AN385 (zpico)CMSDK APB Timer0Hardware 25 MHz free-running counter. Wraps at ~171s, extended via WRAP_COUNT.
STM32F4ARM DWT cycle counterHardware-backed. update_from_dwt() reads elapsed DWT cycles and advances the software counter. Must be called at least once per ~25.6s (at 168 MHz) to avoid missing DWT wraps.
FreeRTOSFreeRTOS kernel tickOS-managed via xTaskGetTickCount().
NuttXPOSIX clock_gettime()OS-managed.
ZephyrZephyr kernel tickOS-managed via k_uptime_get().
POSIX (native)std::time::InstantOS-managed.
XRCE MPS2-AN385CMSDK APB Timer0Same hardware timer as zpico MPS2-AN385. Call init_hardware_timer() before use.

Porting checklist for new platforms

  1. Identify a hardware timer — SysTick, a general-purpose timer, or DWT cycle counter. On RTOS platforms, use the OS tick API.
  2. Export smoltcp_clock_now_ms() -> u64 — called by zpico-smoltcp for TCP/IP timestamping.
  3. Export zenoh-pico clock symbols — z_clock_now(), z_clock_elapsed_us/ms/s(), z_clock_advance_us/ms/s(). These read from the same underlying counter.
  4. Never advance the clock inside smoltcp_network_poll() — the poll callback runs during network I/O and is not a reliable time source. Read the hardware timer directly.
  5. Handle timer wraps — 32-bit timers wrap. Track wrap count in an atomic or use a 64-bit hardware counter if available.

QEMU clock synchronization

QEMU’s virtual clock races ahead of wall-clock time during WFI, causing hardware timer-backed timeouts to fire before TAP network I/O completes. This is solved with -icount shift=auto, which makes virtual time advance at wall-clock speed during CPU sleep states.

See QEMU icount reference for the full explanation, parameter reference, and tradeoffs.

Networking

Ephemeral port conflicts

smoltcp’s ephemeral port allocator starts at port 49152 with a static counter that resets to zero on each boot. When QEMU instances are killed and restarted, the new instance picks the same source port, creating a 4-tuple collision with stale host-side TCP sockets.

Symptom: ConnectionFailed or TransportOpenFailed on the second test run. ss -tnap shows FIN-WAIT-1 sockets from the previous QEMU instance.

Fix (test infrastructure): Kill stale host TCP sockets between test runs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Clean stale TCP connections to QEMU IPs
for ip in &["192.0.3.10", "192.0.3.11"] {
    let _ = Command::new("ss")
        .args(["-K", "dst", ip])
        .status();
}
}

Fix (Zephyr native_sim): Pass different --seed values to each instance so the entropy source produces different ephemeral ports:

./build-listener/zephyr/zephyr.exe --seed=12345
./build-talker/zephyr/zephyr.exe --seed=67890

QEMU single-threaded I/O starvation

QEMU emulates the CPU and processes TAP network I/O in one thread. If the guest never executes WFI (Wait For Interrupt), QEMU never yields to its I/O event loop, and the TAP file descriptor is never serviced.

Symptom: First few packets work (buffered), then all networking stops. Services and actions time out. Pub/sub may appear to work because subscriber callbacks fire inline during zp_read().

Fix: In RTIC, yield between spin_once() calls:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// CORRECT — yields to idle task → WFI → QEMU processes TAP
cx.local.executor.spin_once(0);
Mono::delay(10.millis()).await;

// WRONG — busy-loops, starving QEMU I/O
loop {
    cx.local.executor.spin_once(0);
}
}

In bare-metal (no RTIC), call cortex_m::asm::wfi() in your idle loop.

TAP device assignment

Each QEMU peer must use a different TAP device. Two QEMU instances on the same TAP cause packet collision and loss.

QEMU talker  → tap-qemu0 ─┐
                           ├── qemu-br (192.0.3.1/24)
QEMU listener → tap-qemu1 ─┘

Subscriber startup ordering

Zenoh does not buffer messages for unknown subscribers. If the publisher starts before the subscriber’s declaration propagates through the router, early messages are lost.

Rule: Start subscriber first, wait 5 seconds for stabilization, then start publisher.

TAP queue discipline

The default fq_codel qdisc drops packets when QEMU emulation is slow (CoDel’s default 5ms target interprets emulation pauses as congestion, and per-flow scheduling disrupts zenoh-pico’s service reply timing). This causes TCP data segments to be dropped, breaking zenoh session establishment.

Fix: Use pfifo instead:

sudo tc qdisc replace dev tap-qemu0 root pfifo limit 1000
sudo tc qdisc replace dev tap-qemu1 root pfifo limit 1000

pfifo queues packets without dropping, which QEMU needs to absorb bursts during emulation pauses. Stale packets from killed QEMU processes accumulate in the queue but are harmless — the firmware seeds smoltcp’s ephemeral port from the host’s wall clock via ARM semihosting SYS_TIME, so each QEMU run uses a different source port and stale packets are silently ignored.

See TAP qdisc analysis for why fq_codel and noqueue don’t work for QEMU TAP devices.

zenoh-pico

Z_FEATURE_INTEREST causes multi-client failures

When multiple zenoh-pico clients connect to the same router, the interest protocol’s write filter creation can fail with -78 (_Z_ERR_SYSTEM_OUT_OF_MEMORY) even when memory is available.

Fix: Disable in all builds:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// build.rs
cmake::Config::new(&zenoh_pico_path)
    .define("Z_FEATURE_INTEREST", "0")
    .define("Z_FEATURE_MATCHING", "0")
    .build();
}

Z_FEATURE_MATCHING depends on Z_FEATURE_INTEREST — both must be disabled.

See Troubleshooting: zenoh-pico Multiple Client Issues.

Blocking TCP reads in cooperative schedulers

_z_read_tcp() can block for up to SOCKET_TIMEOUT_MS (default 10 seconds). In cooperative schedulers (RTIC, bare-metal main loop), this blocks the entire system since C FFI cannot yield.

Impact: Pub/sub works (callbacks fire inline during zp_read()), but services and actions fail because z_get() query replies need multiple zp_read() cycles, and the 5-second query timeout expires while _z_read_tcp blocks.

Current status: zpico_spin_once(0) is non-blocking (single_read=true), but the underlying z_get() timeout is still 5 seconds. RTIC service/action E2E tests are #[ignore]d pending a fully non-blocking TCP read path.

Version pinning

The zenoh router is ROS 2’s own (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd) — nano-ros no longer vendors one, so the router version always matches the rmw_zenoh_cpp your ROS nodes use. zenoh-pico is pinned at zpico-sys/zenoh-pico/ (1.10.1 — read its version.txt); its wire protocol is stable across zenoh 1.x, so it interoperates with a newer ROS-shipped router. A transport-level failure (-100, _Z_ERR_TRANSPORT_TX_FAILED) that looks like a network issue can still be a protocol-major mismatch — check both versions before debugging the network.

Bare-metal RISC-V

picolibc errno TLS crash

picolibc’s errno.h uses __thread (thread-local storage), which crashes on bare-metal RISC-V because TLS is not initialized. The crash is a hard fault with no useful backtrace.

Fix: Shadow errno.h with a non-TLS version:

// errno_override.h — no __thread, just a global
extern int errno;
#define EPERM  1
#define ENOENT 2
// ... subset of errno codes

Include this with -include errno_override.h in CFLAGS before picolibc headers.

FreeRTOS

Task priority inversion

The LAN9118 RX FIFO poll task and zenoh-pico read task must run at the same priority (typically priority 4). If the read task has higher priority, it monopolizes the CPU, preventing RX FIFO drain. TCP keep-alives are missed, and zenoh sessions expire.

Similarly, lwIP’s tcpip_thread must run at the same priority. Lower priority stalls packet processing.

Recursive mutexes required

zenoh-pico’s FFI layer requires recursive mutexes. Enable in FreeRTOS config:

#define configUSE_RECURSIVE_MUTEXES 1

Interrupt priority constraints

On Cortex-M3 (3-bit priority, 8 levels): ISRs at priority >= 5 (configLIBRARY_MAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY) cannot call FreeRTOS APIs. Ethernet IRQ handlers that signal tasks must use a lower (numerically higher) priority.

Build System

Parallel test build races

When nextest runs test files in parallel and multiple tests build the same example with different features, cargo fingerprinting creates race conditions — one test overwrites the binary another test is about to execute.

Fix: Use --target-dir for each feature variant:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
Command::new("cargo")
    .args(["build", "--release", "--features", "safety-e2e"])
    .arg("--target-dir").arg("target-safety")
    .status()?;
}

Add each target dir to the example’s .gitignore:

/target/
/target-safety/
/target-zero-copy/

CMake cache invalidation

Changes to CMake defines (like Z_FEATURE_INTEREST=0) are cached. Changing the value without cleaning the build has no effect.

Fix:

# Cargo (native)
cargo clean -p zpico-sys && cargo build

# Zephyr (west)
west build --pristine

Feature flag mutual exclusivity

The three platform axes — RMW backend, platform, ROS edition — are mutually exclusive within each axis. Enabling two platforms (e.g., platform-posix,platform-zephyr) causes compile errors with confusing messages about duplicate symbol definitions, not a clear “pick one” error.

Design background

  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance and the unstable seam

Runner packages

A runner package teaches nros run, nros flash and nros monitor to drive a launcher, flasher or console that nano-ros does not ship a runner for. It is an ordinary package in your workspace, with a package.xml and a small descriptor, built for the host by nros build.

This page is coming soon.

Design background

  • RFC-0119: CLI extension packages

Command packages

A command package adds a verb to nros. It is an ordinary package in your workspace, with a package.xml and a small descriptor, built for the host by nros build. nros help --all lists each extension verb with the package that provides it.

This page is coming soon.

Design background

  • RFC-0119: CLI extension packages

nros CLI reference

The nros binary is the user entry point for nano-ros: it provisions toolchains, scaffolds workspaces, generates message bindings, builds and runs images, and inspects boards, configuration and plans.

nros --help prints the verbs below, in the same groups. This page documents those verbs: the user tier. The verbs that build systems call (the build-system tier) and the older spellings that still parse are not part of it; nros help --all lists the first and nros help --aliases the second.

Install

Install a release, with no checkout and no cargo:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

It verifies the sha256, installs into ~/.nros/sdk/nros/<version>/ and points ~/.nros/bin/nros at the newest installed version. --version <v> installs a named release instead of the newest; the repository’s GitHub Releases page lists them. The release carries the CLI and its SDK root, the library source your build compiles (share/nano-ros in the install). There is no crates.io, Arduino zip or ESP-IDF binary channel. See Installation.

Start

nros new

Scaffold a workspace, a package, an image or a host. Outside a workspace it writes a new one, for one board:

nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker [--lang c|cpp] [--rmw <rmw>]

sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # node package: a library, no main(), names no board
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # package.xml and system.toml: one component row, one image

The node package is named from the workspace (<x>_ws gives <x>_node), and the bringup is <node>_bringup. Its system.toml names the board, the RMW, the one component and one image, so nros run <node> runs it with nothing edited (First Project).

Inside a workspace, nros new <name> adds a node package under src/ instead:

nros new monitor_node --template listener --to sensor_node_bringup

--to <bringup> also adds the node’s [[component]] row and its <exec_depend> to that bringup. Without it the package is written and no bringup runs it yet.

The node is the --template role, the in-tree example of that role under the package’s names:

--templateNodeInterface
talker (default)publishes Hello World: N once a secondstd_msgs/String on /chatter
listenerlogs what /chatter carriesstd_msgs/String on /chatter
serveradds two integersexample_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts on /add_two_ints
clientcalls the server once it is upexample_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts on /add_two_ints
action-servercomputes a Fibonacci sequence, with feedbackexample_interfaces/action/Fibonacci on /fibonacci
action-clientsends one goal, logs feedback and the resultexample_interfaces/action/Fibonacci on /fibonacci

The roles and interfaces are the ROS 2 demos’ (demo_nodes_cpp’s talker and listener, add_two_ints_server / _client, the Fibonacci action pair), so a scaffolded node talks to the demo it is named after.

The package flags follow ros2 pkg create:

FlagWritesDefault
--node-name <name>the node’s ROS namethe package name (- spelled _)
--dependencies <pkg>...extra <depend> rows, after the role’s interface packagenone
--license <id><license>Apache-2.0
--description <text><description>a one-line summary
--maintainer-name / --maintainer-email<maintainer>git config user.name / user.email
--destination-directory <dir>where the package directory is createdthe current directory (src/ inside a workspace)

ros2 pkg create --build-type has no counterpart: --lang decides the package’s build type (cargo for Rust, CMake for C/C++). --library-name has none either: every node package is a library. --use-case is retired and refused, naming --template.

FlagValuesDefault
--boarda board id (Supported Boards)(required for a new workspace)
--langrust, c, cpprust
--rmwzenoh, xrce, cycloneddszenoh
--ros-editionhumble, iron, jazzyhumble
--templatetalker, listener, server, client, action-server, action-clienttalker
--toa bringup package in this workspacenone
--forceoverwrite an existing directoryoff

The scaffold names the image after the board’s platform: [image.baremetal], [image.linux], [image.freertos], [image.zephyr], each with board = "<board>".

--board native and --board posix are refused with a hint naming linux — the host board’s one name. There is no standalone package shape: a system.toml lives only in a bringup, and nros build refuses one beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt, naming where to move it. Zephyr is no exception: nros build and nros run generate the Zephyr application under build/ from the image (the Zephyr chapter), and nros materialize turns it into a package of yours when you need to edit it.

Image / host mode: nros new --image <name> [--board <b>] scaffolds an [image.<name>] — a buildable image — into the bringup package’s system.toml; nros new --host <name> scaffolds a [host.<name>], a machine nodes run on. Both accept [--bringup <pkg>] [--from-launch <path>] [--from-profile <name>]. The bringup package is discovered automatically when the workspace exposes exactly one; pass --bringup <pkg> to pick one when there are several. --from-launch also seeds the bringup [system].default_launch; --from-profile forks an existing block of the same table.

An image names a --board and derives its rustc triple from that board’s descriptor, so there is no --target. A host takes no board: a host says WHERE nodes run, and a board is what an image is BUILT for — passing one is refused rather than written.

nros new --deploy <name> is DEPRECATED: [deploy.*] split into those two tables, and a system.toml that still carries one is refused by name. The flag still works, dispatched by the --kind it always took — self scaffolds a host, anything else an image — and says which flag to use instead. It never writes [deploy.*].

nros setup

Provision the toolchain/SDK for a board. nros setup is the single canonical provisioning command. Inside a workspace, bare nros setup provisions what the workspace’s images declare. Most components are prebuilt per platform per RMW (cross-compiler, emulator, RMW host tools, SDK sources), fetched from a pinned index into a shared store (${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk). No hand-installed cross-toolchains.

Packages are prebuilt where the index has a binary for your host and built from source otherwise; the vendored submodules (zenoh-pico, mbedtls, RTOS sources) are the source builds. --dry-run prints the plan without fetching. Full explanation: Installation.

Note setup does not provision a zenoh router: the router is ROS’s rmw_zenoh_cpp/rmw_zenohd, so a zenoh run needs a ROS 2 install; Cyclone DDS needs no daemon. See Do I need ROS 2 installed?.

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh            # host build (router comes from ROS)
nros setup mps2-an385-freertos --rmw xrce  # arm-none-eabi-gcc, qemu, FreeRTOS, XRCE agent
nros setup zephyr                        # the Zephyr SDK + RMW transport sources
FlagEffect
<board>resolve + fetch this board’s package set (see Supported Boards)
--rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds>also provision the RMW’s host tools — the XRCE agent, Cyclone’s idlc; zenoh has none here (default zenoh); resolves board ∪ rmw packages
--tool <name>install tools by name (e.g. --tool qemu); repeatable — --tool ninja --tool make is one plan, with one system-package ask for the union
--source <name>provision a single source package by name (repeatable)
--prefix <dir>install a --tool here instead of the shared store
--listlist every package in the index + its version
--licensesshow license-gated packages + how to install them
--systemresolve the OS-package closure for this host’s package manager and PRINT the one install command (it never runs it without --sudo)
--workspace [<path>]provision what the workspace at <path> (default .) declares: every [image.*]’s board and RMW, then the OS packages its build types and <depend>s name (installed with --sudo, otherwise printed). An unresolvable <depend> stops it before any fetch. Bare nros setup at a workspace root is the same; --check only reports
--role <role>narrow --system to entries of this role (repeatable)
--checkrun presence probes instead of installing; exits 1 when anything is missing. With --system, the OS packages only; alone, every declared class
--sudoEXECUTE the plan’s composed OS-package install command instead of printing it — with a <board> (its tools’ and sources’ system = [..], before any download), --workspace, --system, or a --tool that declares OS build deps. Any other selector refuses it, naming these
--full / --shallowfull git history / force --depth 1 for provisioned sources
-j, --jobs <n>packages installed at once (default: CPU count; NROS_SETUP_JOBS)
--index <path>the SDK index to read (default nros-sdk-index.toml)
--dry-runresolve + print the plan without fetching anything

nros setup board <name> --zephyr-workspace <dir> [--workspace <nano-ros>] provisions a downstream Zephyr consumer’s tree for a nano-ros board.

--tool and --source combine: nros setup --tool arm-none-eabi-gcc --source freertos-kernel --source lwip installs the tool, then the sources, in one command. Selectors that do not combine — a <board> beside --tool/--source, anything beside --list/--licenses/ --system, --source with --check, --rmw without a <board> — are refused, naming the flag, never silently ignored.

Board names (the full set — the index’s [board.*] keys; each board is named for the reach of its build):

freertos-posix, fvp-aemv8r-smp, linux, mps2-an385-baremetal, mps2-an385-freertos, mps2-an385-zephyr, mps3-an536-freertos, nucleo-f767zi-zephyr, qemu-armv7a-nuttx, rpi-pico-w-zephyr, rv-virt-nuttx, rv-virt-threadx, s32z270-freertos, threadx-linux, zephyr.

A wrong one lists the rest; nros setup <board> --dry-run resolves without fetching. native and posix are refused with a hint naming linux (Retired names); older retired board names are in the retired board names ledger.

nros setup presets

Write a project CMakePresets.json (into [<dir>], default the current directory) that includes the per-board preset fragments nros setup <board> wrote under ~/.nros/presets/. Each preset names the SDK root, the board’s toolchain file (for a cross board) and the build directory build/<board>, so cmake --preset <board> configures a nano-ros CMake package with no hand-set -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE or -Dnano_ros_ROOT. Idempotent: re-run it after provisioning another board. Zephyr boards have no preset, because west is their build tool.

nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx
nros setup presets                 # writes ./CMakePresets.json
cmake --preset qemu-armv7a-nuttx

Build

nros build

Build the workspace. The colcon-like build verb: discover packages, resolve the image, preflight, generate the build root, then hand off to the native tool. The final stage is an exec, so compiler diagnostics are byte-identical to running cargo / cmake / west yourself. With no image argument it builds [system] default_images; --all builds every declared image. An image is named <bringup>:<image>, or <image> when exactly one bringup declares it.

Each build first prepares what the image reads, as nros configure does (below): message bindings, the resolved launch model, the generated entry and the tool’s settings. A part whose inputs did not change is not redone, so a build with nothing changed costs a digest comparison. There is no step to run before it.

cd <workspace>
nros build                       # every default image
nros build linux                # one image by id
nros build linux -- --release   # arguments after `--` go to the native tool

--board <board> builds the image whose [image.*] board is that board — the authored word in any case, another alias of the same board, or the nros setup key it provisions through (--board mps2-an385-baremetal finds a mps2-an385-baremetal image). One match is the same as naming the image; several or none is refused with the image ids listed, so name one. It cannot be combined with image arguments or --all.

After a successful build (not --dry-run, not --check) nros build prints, per image, where the artifact is and the platform’s own next command — it runs nothing:

nros build: next for `demo:qemu`:
  artifact: <ws>/build/…/qemu_entry/target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/debug/qemu_entry
  run:
    <store>/sdk/qemu/<ver>/bin/qemu-system-arm -cpu cortex-m3 -machine mps2-an385 … -kernel <artifact>

A host board prints the binary; a cargo board with a descriptor runner prints that runner; NuttX and ThreadX riscv64 print the QEMU line the tests use; a Zephyr image prints west build -d <dir> -t run and/or west flash -d <dir>, read from what its build supports. QEMU is the store’s patched build (nros locate tool qemu-system-arm), never whatever $PATH holds. A board with no derivable command (S32Z270) gets a pointer to its platform chapter.

colcon’s flags work with colcon’s names: --packages-select, --packages-up-to, --packages-above, --packages-skip and --base-paths choose the packages (nros list -n with the same flags prints the set), and --continue-on-error, --cmake-args and --build-base act as colcon’s do. The differences are refusals rather than different answers: a package name that matches nothing is an error, and a selection that leaves out a package a selected one depends on is refused, because nano-ros has no install prefix for it to come from. In a workspace with images the unit of --continue-on-error is the image, and --build-base is refused there.

-j N / --jobs N (default: the number of CPUs, as cargo) caps the TOTAL number of jobs. nros build runs one GNU make jobserver of N tokens and every cargo, make and ninja below it draws from it, so independent packages building side by side never run more than N compilers between them. Run under a make -jN that already has a jobserver, it joins that one. Ninja older than 1.13 cannot read a jobserver; when one would run, nros build says so. colcon’s --parallel-workers is refused with a pointer to -j: colcon counts packages because it has no shared job pool, and nros build does.

nros build --packages-up-to talker_pkg          # it and its dependencies
nros build --packages-above msgs_pkg            # it and what depends on it
nros list -t -n --packages-skip other_pkg      # the set, in build order

A runner or command package is a host tool. nros build builds it for the host triple, in release, into build/nros/host/<package>/, whatever board the images beside it target. It has its own target directory and never joins an image’s generated root, so editing it rebuilds only it, and editing an image does not rebuild it. --build-base does not move it, because nros run and extension verbs look for its executable there. An image depends on the workspace package providing its runner, so nros build --packages-up-to <bringup> builds that runner too. With no selection every host tool in the workspace builds, and a selection that keeps only host tools builds no image:

nros build --packages-select acme_tools         # one command package, alone

A workspace package may replace one of nano-ros’s own providers by announcing the same kind and name: the workspace overlays the nano-ros packages, as a colcon overlay does its underlay. For a runner or a command, which run host code and flash hardware, the replacement must be declared in the workspace’s nros.toml, pinned to the package’s path; otherwise the build or run that resolves the name refuses it and prints the line to add. --allow-overriding <name> approves it for one invocation, as colcon’s flag does. Other kinds (an rmw, a board) only warn when undeclared. The replacement must speak the runner protocol of the one it replaces, and an entry whose path no longer provides the name is an error rather than a quiet return to ours.

The workspace’s own source trees, src/ and every package_paths entry, are peers, as colcon’s base paths are: the same provider in two of them is an error for every kind, and the message names both paths. Declare the one you mean, or pass --allow-overriding <name> to let the later root win for one run. NROS_PACKAGE_PATH overlays everything, with a warning.

--base-paths <path>… names those source trees for one invocation, and means the same on nros build, nros list, nros configure and nros run/flash/monitor (whose build and runner lookup get it). It replaces the workspace (default .) and its package_paths, relative to the workspace, and nothing else: nano-ros’s own packages and NROS_PACKAGE_PATH stay on the search path, so a runner nano-ros provides still resolves. As in colcon, the paths are peers, their order does not matter, a path repeated or inside another counts once, and a package name found in two of them is an error naming both. A path that does not exist is an error; one holding no package is a warning. A path outside the workspace is allowed, and nros doctor and nros run --dry-run --why say so.

nros build --base-paths src ../vendor   # src/ and a vendor tree beside the workspace
nros list -n --base-paths src           # what that build would see

# nros.toml, at the workspace root
[workspace]
package_paths = ["../vendor"]

[workspace.overrides]
qemu = "src/my_qemu"   # this workspace's package answers the qemu runner

Overrides are the workspace’s to declare: a system.toml under src/ that carries [overrides] is refused. nros doctor lists every override, whether it was declared, and which file the declarations came from.

-v / --verbose shows the configure’s detail notes: why a re-configure happened, which message bounds were refused and why. Without it each is one line. A raw cmake run gets the same with --log-level=VERBOSE.

--dry-run prints the stages and the command that would run, and performs no I/O.

--check type-checks a cargo image instead of building it: every stage runs as for a build (the image’s settings file, its lock), and only the final command becomes cargo check, or cargo clippy with --check=clippy. Lint flags go after a second --. A cmake or west image is refused, since neither tool has a check that is not a build. Like a build, a check prepares the image first.

nros build linux --check                          # cargo check
nros build linux --check=clippy -- -- -D warnings # cargo clippy, warnings denied

Zephyr keeps west build as its build verb: nros build prepares the image, then runs west build on the application it generated.

Driving the native tool yourself is supported: nros build <image> --dry-run prints the exact cargo / cmake / west line, against the generated entry under build/. Run nros configure first to write that entry without building.

nros configure [<workspace>] [--image <id>] [--generated-base <d>] [--ros-edition <e>] [--dry-run] [--check] [--force] [--offline] [--no-metadata] [--no-provider-index] [--model-dir <d>] [--nano-ros-path <p>] [--nano-ros-root <p>] [--base-paths <p>…] [-v]

Configure a project without building it: codegen every *.msg package the declared deps name, write the generated build settings for each declared image, then resolve and generate the image’s build inputs (discover, preflight, census, resolve, generate). It works on a standalone package or a colcon-style workspace (it picks single-pkg vs workspace mode by layout) and runs no target build tool.

You rarely type it. nros build and nros run run it first when it is stale, the way cargo build fetches what it needs. Run it yourself when you want the files without a build (an IDE, a CI step), after editing *.msg, package.xml or system.toml.

nros configure               # generated/ msg crates + build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml
nros build                   # or: nros build <image-id>

The interface search path is computed inside configure, so no environment step is needed before it.

What it writes into build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml: the board’s cargo_config (its [build] target, [target.*] rustflags/linker, [unstable]), this image’s target-dir, its entity facts and derived pool knobs as [env], the in-repo [patch.crates-io] rows, and the nano-ros cargo profiles. Nothing generated is written beside the package, and [env] never uses force = true, so a value you set in the environment wins.

Transitionally, configure also still maintains the [patch.crates-io] block in each Rust consumer’s patch-authority .cargo/config.toml (never in Cargo.toml). That road is being removed, and it is what the ws clean / ws doctor subcommands below still talk about.

The stamp. Each image gets a stamp at <project>/build/nros/configured/<image>/stamp.toml, holding a digest of its inputs: package.xml, Cargo.toml, system.toml, the launch files, the environment variables configure reads (such as AMENT_PREFIX_PATH), the nros-launch-resolve path, and the content of the ROS install the generated message crates came from. A second run with nothing changed reads the stamps and exits without doing any work. An image this host cannot build is recorded as skipped, and is configured only when you name it. The flags that change what configure writes (--ros-edition, --generated-base, --model-dir, --no-metadata, --base-paths, --nano-ros-path, --nano-ros-root) and NROS_MODEL_DIR are inputs too, and a deleted output (generated/, a model, the selection package) makes the stamp stale. --force configures even when every stamp is current. --dry-run records no stamp.

Named images. An image you did not name that fails to configure is reported on stderr (configure: <image>: not configured — …) and the configure still succeeds. An image you name with --image, in a workspace as in a single-package leaf, must configure: its failure, a missing toolchain included, is an error.

The lock. A per-project file lock serialises writers, so several configures reaching one workspace at once (a parallel fixture build) queue instead of racing.

FlagMeaning
[<workspace>]Workspace root (the dir containing src/); defaults to the cwd
--image <id>Single-package leaf only: configure this [image.<id>] (its selection package, build/<id>/nros-cargo.toml, message codegen for its edition)
--generated-base <d>Output dir for the generated message crates, relative to the workspace (default generated)
--ros-edition <e>humble | iron | jazzy; inherits [system].ros_edition, else humble
--dry-runDon’t write; print what would happen
--checkExit non-zero if any patch block is missing or stale (CI hook; also used by nros ws status)
--forceConfigure even when every image’s stamp is current
--offlineNever touch the network. Reaches the cargo update --workspace that prunes a single-package leaf’s freshly seeded Cargo.lock, the one step that resolves crates
--no-metadataSkip the per-Node-package host probe; bakes fall back to the model’s entity lower bound
--no-provider-indexSkip the provider index (build/nros/providers.json)
--model-dir <d>Write resolved SystemModels here instead of each bringup’s config/
--nano-ros-path <p>The SDK root the probes and board lookups read
--nano-ros-root <p>nano-ros source tree scanned as the first provider search root
--base-paths <p>…Provider search roots, replacing the default (as colcon’s --base-paths)
-v, --verboseVerbose codegen output

--check exits non-zero when anything is missing or stale — the CI hook, and what nros ws status reports non-fatally.

nros clean

Remove the generated message bindings (generated/, or --build-dir <dir>) and anything nros configure wrote for them under build/. Sections you wrote are left alone. --dry-run prints what it would remove.

nros clean --dry-run

nros materialize

Take ownership of a generated entry package: the last resort, after which nros build stops regenerating it. It writes the entry into src/<image>_entry/, for a Zephyr image the whole west application. panic, profile and before_boot are declarations on the image and need no materialising. A second run without --force is refused, because it would discard the edits the first one existed to enable. --workspace <dir> names the workspace root.

nros materialize linux            # or <bringup>:linux when two bringups share the id

Run on a target

nros run

Run an image on its target: a host process or an emulator. It builds the image if it is stale, starts the router or agent its link needs, streams the console and stops everything on exit. Arguments after -- go to the target.

The target argument is tried in this order:

You typeIt means
<bringup>:<image>that bringup’s image; always works
<image>the image of that name, when exactly one bringup declares it
<node>the one bringup whose [[component]] rows name only that node package, with its only image
nothingthe workspace’s only image

Anything else refuses and lists the <bringup>:<image> spellings that would resolve; a shortcut never picks one of several. --why names the rung that resolved. The <node> rung is nros run’s alone; nros build, nros flash and nros monitor take the other spellings.

FlagEffect
--expect <text> / --expect-regex <re>exit 0 as soon as a console line matches; exit 1 if the target ends, or --timeout passes, first
--timeout <seconds>stop the target after that long
--router <auto|none|LOCATOR>auto starts the zenoh router or XRCE agent when the link needs one on this host; none starts nothing; a locator names one already running
--port <device>the console device
--prefix <cmd>run a host image under a command (--prefix 'valgrind -q')
--dry-run [--why] [--json]print the resolved run plan instead of running it; --why adds the rung that supplied each field
--plan <file>execute a plan file exactly as written: resolve nothing, build nothing
--workspace <dir>the workspace root (default: found from the current directory)
 
nros run sensor_node                                   # the node rung
nros run linux --expect 'Received: 2' --timeout 30

A board with no host process or emulator is real silicon; nros run refuses it and names the flashing step. See Running an Image.

nros flash

Flash an image onto a board. Reserved: not available in this version. It exits with an error that says so. Until it ships, flash with the command nros build prints after a successful build. See Flash and Monitor.

nros monitor

Attach to a running board’s console. Reserved: not available in this version, with the same error and the same advice as nros flash.

nros bench

This machine’s boards. nros bench scan records which attached USB device is which board, matching each device against the USB id a board descriptor’s [board.console] usb states, in $NROS_HOME/bench.toml (--dry-run prints what it would record). nros bench list prints that file and whether each device is attached now. The bench file supplies ports and probes; it never decides what is tested. See Your Bench.

nros bench scan --dry-run
nros bench list

nros debug

Debug an image on its target. Reserved: not available in this version.

Workspace

nros list

List the workspace’s packages: kind, name and directory per row. Any of -t (build order, as colcon list -t), -n (names only), -p (paths only) or the colcon selection flags (--packages-select, --packages-up-to, --packages-above, --packages-skip, --base-paths) switches to colcon list’s format, one name<TAB>path<TAB>(type) line per package, found the way nros build finds them.

nros list -t -n --packages-up-to talker_pkg

nros graph

Print the workspace’s packages in dependency order, each with the workspace packages it depends on. --workspace <dir> names the workspace (default: the current directory).

nros graph

Interfaces

nros interface

Message interfaces, with three subcommands:

SubcommandEffect
generate <rust|c|cpp|all>generate bindings from a package.xml (--manifest, default package.xml) into --output (default generated), for --ros-edition (default humble); --codegen-config names an explicit per-field capacity file, --rename old=new renames a generated Rust package, --force overwrites
listlist the interface types the search path reaches; -m, -s, -a keep only messages, services or actions
show <package>/<msg|srv|action>/<Name>show one type’s definition with nested types expanded

nros build generates the bindings a workspace needs (for Rust together with the image’s build settings; for C and C++ during the CMake configure). interface generate is the codegen step alone.

nros interface show std_msgs/msg/Header

nros px4 msgs

Generate CDR-serializable px4_msgs::msg::* bindings from a PX4-Autopilot .msg tree (--px4 <dir>, default $PX4_AUTOPILOT_DIR) into --output. --lang rust (the default) writes a px4_msgs crate for an XRCE companion; --lang cpp writes headers and FFI glue for an in-firmware PX4 module. --topics keeps only the messages a bridge carries (by message name or uORB topic name), pulling in nested types. See the PX4 starter.

nros px4 msgs --output generated/px4_msgs --topics vehicle_status

nros px4 is a command package (nros_px4_tools), not a built-in: nros runs its executable with the arguments unchanged. In a checkout just setup-cli builds it. The old spelling, nros generate-px4-msgs, still works and runs the same package.

nros router config --model <model>

Print the zenoh router downsampling rule nros configure wrote beside a resolved model, as the ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE entry rmw_zenohd reads (--format json5 prints the artifact itself):

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE="$(nros router config --model build/nros/models/<bringup>/<stem>.yaml)" rmw_zenohd

It fails when there is no rule: no subscriber declares an ingress, no image links zenoh, or the model was never configured. Like nros px4, it is a command package (nros_zenoh_tools); the old spelling nros ws router-config runs the same package.

Extension commands

A verb nros does not know is looked up as an announced command package (<nano_ros_provides kind="command" name="<verb>"/>). nros help --all lists every one this workspace reaches, with its summary and package. The command runs with NROS_WS_ROOT, NROS_TOOLCHAIN and NROS_CLI set, and its exit status is nros’s. A package announcing a built-in verb is refused.

Inspect

nros doctor

Health-check the install and the project. With no workspace it verifies the install: the launcher, the SDK store, and that the pin in this directory resolves. In a workspace it also checks the bringup’s [image.*] and [host.*] blocks (--config <system.toml> names another) and the license-gated SDKs the images’ boards need (--board <board> narrows that to one board). --platform <name> restricts the check to one platform. --report prints the support status of every board the bringup’s images name, from the board support registry, and stops: a read-only report you can attach to a bug or a review.

nros doctor --report

nros board

The boards this nros knows: the board packages in its SDK root, plus any found through NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH.

SubcommandEffect
listevery board package, with its support status and cadence
show <board>a board’s support evidence: status, where it runs, cadence, breadth and the book chapters that run it
info <board>the board’s resolved descriptor, as JSON
new <name> --platform <platform>scaffold a board package; --out-of-tree <dir> writes it outside nano-ros and prints the NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH that reaches it; --west-board for Zephyr; --dry-run

The status and cadence come from the board support registry, the same source as Supported Boards.

nros board show mps2-an385-freertos

nros config

The resolved configuration, with where each value came from.

nros config show [--system [<bringup>]] [--workspace <dir>] prints the effective config of a bringup system (rmw, domain_id, locator, and the safety, param_services and lifecycle capability axes) with a provenance column: system.toml [section] or the built-in default. Without a bringup it uses the workspace’s default_system, or its only bringup. A legacy per-package nros.toml overlay that still declares one of those blocks is flagged as deprecated.

nros config explain --platform <name> [--board-toml <file>] prints the build-time knob ladder for a platform: every knob’s final value and the rung that set it (builtin, platform, board or env). When a pool size or a hardware budget is not what you expected, it says which rung decided.

nros config show
nros config explain --platform freertos

nros plan

Resolve a bringup’s launch file, its manifests and the components’ source metadata into a typed nros-plan.json under build/<system_pkg>/nros/: the component graph, topic wiring, parameter remaps and scheduling-context bindings. The arguments are the system package, then a launch file or a package directory, then name:=value launch arguments.

FlagUse
--model <system_model.yaml>plan from a resolved SystemModel
--record <file>use a precomputed record.json instead of parsing the launch file
--image <id>resolve per-image values (RMW, build tuning, target triple) against this [image.<id>]
--rmw <rmw>override the RMW: --rmw beats [image.<id>].rmw, which beats [system].rmw
--workspace <dir> / --out-dir <dir>the workspace root / the output root
 
nros plan demo_bringup src/demo_bringup

nros check

Validate a generated nros-plan.json (default build/nros/nros-plan.json) before the platform build runs: unconnected required topics, conflicting QoS, missing parameters and scheduling-context binding errors. A bringup’s system.toml (or its directory) is validated as a deployment instead. --bringup lints a bringup package directory (it must be purely declarative), and --workspace [<dir>] runs the workspace layout checks.

nros check

nros explain

Render a generated nros-plan.json (default build/nros/nros-plan.json) in human-readable form: the component graph, topic wiring, parameter bindings and scheduling-context assignments.

nros explain path/to/nros-plan.json

Toolchain

nros toolchain

The installed toolchains and SDK packages in the store (${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk), which only grows: provisioning never overwrites, so a new version lands beside the old one.

SubcommandEffect
list [--root <dir>]every entry with its version, size and when it was last read
gc --older-than <dur> [--delete] [--pin-file <f>…] [--ignore-pins] [--root <dir>]propose removing entries not read for <dur> (90d, 12h, 2w); removes nothing without --delete, and never an entry a pin names
remove <version> [--dry-run] [--pin-file <f>…] [--ignore-pins] [--root <dir>]remove one installed nano-ros toolchain; refuses while a pin names it, or when no pin file could be consulted
 
nros toolchain gc --older-than 90d

nros toolchain <uninstall|manifest|stage-packages>

SubcommandEffect
uninstall <version> [--dry-run] [--pin-file <f>…] [--ignore-pins] [--root <dir>]remove one installed nano-ros toolchain; refuses while a pin names it, or when no pin file could be consulted
manifest [--store-version <v>] [--index <date>] [--nano-ros <commit>] [--write <path>]read (or, with --write, stamp) the share/nros/manifest.toml a release declares it is made of
stage-packages <prefix> [--checkout <dir>]release-only: stage every runner and command package of <prefix>/share/nano-ros prebuilt into <prefix>/share/nros/packages/<package>/ (package.xml, descriptor, bin/), the underlay a released nros resolves runners from

nros pin [<version>] [--dir <dir>] [--root <dir>] [--dry-run]

Report this project’s nros-toolchain.toml pin, or move it to <version> (the store version, e.g. 0.6.0-nros3, not the crate version nros --version prints). A move reports the codegen delta between the two toolchains first, so an upgrade that would invalidate already-generated code warns before anything is written.

nros pin 0.6.0-nros4 --dry-run

nros update

Move one pin of a pin set and leave one diff to review: a registry crate (--crate <name> [--precise <v>]), a vendored source (--source <name> --ref <sha>, forward only unless --allow-rewind), a host tool (--tool <name> --to-version <v>) or a Zephyr west project (--west <module> --revision <rev>). --pins [--prune] regenerates the registry pin set from the locked roots. It edits the pin set of a nano-ros source tree (--nano-ros-path); an installed release’s pin set is read-only, so a project that only consumes a release never runs it. To move your project to another release, use nros pin.

nros update --crate heapless --precise 0.8.0

nros locate

Print where a resource is, and with --why, every rung of the lookup ladder (argument, environment, the project’s system.toml [sources], a local edit, the store) and what each saw. A name is an index [source.<name>], or store for the store root. nros locate tool <name> locates a host binary (qemu-system-<arch> through the same QEMU lookup nros build uses, renode, or nros-launch-resolve) or an SDK tool’s directory (below). --all locates every [source.*] row, and --format sh|cmake prints shell or CMake assignments instead of bare paths.

nros locate zenoh-pico --why
nros locate tool qemu-system-arm

The SDK root. nros locate nano-ros prints the nano-ros SDK root the project in the current directory builds against: the directory that holds nano-ros’s CMake modules, its Zephyr module and its board descriptors. Use it wherever a build tool needs that path, for example -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)". It needs no network and no index, so it is safe in a CMake execute_process or a script.

Each project can pin its own nano-ros version (nros-toolchain.toml, written by nros build and changed with nros pin). Inside a pinned project, nros runs the pinned toolchain, so nros locate nano-ros prints that version’s SDK root. Two projects pinned to two versions get two different answers, and a script that asks in each project gets each one right. --why shows which version answered and which pin file chose it:

cd ~/robots/arm-controller && nros locate nano-ros --why
cd ~/robots/old-gateway    && nros locate nano-ros     # a different pinned version

--project <dir> asks about another project. If that project is pinned to a different version from the nros answering, the command refuses rather than print the wrong version’s root, and tells you to run it inside that project.

An SDK tool. nros locate tool <name> also prints the install directory of a tool that nros setup <board> provisioned, such as the Zephyr SDK or a cross compiler. The answer is the version this release of nano-ros pins, never another version that happens to sit beside it, so a build that asks keeps working when the pin moves:

nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"

A tool that is not installed, or that nano-ros does not know, makes the command fail with a message that names nros setup <board>. A project’s system.toml can point a tool somewhere else with a [tools] entry, and that entry wins.

Other

nros version

Print the CLI version, its codegen version and the versions of the libraries it was built with.

nros version

nros completions

Emit shell completion scripts to stdout.

ShellInstall snippet
bashnros completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/nros
zshnros completions zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_nros"
fishnros completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/nros.fish
powershellnros completions powershell > $PROFILE.parent\nros.ps1

nros help

Print the grouped verb list, or one verb’s help (nros help build, the same as nros build --help). nros help --all adds the build-system tier and nros help --aliases lists the older spellings that still parse.

C API

The C user-facing surface lives in packages/api/nros-c/include/, at upstream’s paths (rclc/, rcl/, rcl_action/, …). rclc/detail/ is internal. Generated by Doxygen; always reflects the current main branch.

API reference

C API Doxygen — start here.

The umbrella header rclc/rclc.h pulls in every public surface a user application needs.

Where to start

  • rclc/rclc.h — convenience umbrella include
  • rclc/init.h — rclc_support_init, rclc_support_fini
  • rclc/node.h — rclc_node_init_default, rcl_node_fini
  • rclc/executor.h — spin loop, executor lifecycle
  • rclc/publisher.h / subscription.h — pub/sub
  • rclc/service.h / client.h — services
  • rclc/action.h — actions
  • rclc_parameter/rclc_parameter.h — parameter services
  • rclc_lifecycle/rclc_lifecycle.h — REP-2002 lifecycle states

Two-layer API. Every entity exposes two parallel C entry-point sets: rclc_*_init_default (Layer 1, caller polls) and rclc_executor_add_* (Layer 2, executor callback). Layer 1 grew an _init_polling + take_*_raw / send_*_raw family for inline-storage callers (no executor arena). Layer 2 pairs the same rclc_*_init_default with the executor-add call, which is where the callback is supplied (rclc’s binding site). See Two-Layer API for the verb discipline and per-layer trade-offs.

Event-driven wake callbacks. Each L1 polling entity supports nros_*_set_wake_callback(entity, &state, cb, ctx) for event- driven RTOS / embassy callers. State is a caller-owned rclc_wake_state_t POD; the backend fires cb(ctx) on rx / reply / request arrival. Per-channel for actions (set_{goal,cancel,get_result}_wake_callback on the server, set_{goal_response,cancel_response,result,feedback}_wake_callback on the client). See the Doxygen for signatures.

Action server

<rclc/action_server.h> follows rclc’s model:

example_interfaces__action__Fibonacci_SendGoal_Request goal_requests[2];

rclc_action_server_init_default(&server, &node, &support,
    ROSIDL_GET_ACTION_TYPE_SUPPORT(example_interfaces, action, Fibonacci), "/fibonacci");
rclc_executor_add_action_server(&executor, &server, 2, goal_requests,
    sizeof(goal_requests[0]), goal_callback, cancel_callback, &ctx);

Each incoming goal takes one of the handles_number goal handles (rclc_action_goal_handle_t, at most NROS_MAX_CONCURRENT_GOALS); its request is deserialised into the matching element of the array, and goal_callback returns RCL_RET_ACTION_GOAL_ACCEPTED or RCL_RET_ACTION_GOAL_REJECTED. Do the work OUTSIDE the callback — between rclc_executor_spin_some() calls, or from a timer in a C component — and answer with rclc_action_publish_feedback(handle, &feedback_message) and rclc_action_send_result(handle, GOAL_STATE_SUCCEEDED, &get_result_response). Two bounds differ from rclc: a goal arriving with every handle in use is rejected (rclc queues it), and an accepted goal executes at once, so a result may be sent before the client asks for it. A component, which has no rclc_support_t, passes NULL for support. See action_server_pkg in the C language workspace, examples/workspaces/c; nros run action_bringup:linux_action_server runs it on Linux.

Async action client

<rclc/action.h> exposes two parallel entry-point families for sending goals, requesting results, and cancelling:

  • Async (non-blocking): rclc_action_send_goal_async(), rclc_action_get_result_async(), rclc_action_cancel_goal(), rclc_action_try_recv_feedback(). Return immediately. Replies are delivered through the callbacks registered with rclc_action_client_set_goal_response_callback(), rclc_action_client_set_feedback_callback(), rclc_action_client_set_result_callback(), and (for a cancel’s reply: its return code and how many goals are canceling) rclc_action_client_set_cancel_response_callback(). The callbacks fire from rclc_executor_spin_some() — your spin loop is the only place callbacks run.
  • Blocking convenience: rclc_action_send_goal() and rclc_action_get_result(). These call the async variant and then drive rclc_executor_spin_some() internally on a wall-clock budget until the reply lands (or 15 s / 30 s timeout). They take the rclc_executor_t* explicitly because the action client stores its handle as an opaque slot inside the executor (registered via rclc_executor_attach_action_client()). The same applies to rclc_action_client_wait_for_action_server() and rclc_action_client_action_server_is_ready(). Calling any of them from inside a dispatch callback returns RCLC_RET_REENTRANT.
  • Teardown: rcl_action_server_fini() / rcl_action_client_fini() reset only the struct. To take an action off an executor that keeps running, call rclc_executor_remove_action_server() / rclc_executor_remove_action_client() first: they drop the arena entry (the action leaves the graph), free its callback slot and arena bytes for reuse, and bring rclc_executor_get_handle_count() back down. A program that tears the executor down with rclc_executor_fini() needs neither — that drops every entry.
  • The same holds for every other entity the executor registers: rclc_executor_remove_subscription(), rclc_executor_remove_timer(), rclc_executor_remove_service() and rclc_executor_remove_client() — rclc’s rclc_executor_remove_* shape — each drop the arena entry (receive ring included), free the slot and bring handle_count back down. Call one before the entity’s fini when the executor keeps running; a timer or client that is fini’d without it is still dispatched into. A removed client returns to INITIALIZED and can be re-added. All return RCLC_RET_NOT_FOUND for an entity not registered on that executor and RCLC_RET_REENTRANT from inside a callback. A subscription whose callback also receives the sample’s attachment is registered with rclc_executor_add_subscription_with_info() into a rcl_subscription_t and removed the same way; the older direct-arg rclc_executor_add_subscription_raw_with_info() takes no subscription object, so its entry lives until rclc_executor_fini().

The equivalent service client helper rclc_client_call() does not take an explicit executor — the client stashes the executor pointer during rclc_executor_attach_client() and recovers it internally — but it follows the same async-then-spin contract.

Canonical pattern: declare the executor, register the client, then either call the blocking helper or drive rclc_executor_spin_some() yourself between async calls until your callback flags the result. See action_client_pkg in the C language workspace, examples/workspaces/c. The same package runs on Linux and on FreeRTOS: its linux_action_client and freertos_action_client image rows in action_bringup differ only in the board.

A separate L1 polling family (rclc_polling_action_client_init + the _raw send/recv siblings) stores ActionClientCore inline in the separate type rclc_polling_action_client_t and skips the executor entirely; see the Doxygen for the full L1 verb list.
