Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups in the language workspaces.

C++ API

The nano-ros C++ API is a freestanding C++14 interface for ROS 2 nodes on embedded and host targets. It needs no standard library, no exceptions and no RTTI, so the same code builds for Zephyr, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, bare metal and Linux.

  • Upstream’s names, in upstream’s namespaces. rclcpp::Node, Publisher<M>, Subscription<M>, Service<S>, Client<S>, Timer, GuardCondition, Executor, and rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A>. Every user-facing name is in rclcpp::, rclcpp_action:: or rclcpp_lifecycle::; there is no nros:: namespace. The extensions with no upstream counterpart (the Poll* types, the *Storage types, FixedString, …) are in rclcpp:: too.
  • Errors are values. Every fallible call returns rclcpp::Result, and RCLCPP_TRY returns early on failure. Nothing throws.
  • Generated message types. std_msgs::msg::Int32, example_interfaces::srv::AddTwoInts and so on, generated by the build from the packages your node depends on (see Message Generation).
  • An opt-in std surface for ported code. Defining NROS_CPP_STD adds the std::string / std::function / std::chrono overloads and the std::shared_ptr-returning rclcpp::Node factories. The build requests it; it is never detected from the toolchain. See Two surfaces.

The headers live in the SDK’s C++ include directory at upstream’s paths: rclcpp/, rclcpp_action/ and rclcpp_lifecycle/. rclcpp/detail/ is internal.

To build and run a first C++ node, start with First Node — C++; to grow it into a workspace, see C++ in a workspace. To bring an existing ROS 2 node across, see Porting a ROS 2 C++ node. This page is the API itself.

API reference

C++ API Doxygen — start here.

The Doxygen site is generated from the current main branch. The umbrella header rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp pulls in every public surface a user application needs.

Where to start

  • rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp — convenience umbrella include
  • rclcpp::init_in / rclcpp::shutdown — session lifetime
  • rclcpp::Node — node + create_publisher/subscription/service/client/action_*
  • rclcpp::Publisher<M> / Subscription<M>. Hosted, a subscription callback may also take upstream’s const rclcpp::MessageInfo& as its second argument (see Subscription)
  • rclcpp::Service<S> / Client<S> — the DISPATCH service server and client. A handler is registered into the executor arena, which owns the entity. Service<S>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::ServiceHandle<S>, a two-word keep-alive with nothing to dereference; Client<S>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::ClientHandle<S>, the same two words with one verb, async_send_request. Neither has an operator->.
  • rclcpp::PollService<S> — L1 polling service server. The caller owns the server and drains it with take_request / send_response from its own spin loop. node.create_service<S>(name) with no handler hands one back.
  • rclcpp::PollClient<S> — L1 future-style service client, the client half of the same split. The caller owns the client and drains the reply itself: send_request returns a rclcpp::Future<T> (on a hosted build async_send_request(shared_ptr) returns upstream’s FutureAndRequestId — .future, .request_id, share()), call blocks while driving the executor, call_polling blocks without driving it, and wait_for_service / service_is_ready probe the server. node.create_client<S>(name) with no handler hands one back.
  • rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A> — L2 callback model (executor-arena registered). rclcpp::ActionServer<A> / rclcpp::ActionClient<A> are the same two types. Hosted, upstream’s goal handles too (see Actions with upstream’s goal handles).
  • rclcpp::PollingActionServer<A> / PollingActionClient<A> — L1 polling model. Caller drives take_* / accept_goal / complete_goal from a spin loop.
  • rclcpp::Future<T> — async result handle
  • rclcpp::Executor, Timer, GuardCondition
  • Parameters are methods ON the node — declare_parameter<T> / get_parameter<T> / set_parameter<T> / has_parameter, upstream’s names, forwarding to the one store the rcl_interfaces services read. rclcpp::Seq<T, N> is the array VALUE a freestanding node declares with (std::vector<T> under NROS_CPP_STD). There is no standalone rclcpp::ParameterServer: a second store would be invisible to ros2 param get. See Differences from ROS 2 §9 for what is intentionally smaller than rclcpp, and Parameters below.

Two-layer API. The rclcpp::ActionServer<A> / ActionClient<A> templates are L2 callback handles, dispatched by the executor. The rclcpp::PollingActionServer<A> / PollingActionClient<A> are L1 polling templates with the same typed serialization glue but caller-driven control flow. Subscriptions, services and service clients have both shapes too (Subscription / PollSubscription, and so on). See Two-Layer API for the per-layer rationale.

Event-driven wake callbacks. PollingActionServer<A> and PollingActionClient<A> expose a nested WakeState POD and typed set_{goal,cancel,get_result,goal_response, cancel_response,result,feedback}_wake_callback(state, cb, ctx) methods. Pair an nros_cpp_wake_state_t with each entity / channel to wake on rx instead of polling.

Core API

The snippets below use the freestanding surface. Each create_* writes the entity through an out-reference and returns a Result.

Initialization

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

// Global init (simple applications). `init_in` is the Result-returning form:
// upstream's `rclcpp::init(argc, argv)` returns `void`, so the name differs
// where the contract does.
rclcpp::Result ret = rclcpp::init_in("tcp/127.0.0.1:7447", 0);

// Or an explicit executor (multi-executor patterns)
rclcpp::Executor executor;
RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::Executor::create(executor, "tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"));

Node

rclcpp::Node node;
RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::create_node(node, "my_node"));

// Or with an explicit executor:
RCLCPP_TRY(executor.create_node(node, "my_node", "/namespace"));

Publisher

#include "std_msgs.hpp"

rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::Int32> pub;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_publisher(pub, "/chatter"));

std_msgs::msg::Int32 msg;
msg.data = 42;
RCLCPP_TRY(pub.publish(msg));

A publisher can be marked express (it bypasses transmit batching) through its QoS profile; see TX Throughput & Latency Tuning.

Subscription

A poll-style subscription is rclcpp::PollSubscription<M>: the caller owns the subscriber, so the caller is the one that takes from it. Call spin_once() to drive I/O, then take() to check for a message. rclcpp::Subscription<M> is the DISPATCH subscription, whose samples the executor arena delivers to a callback.

rclcpp::PollSubscription<std_msgs::msg::Int32> sub;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_subscription(sub, "/chatter"));

rclcpp::spin_once(100);

std_msgs::msg::Int32 msg;
if (sub.take(msg).ok()) {
    printf("Received: %d\n", msg.data);
}

On a hosted build (NROS_CPP_STD) a dispatch subscription’s callback may take upstream’s const rclcpp::MessageInfo& as a second argument, after the message in any of its four forms (const M&, std::shared_ptr<const M>, std::shared_ptr<M>, std::unique_ptr<M>):

auto sub = node->create_subscription<std_msgs::msg::Int32>(
    "/chatter", 10, [](const std_msgs::msg::Int32& msg, const rclcpp::MessageInfo& info) {
        const auto& r = info.get_rmw_message_info();
        printf("%d from seq %llu at %lld ns\n", msg.data,
               (unsigned long long)r.publication_sequence_number, (long long)r.source_timestamp);
    });

get_rmw_message_info() carries source_timestamp, received_timestamp, publication_sequence_number, reception_sequence_number and the 24-byte publisher_gid, as the backend reported them. A backend that reports none (XRCE, uORB) leaves every field zero. from_intra_process is always false. A freestanding build refuses the shape at compile time: the metadata path keeps the callable on the heap. SubscriptionOptions::message_info = true with a callback that takes no MessageInfo aborts the create, because it would otherwise configure nothing.

Service server

rclcpp::PollService<S> is the polled server: the caller owns it and drains it. rclcpp::Service<S> is the DISPATCH server, which takes a handler.

#include "example_interfaces.hpp"

using AddTwoInts = example_interfaces::srv::AddTwoInts;

rclcpp::PollService<AddTwoInts> srv;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_service(srv, "/add_two_ints"));

// In your main loop:
rclcpp::spin_once(10);
AddTwoInts::Request req;
int64_t seq;
if (srv.take_request(req, seq).ok()) {
    AddTwoInts::Response resp;
    resp.sum = req.a + req.b;
    srv.send_response(seq, resp);
}

Service client

rclcpp::PollClient<S> is the polled client: the caller owns it and drains the reply. rclcpp::Client<S> is the DISPATCH client, whose one verb is async_send_request and whose reply reaches a handler during spin_once.

rclcpp::PollClient<AddTwoInts> client;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_client(client, "/add_two_ints"));

AddTwoInts::Request req;
req.a = 1; req.b = 2;
AddTwoInts::Response resp;
RCLCPP_TRY(client.call(req, resp));
// resp.sum == 3

Action server

rclcpp_action::Server<A> is a DISPATCH server: the executor answers goal and cancel requests through callbacks you install, and the goal itself is driven through the server by its 16-byte id. Upstream hands handle_accepted an owning std::shared_ptr<ServerGoalHandle>; here the goals live in the server’s static arena, so the callback receives the id instead. A polled form, where the caller takes each goal request itself, is rclcpp::PollingActionServer<A>.

#include "example_interfaces.hpp"

using Fibonacci = example_interfaces::action::Fibonacci;

rclcpp_action::Server<Fibonacci> srv;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_action_server(srv, "/fibonacci"));

// Stateless callables: an empty-capture lambda or a plain function pointer.
// The `*_with_ctx` forms add a `void*` for state.
RCLCPP_TRY(srv.set_goal_callback([](const uint8_t id[16], const Fibonacci::Goal& goal) {
    return goal.order > 0 ? rclcpp_action::GoalResponse::ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE
                          : rclcpp_action::GoalResponse::REJECT;
}));
RCLCPP_TRY(srv.set_accepted_callback([](const uint8_t id[16]) {
    // Record `id`; the work happens outside the callback, which must return
    // promptly.
}));

// Later, from the main loop, for an accepted goal `goal_id`:
Fibonacci::Feedback fb;
// ... fill feedback ...
srv.publish_feedback(goal_id, fb);

Fibonacci::Result result;
// ... fill result ...
srv.complete_goal(goal_id, result);  // GoalStatus::Succeeded; another overload takes a status

Action client

rclcpp_action::Client<A> keeps its goal, feedback and result buffers (and the four transport channels underneath) in fixed-size storage inside the Client<A> instance itself. Nothing is heap-allocated per send_goal call, and the type is move-only.

Blocking convenience. send_goal() and get_result() spin the executor internally until the server replies or the per-call timeout expires:

rclcpp_action::Client<Fibonacci> client;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_action_client(client, "/fibonacci"));

Fibonacci::Goal goal;
goal.order = 10;
uint8_t goal_id[16];
RCLCPP_TRY(client.send_goal(goal, goal_id));

Fibonacci::Result result;
RCLCPP_TRY(client.get_result(goal_id, result));

These helpers are sugar over send_goal_async() + spin_once(). They cannot be called from inside a dispatch callback; a blocking call made there fails with ErrorCode::Reentrant.

Future-based async. send_goal_future() / get_result_future() return a Future<T> keyed by its goal: each future receives only its own goal’s acceptance or result, whether the executor dispatched it during spin_once or the future’s own poll took it, and a result for a goal nobody waits on is dropped. At most MAX_CONCURRENT_GOALS of each may be pending per client; past that the send is refused and the future is empty (valid() false):

auto fut = client.send_goal_future(goal);
typename decltype(client)::GoalAccept accept;
RCLCPP_TRY(fut.wait(executor.handle(), 5000, accept));
if (accept.accepted) {
    auto rfut = client.get_result_future(accept.goal_id);
    Fibonacci::Result result;
    RCLCPP_TRY(rfut.wait(executor.handle(), 10000, result));
}

GoalAccept is a nested type on rclcpp_action::Client<A> (16-byte UUID + bool accepted).

Feedback. Feedback is not goal-scoped at the stream layer: feedback_stream() yields FeedbackType across every active goal for this client.

auto& fb_stream = client.feedback_stream();
Fibonacci::Feedback fb;
while (fb_stream.try_next(fb).ok()) { /* ... */ }
// Or blocking:
RCLCPP_TRY(fb_stream.wait_next(executor.handle(), 500, fb));

For per-goal feedback dispatch, use the callback API.

Callback API: SendGoalOptions + set_callbacks(). This is the rclcpp-style entry point. SendGoalOptions is a nested POD on rclcpp_action::Client<A>; populate the three function-pointer fields (goal_response, feedback, result) plus an optional context pointer, then install once. Callbacks fire from spin_once():

typename decltype(client)::SendGoalOptions opts;
opts.goal_response = [](bool accepted, const uint8_t id[16], void* ctx) {
    auto* state = static_cast<MyState*>(ctx);
    state->accepted = accepted;
    std::memcpy(state->goal_id, id, 16);
};
opts.feedback = [](const uint8_t id[16], const uint8_t* data, size_t len, void* ctx) {
    Fibonacci::Feedback fb;
    if (Fibonacci::Feedback::ffi_deserialize(data, len, &fb) == 0) {
        // dispatch on `id`
    }
};
opts.result = [](const uint8_t id[16], int32_t status, const uint8_t* data, size_t len, void* ctx) {
    // status: 4=Succeeded, 5=Canceled, 6=Aborted
};
opts.context = &my_state;
RCLCPP_TRY(client.set_callbacks(opts));

RCLCPP_TRY(client.send_goal_async(goal, goal_id));  // fire-and-forget
while (!my_state.done) { rclcpp::spin_once(10); }

set_callbacks() may be called before or after send_goal_async(): the executor reads the latest callbacks on each dispatch. The client also keeps the most recent feedback and result bytes, so the same Client can drive feedback_stream().try_next() and get_result_future().wait() even with callbacks installed.

Actions with upstream’s goal handles (hosted)

On a hosted build (NROS_CPP_STD) the stock rclcpp_action spellings are drop-ins over the two classes above:

using Fibonacci = example_interfaces::action::Fibonacci;
using GoalHandle = rclcpp_action::ServerGoalHandle<Fibonacci>;
using namespace std::placeholders;

// Server: free factory over the node interfaces, std::bind-ed members.
rclcpp_action::Server<Fibonacci>::SharedPtr server = rclcpp_action::create_server<Fibonacci>(
    get_node_base_interface(), get_node_clock_interface(), get_node_logging_interface(),
    get_node_waitables_interface(), "fibonacci",
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_goal, this, _1, _2),    // (const GoalUUID&, shared_ptr<const Goal>)
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_cancel, this, _1),      // (shared_ptr<GoalHandle>)
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_accepted, this, _1));   // (shared_ptr<GoalHandle>)
// in handle_accepted: goal_handle->get_goal(), ->publish_feedback(fb),
// ->is_canceling(), ->succeed(result) / ->abort(result) / ->canceled(result)

// Client: SendGoalOptions' upstream fields, bound per goal by async_send_goal.
auto client = rclcpp_action::create_client<Fibonacci>(this, "fibonacci");
auto opts = rclcpp_action::Client<Fibonacci>::SendGoalOptions();
opts.goal_response_callback = [](rclcpp_action::ClientGoalHandle<Fibonacci>::SharedPtr h) {};
opts.feedback_callback = [](auto h, const std::shared_ptr<const Fibonacci::Feedback> fb) {};
opts.result_callback = [](const rclcpp_action::Client<Fibonacci>::WrappedResult& r) {
    // r.code: rclcpp_action::ResultCode::SUCCEEDED / ABORTED / CANCELED; r.result
};
auto fut = client->async_send_goal(goal, opts);   // rclcpp::Future<GoalAccept>

// The handle-taking calls return upstream's std::shared_future.
auto result = client->async_get_result(goal_handle);   // shared_future<WrappedResult>
auto cancel = client->async_cancel_goal(goal_handle);  // shared_future<CancelResponse::SharedPtr>
if (rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, result) == rclcpp::FutureReturnCode::SUCCESS) {
    const auto& wrapped = result.get();
}
// server, after handle_goal returned ACCEPT_AND_DEFER:
goal_handle->execute();   // ACCEPTED -> EXECUTING, status array published

X<A>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::Owned<X<A>> (the entity by value), and the get_node_*_interface() handles name the node and do nothing else. A goal handle is a heap token over the goal id: every call forwards to the server or client keyed by it, and the goal’s state stays in the arena. Drive it from the executor’s task only — not from a thread you started — and do not move the server while a handle is in use. The callbacks run from the executor’s dispatch, beside the client-wide set_callbacks ones. async_send_goal returns the goal-keyed rclcpp::Future<GoalAccept>, not a std::shared_future; get_goal_stamp is absent.

async_get_result / async_cancel_goal / async_cancel_all_goals / async_cancel_goals_before return a rclcpp_action::detail::DrivenSharedFuture<T>, which IS-A std::shared_future<T>: its is_ready() (what spin_until_future_complete polls), wait_for and get drive the client’s dispatch and executor while they wait, since no other thread fulfils it. Converted to a bare std::shared_future it still completes, but only when something else drives the client. Every async_get_result for one goal returns the handle’s own future; a result-aware goal’s handle is kept by the client until its result arrives, as upstream’s pending request keeps it. Cancel replies are taken by the executor’s spin, as upstream’s executor delivers them: the spin settles the waiting async_cancel_* future and runs its cancel_callback, so a caller that keeps only the callback needs no poll(). A reply no future claims is kept for try_recv_cancel_response, oldest first, up to rclcpp_action::CANCEL_STASH_CAP (4) per client. These need std::promise, so they are hosted-only twice over: a libstdc++ built without threads (arm-none-eabi) refuses them as a freestanding build does.

ServerGoalHandle::execute() and Server<A>::execute(goal_id) move an ACCEPTED goal to EXECUTING and publish the status array; the latter reports NotFound / NotAllowed where upstream raises. create_server executes an ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE goal before handle_accepted; the goal-id API leaves it ACCEPTED.

Goal slots. Each action sub-client holds at most MAX_CONCURRENT_GOALS (4) requests in flight. A future dropped (or cancel()ed) before its reply frees its request’s slot, unless something else still waits on that reply — a client-wide set_callbacks hook, or an upstream goal (async_send_goal with callbacks, async_get_result). A late reply for a freed slot is dropped. On a freestanding build each of these shapes is a compile error (NROS_RCLCPP_REFUSE_ACTION_GOAL_HANDLE) naming the goal-id-keyed form above; create_client alone works there.

Timer

Timers fire during spin_once():

void on_timer(void* ctx) {
    // periodic work
}

rclcpp::Timer timer;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_wall_timer(timer, 1000, on_timer));     // 1000 ms period
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_timer_oneshot(timer, 5000, on_timer));  // one-shot after 5 s

timer.cancel();
timer.reset();  // restart from zero

GuardCondition

Guard conditions allow cross-thread signalling:

void on_signal(void* ctx) {
    // handle event
}

rclcpp::GuardCondition guard;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_guard_condition(guard, on_signal));

// From another thread:
guard.trigger();
// Callback fires on the next spin_once()

Executor

rclcpp::Executor executor;
RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::Executor::create(executor));

rclcpp::Node node;
RCLCPP_TRY(executor.create_node(node, "my_node"));

// Create publishers, subscriptions, etc. on node...

while (executor.ok()) {
    executor.spin_once(10);
}
executor.shutdown();

Spinning

// Global spin (after rclcpp::init_in())
rclcpp::spin_once(10);           // single poll, 10 ms timeout
rclcpp::spin_in(5000);           // spin for 5 seconds
rclcpp::spin_in(5000, 50);       // spin for 5 s, 50 ms poll interval
rclcpp::spin_in();               // until rclcpp::shutdown() flips rclcpp::ok()

// Explicit executor
executor.spin_once(10);
executor.spin_for(5000, 50);    // bounded; executor.spin() blocks until shutdown

How spinning maps onto RTOS tasks and priorities is the subject of Execution Model.

Parameters and /parameter_events

Parameters are methods on the node (declare_parameter<T>, get_parameter<T>, set_parameter<T>, undeclare_parameter), over the executor’s one store. node.start_parameter_services() serves them on the six rcl_interfaces services, so ros2 param reaches them, and publishes /parameter_events (rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent, rmw_qos_profile_parameter_events) as rclcpp’s node does:

rclcpp::Node node;
RCLCPP_TRY(executor.create_node(node, "ctrl"));
node.declare_parameter<int64_t>("gain", 3);   // before or after: both reported
RCLCPP_TRY(node.start_parameter_services());  // start-up event: new_parameters = [gain]
node.set_parameter<int64_t>("gain", 4);       // changed_parameters = [gain]
node.undeclare_parameter("gain");             // deleted_parameters = [gain]

Each event names the node’s fully qualified name in node; the events are published on the next spin. The image needs the param_services capability. One publisher per executor serves every node. It is on for every served node unless the node was built with rclcpp::NodeOptions().start_parameter_event_publisher(false), which opts that one node out; the other nodes keep publishing.

To react to OTHER nodes’ changes, a hosted build has rclcpp::ParameterEventHandler. It subscribes to /parameter_events once, on the node you give it:

auto handler = std::make_shared<rclcpp::ParameterEventHandler>(node);
auto h = handler->add_parameter_callback(
    "gain", [](const rclcpp::Parameter& p) { use(p.as_int()); }, "/controller");
auto e = handler->add_parameter_event_callback(
    [](const rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterEvent& ev) { /* every event */ });

Keep the handles: dropping one unregisters it, as upstream’s do. An empty node name means this node, and a relative one resolves against this node’s namespace. A parameter callback sees new and changed values, never deletions. An event callback receives the type it takes, so rcl_interfaces must be generated for the image. The per-parameter handle is rclcpp::ParameterCallbackHandle, as upstream (the handler’s nested ParameterEventHandler::ParameterCallbackHandle names the same type). A freestanding build refuses the handler at compile time; there, subscribe to /parameter_events with create_subscription yourself.

Error handling

All fallible operations return rclcpp::Result. Use RCLCPP_TRY for early return:

rclcpp::Result setup() {
    RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::init_in());
    RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::create_node(node, "my_node"));
    RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_publisher(pub, "/topic"));
    return rclcpp::Result::success();
}

Check results manually when needed:

rclcpp::Result ret = pub.publish(msg);
if (!ret.ok()) {
    printf("Error: %d\n", ret.raw());
}

ret.raw() is an rclcpp::ErrorCode. The numbering matches rcl_ret_t:

CodeValueMeaning
Ok0success
Error-1generic failure not covered by a more specific code
Timeout-2the deadline elapsed before completion
InvalidArgument-3null pointer, empty topic name, or out-of-range value
NotFound-4entity not found (topic, parameter, service, goal)
AlreadyExists-5duplicate declare or register
Full-6a static pool is exhausted (executor slots, subscription buffers, …)
NotInitialized-7init was never called, or the entity is in its default state
BadSequence-8the call is invalid in the current state
ServiceFailed-9a service request or reply failed
PublishFailed-10publish failed
SubscriptionFailed-11subscription create or take failed
NotAllowed-12not allowed for this entity or backend
Rejected-13the peer considered the request and declined (a rejected goal, a QoS mismatch)
TryAgain-14no data ready yet (non-blocking take); retry later
Reentrant-15a blocking call was made from inside a callback
Unsupported-16not implemented by the active backend
TransportError-100the transport rejected the operation

A Full from a create_* usually means a build-time pool is too small; see Static Pool Inventory for the knob that sizes it.

Two surfaces: freestanding, and NROS_CPP_STD

One set of headers ships two API shapes, and a build picks one.

The freestanding surface is the default and it is not a fallback. It is plain C++14 with no standard library, no exceptions and no RTTI: rclcpp::Node, create_* writing through an out-reference and returning an rclcpp::Result, const char* for names, uint64_t period_ms for durations. It is the surface for every node written for nano-ros, native host builds included.

The std surface is an opt-in and it is reached only by defining NROS_CPP_STD. Defining it turns on the six NROS_CPP_HAS_* capability macros in rclcpp/detail/std_detect.hpp, and with them: the std::string / std::function / std::chrono / std::vector convenience overloads in nros/std_compat.hpp, the RCLCPP_*_STREAM logging macros, and — the piece that actually motivates the flag — rclcpp::Node’s upstream-shaped factories, which return std::shared_ptr and take const std::string& names.

Do I need this flag?

The split is ported rclcpp code versus code written for nano-ros. It is not host versus embedded. A native Linux build does not want the flag any more than a Cortex-M3 build does; a ported node wants it on both.

You are…FlagWhy
writing a new node against rclcpp::Node / rclcpp::Publisher<M> / rclcpp::ExecutornoThe freestanding surface is the whole API you are using. This is the common case on every platform, native included.
compiling an upstream ROS 2 .cpp unmodified — it says class MyNode : public rclcpp::Node, std::make_shared<MyNode>(), create_publisher<M>(...) returning a SharedPtryesThose signatures are spelled in std::shared_ptr and std::string. Without the flag they do not exist and you get a compile error naming a missing overload.
passing a std::string topic name or a std::chrono period into an otherwise nano-ros-native fileyesThose are the std_compat.hpp overloads.
building for Zephyr, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, or any -ffreestanding toolchainnoAnd here it is not merely unnecessary: asking for the std surface asks the headers to #include <string>, which on those toolchains is either absent or a hard #error.

If you are unsure, build without it. The failure direction is loud: a missing overload at compile time, never a silent behaviour change.

Turning it on

Define it on the target, not per file:

target_compile_definitions(my_ported_node PRIVATE NROS_CPP_STD=1)

Per target rather than per #define-before-include, because the macro changes the layout of rclcpp::Node (it carries hosted-only members and an enable_shared_from_this base), so two translation units of one image that disagree about it are an ODR/layout break rather than a missing function. An image may set the flag on one module and not another, so keep the definition at target granularity and give every translation unit of a target the same answer.

A ported package usually needs none of this. nano-ros’s ament surface sets NROS_CPP_STD=1 on every target its ament_* verbs create, and find_package(rclcpp) sets it on whatever links rclcpp::rclcpp, so a ported package already has the surface it needs; see Porting a ROS 2 C++ node.

The ported shape

With the flag set, an upstream node’s own spelling compiles: std::make_shared, SharedPtr returns, a std::string topic, a QoS depth, a capturing lambda and a std::chrono period.

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs/std_msgs.hpp"

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
    auto node = std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>("talker");
    auto pub = node->create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::Int32>("chatter", 10);
    int count = 0;
    auto timer = node->create_wall_timer(1s, [&]() {
        std_msgs::msg::Int32 msg;
        msg.data = ++count;
        pub->publish(msg);
    });
    rclcpp::spin(node);
    rclcpp::shutdown();
}

A failed create_* here ABORTS, naming the call, because upstream throws and nano-ros has no exceptions. To handle the failure instead, use the Result-returning forms above.

Why it is not detected for you

Earlier releases discovered the capability macros from the include path with __has_include, so a hosted compiler handed you the std-flavoured API whether you asked for it or not. That was removed because no probe answers the question correctly on both embedded toolchains:

__STDC_HOSTED____has_include(<string>)#include <string>
arm-none-eabi 13.2, -ffreestanding (FreeRTOS)0TRUEhard #error
Zephyr -nostdinc++, minimal libcpp1FALSEabsent
hosted g++ 12.31TRUEworks

Each probe is right on exactly one embedded toolchain and wrong on the other: libstdc++ 13 added bits/requires_hosted.h, so header presence stopped implying usability. Only the request is right on both, because it is not a probe — it is you saying which surface you want. The full measurement is in the comments of rclcpp/detail/std_detect.hpp.

Zephyr

A Zephyr application reaches the C++ API through the nano-ros Zephyr module. The module, the image’s system.toml and the prj.conf split are covered in Zephyr integration; the RMW, locator and domain come from the image, never from CONFIG_NROS_* lines in prj.conf. The C++ side needs CONFIG_CPP=y and CONFIG_STD_CPP14=y in prj.conf (Zephyr’s own settings), and the application’s CMakeLists.txt generates the message bindings:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20.0)
find_package(Zephyr REQUIRED HINTS $ENV{ZEPHYR_BASE})
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

nros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs LANGUAGE CPP)
target_sources(app PRIVATE src/main.cpp)

A minimal main() waits for the network, opens the session with the locator and domain the image rendered into Kconfig, and spins:

#include <zephyr/kernel.h>
#include <zephyr/logging/log.h>

#include <nros/platform_zephyr.h>

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs.hpp"

LOG_MODULE_REGISTER(my_app, LOG_LEVEL_INF);

int main(void)
{
    nros_platform_zephyr_wait_network(CONFIG_NROS_INIT_DELAY_MS);

    rclcpp::Result ret = rclcpp::init_in(CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR, CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID);
    if (!ret.ok()) return 1;

    rclcpp::Node node;
    if (!rclcpp::create_node(node, "my_node").ok()) return 1;

    // ... create publishers, subscriptions, etc.

    while (true) {
        rclcpp::spin_once(100);
    }
}

nros_platform_zephyr_wait_network (<nros/platform_zephyr.h>) is defined in every Zephyr image. On an image with no IP stack (CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS off, for example a serial-only zenoh image) it returns 0 at once, so the call needs no guard. CONFIG_NROS_INIT_DELAY_MS is the module’s start-up delay; your main() is its only reader.

RMW API

The RMW (ROS middleware) vtable is the porting boundary between nano-ros and a concrete pub/sub transport (zenoh-pico, XRCE-DDS, Cyclone DDS, uORB, …). RMW is internal — user applications use the Rust / C / C++ APIs, not the vtable directly.

Canonical reference

The C vtable nros_rmw_vtable_t is the source of truth. Every function pointer’s brief, parameter docs, ownership rules (buffer-borrowed vs caller-owned), blocking / non-blocking classification, return-code conventions, and lifetime contract for loaned slots live in the Doxygen output.

Platform API

The platform API is the porting boundary between nano-ros and a concrete OS / RTOS / bare-metal target. Each platform provides a clock, optionally a heap, optionally threading, optionally networking. Platform is internal — user applications use the Rust / C / C++ APIs, not the platform vtable directly.

Canonical reference

The SSoT C headers in packages/platform/nros-platform-api/include/nros/ (platform.h + platform_net.h, platform_timer.h, platform_zephyr.h; Rust consumes committed bindgen output from them) are the source of truth. Every symbol’s brief, parameter docs, ownership rules, blocking / non-blocking classification, and ISR-safe contract live in the Doxygen compiled from those headers.

Canonical interface contract. What “Yes” / “—” / specific functions mean — buffer ownership, blocking allowance, valid value ranges — is in the platform-cffi Doxygen reference. This page is a comparison table, not a spec.

Behaviour notes by trait group

Time (PlatformClock)

All ports surface a monotonic clock. Resolution varies:

  • POSIX / NuttX: nanosecond-resolution clock_gettime, exposed at ms + µs.
  • FreeRTOS: xTaskGetTickCount ticks (typically 1 ms). clock_us = clock_ms × 1000 — the resolution lie is documented.
  • Zephyr: k_uptime_get ms + k_cyc_to_us_floor64(k_cycle_get_64()) µs.
  • ThreadX: tx_time_get ticks (default 100 Hz; bump via TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND for finer resolution).
  • Bare-metal (Cortex-M): hardware timer counter (CMSDK Timer0, DWT cycle counter). µs is the native resolution; ms is µs / 1000.

The clock is monotonic and wraparound-free from init to shutdown. Platforms with 32-bit timers run a software extender on overflow.

Memory (PlatformAlloc)

Only zenoh-pico calls PlatformAlloc::{alloc, realloc, free}. XRCE-DDS does not allocate. Recommended heap budget: 64 KB minimum for zenoh-pico’s working set; bare-metal ports typically allocate 128 KB+ via a bump allocator (linked-list-allocator or embedded-alloc).

The RTOS allocators (pvPortMalloc, tx_byte_allocate, k_malloc, libc malloc) honour their respective heap-region configurations. On bare-metal the heap region is defined in the linker script and consumed at startup by the bump allocator.

Threading (PlatformThreading)

Multi-threaded ports (POSIX, NuttX, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, ThreadX) expose real tasks, mutexes, and condition variables. zenoh-pico’s lease task and read task spawn into these. Single-threaded bare-metal ports stub task_init to return -1 so the spawn fails gracefully; the application drives spin_once from a single context.

Recursive mutexes are required by zenoh-pico. FreeRTOS uses xSemaphoreCreateRecursiveMutex; ThreadX uses tx_mutex_create(..., TX_INHERIT, ...); POSIX uses PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE.

Sleep / Random / Wall-time (PlatformSleep, PlatformRandom, PlatformTime)

PlatformSleep on RTOS ports uses the kernel’s tickless sleep (vTaskDelay, tx_thread_sleep, k_msleep, libc usleep). On bare-metal with smoltcp, the sleep helper also runs network_poll() in a busy loop — packets must keep flowing during otherwise-idle waits or the zenoh lease times out.

PlatformRandom is a 32-bit xorshift PRNG seeded with hardware entropy (getrandom, RNG peripheral) or a build-time constant on platforms without entropy. Used for session IDs and protocol nonces; not cryptographic.

PlatformTime returns wall-clock for log timestamps. Bare-metal platforms with no RTC fall back to the monotonic clock — log timestamps then count from boot, not Unix epoch.

Networking (PlatformTcp, PlatformUdp, PlatformSocketHelpers, PlatformUdpMulticast, PlatformNetworkPoll)

The split into four traits maps directly onto zenoh-pico’s unix/network.c interface. Each port wires the four traits independently:

  • C-backed networking (NuttX, ThreadX): the platform shim forwards into zenoh-pico’s bundled unix/network.c (NuttX) or a NetX-Duo equivalent (ThreadX) — the C code talks to BSD-shape sockets directly.
  • Rust-backed networking (POSIX, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, bare-metal): the platform crate implements TCP / UDP in Rust. POSIX wraps libc, FreeRTOS wraps lwIP via freertos-lwip-sys, Zephyr wraps the POSIX layer, bare-metal goes through nros-smoltcp.

PlatformUdpMulticast (RTPS SPDP, zenoh scouting) ships fully wired on POSIX, NuttX, Zephyr, and bare-metal (smoltcp 0.12 IGMP group join). FreeRTOS and ThreadX have no multicast yet — gated by lwIP’s IGMP=1 (untested) and NetX Duo’s nx_igmp_* (untested).

PlatformNetworkPoll is bare-metal only. The implementation advances the smoltcp state machine; without it, smoltcp would only receive when the application explicitly asked. PlatformSleep and the wait_event helper both run network_poll() while waiting so packets continue flowing.

Libc (PlatformLibc)

zenoh-pico uses strlen, memcpy, errno, etc. directly. Bare-metal targets that link picolibc or newlib-nano satisfy these for free; the trait exists for no_std targets without a C runtime, which forward to Rust implementations.

Common pitfalls

For platform-specific gotchas (DMA buffer placement, ephemeral port conflicts, picolibc errno TLS, QEMU clock synchronization, Z_FEATURE_INTEREST mutex exhaustion, etc.), see Platform Porting Pitfalls.

For the design rationale (why these trait groups, why both ms and µs, why split PlatformNetworkPoll), see Platform API Design.

For writing a new port, see Custom Platform. For the canonical interface spec, see the Doxygen reference.

Humbleros-humble (default)SupportedTypeHashNotSupported key expressions, XCDR1. No rmw_zenoh_cpp apt package — zenoh interop on Humble needs a source overlay, or use Cyclone DDS.

Pick the edition of the ROS system you interop with — mismatched editions discover nothing (different key expressions).

Supported means WIRE interop, not API parity. nano-ros’s API is compared against Humble and Jazzy — Jazzy from pinned upstream sources, since it cannot be installed beside Humble (how the comparison runs). Iron is not compared on its own; what it added and Jazzy kept is covered there. Jazzy’s additions over Humble are each RULED, not each implemented: matched/incompatible-type events, timer call info, the small rclcpp accessors, count_clients/count_services, the client GID and event_type_is_supported are implemented; BEST_AVAILABLE QoS is implemented, resolved at creation against the discovered graph; dynamic typesupport, service introspection and the ~/get_type_description service are declined on RAM/flash grounds; rmw_discovery_options_t is answered by the session locator and localhost_only. Type hashes (RIHS01) are on the wire today.

Per-RMW Feature Matrix

One table per question the capability pages used to answer in contradictory prose. Derived from the backend sources — the C vtables (vtable.c (XRCE-DDS), vtable.cpp (Cyclone DDS), vtable.cpp (uORB)) and the zenoh shim’s trait overrides — so a backend gaining or losing a slot moves this page in the same commit or fails the gate.

wired = the backend implements it. — = not wired: the runtime surfaces UNSUPPORTED or falls back where a fallback exists (the vtable comments name which). A slot filled with a function that only returns UNSUPPORTED (uORB’s service stubs) is —, not wired. Status events count as wired whether the backend calls back (*_event_init) or the runtime polls it (*_take_event). The rows below the parity marker are slots declared in the ABI whose backend wiring is still landing; all-dash rows there mean declared, not yet wired anywhere, and they flip automatically as backends land implementations.

Scheduling Wiring Matrix

Which scheduling capabilities nano-ros delivers per platform, and which portable executor classes are live in dispatch — derived from the two artifacts the runtime executes, not from prose. The per-platform rows are parsed from sched_caps_for() (nros-orchestration-ir), the exact function the workload realizer calls to decide Native-vs-Degrade for a deployment; its rule, quoted from the source: caps describe what nano-ros DELIVERS, not what the OS could do.

Kernel capabilities per platform

PlatformKernel EDFReservation / sporadic serverPreemption thresholdSMP affinityPriority levelsLow number = high priority
Linux host———✓99—
Zephyr✓——✓32✓
FreeRTOS———✓16—
ThreadX——✓✓32✓
NuttX—✓—✓255—
Bare-metal (RTIC / NVIC)————8—

Notes carried from the source arms: the Linux row is deliberately conservative — no SCHED_DEADLINE consumer exists, so edf is false even though Linux could; its affinity is sched_setaffinity, which is Linux and not POSIX (absent from libc’s apple module), so the row’s reach is linux while the platform layer beneath it stays posix; Zephyr’s EDF is CONFIG_SCHED_DEADLINE; NuttX’s reservation is POSIX SCHED_SPORADIC; ThreadX’s preemption threshold is native; the bare-metal row is NVIC hardware priorities with SRP ceilings (RTIC), single core. These are PLATFORM DEFAULTS and there is no per-image override today. ([deploy.<board>] edf / cores, documented in older releases, never took effect and is retired.)

Portable executor classes (SchedClass)

These run inside the executor on every platform — they need no kernel support, which is what makes them portable; where the kernel HAS the native capability (table above), the realizer places the workload natively instead. “Dispatch sites” counts SchedClass::<X> references in the executor’s spin path — a class with zero sites is a type, not a behavior.

ClassDispatch sites in spin.rsStatus
Fifo3Live — the default class; bucketed FIFO ready-set.
Edf2Live — earliest-deadline-first ready-set ordering.
Sporadic6Live — budget/period enforcement in dispatch.

To add a board, as a package of your own or contributed to nano-ros, see Adding a Board to the Registry.

Caveats by chip family

  • Cortex-M0+ (RP2040, STM32F0, nRF51): only 4 NVIC priority levels. Per-callback OS-priority dispatch (a research scheduler shape originally proposed by Choi et al. as PiCAS, RTAS ’21) is disqualified on this class; nano-ros’s user-space EDF / FIFO scheduler is the only option. Pub/sub works fine.
  • Xtensa (ESP32, ESP32-S2, ESP32-S3): not supported. nano-ros has no Xtensa board, and the RISC-V ESP32 boards are retired (ESP32 — retired).
  • Cortex-A9 / A53: hosted-RTOS only (NuttX, Zephyr). Heap + libc required; bare-metal Cortex-A is not in the coverage matrix.
  • PX4 boards: NuttX is the underlying kernel; the PX4 module template is the canonical entry path — see PX4 Autopilot.

Environment Variables Reference

Set a runtime variable in the shell that starts the program. Set a build-time knob in the shell before nros build, or per image in system.toml (an [image.<id>] env row, or the knob-registry table where the section below says so).

The checkout’s .env file for in-tree builds: see Internals → Build Commands.

Runtime Configuration

Examples use ExecutorConfig::from_env() for configuration:

VariableDescriptionDefault
ROS_DOMAIN_IDROS 2 domain ID0
NROS_LOCATORRMW locator (tcp/…, udp/…, serial/…, or tls/…)tcp/127.0.0.1:7447
NROS_SESSION_MODESession mode: client or peerclient
ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATEPath to CA certificate (PEM) for TLS(none)
ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATE_BASE64Base64-encoded CA certificate for TLS(none)
ZENOH_TLS_VERIFY_NAME_ON_CONNECTVerify server hostname in TLS (true/false)(none)

Retired legacy names: ZENOH_LOCATOR and ZENOH_MODE are no longer read. Setting either is a startup ERROR naming its replacement (NROS_LOCATOR / NROS_SESSION_MODE) — Rust panics in resolve_hosted / returns InitError::RetiredEnvVar from nros::init, C / C++ init returns RCL_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT / NROS_CPP_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT and logs the reason. Refused rather than ignored: an ignored locator would dial the default router and read as “no delivery”. ZENOH_TLS_* names are kept because TLS is currently zenoh-specific.

TLS Notes

  • POSIX: requires libmbedtls-dev (install it with your host’s package manager). File-path and base64 cert loading are both supported.
  • Bare-metal: only ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 is supported (no filesystem). The certificate is embedded at build time.
  • The link-tls Cargo feature must be enabled on both the example and the nros crate.

Build-Time Configuration

VariableDescriptionRequired
ZENOH_PICO_DIRCMake install prefix for pre-built zenoh-pico (use with system-zenohpico feature on zpico-sys)Only with system-zenohpico
NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATHExtra board-search roots (PATH-style : separated). Each entry is a directory shaped like packages/boards/ — subdirs carrying nros-board.toml crates or */boards/<name>/board.cmake bundles. Read by the nros CLI’s board catalog AND nano_ros_use_board() (also settable as a CMake cache var there). Board keys stay global: a name found under two roots is an error, never shadowed.(unset)

ARM FVP (FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R)

Not license-gated: nros setup --tool arm-fvp fetches the model from a pinned Arm CDN permalink ([tool.arm-fvp] in nros-sdk-index.toml, digest-checked) into the SDK store. Arm publishes it for x86_64 Linux only. You need none of the variables below unless you installed a model yourself. See the ARM FVP getting-started chapter for the end-to-end build+run walk-through.

VariableDescriptionDefault
ARMFVP_BIN_PATHDirectory containing FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R (Zephyr-canonical, highest priority).(unset)
ARM_FVP_DIRInstall root; resolver scans models/Linux64_GCC-*/ underneath.(unset)

The model is found in this order: ARMFVP_BIN_PATH, ARM_FVP_DIR, FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R on PATH, then the store copy that nros setup --tool arm-fvp installs. Set ARMFVP_BIN_PATH at BUILD time as well as run time, because Zephyr’s armfvp.cmake caches the location at configure. For a model you downloaded by hand, set ARM_FVP_DIR to the extraction root. nros doctor --board fvp-aemv8r-smp reports whether the model resolves.

Changing how the FVP is resolved or run in the tree: see Internals → Zephyr in-tree examples.

Vendored source trees

You normally set none of these. nros setup puts each tree in the shared store, and every build locates it through one ladder: this variable, then the project’s [sources] row in system.toml, then a checkout submodule you are editing, then the store, then the checkout’s own copy. nros locate <name> --why prints which rung answered. Set a variable only to build against a tree of your own.

VariableTree
FREERTOS_DIRFreeRTOS kernel source
LWIP_DIRlwIP source
NUTTX_DIRNuttX RTOS source
NUTTX_APPS_DIRNuttX apps source
THREADX_DIRThreadX kernel source
NETX_DIRNetX Duo source
CYCLONEDDS_SOURCE_DIRCyclone DDS source

FREERTOS_PORT, FREERTOS_CONFIG_DIR, THREADX_CONFIG_DIR and NETX_CONFIG_DIR are board facts: each board’s nros-board.toml states them, and the build carries them from there. They are not user inputs.

NROS_ZENOH_MAX_LARGE_SUBSCRIBERSHow many large-class blocks this image reserves. 0 is legal: an image whose subscribed types all fit NROS_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZE declares 0 and stops paying RING_DEPTH x LARGE_SIZE — 65,536 B at the defaults — for a class it never routes into. A hint no class can hold then fails create_subscription rather than dropping every sample. DERIVED, on both lanes — a Zephyr image gets it from Kconfig’s -1 sentinel, and a cargo image gets it from the build settings nros build generates under build/, joined over the types the image’s components subscribe to. Setting it here still wins.2nros-rmw-zenoh
NROS_ZENOH_SERVICE_BUFFER_SIZEPer-service-server static buffer in zenoh shim1024nros-rmw-zenoh
NROS_PARAM_SERVICE_INBOX_BYTESBytes one request slot holds in the inbox ring of a ROS parameter service queryable (six per node) or a REP-2002 lifecycle one (five per node) – the BUILTIN family, which the zenoh shim selects by service name. DERIVED: with nothing stated, the contract’s declared parameters bound it, as the largest request a set_parameters over the worst-declared node can produce (672 B on the Autoware Safety Island, against the transport’s 1,024). A contract declaring a string- or array-valued parameter needs the parameter store’s capacities to price, which the RMW cannot see, so the shim abstains there and the user-service slot stands. Setting it here still wins.derived, else NROS_SERVICE_INBOX_BYTESnros-rmw-zenoh
NROS_PARAM_SERVICE_INBOX_DEPTHRequests one parameter or lifecycle service queryable holds before the newest is dropped. One, because this traffic is one request and one reply from a client that waits (ros2 param, rclcpp’s SyncParametersClient) and a node’s services are polled serially in one spin. Raise it to 2 for an image serving a parameter dashboard. Must be >= 1.1nros-rmw-zenoh
NROS_ZENOH_GET_REPLY_BUF_SIZEStack buffer for service client replies4096zpico-sys
NROS_ZENOH_GET_POLL_INTERVAL_MSSingle-threaded polling interval in zenoh_shim_get()10zpico-sys
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_SOCKETSMax concurrent TCP sockets (smoltcp); brokered default. (ZPICO_SMOLTCP_MAX_SOCKETS is retired.)1 (brokered)nros-smoltcp
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_UDP_SOCKETSMax concurrent UDP sockets (smoltcp); 1 by default, 4 with the nros-smoltcp/rtps feature. (ZPICO_SMOLTCP_MAX_UDP_SOCKETS is retired.)1 (brokered)nros-smoltcp
NROS_SMOLTCP_BUFFER_SIZEPer-socket staging buffer (smoltcp). (ZPICO_SMOLTCP_BUFFER_SIZE is retired.)2048nros-smoltcp
NROS_SMOLTCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MSTCP connection timeout (smoltcp). (ZPICO_SMOLTCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS is retired.)30000nros-smoltcp

XRCE-DDS (NROS_XRCE_*)

These are read by nros-rmw-xrce-cffi’s build script, either from the environment or — on Zephyr — from CONFIG_<name> in .config. They set C #defines of the same name without the NROS_ prefix; the define is not itself an environment variable, so exporting XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE has no effect and reports no error.

VariableDescriptionDefaultMinCrate

NROS_XRCE_SERVICE_REQUEST_BUFFER_SIZEApplication service-server request entry size. DERIVED from the declared servers’ requests beside the builtin splitBUFFER_SIZE1nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_SERVICE_REPLY_BUFFER_SIZEService-client reply slot size. DERIVED from the declared clients’ repliesBUFFER_SIZE1nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_BUILTIN_SERVICE_SERVERSHow many service-server slots are the parameter / lifecycle services’. DERIVED beside the total0 (no split)0nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_BUILTIN_SERVICE_REQUEST_BUFFER_SIZERequest entry size of a builtin-family slotBUFFER_SIZE, raised to the parameter request1nros-rmw-xrce

Dropping MAX_SUBSCRIBERS, MAX_SERVICE_* and SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH to 1, BUFFER_SIZE to 256, STREAM_HISTORY to 4 and CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU to 512 takes the session struct from ~390 KB to ~10-20 KB.

Every variable in this table is a knob-registry row, so a project states it per image as [image.<id>.knobs.xrce] buffer_size = 256 — the name without NROS_XRCE_, lowercased (max_subscribers, max_service_servers, max_service_clients, subscriber_ring_depth, subscriber_buffer_size, service_request_buffer_size, service_reply_buffer_size, stream_history, transport_mtu, custom_transport_mtu) — rather than as an env row.

On Zephyr the three entity caps DERIVE, and the minimum is 0

CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS and CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_SERVERS default to -1, which means take the number from the entities this image declares (the contract sidecar beside the bringup’s launch file, or beside the bringup’s system.toml when it has no launch/). A listener that declares one subscription and no service is built with one subscriber slot and zero service-server slots, which is what took the session struct from 427,968 bytes to 59,088 on the zephyr cpp listener. Stating a number in Kconfig or the environment still wins over the derivation, in both directions.

CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_CLIENTS also defaults to -1, and its number comes from the image’s sizing descriptor on every road that writes one: the declared service clients plus three per action client (send_goal, cancel_goal, get_result). With no descriptor, or one that does not state both counts, the crate default of 4 stands.

Zero is a legal, honoured value for all three caps — it is not rounded up to 1. So creating an entity the image never declared does not truncate silently: the create fails with InvalidConfig and the backend logs which cap it hit, which knob moves it, and that the count came from the declaration.

NROS_XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH is deliberately NOT derivable — no inventory knows how deep a burst a subscriber must survive — but it does have a Kconfig symbol, and on Zephyr that is the way to set it: a Zephyr cargo build sees only the knobs nros_cargo_build.cmake forwards, and shell exports do not survive that.

NROS_XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE is the XRCE receive ceiling

A subscriber’s receive ring entry is a fixed uint8_t data[XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE], so a subscription’s own buffer size cannot raise it: asking for create_subscription_sized::<M, 16384> still stops at 1024, because the 16384 buffer is the destination of a copy that never happens. A sample that does not fit is refused on take with MessageTooLarge.

The static cost is XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH x XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE per subscriber, which is why the default is small — raise it deliberately, and consider lowering the ring depth at the same time.

A payload at or above the transport MTU (4096) arrives fragmented; the receive path reads the fragment chain and delivers it whole.

Design background

  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact — the one source-location ladder, the NROS_<ID> knob spelling, and knob-registry rows

nros-bridge.toml — bridge configuration schema

Consumed by nros::run_from_config (Rust) and the future C/C++ mirror (nros::run_from_config in nros-cpp).

Not the orchestration nros.toml. This is the bridge runtime config (multi-RMW byte forwarding). It is named nros-bridge.toml to avoid colliding with the orchestration nros.toml (component/system build config) — different lifecycle, different schema.

The file lives next to the binary (or anywhere the program can read it) and selects:

  1. Which RMW backends to open, under what locator / domain.
  2. How those backends are wired into bridge entries that forward traffic between them.

The binary’s Cargo.toml (or target_link_libraries) still selects which backends are linked — the TOML file selects which of the linked backends are used in this run. Backend names in the file that don’t match a linked backend surface as ConfigError::OpenSession.

Top-level structure

# nros-bridge.toml — sibling of the binary
[[node]]
name    = "field"
rmw     = "zenoh"
locator = "tcp/10.0.0.1:7447"

[[node]]
name    = "control"
rmw     = "cyclonedds"
locator = "domain=0"

[[bridge]]
type      = "std_msgs/Int32"
type_hash = "RIHS01_..."
from      = { node = "field",   topic = "/sensor/raw" }
to        = { node = "control", topic = "/sensor/raw" }

Run via:

fn main() -> Result<(), nros_bridge::ConfigError> {
    nros_bridge::run_from_config("nros-bridge.toml")
    // or, via the umbrella feature: nros::run_from_config("nros-bridge.toml")
}

[[node]]

One block per backend session. The first [[node]] becomes the primary session (extra_sessions[0] in Executor::open_multi); the rest open as extras keyed by rmw.

KeyTypeDefaultNotes
namestringrequiredLogical name. Bridge entries reference this.
rmwstringrequiredCanonical backend name: "zenoh", "xrce", "cyclonedds". Must match a backend the binary linked in.
locatorstring""Backend-specific locator. Zenoh uses tcp/..., udp4/..., serial/...; DDS uses domain=<n>; XRCE uses udp4://...:port.
domain_idu320ROS domain id passed to the backend.
namespacestring"/"Default namespace applied to handles created on this node.

Locator scheme grammar (zenoh)

SchemeExampleMeaning
tcp/<host>:<p>tcp/10.0.0.1:7447TCP unicast
udp/<host>:<p>udp/10.0.0.1:7447UDP unicast
serial/<dev>serial//dev/ttyUSB0UART (host-side) or board UART (bare-metal)
tls/<host>:<p>tls/router.example.org:7447TLS over TCP (requires link-tls on backend)

DDS / XRCE follow their native locator conventions; consult each backend’s docs for the exact form.

[[bridge]]

One block per topic forwarded between two [[node]]s. Each bridge creates a RawSubscription on the source side and an EmbeddedRawPublisher on the destination side and pumps bytes once per executor tick.

KeyTypeDefaultNotes
typestringrequiredROS type name ("std_msgs/Int32"). Backends use it for liveliness / discovery.
type_hashstring""ROS 2 RIHS type hash for the typed binding. May be left empty if both sides ignore it.
fromendpointrequired{ node = "<name>", topic = "<topic>" }. The source node + topic.
toendpointrequired{ node = "<name>", topic = "<topic>" }. The destination node + topic.

Bidirectional bridges are two [[bridge]] entries — one in each direction. The runtime stamps a bridge_origin attachment field on forwarded frames and drops on receive when the origin matches the local backend, so an echo pair does not loop.

Error semantics

run_from_config returns ConfigError:

VariantCause
IoFile read failed (missing / unreadable).
ParseTOML malformed or a required field missing.
UnknownNodeA [[bridge]] references a node name no [[node]] declared.
OpenSessionExecutor::open_multi rejected a spec — usually a backend name no RMW_INIT_ENTRIES entry registered under.
BuildNodecreate_node_on failed (registry exhausted, name too long, …).
BuildEntityCreating the source subscription or destination publisher failed (typically backend rejection of the topic name / type / QoS).

Any error short-circuits the runtime; bridges that opened cleanly before the failure are not pumped.

Linked-backend matrix

Backend nameCargo dep that contributes the RMW_INIT_ENTRIES entry
zenohnros-rmw-zenoh = { ... }
xrcenros-rmw-xrce-cffi = { ... }
cycloneddsnros-rmw-cyclonedds static lib (CMake side, --whole-archive)

Add a backend to your Cargo.toml (or target_link_libraries) to make its name available in the TOML; remove it to fence off use even when the TOML file lists it (yields OpenSession at startup).

Static pool inventory

Every build-time sizing knob nano-ros reads, with the default it uses when you do not set it. Set them as environment variables at BUILD time.

This page exists because knowing a knob exists is the hard part. An audit of a 256 KB image found it already tuned nine of these and still carried ~145 KB of defaults it did not know to change — every knob it needed was already there. Four separate features had each added a static pool with a knob, silently.

Every sizing knob

Every knob says what it costs: a byte figure where a formula prices it, otherwise WHERE its bytes go and why no static figure exists. Nothing in this column is blank, and nothing here is free unless it says so.

knobdefaultread bycost

NROS_ACTION_INBOX_DEPTHcomputed — see packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenoh/build.rs:171packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenohpool nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::service::ACTION_INBOX: ring depth of each action-family inbox; same InboxStorage element

Conflicting defaults

These knobs are read in more than one place with DIFFERENT defaults, so setting one moves only part of the tree: one setting, two values in the same image.

  • NROS_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZE

Configuration surface

One fact can be spelled several ways. Only one of them is a place to make a decision; the rest carry that decision across a layer boundary. This page separates the two, because a list that does not is a list of nine ways to set a locator.

Every symbol on this page is one a user may set. Kconfig says so itself: each carries a PROMPT, which is what a prompt means. An earlier draft split these into public and carrier by asking who read them, and got the layer wrong — cmake reading ${CONFIG_X} to emit ZPICO_X=<value> is cmake CARRYING the choice, not owning it.

The real carriers are one layer down and are NOT Kconfig symbols: the ZPICO_* / NROS_* environment variables, the -D cache variables and the compile definitions this page’s symbols feed. Setting one of those by hand bypasses the question Kconfig asked.

The evidence column is where each value is consumed, so a symbol with no reader stands out: a prompt asking a question whose answer is discarded is worse than no prompt.

139 Kconfig symbols — 66 settable, 1 provided for application code, 72 derived, 0 dead.

Facts with more than one spelling

Where a decision has an authority OUTSIDE Kconfig, that authority is the place to set it and these symbols carry it.

RMW backend

Set it here: [system].rmw in the bringup’s system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends

nano_ros_workspace(BACKEND …) and -DNROS_RMW are the cmake carriers. cmake already warns that BACKEND silently beats the cache var; nothing yet compares either against [system].rmw.

ROS domain id

Set it here: [system].domain_id in system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID0publicforwarded-to-cargo, c-source, cmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_CYCLONE_DOMAIN_IDNROS_DOMAIN_IDpublicc-define, c-source, cmake, rust-source

CONFIG_NROS_CYCLONE_DOMAIN_ID defaults FROM NROS_DOMAIN_ID — the one derivation edge in this cluster. Do not pin it to a literal: a Cyclone DDS image would then run on that domain whatever domain_id says.

Router / agent endpoint

Set it here: [system].locator in system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATORtcp/127.0.0.1:7447publicc-source, cmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_ADDR127.0.0.1publiccmake, rust-source

Zephyr is exempt from the cmake precedence chain by design (see the exemption comments in NanoRosEntry.cmake — no line ref, they move), so the Kconfig spelling is the carrier there rather than an override.

Board Support Levels

What nano-ros can show for each board it knows about. Each level is derived from evidence, never typed: where the board’s image runs (on a host, in an emulator, on hardware, or nowhere yet), how often that run happens (every merge, daily, weekly, or by hand on a date) and which board’s test matrix stands for its breadth.

StatusWhat it means
Verified on host / in emulator / on hardware (cadence)an automated lane boots it and asserts a message, at that cadence
Boots, manual (date)a maintainer booted it by hand on that date; after 120 days it reads Builds until booted again
Buildsa lane builds it; nothing boots it
Not supportednothing builds or boots it

A witness board runs its platform family’s test matrix; a board that inherits shares the witness’s code path and adds its own smoke evidence. Each board links to its evidence page.

Notes

Raspberry Pi Pico W (RP2040, Cortex-M0+, 264 KiB SRAM) on Zephyr 3.7, serial only. Its Wokwi twin boots the C talker over UART0 (the Wokwi serial monitor), with the console on UART1. The image needs CONFIG_TICKLESS_KERNEL=n (in the board’s prj.conf) and five RAM knobs, which are the descriptor’s [knobs] and every image inherits. Each twin run needs your own WOKWI_CLI_TOKEN and spends that account’s simulation minutes, so the twin is run by users and not in nano-ros CI.

See Board Support Levels for what each status means.

Retired names

nano-ros’s cmake variables use one prefix, NROS_. Older releases used NANO_ROS_ for some of them, and the release before this one still accepted those spellings as deprecated aliases. They are now retired: a configure that sets one — in a CMakeLists.txt, with -D on the command line, or left behind in a build directory’s CMakeCache.txt — stops with an error that names the replacement. Nothing is adopted under the new name any more, so rename the old spelling where you set it.

RetiredUse instead
NANO_ROS_PLATFORMNROS_PLATFORM
NANO_ROS_FEATURESNROS_FEATURES
NANO_ROS_SAFETY_E2ENROS_SAFETY_E2E
NANO_ROS_ROS_EDITIONNROS_ROS_EDITION
NANO_ROS_GEN_CACHE_DIRNROS_GEN_CACHE_DIR
NANO_ROS_SKIP_BOOTSTRAPNROS_SKIP_BOOTSTRAP
NANO_ROS_BUILD_CODEGENNROS_BUILD_CODEGEN
NANO_ROS_CMAKE_DIRNROS_CMAKE_DIR
NANO_ROS_RMWNROS_RMW
NANO_ROS_BOARDNROS_BOARD
NANO_ROS_ROOT (cmake variable)NROS_REPO_DIR
NANO_ROS_ROOT <path> (keyword of nano_ros_workspace() and friends)NROS_REPO_DIR <path>

Retired board names

The host board is linux. Two other words used to name it and are now refused wherever a board is named — nros setup <board>, nros new --platform, nros new --image … --board, an [image.<id>] board row — with an error that names linux. One more word named the bare-metal MPS2-AN385 board by its emulator, and another the RISC-V ThreadX board; both are refused the same way, naming the board’s one name:

RetiredUse insteadWhy
nativelinuxnative names every general-purpose host, and the host board builds on Linux only
posixlinuxposix is the platform (nros-platform-posix), not a board
qemu-mps2-an385mps2-an385-baremetalnames the emulator, not the board: QEMU is how the AN385 image is run
threadx-qemu-riscv64rv-virt-threadxnames the emulator, not the board: QEMU is how the RISC-V virt image is run

posix stays correct as a PLATFORM name and in [tasks.*.posix]. This page is the only place in the book that spells any of these words as a board.

Retired knob spellings

Build-time knobs have one env spelling, NROS_<ID>, held in the knob registry packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-build/knobs.toml. The older spellings below were read with a deprecation warning for one release. They are now retired: a build that finds one set — exported in the environment, in a cargo [env] table, or as an [image.<id>] env row in system.toml — stops with an error that names the replacement. Nothing is read under the old name any more, so rename it where you set it.

RetiredUse instead
ZPICO_BATCH_MULTICAST_SIZENROS_ZENOH_BATCH_MULTICAST_SIZE
ZPICO_BATCH_UNICAST_SIZENROS_ZENOH_BATCH_UNICAST_SIZE
ZPICO_FRAG_MAX_SIZENROS_ZENOH_FRAG_MAX_SIZE

ZPICO_MAX_PENDING_GETSNROS_ZENOH_MAX_PENDING_GETS

The same ZPICO_* words remain the zenoh-pico shim’s own C macro names (a -DZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES=… the build passes to the C compiler). Those are generated from the knob, never set by hand, and are not on this list.

Retired knobs

Some knobs are gone, not renamed: what they configured no longer exists. Every spelling of one is refused with an error that says why and what to set instead.

zenoh-pico 1.10 runs the lease and keep-alive on its executor thread, which is the read task, so the separate lease task and its settings are retired:

RetiredWhere it was setWhat to do
NROS_ZENOH_LEASE_PRIORITY, ZPICO_LEASE_TASK_PRIORITYenvironment, cargo [env], [image.<id>] envremove it; NROS_ZENOH_READ_PRIORITY prioritises the thread that now runs the lease
[image.<id>.knobs.zenoh] lease_prioritysystem.tomlremove it; use read_priority
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LEASE_PRIORITYprj.conf / Kconfig fragmentsremove it; Kconfig reports it as an undefined symbol. Use CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_READ_PRIORITY
zenoh_lease_priority, zenoh_lease_stack_bytes[node.rt] / [node.rt.freertos]remove them; zenoh_read_priority / zenoh_read_stack_bytes configure that task
.keepalive_priority, .keepalive_stack_bytesnros_app_config_t.schedulingremove them; the C compiler rejects an initializer that names either
ZPICO_LEASE_TASK_PRIORITY (C define)-D to the zenoh shimremove it; the shim #errors on it

zpico_set_task_config takes two arguments now, the executor task’s priority and stack size.

A board descriptor’s knobs are a top-level [knobs.<group>] table. The per-board [board.knobs.<group>] spelling is retired the same way: a descriptor that still states it fails to load, naming [knobs].

Retired runtime aliases and macro forms

Deprecated in release 0.5.0-nros2, retired after it. Each is now an ERROR naming its replacement — never silently ignored, because an ignored locator dials the default router and reads as “no delivery”.

RetiredUse insteadWhat happens now
ZENOH_LOCATOR (env)NROS_LOCATORstartup error (Rust panic / InitError::RetiredEnvVar; C/C++ init returns invalid-argument and logs it)
ZENOH_MODE (env)NROS_SESSION_MODEsame
nros::main!(board = X)nros::main!() + [image.<id>] board in system.toml; an out-of-tree board crate states [package.metadata.nros.board] type = "::my_board::MyBoard"compile_error!
--features rmw-xrce on the PX4 companionsnothing — the xrce backend is unconditionalthe feature no longer exists (cargo: unknown feature)

Retired commands

RetiredUse insteadWhat happens now
nros new entry <name> --platform zephyrnros materialize <bringup>:<image>, which writes the image’s generated entry into your workspace as a package you own under src/; or, for an application that owns its west build, A Zephyr App You Build with Westthe book no longer teaches it: a workspace generates the entry for each image, so there is nothing to scaffold by hand

A build directory from an older release

An older nano-ros wrote some of these names into the cache itself, so a build directory it first configured carries them even though nothing sets them now. The error lists those entries and prints the command that drops exactly them:

cmake -U NANO_ROS_PLATFORM -U NANO_ROS_RMW <build-dir>

Deleting the build directory’s CMakeCache.txt works too.

What is not on this list

nano_ros_DIR and nano_ros_ROOT are CMake’s own find_package(nano_ros) hints and keep their spelling.

NANO_ROS_ROOT as an environment variable is retired by its own rule: a configure that finds it set stops, naming NROS_REPO_DIR.

The error table stays: a retired name is refused for good, naming what to type. Dropping the rows would turn -DNANO_ROS_PLATFORM=zephyr (or a stale cache entry an older nano-ros wrote) into an unknown variable, and the configure would build the default platform without a word.

Design background

  • RFC-0093: board naming states reach — why a board is not named for its emulator
  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact — the one NROS_<ID> knob spelling
  • RFC-0110: zenoh-pico executor driving — why the lease task is gone

Migrating off the install-local prefix

TL;DR. nano-ros no longer has a CMake install step: the install-local recipe, the build/install/ prefix, every install(...) rule, every Config.cmake.in template, and the find_package(NanoRos) consumption path are gone. nano-ros is consumed exclusively via add_subdirectory(<repo-root>) from the user’s CMakeLists.txt.

If your project still consumes nano-ros through an installed prefix, this page is the one-page rewrite that gets you onto the supported shape.

Before (installed prefix)

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(my_app C)

find_package(NanoRos REQUIRED CONFIG)
nano_ros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs SKIP_INSTALL)
add_executable(my_app src/main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE
    std_msgs__nano_ros_c
    NanoRos::NanoRos)

Build:

# In the nano-ros checkout: the install-local recipe populated build/install/

# In the user project:
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<nano-ros>/build/install
cmake --build build

After (no install step)

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_app C)

set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)
set(NROS_RMW     zenoh)
add_subdirectory(<path-to-nano-ros> nano_ros)

nano_ros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs SKIP_INSTALL)
add_executable(my_app src/main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE
    std_msgs__nano_ros_c
    NanoRos::NanoRos)
nros_platform_link_app(my_app)

Build:

# No nano-ros-side install step. Just configure your project.
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build

What changed

BeforeAfter
find_package(NanoRos REQUIRED CONFIG)add_subdirectory(<path-to-nano-ros>) after set(NROS_PLATFORM ...) + set(NROS_RMW ...)
the install-local recipe(deleted) — nano-ros builds in-tree per-example via Corrosion
cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<nano-ros>/build/install(not needed)
nano_ros_link_platform(target) / nano_ros_link_rmw(target)(folded into NanoRos::NanoRos’s INTERFACE link libraries)
nros_freertos_compose_platform(target) / nros_threadx_compose_platform(target)nros_platform_link_app(target) — single per-app fixup hook
find_package(NrosRmwCyclonedds CONFIG REQUIRED)(auto-wired when NROS_RMW=cyclonedds)
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22) (matches root nano-ros)

RTOS-specific notes

  • Zephyr. Consume nano-ros via the zephyr/ module — drop nano-ros into your west.yml, set CONFIG_NROS=y in prj.conf, and state the RMW as the image’s rmw in a system.toml beside it.
  • ESP-IDF. No longer supported: the component was removed too (ESP32 — retired).
  • NuttX. integrations/nuttx/ is a apps/external/ shim — symlink (or copy) and enable via make menuconfig.
  • PX4. integrations/px4/module-template/ is a EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION template — copy out, edit the user glue, point PX4 at it.

Each shell internally does add_subdirectory(<nano-ros>) with the right NROS_PLATFORM cache var set; user-side code is the same as the C/C++ snippet above.

What you lose

  • A pre-built <prefix>/lib/libnros_c.a you could link from arbitrary external projects. Now each consumer builds the staticlib in its own build tree (Corrosion handles caching via the Cargo target dir).
  • The build/install/share/nano-ros/interfaces/ bundled-interface drop. Codegen now resolves interface files via the ament index (when colcon-discovered) or directly from packages/cli/interfaces/ inside the nano-ros checkout.
  • The cmake --install build step. There is nothing nano-ros-side to install. Your own project ships its binary; nano-ros is a static dependency.

Why this change

find_package(NanoRos) was a Debian-style “library installed once, consumed by many projects” model. The RTOS workflows that nano-ros actually targets (Zephyr west, NuttX apps/external, PX4 EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION) all consume dependencies as source trees inside the user’s workspace — not from an installed prefix. The install path drifted out of sync with the cargo path more than once (UDP multicast linker error was the proof) and added ~30 s warm / ~10 min cold to every test-all run. Removing it collapses two surfaces into one.

ESP32 — retired

nano-ros no longer supports the ESP32. Two paths existed, and both have been removed: the ESP32-C3 bare-metal board over esp-hal, and the ESP-IDF component with its idf.py build driver. This page says what each was, why it went, and what an ESP32 port would need today.

The ESP32-C3 bare-metal board (esp-hal), retired 2026-11-02

esp32 was the ESP32-C3 under Espressif’s QEMU fork, over esp-hal: the nros-board-esp32-qemu board crate, the nros-platform-esp32-qemu platform crate and the examples/esp32-c3-baremetal/ projects. It had already been dormant: nothing built or ran it.

nano-ros supports a way of running only where it keeps its real-time promise: an executor parks until an arrival or its next deadline, and wakes for nothing else. On a bare-metal board that needs a receive interrupt and a one-shot timer behind the port’s wake object, as mps2-an385-baremetal has. The ESP32-C3 board had neither, so its executor could only poll the network. nano-ros refuses such a board rather than serve it by polling, so the board was retired instead of ported.

Every name the board answered to (esp32-c3-baremetal, esp32-qemu, esp32-c3, esp32c3, esp32) is refused with that reason wherever a board is read: system.toml, nros build, nros setup, nros::main!. The esp32 framework name is refused the same way.

The ESP-IDF component and idf.py driver, retired 2026-09

integrations/nano-ros/ was an ESP-IDF component shim. Nothing built it, it had no platform descriptor or package.xml, and it was never published to the Espressif Component Registry, so it was removed rather than kept as an untested promise.

nros build also had an idf.py driver for ESP32 boards whose package graph crossed languages. With the component gone there was nothing for a project to depend on, no ESP-IDF project for idf.py to find, and no way to carry a resolved nano-ros setting into that build, so the driver was deleted. That combination now refuses with those reasons instead of running a tool with no project to build. C and C++ on an ESP32 have no build road.

If you need an ESP32

The platform ABI and the C API are unchanged, and nothing forbids an out-of-tree port. A port has to bring what every supported board has:

  • for bare metal, the network driver’s receive interrupt and a one-shot timer signalling the port’s wake object, so the session reports arrivals instead of being polled;
  • for ESP-IDF, a component, a way to carry nano-ros’s resolved settings into the ESP-IDF build, and a build that something runs.

Extending nano-ros describes what a port provides.

Retired Configuration Files

These files used to carry configuration and no longer do. If a guide, an old project or a blog post tells you to write one of them, its content now belongs in system.toml (an image’s settings, under [image.<id>]) or, for a hand-written no_std app with no codegen, in the standalone config.toml that Configuration describes.

  • nros.toml — retired in full. A workspace-root nros.toml is rejected by the CLI (NrosTomlNotSupported; migrate with the nros-v0.5.0 tag’s nros migrate workspace — the one-shot verb is retired on newer trees); the legacy per-package overlay is a deprecated fallback that nros check flags; the embedded-runtime role never shipped (no example ever declared one). If a doc tells you to write nros.toml, it predates the migration — the content belongs in system.toml.
  • Old config.toml schemas — [network]/[zenoh]/[scheduling], and the [[transport]] table — retired; the direct-mode config.toml above is the kept, supported shape.
